saindhava-dynasty.t: A dynasty of western Saurashtra that ruled from Bhutambilika and fought Arab raiders from the sea.
saindhava-dynasty.o: The Saindhavas established themselves in western Saurashtra, in modern [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], around the early 8th century, probably after the decline of the [[s:maitraka-dynasty|Maitraka dynasty]]. Their founder was Pushyadeva, and their capital was Bhutambilika, modern Ghumli near [[s:porbandar-state|Porbandar]].
saindhava-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known from [[e:copper|copper]]-plate grants dated in the Gupta era. They record that King Agguka I defeated a naval attack, probably by Arab raiders, which shows the dynasty's role in guarding the coast. The Saindhavas were Shaivas and appear to have acknowledged the [[s:gurjara-pratihara|Gurjara-Pratihara]] as overlords at times.
saindhava-dynasty.e: The Saindhava line disappears after the early 10th century. Ghumli later became a seat of the Jethwa rulers of the region.

cr.a: Jean-Michel Moullec from Vern sur Seiche (35, Bretagne), France

sultanate-of-fezzan.t: The Awlad Muhammad sultanate of Murzuk, a Saharan state that controlled the caravan route between Bornu and Tripoli.
sultanate-of-fezzan.o: Around 1550 Muhammad al-Fasi, a sharif said to have come from [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], established himself in the [[e:fezzan|Fezzan]] oases of southern [[e:libya|Libya]], founding the Awlad Muhammad dynasty. He made Murzuk his capital, displacing earlier local rulers, and the dynasty soon acknowledged the overlordship of [[s:ottoman-tripolitania|Ottoman Tripolitania]].
sultanate-of-fezzan.r: The sultans controlled the oasis towns, date gardens and [[e:well|wells]] of the [[e:fezzan|Fezzan]] and taxed caravans crossing between the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]] and the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]], trading slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and goods. They paid annual tribute to [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]], but repeatedly withheld it, provoking Tripolitanian expeditions that occupied Murzuk for periods in the 17th and 18th centuries.
sultanate-of-fezzan.e: In 1812 Muhammad al-Mukni, acting for Yusuf Karamanli of [[s:karamanli-tripoli|Karamanli Tripoli]], killed the last Awlad Muhammad sultan and annexed the [[e:fezzan|Fezzan]]. It was later governed directly by the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in the [[s:tripolitania-vilayet|Tripolitania Vilayet]].

cr.a: Lapie, P. and Lapie, A. E., Atlas Universel de Geographie Ancienne et Moderne, (1829 first edition).

sedetani.t: An Iberian people of the middle Ebro around Salduie, the native town on whose site Augustus founded Caesaraugusta, modern Zaragoza.
sedetani.o: The Sedetani occupied the middle [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] valley around modern [[e:zaragoza|Zaragoza]] from at least the 5th century BCE. They belonged to the Iberian world, with fortified towns on hills and terraces above the river and its tributaries.
sedetani.r: Their main centre was Salduie, which minted coins with the Iberian legend Salduie. Farming of the fertile [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]] plain, livestock and trade along the river underpinned their economy. They are sometimes confused in ancient texts with the [[s:edetani|Edetani]] of [[e:valencia|Valencia]]. Horsemen from Salduie served [[e:rome|Rome]] in the Social War and received citizenship in 89 BCE, recorded on the [[e:bronze|Bronze]] of Ascoli.
sedetani.e: The Sedetani were brought under Roman control during Cato's campaign of 195 BCE and became part of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]]. Around 14 BCE Augustus founded the colony of Caesaraugusta on the site of Salduie, and the Sedetani merged into Roman provincial society.

selinous.t: The westernmost Greek city in Sicily, famed for its great temples, which was destroyed by Carthage in 409 BCE.
selinous.o: Colonists from [[s:megara-hyblaea|Megara Hyblaea]], led by Pammilus, founded Selinous around 628 BCE on a coastal plateau between two rivers in south-western [[e:sicily|Sicily]], according to Thucydides; some ancient sources give an earlier date. The name came from wild celery (selinon), which appears on its coins.
selinous.r: Selinous grew rich from its grain-growing lands and trade with [[e:carthage|Carthage]] and the Elymians, and it built more large temples than almost any other Greek city: on its acropolis and on the eastern hill stand the remains of at least eight, including the colossal Temple G, and their sculpted metopes are now in Palermo. It sided with Carthage in 480 BCE but later quarrelled over borders with [[s:segesta|Segesta]], which called in [[s:athens|Athens]] and Carthage.
selinous.e: In 409 BCE a Carthaginian army under [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] Mago stormed Selinous after nine days, killing thousands. The city revived under Carthaginian control, but in 250 BCE [[e:carthage|Carthage]] moved its inhabitants to [[s:lilybaeum|Lilybaeum]] and abandoned it. Its archaeological park is one of the largest in [[e:europe|Europe]].

state-of-yue.t: The kingdom of Goujian, who endured humiliation, rebuilt his state and destroyed Wu in 473 BCE, a story of patient revenge known to every Chinese reader.
state-of-yue.o: Yue, or Yuyue, was a state of the Yue peoples around Kuaiji (Shaoxing) in northern Zhejiang. Its rulers claimed descent from a son of a Xia king sent to tend the tomb of Yu the Great. Yue appears in the record from the late 6th century BCE under King Yunchang, already at war with its northern neighbour, the [[s:state-of-wu|State of Wu]].
state-of-yue.r: Defeated by Wu in 494 BCE, King Goujian served Fuchai as a near-hostage, then rebuilt Yue with his ministers Fan Li and Wen Zhong, by tradition sleeping on brushwood and tasting bitter gall to keep his resolve. The Yue people tattooed their bodies, cut their hair short and fought on water; their bronze swords, like the Sword of Goujian found in 1965, were the finest of the age.
state-of-yue.e: Goujian destroyed Wu in 473 BCE and was briefly hegemon, moving his court north to Langya. His successors declined, and the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] crushed Yue around 306 BCE. Its royal kin scattered south and founded states such as [[s:minyue|Minyue]] and [[s:dongou|Dong'ou]].
state-of-yue.re: Yue local religion and ancestral cults

semigallians.t: Baltic people of the fertile Lielupe plain who fought the Livonian crusaders longer than any other, finally abandoning their land in 1290.
semigallians.o: The Semigallians settled the plain of the Lielupe river in central [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]] and northern [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] in the first millennium. By the 12th century they had a network of strong hillforts, with Tērvete and Mežotne among the most important, and their land was the granary of the region.
semigallians.r: Regional leaders sometimes acted together under a single war chief. Viesturs allied with the Germans of Riga against the Lithuanians early in the 13th century, then turned against them and joined the Lithuanian victory over the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]] at Saule in 1236. Trade along the Daugava and Lielupe brought them [[e:silver|silver]] and connections with Rus'.
semigallians.e: The [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] fought them through the 1270s and 1280s; Nameisis led a major revolt. In 1290 the last Semigallians burned their hillforts and many moved south into [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]]. Their land was divided between the Order and the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]], and Zemgale remains a region of [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]].

second-dynasty-of-isin.t: The native Babylonian dynasty that restored Babylon after Elamite conquest, and under Nebuchadnezzar I brought the statue of Marduk home from Susa.
second-dynasty-of-isin.o: After the [[e:elamites|Elamites]] ended [[s:kassite-babylonia|Kassite Babylonia]] around 1155 BCE, Marduk-kabit-ahheshu, a ruler from the city of [[s:isin|Isin]], established a new line around 1157 BCE. Within decades his successors controlled [[e:babylon|Babylon]] and claimed to be kings of all [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]].
second-dynasty-of-isin.r: The dynasty's high point was [[e:nebuchadnezzar-i|Nebuchadnezzar I]] (c. 1125 to 1104 BCE), who defeated Hutelutush-Inshushinak of the [[s:middle-elamite-kingdom|Middle Elamite kingdom]] and returned the statue of [[e:marduk|Marduk]], an event celebrated in literary texts and possibly linked to the rise of Marduk as king of the gods in the Enuma Elish. Kudurru stones recorded land grants to loyal officers. Marduk-nadin-ahhe fought Tiglath-Pileser I of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]], who raided [[e:babylon|Babylon]].
second-dynasty-of-isin.e: From the late 11th century Aramean and Sutean migrations, famine and Assyrian pressure weakened [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]]. Adad-apla-iddina was a usurper of Aramean origin, and the dynasty ended with Nabu-shumu-libur in 1026 BCE, followed by the [[s:second-sealand-dynasty|Second Sealand Dynasty]].

sasanian-yemen.t: Yemen as a province of the Persian Empire, ruled by a Persian garrison whose descendants, the Abna, helped bring the country into Islam.
sasanian-yemen.o: Around 570 the Sasanian king [[e:khosrow-i|Khosrow I]] sent a small force under the general Wahriz at the request of [[e:sayf-ibn-dhi-yazan|Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan]] to expel the Ethiopians of [[s:aksumite-yemen|Aksumite Yemen]]. Sayf was set up as a client ruler, but after his murder [[e:persia|Persia]] took direct control, governing from Sanaa through a [[e:marzban|marzban]].
sasanian-yemen.r: Persian rule was light and focused on Sanaa and the trade routes. Persian soldiers settled and married locally, forming the Abna, a distinct elite group. [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] gave the [[s:sasanian-empire|Sasanian Empire]] a foothold on the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] and [[e:indian-ocean-trade|Indian Ocean trade]] against the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] and its allies, but the provincial governors had limited reach into the tribal highlands.
sasanian-yemen.e: As [[e:persia|Persia]] weakened after its wars with [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], the governor Badhan accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] around 628 and [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] came under the [[s:islamic-state-of-medina|Islamic state of Medina]]. The Abna remained influential in early Islamic Sanaa.

sarangarh-state.t: A Raj Gond state of the Chhattisgarh plain on the Mahanadi, whose last ruler became Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh.
sarangarh-state.o: Sarangarh was ruled by a [[e:british-raj|Raj]] Gond family, one of several Gond dynasties of eastern Chhattisgarh. Its traditions date the state to around 1600, and it was long a dependency of larger neighbours, including the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Bhonsles of Nagpur]] in the 18th century.
sarangarh-state.r: The Raja ruled a modest territory of [[e:rice|rice]] fields and forest near the Mahanadi. Under British paramountcy Sarangarh was one of the Chhattisgarh Feudatory States, later in the Eastern States Agency. Its last ruler, Naresh Chandra Singh, took an active part in politics.
sarangarh-state.e: Sarangarh merged into the Central Provinces and Berar in 1948. Naresh Chandra Singh later served briefly as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh in 1969. The area is now in Chhattisgarh.

satsuma-domain.t: The powerful Shimazu domain of southern Kyushu, overlord of Ryukyu and, with Choshu, the driving force behind the Meiji Restoration.
satsuma-domain.o: The Shimazu had fought against [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] in 1600, but by negotiation they kept Satsuma, Osumi and part of Hyuga, assessed at about 770,000 koku and ruled from Kagoshima. In 1609 the domain invaded the [[s:ryukyu-kingdom|Ryukyu Kingdom]] and made it a [[e:vassal|vassal]].
satsuma-domain.r: Satsuma had an unusually large [[e:samurai|samurai]] class, many living as rural warriors, and a strict youth training system. Its control of [[s:ryukyu-kingdom|Ryukyu]] gave it a hidden window on Chinese trade, including [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]]. Zusho Hiromichi restored its finances in the 1830s, and Shimazu Nariakira built Western-style furnaces, shipyards and factories at the Shuseikan.
satsuma-domain.e: After the Namamugi incident a British squadron bombarded Kagoshima in 1863. Satsuma then modernised, allied with [[e:choshu-domain|Choshu]] in 1866, and its men Saigo Takamori and Okubo Toshimichi led the Restoration of 1868. It became Kagoshima Prefecture in 1871; Saigo's Satsuma Rebellion of 1877 was crushed.

shimashki-dynasty.t: An Elamite highland dynasty whose king Kindattu sacked Ur in 2004 BCE and carried off its last king, ending the Neo-Sumerian Empire.
shimashki-dynasty.o: Shimashki was a group of highland lands in western [[e:iran|Iran]], probably north of [[s:kingdom-of-anshan|Anshan]] in the [[e:zagros-mountains|Zagros]] between [[e:isfahan|Isfahan]] and Luristan. Under the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]] its rulers were both enemies and allies of Ur, receiving Sumerian princesses in marriage. As Ur weakened at the end of the 21st century BCE, Shimashki kings took over [[e:susa|Susa]].
shimashki-dynasty.r: The [[e:susa|Susa]] king list names twelve Shimashki kings, but few are well documented. They ruled a federation of Elamite lands joined to Susa and [[s:kingdom-of-anshan|Anshan]], combining highland and lowland power, a pattern that later Elamite states kept. Religion centred on Elamite gods such as Inshushinak and Humban. The dynasty's greatest moment came when [[e:kindattu|Kindattu]] sacked Ur in 2004 BCE and took Ibbi-Sin captive to [[e:anshan|Anshan]].
shimashki-dynasty.e: Ishbi-Erra of [[s:isin|Isin]] expelled the Elamite garrison from Ur soon after. Around 1970 BCE power passed to the [[s:sukkalmah-dynasty|Sukkalmah dynasty]], founded by Ebarat, whose rulers continued to govern [[e:elam|Elam]].

sumedang-larang.t: A Sundanese kingdom in the highlands of West Java that claimed the heritage of the Sunda Kingdom before submitting to Mataram in 1620.
sumedang-larang.o: Sumedang Larang was a principality in the Priangan highlands, long subordinate to the [[s:sunda-kingdom|Sunda Kingdom]]. Its rulers accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 16th century, under Pangeran Santri. When Banten destroyed Pakuan Pajajaran in 1579, [[e:sunda-strait|Sunda]] nobles are said to have carried the royal crown, the Binokasih, to Sumedang.
sumedang-larang.r: Prabu Geusan Ulun, who received the regalia, claimed to rule as heir of [[e:sunda-strait|Sunda]] over much of the Priangan, from his capital at Kutamaya. The realm was agricultural, based on [[e:rice|rice]] farming, and kept Sundanese court traditions while adopting [[e:islam|Islam]].
sumedang-larang.e: Squeezed between Banten, Cirebon and the expanding [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram Sultanate]], Sumedang submitted to [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Agung of Mataram in 1620, and its ruler became a regent. It later passed under the [[e:dutch|Dutch]], and the Binokasih crown is kept today in the Prabu Geusan Ulun Museum in Sumedang.

spanish-tripoli.t: Tripoli under Spanish rule after its capture by Pedro Navarro in 1510, a brief Habsburg outpost later handed to the Knights of St John.
spanish-tripoli.o: In July 1510, following his capture of Bejaia, Pedro Navarro stormed [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] for [[e:ferdinand-ii-of-aragon|Ferdinand II of Aragon]]. The town, then an autonomous city loosely tied to the [[s:hafsid-sultanate|Hafsid Sultanate]], was sacked and much of its population fled or was killed.
spanish-tripoli.r: Spanish [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] was a small garrison administered through the viceroyalty of the [[s:kingdom-of-sicily|Kingdom of Sicily]]. Costly to supply and isolated, it served mainly to deny the port to corsairs. Its fortifications were rebuilt, but the town recovered little of its former trade.
spanish-tripoli.e: In 1530 [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] granted [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]], together with Malta, to the Knights Hospitaller, who had lost [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]], creating [[s:hospitaller-tripoli|Hospitaller Tripoli]].

sangri-state.t: A tiny Himalayan hill state above the Sutlej, ruled by a branch of the Kullu royal family.
sangri-state.o: Sangri was one of the small Simla Hill States, held by a branch of the ruling family of Kullu. When Kullu fell to the [[e:sikhism|Sikhs]] and then the British, this outlying fragment survived as a separate chiefship. The register dates it to around 1700.
sangri-state.r: The Rai or Rana ruled a few mountain villages on the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]], with terraced farming and [[e:pastoralism|pastoralism]]. After the Gurkha war of 1814 to 1815 it held a British sanad as one of the Simla Hill States. Little else is recorded.
sangri-state.e: Sangri joined Himachal Pradesh in 1948. Its lands lie in Kullu and Shimla districts.

second-taifa-of-cordoba.t: Córdoba's brief independence under the qadi Ibn Hamdin during the collapse of Almoravid rule in al-Andalus in the 1140s.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.o: In 1144, amid revolts across [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]] against the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], the Córdoban qadi Ibn Hamdin, from a leading family of jurists, was proclaimed emir by the city's notables and expelled the Almoravid garrison.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.r: Ibn Hamdin's authority rested on his religious office and local support rather than on an army. He briefly claimed recognition from other cities, but was driven out for a time by the Hudid prince Zafadola and had to seek help from Alfonso VII of [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], while the Almoravid commander Yahya ibn Ghaniya fought to retake the city.
second-taifa-of-cordoba.e: Ibn Hamdin fled to [[e:north-africa|North Africa]], and by 1148 [[e:cordoba|Córdoba]] had passed to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]], who made [[e:seville|Seville]] their main Andalusi capital. Córdoba fell to [[e:ferdinand-iii-of-castile|Ferdinand III]] of the [[s:crown-of-castile|Crown of Castile]] in 1236.

state-of-qatar.t: Independent Qatar since 1971, whose vast gas reserves made it one of the world's richest states and an outsized diplomatic and media power.
state-of-qatar.o: When [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] withdrew from the Gulf, the [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Sheikhdom of Qatar]] chose not to join the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] and became independent on 3 September 1971. In February 1972 [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]] bin Hamad Al Thani deposed his cousin Ahmad and took power.
state-of-qatar.r: [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Qatar]] is an absolute monarchy of the Al Thani with an advisory council. The North Field, the world's largest gas field shared with [[e:iran|Iran]], made it a leading exporter of liquefied natural gas from the 1990s. Hamad bin [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]], who displaced his father in 1995, founded Al Jazeera in 1996, hosted a large US air base and pursued an independent foreign policy. Most residents are foreign workers.
state-of-qatar.e: Tamim bin Hamad succeeded his father in 2013. [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]], the UAE, [[s:state-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] and [[e:egypt|Egypt]] blockaded [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Qatar]] from 2017 to 2021, and in 2022 it hosted the FIFA World Cup.

state-of-xue.t: An old Ren-clan state in southern Shandong that ended as the fief of Lord Mengchang, the most famous patron of retainers in the Warring States.
state-of-xue.o: Xue was ruled by the Ren clan, who traced their line to Xi Zhong, legendary inventor of the cart and a minister of the Xia. The Zhou recognised it as a minor state with its capital near modern Tengzhou in Shandong, between the [[s:state-of-lu|State of Lu]] and the [[s:state-of-song|State of Song]].
state-of-xue.r: Xue played a small part in the alliances of the Spring and Autumn period, sending its rulers to interstate covenants led by Qi and Jin. Its walled city, whose remains survive south of Tengzhou, was large for so minor a state, suggesting a prosperous agricultural and trading centre on the eastern plain.
state-of-xue.e: The [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]] absorbed Xue in the 4th century BCE and granted it as a fief to Tian Ying. His son Tian Wen, Lord Mengchang, ruled from Xue and kept thousands of retainers there, making the name famous long after the old state had gone.

state-of-deng.t: A small kingdom of the Man clan on the Han River, older than the Zhou, whose marriage ties with Chu did not save it from being swallowed by that rising power in 678 BCE.
state-of-deng.o: Deng appears in [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] oracle-bone inscriptions and survived the Zhou conquest as a minor state ruled by the Man clan, centred near modern [[e:xiangyang|Xiangyang]] in Hubei and the Nanyang basin of Henan. It lay on the route between the Central Plain and the middle [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]].
state-of-deng.r: Little is recorded of its institutions. Deng is known mainly through the Zuo zhuan, which notes marriages between its ruling house and the kings of Chu: Deng Man was the wife of King Wu of Chu and mother of King Wen. [[e:bronze|Bronze]] vessels inscribed with the name of Deng rulers have been found in Hubei and Henan.
state-of-deng.e: When King Wen of Chu passed through Deng on campaign, the Marquis of Deng refused his advisers' urging to kill his visiting nephew. Chu attacked Deng soon afterwards and annexed it in 678 BCE, an early step in the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]]'s expansion northwards.

seuna-yadava-dynasty.t: The Deccan dynasty of Devagiri, whose wealth drew the first Delhi Sultanate raid into southern India in 1296.
seuna-yadava-dynasty.o: The Seunas were long-standing feudatories of the [[s:western-chalukya-empire|Chalukyas of Kalyani]] in the northern [[e:deccan|Deccan]]. When Chalukya power collapsed, Bhillama V proclaimed independence around 1187, founded the fortress city of Devagiri (later [[e:daulatabad|Daulatabad]]) and fought the [[s:hoysala-empire|Hoysalas]] for control of the former Chalukya territories.
seuna-yadava-dynasty.r: Singhana II, the greatest ruler, extended Seuna power over most of Maharashtra and northern Karnataka. The court supported [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] and early [[e:marathi|Marathi]] literature: the astronomer Bhaskara's grandson ran a school under Seuna patronage, and Hemadri, minister to Mahadeva and Ramachandra, wrote the Chaturvarga Chintamani and is credited with the Hemadpanti temple style. The poet-saint Jnaneshwar wrote his Marathi commentary on the Gita in this period.
seuna-yadava-dynasty.e: [[e:alauddin-khalji|Alauddin Khalji]] raided Devagiri in 1296 and extracted vast tribute, and Ramachandra became a [[e:vassal|vassal]] of the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. After revolts, the kingdom was annexed in 1317 under Mubarak Shah. Devagiri, renamed [[e:daulatabad|Daulatabad]], later served briefly as Muhammad bin Tughluq's capital.

sarmatians.t: Iranian-speaking horse nomads who replaced the Scythians as masters of the Pontic steppe and fought Rome for four centuries.
sarmatians.o: The Sarmatians grew out of the [[s:sauromatae|Sauromatae]], whom [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] placed east of the Don. From the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE their tribes pushed west across the Don and [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], breaking the power of the [[e:scythians|Scythians]] and taking over the steppe as far as the [[e:danube|Danube]]. Leading tribes included the [[s:iazyges|Iazyges]], [[s:roxolani|Roxolani]], [[s:aorsi|Aorsi]], Siraces and later the [[s:alans|Alans]].
sarmatians.r: They formed a loose confederation of tribes under their own kings rather than a single state. Their armoured [[e:lance|lancers]] on horseback impressed Greek and Roman writers, and rich female burials with weapons suggest women held unusual status, feeding Greek tales of the [[e:amazon|Amazons]]. They traded with the Bosporan cities and took Roman [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] or raided the frontier in turn.
sarmatians.e: Many Sarmatians were absorbed by the Goths in the 3rd century, and the Hunnic invasion of the 370s scattered the rest. Some joined the [[e:huns|Huns]], others entered Roman service, including 5,500 [[s:iazyges|Iazyges]] sent to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 175, while the [[s:alans|Alans]] migrated as far as Gaul, [[e:spain|Spain]] and [[e:north-africa|North Africa]].

senones.t: Gallic people of the Yonne around Sens, a branch of whom sacked Rome in about 390 BCE and settled on the Adriatic coast.
senones.o: The [[s:senones-400|Senones]] held the land along the Yonne and the upper Seine, with Agedincum (Sens) as their chief town. Livy and Polybius record that part of the people crossed the [[e:alps|Alps]] around 400 BCE; led by Brennus, they defeated the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] at the Allia and sacked [[e:rome|Rome]], then settled on the Adriatic coast around Sena Gallica (Senigallia).
senones.r: In Gaul they were a powerful people with a council of nobles. Caesar made Cavarinus their king, but the [[s:senones-400|Senones]] drove him out in 54 BCE, a sign of resistance to Roman-backed kingship.
senones.e: The Italian [[s:senones-400|Senones]] were defeated by [[e:rome|Rome]] in 283 BCE. In Gaul Caesar had the rebel leader [[s:acco|Acco]] flogged to death in 53 BCE, and the Senones joined Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. Agedincum became Sens, later the seat of a powerful archbishop.

sybaris.t: Achaean Greek city in southern Italy so rich that its name became a byword for luxury, destroyed by its neighbour Croton in 510 BCE.
sybaris.o: Achaean colonists from the northern Peloponnese, led by Is of Helike, founded Sybaris around 720 BCE on the plain between the Crathis and Sybaris rivers, near the Gulf of [[s:principality-of-taranto|Taranto]]. The fertile plain and routes across the Calabrian isthmus to the Tyrrhenian Sea gave it rapid growth.
sybaris.r: Sybaris became one of the largest Greek cities in the West. Strabo says it ruled four native peoples and twenty-five subject towns and could field an enormous army. It founded [[s:poseidonia|Poseidonia]] and other colonies, and its traders worked closely with [[s:miletus|Miletus]] and the Etruscans. Later Greek writers delighted in tales of Sybarite excess, which gave English the word 'sybarite'. Around 510 BCE a popular leader, Telys, seized power and expelled the wealthy.
sybaris.e: When [[s:croton|Croton]] sheltered the Sybarite exiles, war followed. In 510 BCE Croton's army, led by the athlete Milo, defeated Sybaris, and the victors are said to have diverted the Crathis over the ruins. Attempts at refoundation led to the Panhellenic colony of [[s:thurii|Thurii]] in 444 BCE nearby.

southern-han.t: A kingdom ruled from Guangzhou by the Liu family, rich from maritime trade but notorious for its cruelty and its vast corps of eunuchs.
southern-han.o: Liu Yin, of a family that had grown wealthy in the southern trade, became military governor of Lingnan at [[e:guangzhou|Guangzhou]] late in the [[s:later-tang|Tang]]. His brother Liu Yan inherited the post and in 917 proclaimed himself emperor of Great Yue, renaming the state Han in 918, with the capital renamed Xingwang.
southern-han.r: Southern Han controlled modern Guangdong and Guangxi and grew rich on the sea trade with South-east [[e:asia|Asia]] and the [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]], handled by Arab, Persian and other foreign merchants at [[e:guangzhou|Guangzhou]]. Its rulers were notorious for elaborate tortures and lavish palaces; under Liu Chang [[e:eunuch|eunuchs]] numbered in the thousands and dominated government. In 938 its fleet was destroyed by Ngô Quyền at the Bạch Đằng river, ending Chinese rule in northern [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]].
southern-han.e: In 971 a [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] army under Pan Mei invaded; Liu Chang burned his treasures and surrendered. He lived on at [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]] as a pensioned noble, and the far south was reunited with the rest of [[e:china|China]].

shaddadids-of-ani.t: A Kurdish Muslim dynasty that governed the old Armenian capital Ani for the Seljuks, alternating with Georgian conquerors for over a century.
shaddadids-of-ani.o: After the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] took Ani in 1064, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:malik-shah-i|Malik Shah]] granted the city in 1072 to Manuchihr, son of the [[s:shaddadid-emirate|Shaddadid Emirate]]'s ruler Shavur. The branch at Ani outlived the main line in [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]], which the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] deposed in 1075.
shaddadids-of-ani.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] governed a largely Armenian Christian city, maintaining its walls and trade and treating the population with some tolerance. Manuchihr built the mosque that still stands at Ani, among the earliest Turkic-era mosques in [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]. The [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]] repeatedly captured the city, in 1124, 1161 and 1174, and the [[s:shaddadid-emirate|Shaddadids]] regained it each time.
shaddadids-of-ani.e: In 1199 Queen Tamar's generals Zakare and Ivane took Ani for good and made it the centre of [[s:zakarid-armenia|Zakarid Armenia]], ending Shaddadid rule. The Manuchihr mosque, later used as a museum, remains one of the few standing buildings in the ruins of Ani.

state-of-kuwait.t: Independent Kuwait since 1961, an oil-rich emirate with an elected parliament that survived Iraqi invasion and occupation in 1990-1991.
state-of-kuwait.o: On 19 June 1961 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ended the 1899 protection agreement and the [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Sheikhdom of Kuwait]] became fully independent under Abdullah Al-Salim Al-Sabah. [[e:iraq|Iraq's]] ruler Abd al-Karim Qasim immediately claimed Kuwait, and British and then Arab League troops deployed to deter an invasion.
state-of-kuwait.r: A constitution of 1962 created the National Assembly, the most powerful elected parliament in the Gulf, though the emir retains wide powers and has suspended it several times. Oil revenues financed a welfare state, free education and health care, and the [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] Fund for Arab development aid. Kuwaiti citizens are a minority among a large foreign workforce.
state-of-kuwait.e: [[e:iraq|Iraq]] invaded on 2 August 1990 and occupied [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] until a US-led coalition liberated it in February 1991. Kuwait rebuilt and remains a constitutional [[e:emirate|emirate]] under the Al Sabah.

spanish-formosa.t: A small Spanish colony on Taiwan's northern tip, founded from Manila to protect the galleon trade, which the Dutch captured in 1642.
spanish-formosa.o: Alarmed by the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] presence in the south of [[s:republic-of-china|Taiwan]], which threatened the trade between [[e:china|China]] and Spanish [[e:manila|Manila]], the Spanish sent an expedition under Antonio Carreño de Valdés in 1626. It occupied the harbour of Keelung, founding the settlement of Santísima Trinidad and Fort San [[e:salvador|Salvador]], and in 1628 built Fort Santo Domingo at Tamsui.
spanish-formosa.r: The colony was a garrison outpost governed from [[e:manila|Manila]], with Dominican and Franciscan missionaries working among the Basay and other indigenous peoples. Hopes of drawing Chinese and Japanese trade away from the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] were disappointed, and the colony was costly and disease-ridden.
spanish-formosa.e: [[e:manila|Manila]], needing troops against Muslim sultanates in the southern [[s:philippines|Philippines]], reduced the garrison in 1637 and abandoned Tamsui. In 1642 a [[e:dutch|Dutch]] force besieged Keelung, and the governor Gonzalo Portillo surrendered. Northern [[s:republic-of-china|Taiwan]] passed to [[s:dutch-formosa|Dutch Formosa]].

shambaa-kingdom.t: A mountain kingdom of north-eastern Tanzania, ruled by the Kilindi dynasty from Vugha, which dominated the Usambara range until German conquest.
shambaa-kingdom.o: According to Shambaa tradition, the hunter Mbegha came to the Usambara Mountains around the early 18th century, settled disputes, killed wild pigs that ravaged the fields and married into local lineages. His son Buge founded the Kilindi dynasty, and the kingdom grew under Kimweri I.
shambaa-kingdom.r: The king, the simba mwene, ruled from the capital at Vugha through sons and relatives placed as chiefs of districts, with ritual authority over rain and land. Under Kimweri ye Nyumbai, who died in 1862, the kingdom reached its height, controlling the mountains and receiving tribute from the coastal plains. Missionaries Johann Krapf and Erhardt visited his court.
shambaa-kingdom.e: After Kimweri's death succession wars split the kingdom, with rival lineages backed by coastal traders. The Germans conquered Usambara in the 1890s, making it part of [[s:german-east-africa|German East Africa]]. The Kilindi survived as local chiefs until chieftaincies were abolished in [[s:tanganyika|Tanganyika]] in 1963.

cr.a: Böhler, H. (18..-19..). Auteur du texte Reimer, Dietrich (1818-1899). Auteur du texte

sheikhdom-of-fujairah.t: The only Trucial sheikhdom on the Gulf of Oman coast, which broke away from Sharjah in 1902 and was recognised by Britain only in 1952.
sheikhdom-of-fujairah.o: Fujairah, on the east coast of the [[e:oman|Oman]] peninsula, was home to the Sharqiyin tribe and long fell under the [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Qawasim]] of the [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sheikhdom of Sharjah]]. In 1902 the Sharqiyin chief Hamad bin Abdullah Al Sharqi asserted independence, though [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] continued to treat Fujairah as part of Sharjah.
sheikhdom-of-fujairah.r: The sheikhdom lived from date farming, fishing and the trade of its small port, in the mountain-backed valleys of the east coast. In 1925 a British warship shelled Fujairah fort during a dispute with the sheikh. Its claims also brought it into conflict with the [[s:sheikhdom-of-kalba|Sheikhdom of Kalba]]. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] finally recognised Fujairah as one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] in 1952.
sheikhdom-of-fujairah.e: Fujairah joined the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] at its foundation in December 1971. Its port later became a major oil bunkering centre outside the Strait of [[s:kingdom-of-ormus|Hormuz]].

satavahana-dynasty.t: The first great Deccan empire, which linked India's west-coast ports to the Bay of Bengal and patronised the Buddhist caves of the Western Ghats.
satavahana-dynasty.o: The Satavahanas rose in the northern [[e:deccan|Deccan]] after the decline of the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]]. The Puranas call them Andhras and name Simuka as the founder. An early king, Satakarni I, extended their rule over the western Deccan and [[e:malwa|Malwa]], and his queen Naganika recorded his Vedic sacrifices in the Naneghat cave inscription.
satavahana-dynasty.r: Satavahana kings ruled from Pratishthana, modern Paithan, and later from Dharanikota in Andhra, governing through officials called amatyas and local chiefs. Kings were named after their mothers, as in Gautamiputra Satakarni. Ports such as Bharuch and Sopara traded with the Roman world, and merchants and royals funded Buddhist caves at Karle, Nashik and Kanheri and the great stupa at Amaravati. Prakrit was the court language.
satavahana-dynasty.e: Gautamiputra Satakarni defeated Nahapana of the [[s:western-satraps|Western Satraps]] around 125, but Rudradaman later beat the Satavahanas twice. After Yajna Sri Satakarni the empire fragmented in the early 3rd century among the [[s:abhira-dynasty|Abhira dynasty]], the [[s:ikshvaku-dynasty|Ikshvaku dynasty]], the [[s:chutu-dynasty|Chutu dynasty]] and others.

swazi-kingdom.t: The Dlamini kingdom of Eswatini, founded in the 18th century, which survived colonial rule to become one of the world's last absolute monarchies.
swazi-kingdom.o: Around 1745 the Dlamini clan under Ngwane III settled on the lower Pongola river. In the early 19th century Sobhuza I, under pressure from the [[s:ndwandwe-kingdom|Ndwandwe Kingdom]], moved north to the Ezulwini valley and built a new kingdom by absorbing local Sotho and [[e:nguni|Nguni]] chiefdoms.
swazi-kingdom.r: The king (Ngwenyama) rules jointly with the queen mother (Ndlovukati), supported by royal councils and regiments. Mswati II, from whom the Swazi take their name, expanded the kingdom through raiding and alliances in the mid-19th century. Kingship is renewed in the annual Incwala ceremony, and the Umhlanga reed dance is a major national event.
swazi-kingdom.e: Swaziland became a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] of the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] in 1894 and a British territory after the [[e:second-boer-war|Second Boer War]]. It regained independence in 1968 under Sobhuza II, who abolished parliamentary rule in 1973. Renamed Eswatini in 2018, it remains ruled by Mswati III.

state-of-dathina.t: A tribal territory of the Aden hinterland without a ruling family, governed by a council under British advice from 1944.
state-of-dathina.o: Dathina was a district inland from the [[e:gulf-of-aden|Gulf of Aden]] inhabited by tribes who recognised no sultan or sheikh. In 1944 British officials organised it as a state governed by a tribal council, with its centre at Mudiyah, so that it could be brought into the system of protected states.
state-of-dathina.r: Unlike its neighbours, Dathina had no hereditary ruler; a council of tribal representatives chose its head. Its people lived from farming and herding in the valleys. As part of the [[s:aden-protectorate|Western Aden Protectorate]] it joined the [[s:federation-of-arab-emirates-of-the-south|Federation of Arab Emirates of the South]] in 1960.
state-of-dathina.e: Dathina remained a member of the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] until 1967, when the National Liberation Front took over and the territory was incorporated into [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].

socialist-soviet-republic-of-byelorussia.t: The first Soviet Belarusian republic, proclaimed on 1 January 1919 and merged into Litbel within two months.
socialist-soviet-republic-of-byelorussia.o: As German troops withdrew from Belarus at the end of 1918, the Red Army occupied Minsk, displacing the [[s:belarusian-peoples-republic|Belarusian People's Republic]]. On 1 January 1919 a Bolshevik conference in [[e:smolensk|Smolensk]] proclaimed the Socialist Soviet Republic of Byelorussia, partly to counter the nationalist government, and its leaders moved to Minsk.
socialist-soviet-republic-of-byelorussia.r: Its provisional government was headed by the writer Zmitser Zhylunovich, known as Tsishka Hartny. The republic adopted a constitution at a congress of soviets in February 1919, but [[e:moscow|Moscow]] soon cut off several eastern provinces and joined them directly to the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]], leaving it only the Minsk and Grodno regions.
socialist-soviet-republic-of-byelorussia.e: With Polish forces advancing, [[e:moscow|Moscow]] decided to merge the republic with the Lithuanian Soviet republic, and on 27 February 1919 it became part of the [[s:lithuanian-byelorussian-ssr|Lithuanian-Byelorussian SSR]]. A Belarusian Soviet republic was proclaimed again in 1920 as the [[s:byelorussian-ssr|Byelorussian SSR]].

state-of-deseret.t: A vast state proposed by Mormon settlers in 1849, governed in practice by the Latter-day Saint leadership under Brigham Young until Congress created Utah Territory.
state-of-deseret.o: Driven from Illinois, members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints reached the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, then in Mexican territory. After the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo made the region American, church leaders drafted a constitution in 1849 for a State of Deseret, a name from the Book of Mormon meaning honeybee, and petitioned Congress for admission.
state-of-deseret.r: Deseret claimed a huge area covering most of present-day Utah and Nevada, much of Arizona and parts of six other states, with a corridor to the Pacific at San Diego. Brigham Young was elected governor, and church officers filled the legislature and courts, so civil and religious authority were effectively one. The government organised irrigation, roads, a militia and the University of Deseret, the future University of Utah.
state-of-deseret.e: Congress rejected statehood and in the Compromise of 1850 created the much smaller Utah Territory, with Young as governor. The Deseret assembly dissolved itself in April 1851. A shadow legislature met for years afterwards, and Utah became a state in 1896.

sakti-state.t: One of the smallest of the Chhattisgarh feudatory states, ruled by a Gond family in the plains east of Bilaspur.
sakti-state.o: Sakti was held by a Gond ruling family in the Chhattisgarh plain. Its traditions place the founding around 1600, but its early history is known mainly from local accounts.
sakti-state.r: The Raja ruled a small territory of [[e:rice|rice]] villages and forest. In the British period Sakti was one of the Chhattisgarh Feudatory States, attached to the Central Provinces and later to the Eastern States Agency. Few further details are recorded.
sakti-state.e: Sakti merged into the Central Provinces and Berar on 1 January 1948, later Madhya Pradesh. Since 2000 it has been in Chhattisgarh, where it is now a district headquarters.

sequani.t: Gallic people of Franche-Comté whose rivalry with the Aedui led them to invite the German Ariovistus into Gaul.
sequani.o: The Sequani lived between the Saône, the Jura and the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], around their great oppidum of Vesontio ([[s:imperial-city-of-besancon|Besançon]]) in a loop of the Doubs. Their land was famous for salted pork exported to [[e:rome|Rome]].
sequani.r: They contested with the [[s:aedui|Aedui]] for control of tolls on the Saône and for leadership of Gaul. Caesar names Catamantaloedes as a former king who held the title of friend of the Roman people, and his son Casticus as a would-be king.
sequani.e: To defeat the [[s:aedui|Aedui]] they hired the German leader Ariovistus, who then seized a third of their land, until Caesar drove him out in 58 BCE. The Sequani joined the revolt of 52 BCE. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Vesontio became an important town, and their land later formed the province of Maxima Sequanorum.

sant-state.t: A Parmar Rajput state in eastern Gujarat, ruled from Santrampur, one of the states of the Rewa Kantha Agency.
sant-state.o: The ruling family claimed Parmar [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] descent, and tradition dates the state to 1255. Little is reliably known about its early history.
sant-state.r: Sant was a hilly, forested state with a large Bhil population. In the colonial period it was part of the Rewa Kantha Agency and paid tribute to [[s:baroda-state|Baroda State]]. Its capital was the town of Santrampur.
sant-state.e: Sant merged into Bombay State in 1948, and Santrampur is now in Mahisagar district, [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

sikh-misls.t: A confederacy of Sikh warrior bands that took control of the Punjab from the Mughals and Afghans in the 18th century.
sikh-misls.o: After the execution of [[s:kingdom-of-banda|Banda]] Singh Bahadur in 1716, [[e:sikhism|Sikh]] fighters organised in bands during decades of persecution by Mughal governors and invasions by [[e:ahmad-shah-abdali|Ahmad Shah Durrani]]. In 1748, at [[e:amritsar|Amritsar]], they combined into the Dal [[e:khalsa|Khalsa]] under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, grouped into eleven or twelve misls, each led by a sardar.
sikh-misls.r: The misls were largely autonomous units that shared conquered land and met at the Sarbat [[e:khalsa|Khalsa]] assemblies at [[e:amritsar|Amritsar]], where collective decisions, gurmatta, were taken. They collected rakhi, a protection levy, from villages. Despite the [[e:durrani-empire|Durrani]] massacre of 1762, they took [[e:lahore|Lahore]] in 1765 and rebuilt the [[e:golden-temple|Harmandir Sahib]]. Leading misls included the Bhangi, Ahluwalia, Ramgarhia and Sukerchakia.
sikh-misls.e: Rivalries among the misls grew after the [[e:durrani-empire|Durrani]] threat faded. [[e:ranjit-singh|Ranjit Singh]], head of the Sukerchakia misl, captured [[e:lahore|Lahore]] in 1799 and absorbed the other misls into the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]], of which he was proclaimed maharaja in 1801.

sheikhdom-of-kuwait.t: The Al Sabah trading town at the head of the Gulf that passed from pearling and shipbuilding to oil wealth under British protection.
sheikhdom-of-kuwait.o: Clans of the Bani Utbah settled at [[s:state-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] in the early 18th century under the protection of the [[s:banu-khalid-emirate|Banu Khalid Emirate]]. Around 1752 they chose Sabah I as their leader, founding the Al Sabah dynasty that still rules.
sheikhdom-of-kuwait.r: [[s:state-of-kuwait|Kuwait]] was a merchant town of pearl divers, dhow builders and long-distance traders to [[e:india|India]] and [[e:east-africa|East Africa]], governed by the ruler with the consent of leading merchant families. Mubarak al-Sabah, who took power in 1896, signed the Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement of 1899, placing Kuwait under British protection against Ottoman claims. The Uqair conference of 1922 set its borders with the [[s:sultanate-of-nejd|Sultanate of Nejd]].
sheikhdom-of-kuwait.e: Oil was discovered at Burgan in 1938 and exported from 1946, transforming the economy under Abdullah Al-Salim Al-Sabah. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ended the 1899 agreement on 19 June 1961, and the [[s:state-of-kuwait|State of Kuwait]] became independent.

saga-domain.t: The Nabeshima domain of Hizen, home of Arita porcelain and of the samurai classic Hagakure, and a pioneer of Western industrial technology.
saga-domain.o: Nabeshima Naoshige, chief retainer of the Ryuzoji, took over their domain after Ryuzoji Takanobu's death in 1584 and was confirmed by [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] and then by [[e:tokugawa-ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]]. After the last Ryuzoji heir died in 1607, Naoshige's son Katsushige became lord in name as well as fact, with 357,000 koku.
saga-domain.r: Korean potters brought back from the invasions of [[e:korea|Korea]] began making [[e:porcelain|porcelain]] at Arita around 1616, and the domain controlled its export through the port of Imari, while the Nabeshima kilns made pieces for gifts to the [[e:shogun|shogun]]. Saga shared guard duty at [[e:nagasaki|Nagasaki]] with Fukuoka. Hagakure, a [[e:samurai|samurai]] treatise dictated by Yamamoto Tsunetomo, was compiled here. Nabeshima Naomasa built [[e:japan|Japan's]] first reverberatory furnace in 1850.
saga-domain.e: Saga's modern weapons helped the imperial side in 1868. It became part of Saga Prefecture in 1871, and in 1874 Eto Shinpei led the failed Saga Rebellion.

second-bulgarian-empire.t: Restored medieval Bulgarian state of the Asen dynasty, centred on Tarnovo, which defeated the Latin crusaders and led Orthodox culture until the Ottomans came.
second-bulgarian-empire.o: In 1185 the brothers Asen and Peter led a revolt against Byzantine taxes at Tarnovo, restoring Bulgarian independence lost when the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]] fell in 1018. Their younger brother Kaloyan received a crown from [[e:papacy|Pope]] Innocent III in 1204 and in 1205 destroyed the [[e:latin|Latin]] crusader army at Adrianople, capturing Emperor Baldwin I.
second-bulgarian-empire.r: The tsar ruled from the fortified hill of Tsarevets with a council of boyars. Ivan Asen II (1218–1241) defeated Epirus at Klokotnitsa in 1230 and ruled from the Adriatic to the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]], and the Bulgarian patriarchate was restored in 1235. Mongol raids and civil wars weakened the state after 1242. Under Ivan Alexander in the 14th century, Tarnovo became a centre of art and letters, with Patriarch Euthymius reforming church books.
second-bulgarian-empire.e: In 1356 the realm split, with the [[s:tsardom-of-vidin|Tsardom of Vidin]] breaking away. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took Tarnovo in 1393 and Vidin in 1396, and [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] remained under Ottoman rule until 1878.

singhasari.t: The short-lived East Javanese kingdom of Ken Arok and Kertanegara, which defied Kublai Khan and paved the way for Majapahit.
singhasari.o: Ken Arok, a commoner turned ruler of Tumapel, overthrew Kertajaya of the [[s:kediri-kingdom|Kediri Kingdom]] at the Battle of Ganter in 1222 and founded a new dynasty under the name Rajasa. The Pararaton chronicle tells a violent story of murders over the following generations, until Wisnuwardhana restored order in the mid-13th century.
singhasari.r: Its last king [[e:kertanegara|Kertanegara]] pursued an ambitious overseas policy: the Pamalayu expedition of 1275 brought Sumatran [[s:dharmasraya|Dharmasraya]] into his orbit, and he claimed influence over [[e:bali|Bali]] and Madura. He patronised a blend of Tantric [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] and Shaivism, and his reign produced temples such as Candi Jago and Candi Singhasari. In 1289 he humiliated an envoy of [[e:kublai-khan|Kublai Khan]].
singhasari.e: In 1292 Jayakatwang of [[e:kediri-kingdom|Kediri]] killed [[e:kertanegara|Kertanegara]] and set up [[s:gelang-gelang|Gelang-gelang]]. Kertanegara's son-in-law [[e:raden-wijaya|Raden Wijaya]] used the Mongol fleet sent by [[e:kublai-khan|Kublai Khan]] to defeat Jayakatwang in 1293, then drove the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] out and founded [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]].

slovak-soviet-republic.t: Communist puppet state proclaimed in eastern Slovakia in 1919 under the protection of the Hungarian Red Army, which lasted just three weeks.
slovak-soviet-republic.o: In May and June 1919 the Hungarian Red Army of the [[s:hungarian-soviet-republic|Hungarian Soviet Republic]] pushed into Slovakia, recently claimed by [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]], and took Košice and much of the east. On 16 June 1919, in Prešov, local and Hungarian communists proclaimed the Slovak Soviet Republic, led by the Czech communist Antonín Janoušek.
slovak-soviet-republic.r: The republic had a Revolutionary Executive Committee modelled on the Hungarian council and copied its nationalisation decrees. It depended entirely on Hungarian troops and found little support among Slovaks, who largely saw it as a Hungarian attempt to reclaim the region.
slovak-soviet-republic.e: Under Allied pressure, the Hungarian Red Army withdrew from Slovakia at the end of June 1919, and Czechoslovak forces moved in; the republic collapsed by 7 July 1919. Slovakia remained part of [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]].

second-taifa-of-almeria.t: Almería's brief independence in the 1140s, ended when a Castilian, Genoese and Catalan crusade stormed the great port in 1147.
second-taifa-of-almeria.o: In 1145 the people of Almería, then the chief Andalusi port and naval base, rose against the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]]. Power passed to local leaders, notably the admiral Ibn Maymun, whose family had commanded the Almoravid fleet.
second-taifa-of-almeria.r: Almería remained a centre of [[e:silk|silk]] weaving and [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] trade, but also of corsair raiding against Christian shipping, which made it a target for [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]] and Pisa. Its new rulers had little time to establish a stable government.
second-taifa-of-almeria.e: In October 1147 Alfonso VII of [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], with Genoese, Pisan, Catalan and Navarrese forces, captured Almería after a siege, creating [[s:castilian-almeria|Castilian Almería]].

sanjeli-state.t: A minor chiefship in the forested hills of eastern Gujarat, one of the small estates of the Rewa Kantha country.
sanjeli-state.o: Sanjeli was a small estate in the hills of eastern [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], near the border with [[e:malwa|Malwa]], held by a local chiefly family from around 1600. Its founding is poorly documented.
sanjeli-state.r: The ruler governed a few villages with a largely Bhil population and, in the British period, came under the Rewa Kantha Agency. Standard references record little else.
sanjeli-state.e: Sanjeli was merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present Dahod district.

cr.a: Goran tek-en, following request by Nizil Shah

sabirs.t: A powerful nomad people of the North Caucasus steppe who served as mercenaries for both Byzantium and Persia in the 6th century.
sabirs.o: The Sabirs moved west from the steppes of Western [[e:siberia|Siberia]] around 463, when, according to Priscus, they were pushed by the [[e:avars|Avars]] and in turn drove the Saragurs, Urogs and [[s:onogurs|Onogurs]] towards the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]]. By the early 6th century they were settled north of the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] between the Caspian and the Kuban.
sabirs.r: Byzantine authors such as Procopius describe them as numerous and warlike, ruled by several chiefs, and skilled in siege engineering. In 515 they raided [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[s:kingdom-of-cappadocia|Cappadocia]], and they hired themselves to both Justinian and the Sasanian kings in the wars over [[s:kingdom-of-lazica|Lazica]]. Their queen Boa, a widow ruling 100,000 people, allied with Justinian around 527.
sabirs.e: The [[e:avars|Avars]] defeated the Sabirs in the late 550s, and the Turkic Khaganate subdued the remainder in 576. Their people merged into the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]] and [[e:bulgars|Bulgar]] peoples; some are recorded settled in Byzantine and Caucasian territory.

simurrum.t: A Bronze Age kingdom in the Zagros foothills east of the Tigris, repeatedly attacked by the kings of Akkad and Ur and known from its rulers' rock reliefs.
simurrum.o: Simurrum lay on the routes between [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]] and the Iranian highlands, probably near the Lesser Zab or the Sirwan (upper Diyala); its capital has not been securely located. It appears in year names and inscriptions of the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]], whose kings [[e:sargon-of-akkad|Sargon]] and [[e:naram-sin|Naram-Sin]] campaigned against it.
simurrum.r: Little is known of its internal life. It was a Hurrian-influenced hill kingdom with fortified towns controlling trade in metals, [[e:timber|timber]] and horses. [[e:shulgi|Shulgi]] of the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]] boasted of destroying Simurrum several times. A local king, Iddin-Sin, and his son Zabazuna left Akkadian inscriptions and a rock relief showing their victories over the [[s:lullubi|Lullubi]], revealing a brief period of independent power around 2000 BCE.
simurrum.e: Simurrum disappears from the record in the 18th century BCE, when the region fell under [[s:eshnunna|Eshnunna]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-upper-mesopotamia|Kingdom of Upper Mesopotamia]] of Shamshi-Adad.

sugambri.t: A warlike Germanic people of the lower Rhine who repeatedly defied Rome until Augustus deported much of the tribe across the river into Gaul.
sugambri.o: The Sugambri lived on the east bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] between the Sieg and the Lippe. They first appear in 55 BCE, when they sheltered survivors of the Usipetes and [[s:tencteri|Tencteri]]; [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] bridged the Rhine and ravaged their land in retaliation.
sugambri.r: Little is known of their internal organisation beyond war-leaders and a reputation for raiding. In 16 BCE they crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] with the Usipetes and [[s:tencteri|Tencteri]] and defeated the Roman legate Marcus Lollius, capturing the eagle of the Fifth [[e:legion|Legion]], an event known as the clades Lolliana. This defeat helped prompt Augustus' German campaigns.
sugambri.e: Drusus attacked them from 12 BCE, and in 8 BCE Tiberius forcibly resettled tens of thousands on the left bank of the [[e:rhine|Rhine]], where they became the Cugerni. Those who stayed merged into later groups, and the name was later absorbed into the [[s:franks|Frankish confederation]]; Frankish kings were poetically called Sicambri.

siak-sultanate.t: Riau sultanate founded by the adventurer Raja Kecil, once master of the east Sumatran coast and later a model of royal patriotism.
siak-sultanate.o: Raja Kecil, a Minangkabau-backed claimant who said he was the posthumous son of [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mahmud II of [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor]], seized the Johor Sultanate in 1718. Driven out by Bugis allies of the [[e:johor|Johor]] nobility in 1722, he withdrew to the Siak river in [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]] and founded a new sultanate at Buantan in 1723.
siak-sultanate.r: Siak controlled the trade of the Siak river, exporting [[e:timber|timber]], [[e:pepper|pepper]], gold and forest products, and in the 18th century extended its overlordship over the [[s:deli-sultanate|Deli Sultanate]] and other coastal states. Arab-descended sultans of the Syarif line ruled from 1791. The court moved to Siak Sri Indrapura, where the Asserayah Hasyimiah palace was built in 1889.
siak-sultanate.e: A treaty of 1858 made Siak a [[e:dutch|Dutch]] protected state. In 1945 its last sultan, Syarif Kasim II, declared support for the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] and gave it his treasury; the sultanate was merged into the republic in 1946, and he was named a national hero.

souliote-confederacy.t: Self-governing community of Orthodox warrior clans in the mountains of Epirus, famous for resisting Ali Pasha of Ioannina for over a decade.
souliote-confederacy.o: Souli was a group of villages in the rugged mountains of Thesprotia in Epirus. From the mid-17th century [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] Christian families, mainly Albanian-speaking, settled there and built a free community outside effective Ottoman control, growing into a confederation of villages such as Souli, Kiafa, Avariko and Samoniva.
souliote-confederacy.r: Souliote society was organised in clans (fares), each with its own leader; a council of chiefs decided on war. Men were full-time warriors who lived from herding and from tribute imposed on surrounding villages; women also fought. Leading families included the Botsaris and Tzavelas. The Souliotes spoke Albanian and Greek and were [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]].
souliote-confederacy.e: Ali Pasha of Ioannina attacked repeatedly from 1792 and finally forced their surrender in December 1803. Many Souliotes went to [[s:corcyra|Corfu]], while women reportedly threw themselves from the cliffs at Zalongo. They returned to fight in the [[e:greek-war-of-independence|Greek War of Independence]] under Markos Botsaris.

sukkalmah-dynasty.t: The long-lived dynasty of 'grand regents' that ruled Elam from Susa for nearly five centuries, at its height a great power in Hammurabi's world.
sukkalmah-dynasty.o: Around 1970 BCE Ebarat (Eparti), possibly the last of the [[s:shimashki-dynasty|Shimashki]] kings, founded a new royal line in [[e:elam|Elam]]. His successors took the title [[e:sukkalmah|sukkalmah]], 'grand regent', a term borrowed from Sumerian administration, and ruled from [[e:susa|Susa]] over lowland Khuzestan and the highlands of [[s:kingdom-of-anshan|Anshan]].
sukkalmah-dynasty.r: Power was shared in a distinctive system: the [[e:sukkalmah|sukkalmah]] ruled as overlord, a '[[e:sukkal|sukkal]] of [[e:elam|Elam]] and [[e:shimashki-dynasty|Shimashki]]' acted as his deputy, and a 'sukkal of [[e:susa|Susa]]' governed the city, with succession often passing between brothers and nephews claimed as 'sons of the sister'. Susa produced legal contracts in Akkadian alongside Elamite cults of Inshushinak and Humban. Under Siwe-palar-huppak, in the 1760s BCE, Elam intervened deep in [[e:mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]], took [[s:eshnunna|Eshnunna]] and was courted by [[s:mari|Mari]] and [[e:babylon|Babylon]].
sukkalmah-dynasty.e: A coalition led by [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]] of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] drove the [[e:elamites|Elamites]] back in 1764 BCE. The dynasty survived, but sources thin out after the 17th century BCE, and by about 1500 BCE it gave way to the kings of the [[s:middle-elamite-kingdom|Middle Elamite kingdom]].

state-of-ba.t: The kingdom of the Ba warriors in the Three Gorges and Chongqing region, famed for salt springs and war dances, conquered by Qin with its neighbour Shu in 316 BCE.
state-of-ba.o: The Ba were peoples of the eastern [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] basin and the Three Gorges of the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]]. Tradition says their warriors fought alongside King Wu of Zhou against the [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]], singing and dancing as they advanced. A state led by a royal Ba lineage took shape in the 1st millennium BCE, its centre eventually at Jiangzhou in modern Chongqing.
state-of-ba.r: Ba controlled valuable brine springs and salt production along the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]], which gave it wealth and influence over trade with the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]]. Its elite were buried in boat-shaped coffins and used distinctive willow-leaf bronze swords marked with Ba-Shu symbols that remain undeciphered. Relations with Chu alternated between alliance and war.
state-of-ba.e: Fighting between Ba and [[s:ancient-shu|Ancient Shu]] gave the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] its opportunity: in 316 BCE [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] armies conquered both and captured the king of Ba. Qin made the area Ba [[e:commandery|Commandery]], while Ba elites kept local privileges. The name survives in the traditional term Ba-Shu for [[e:sichuan|Sichuan]] and Chongqing culture.

state-of-xu-huaiyi.t: The leading Huaiyi state of the lower Huai River, whose rulers called themselves kings and challenged the Zhou, before Wu destroyed it in 512 BCE.
state-of-xu-huaiyi.o: Xu was ruled by a lineage of the Ying clan among the Huaiyi peoples of northern Jiangsu and Anhui, with its centre near modern Sihong. It resisted the Zhou from the early [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]], and bronze inscriptions record royal campaigns against the Huaiyi and Xu.
state-of-xu-huaiyi.r: Unlike most Zhou states, Xu's rulers used the title of king, and inscribed bronzes of the 'kings of Xu' have been found across the Huai and [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] region. Later tradition celebrated King Yan of Xu as a benevolent ruler who gave up war rather than see his people suffer. Xu was a cultural bridge between the Central Plain and the emerging states of the south-east.
state-of-xu-huaiyi.e: Squeezed between Chu and the rising [[s:state-of-wu|State of Wu]], Xu was conquered by King Helü of Wu in 512 BCE, and its ruler fled to Chu. Xu culture influenced the bronze art of Wu and Yue, and the surname Xu is traced to the state.

state-of-brazil.t: The Portuguese royal government of Brazil set up at Salvador in 1549, which united the captaincies under a governor-general and later a viceroy.
state-of-brazil.o: The hereditary captaincies of 1534 had largely failed, so King John III created a central government in 1549. [[e:tome-de-sousa|Tomé de Sousa]] arrived as the first governor-general with soldiers, officials and the first [[e:jesuits|Jesuits]] under Manuel da Nóbrega, and founded [[e:salvador|Salvador]] on the Bay of All Saints as capital.
state-of-brazil.r: The governor-general oversaw defence, justice and finance, while the captaincies kept their own governors. Mem de Sá expelled the French from [[s:france-antarctique|France Antarctique]] and founded [[e:rio-de-janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]]. In 1621 the north was separated as the [[s:state-of-maranhao|State of Maranhão]], reporting directly to [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]]. From the 1640s governors often held the title of [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]]. A High Court, the Relação, sat at [[e:salvador|Salvador]] from 1609. The capital moved to Rio de Janeiro in 1763.
state-of-brazil.e: After the Portuguese court moved to [[e:rio-de-janeiro|Rio de Janeiro]] in 1808, the colonial government was overshadowed by the monarchy itself. In 1815 the State of [[s:new-republic-brazil|Brazil]] was raised to the [[s:kingdom-of-brazil|Kingdom of Brazil]].

sheikhdom-of-bushehr.t: An Arab-ruled port state on the Persian Gulf coast, under the Al Madhkur sheikhs, that became Iran's main harbour and briefly held Bahrain.
sheikhdom-of-bushehr.o: [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah]] developed [[e:bushehr|Bushehr]] as a naval base in the 1730s. After his death in 1747, the Al Madhkur, an Arab family settled on the Persian coast, ruled the port as hereditary sheikhs. Sheikh Nasir Al Madhkur extended their power across the Gulf, taking [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] in 1753.
sheikhdom-of-bushehr.r: [[e:bushehr|Bushehr]] became the main port of southern [[e:iran|Iran]], linking [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] with [[e:india|India]] and the Gulf. In 1763 [[e:karim-khan-zand|Karim Khan]] of the [[s:zand-empire|Zand Empire]] and the sheikh allowed the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] to open a factory there, and it later became the seat of the British Political Resident in the Gulf. The sheikhs combined trade, customs revenue and a small fleet, paying tribute to the Zand and later [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] rulers.
sheikhdom-of-bushehr.e: The Al Madhkur lost [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] to the Al [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]] in 1783. Under [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]] their authority was steadily reduced, and by about 1850 [[e:bushehr|Bushehr]] was governed by appointed officials.

sarbadars.t: A rebel regime in western Khurasan, born of a revolt against Mongol tax collectors, that ruled through a mix of military leaders and Shia dervishes.
sarbadars.o: In the 1330s, as the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]] disintegrated, villagers at Bashtin near Sabzevar rose against abusive Mongol officials. Their leaders took the name sarbadar, 'head on the gallows', meaning they would rather die than submit. Under Abd al-Razzaq and his brother Wajih al-Din Mas'ud they took Sabzevar and built a state in western Khurasan.
sarbadars.r: The Sarbadars had no hereditary dynasty: power passed among military chiefs, often violently, and alongside them stood the Shaykhiyya, a [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] [[e:sufism|Sufi]] movement founded by Shaykh [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]] and Shaykh Hasan Juri, whose dervishes expected the coming of the [[e:mahdi|Mahdi]]. The state minted coins with Shia formulas and defeated the Mongol claimant Togha Temür. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] described their egalitarian, puritanical regime.
sarbadars.e: The last leader, Ali-yi Mu'ayyad, submitted to [[e:timur|Timur]] in 1381 and died in his service in 1386, after which the Sarbadar lands joined the [[s:timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]]. Historians see them as an early [[e:shia-islam|Shia]] state in [[e:iran|Iran]].

second-taifa-of-murcia.t: The kingdom of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King, who ruled eastern al-Andalus for 25 years in alliance with Christian powers against the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-murcia.o: Muhammad ibn Mardanish, of a family of Muwallad origin from the [[e:valencia|Valencia]] region, took power in [[e:murcia|Murcia]] in 1147 amid the collapse of the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]], soon adding Valencia, Jaén, Dénia and other eastern towns to his domains.
second-taifa-of-murcia.r: Known to Christians as Rey Lobo, he made treaties with [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]], Barcelona, [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]] and Pisa, hired Christian [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] and minted gold coins widely used in Christian [[e:iberia|Iberia]]. He built palaces such as the Castillejo de Monteagudo near [[e:murcia|Murcia]] and kept a sophisticated court while fighting the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]].
second-taifa-of-murcia.e: After losing allies and territory, Ibn Mardanish died in 1172, and his sons submitted to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]], who married into his family. [[e:murcia|Murcia]] later revived as the [[s:third-taifa-of-murcia|Third Taifa of Murcia]].

serdang-sultanate.t: Malay sultanate of eastern Sumatra that split from Deli in 1723 and shared in the plantation wealth of the colonial era.
serdang-sultanate.o: Serdang arose from a succession dispute in the [[s:deli-sultanate|Deli Sultanate]] after the death of Tuanku Panglima Paderap around 1723. One of his sons, Tuanku Umar Johan Alamsyah, was passed over and withdrew with local support to found a separate realm on the Serdang river, south-east of Deli.
serdang-sultanate.r: The sultans ruled Malay coastal communities and drew tribute from neighbouring Karo and Simalungun Batak lands. Like Deli, Serdang came under [[e:dutch|Dutch]] control in the 1860s and leased land for tobacco and [[e:rubber|rubber]] estates. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Sulaiman Shariful Alamshah, who reigned from 1881 to 1946, was known as a patron of Malay arts and education.
serdang-sultanate.e: Serdang survived as a self-governing domain of the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]] until the East Sumatran social revolution of March 1946, when the Malay aristocracy lost its power and the sultanate was absorbed into the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]].

salian-franks.t: Frankish group settled in Toxandria by Rome in 358, whose kings at Tournai founded the Merovingian dynasty.
salian-franks.o: The Salians were one of the Frankish peoples living near the lower [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. In 358 the Caesar Julian forced the submission of those who had settled in Toxandria, in the modern Kempen, and let them remain as allies of the [[s:roman-empire|Roman Empire]]. Over the next century they moved south-west towards the Scheldt.
salian-franks.r: Their kings served [[e:rome|Rome]] as federate commanders. Around the 440s King Chlodio took [[s:prince-bishopric-of-cambrai|Cambrai]] and the land up to the [[e:battle-of-the-somme|Somme]]. The Lex Salica, written down under [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]], preserves their customary law, including the rule later used to bar women from the French throne.
salian-franks.e: Childeric I, traditionally the son of Merovech, ruled from Tournai and fought for [[e:rome|Rome]] on the Loire; his rich tomb, found in 1653, held a signet ring and gold bees. On his death in 481 his son [[e:clovis-i|Clovis]] began the conquests that created the [[s:kingdom-of-the-franks|Kingdom of the Franks]].

serbia.t: Present-day Serbia, independent successor of the Yugoslav states since 2006, an EU candidate that does not recognise Kosovo's independence.
serbia.o: When [[s:montenegro|Montenegro]] voted to leave [[s:serbia-and-montenegro|Serbia and Montenegro]] in 2006, Serbia became the legal successor of the union and of the earlier [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslav states]] on 5 June 2006. A new constitution adopted in October 2006 described Kosovo, then under [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] administration, as an integral part of Serbia.
serbia.r: Serbia is a parliamentary republic with a directly elected president. Kosovo declared independence in 2008, which Serbia rejects, though the EU-brokered Brussels Agreement of 2013 began a normalisation of relations. Aleksandar Vučić's Serbian Progressive Party has dominated politics since 2012, combining EU accession talks with close ties to [[e:russia|Russia]] and [[e:china|China]]. Manufacturing, agriculture and IT drive the economy.
serbia.e: Serbia became an EU candidate in 2012 and opened accession negotiations in 2014. The collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed sixteen people, led to the largest student-led protests in decades against corruption and Vučić's government.

santones.t: Gallic people of Saintonge on the Atlantic coast, whose land was the goal of the Helvetian migration of 58 BCE.
santones.o: The Santones lived north of the Gironde estuary, along the Charente, in the modern Charente-Maritime. Caesar records that the [[s:helvetii|Helvetii]] planned to settle in their land, which alarmed him because it lay close to the Roman Province.
santones.r: Their coast gave them ships and seamen, which Caesar requisitioned in 56 BCE for the war against the [[s:veneti|Veneti]]. They struck coins in large numbers and traded salt and goods along the Atlantic.
santones.e: They joined the revolt of 52 BCE with twelve thousand men. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] Mediolanum Santonum (Saintes) became the first capital of Aquitania, with the Arch of Germanicus and a large amphitheatre. The region kept their name as Saintonge.

sur-empire.t: The Afghan empire of Sher Shah Suri, who drove the Mughals out of India and built roads, coinage and administration that outlived him.
sur-empire.o: Farid Khan, an Afghan noble of the Sur clan in Bihar, earned the title Sher Khan and gathered power in eastern [[e:india|India]]. He defeated the Mughal emperor Humayun at Chausa in 1539 and Kannauj in 1540, drove him into exile and proclaimed himself Sher Shah, ruling from [[e:delhi|Delhi]] over north India.
sur-empire.r: Sher Shah reorganised revenue on measured land, introduced the [[e:silver|silver]] [[e:rupiya|rupiya]] that gave the [[e:rupee|rupee]] its name, built the Grand Trunk Road from [[e:bengal|Bengal]] to the [[e:punjab|Punjab]] with [[e:caravanserai|caravanserais]] and a postal service, and built the Rohtas Fort and the Purana Qila. His son [[e:islam|Islam]] Shah continued centralised rule, while Hemu, a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] general, served his successors.
sur-empire.e: Sher Shah died in an explosion at the siege of Kalinjar in 1545. After [[e:islam|Islam]] Shah's death in 1554 the empire split among rival claimants. Humayun returned in 1555, and [[e:akbar|Akbar's]] victory at the Second Battle of Panipat in 1556 restored the [[s:mughal-empire|Mughal Empire]].

sotiates.t: Aquitanian people of the Sos district whose king Adiatuanus made a last stand against Rome with six hundred sworn companions.
sotiates.o: The Sotiates were one of the Aquitani, living around the oppidum of Sos in the modern Lot-et-Garonne, north of the Pyrenean foothills. They are known almost entirely from Caesar's account of the campaign of his legate Publius [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Crassus]] in 56 BCE.
sotiates.r: Caesar describes their king Adiatuanus surrounded by six hundred soldurii, sworn companions who vowed to share their lord's fate and never survive him. Coins inscribed with the names of the Sotiates and of Adiatuanus confirm the account.
sotiates.e: [[e:marcus-licinius-crassus|Crassus]] defeated the Sotiates in open battle and besieged their oppidum; the defenders, skilled from their [[e:copper|copper]] mines, tried in vain to undermine the Roman siege works. After a failed sortie Adiatuanus surrendered. Their land later formed part of the Roman province of Aquitania.

sawangkhaburi-regime.t: A northern Siamese regime led by a militant monk, Chao Phra Fang, which ruled from Sawangkhaburi after Ayutthaya fell.
sawangkhaburi-regime.o: After the fall of the [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya Kingdom]] in 1767, a senior monk known as Chao Phra Fang, formerly abbot in Fang (Sawangkhaburi, near Uttaradit), gathered followers and established his own regime in the upper Nan river region, retaining his monk's robes while exercising political power.
sawangkhaburi-regime.r: The regime was unusual in being led by monks: Chao Phra Fang and senior monks among his followers held both religious and military authority. In 1768 it absorbed the [[s:phitsanulok-regime|Phitsanulok regime]] after the death of its ruler. Its power rested on control of northern [[e:rice|rice]] lands and the loyalty of local troops.
sawangkhaburi-regime.e: In 1770 Taksin of the [[s:thonburi-kingdom|Thonburi Kingdom]] marched north and captured Sawangkhaburi. Chao Phra Fang fled and disappeared. Taksin then purged and reformed the northern sangha, re-ordaining monks whose conduct was doubted.

second-dominican-republic.t: The restored Dominican state of 1865 to 1916, marked by caudillo rule, Ulises Heureaux's dictatorship, a sugar boom and mounting debt to foreign creditors.
second-dominican-republic.o: The War of Restoration ended Spanish rule in 1865, re-establishing Dominican independence. The victorious generals and rival parties, the Reds of Buenaventura Báez and the Blues led by Gregorio Luperón, fought for power in a long series of revolts.
second-dominican-republic.r: Báez's six-year rule of 1868 to 1874 negotiated annexation to the [[s:united-states|United States]], which President Grant supported but the US Senate rejected in 1870. Ulises Heureaux dominated from 1882, ruling as dictator from 1887 until his assassination in 1899. Cuban and American investors built [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] mills in the southeast, and railways linked the Cibao to the coast. Heureaux's borrowing left huge foreign debts, and in 1905 the [[e:united-states|United States]] took control of Dominican customs to pay creditors.
second-dominican-republic.e: President Ramón Cáceres was assassinated in 1911, and renewed civil strife followed. In 1916 the [[s:united-states|United States]] landed Marines and installed the [[s:military-government-of-santo-domingo|Military Government of Santo Domingo]].

shirvanshah-state.t: A Muslim dynasty that ruled Shirvan on the Caspian coast for nearly seven centuries, patrons of Persian poets and builders of the Palace of the Shirvanshahs in Baku.
shirvanshah-state.o: In 861, as Abbasid control weakened, the governor Haytham ibn Khalid, from the Arab Yazidid family, declared himself Shirvanshah. Using the old Persian title, the family turned the province between the Kura and the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] mountains into a hereditary state with its capital at Shamakhi.
shirvanshah-state.r: The Shirvanshahs became thoroughly Persianised and ruled a land of [[e:silk|silk]], oil and Caspian trade. Their courts hosted the poets Khaqani and Nizami Ganjavi. They survived by paying tribute to stronger powers, from the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] and [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]] to the [[e:mongols|Mongols]]. From 1382 the Derbendi line under Ibrahim I revived the state, and Khalilullah I built the [[e:baku|Baku]] palace complex.
shirvanshah-state.e: Shah [[e:ismail-i|Ismail I]] of Safavid [[e:iran|Iran]] defeated and killed Farrukh Yasar in 1500 to avenge his father. The weakened dynasty lingered as [[e:vassal|vassals]] until 1538, when Tahmasp I annexed Shirvan to the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]].
