state-of-qi-kai.t: The small Zhou state where the descendants of the Xia kings kept up their ancestral sacrifices, remembered in the idiom about the man of Qi who feared the sky would fall.
state-of-qi-kai.o: After the conquest of the [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]], King Wu of Zhou sought out descendants of the Xia royal house and enfeoffed Donglou, of the Si clan, at Yongqiu (modern Qi County, Henan), so that sacrifices to Yu the Great would continue. The name is often written Kai in English to distinguish it from the great [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]].
state-of-qi-kai.r: Qi was weak and repeatedly moved, eventually relocating east into Shandong under pressure from stronger neighbours. Its rulers held the rank of duke or earl but depended on alliances. Confucius complained that Qi preserved too few records to confirm the rites of the Xia, and the Liezi made a man of Qi the proverbial worrier who feared that heaven would collapse.
state-of-qi-kai.e: The [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] annexed Qi in 445 BCE as it expanded into the lands between the Huai and the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]]. Its main legacy is symbolic: it embodied the Zhou practice of preserving defeated royal lines, and its name survives in the Chinese idiom for needless anxiety.

state-of-jiang.t: A small Ying-clan state on the upper Huai River that allied with Qi against Chu and was destroyed by Chu in 623 BCE.
state-of-jiang.o: Jiang was ruled by the Ying clan, which claimed descent from Boyi, an adviser of Yu the Great. It lay near modern Zhengyang in southern Henan, among several small Huai River states recognised by the Zhou.
state-of-jiang.r: Almost nothing is recorded of its government. Jiang appears in the Zuo zhuan when, with the [[s:state-of-huang|State of Huang]], it joined the covenant led by Duke Huan of Qi in the 650s BCE, a gesture of defiance towards the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]], its powerful southern neighbour.
state-of-jiang.e: Once Qi's protection faded, Chu took revenge. King Mu of Chu destroyed Jiang in 623 BCE, and Duke Mu of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] was said to have worn mourning for it. The surname Jiang is traditionally traced to its people.

samudera-pasai-sultanate.t: The first securely dated Muslim kingdom of Southeast Asia, a pepper port in northern Sumatra visited by Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta.
samudera-pasai-sultanate.o: Samudera Pasai arose on the north coast of [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]], near modern Lhokseumawe, in the late 13th century. Its first Muslim ruler, [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Malik al-[[s:salihids|Salih]], is known from his tombstone dated 1297, and the Hikayat Raja Pasai tells of his conversion. [[e:marco-polo|Marco Polo]] stopped at Samara in 1292. It later absorbed neighbouring [[s:peureulak-sultanate|Peureulak]].
samudera-pasai-sultanate.r: Pasai exported [[e:pepper|pepper]], [[e:silk|silk]] and [[e:camphor|camphor]] and issued gold coins, among the earliest in the region. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] visited in 1345 and praised [[e:sultan|Sultan]] al-Malik al-Zahir as a learned [[e:shafii-school|Shafi'i]] ruler who debated with scholars. Pasai became a centre from which [[e:islam|Islam]] and Malay letters spread across the archipelago.
samudera-pasai-sultanate.e: Pasai was raided by [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] around 1350 and later overshadowed by [[e:malacca|Malacca]]. The Portuguese seized it in 1521, and the [[s:aceh-sultanate|Aceh Sultanate]] conquered it in 1524. Its tombstones, carved in [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]], remain important early evidence of [[e:islam|Islam]] in [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]].

sexi.t: A Phoenician colony at Almuñécar on Spain's southern coast, known for its rich tombs and for salted fish exported across the Mediterranean.
sexi.o: Sexi was founded by [[e:phoenicians|Phoenicians]] in the 8th century BCE on the headland of modern Almuñécar, in [[e:granada|Granada]] province. It formed part of the string of Phoenician harbours along the Andalusian coast, between [[s:malaka|Malaka]] and [[s:abdera|Abdera]].
sexi.r: Its Laurita necropolis has yielded Egyptian alabaster vases reused as burial urns, evidence of the colonists' wide contacts. The city's economy rested on trade and on fish salting, and its later Punic-legend coins carried tuna, the source of its wealth. Its government is not recorded.
sexi.e: With the Roman conquest of the south after 206 BCE, Sexi passed under Roman control. It kept its fish-salting industry and became the Roman town of Firmum Iulium Sexi, ancestor of modern Almuñécar.

state-of-the-presidi.t: A string of Spanish-held fortresses on the Tuscan coast that let Spain and later Naples watch over central Italy for nearly 250 years.
state-of-the-presidi.o: When [[e:philip-ii-of-spain|Philip II of Spain]] granted the conquered [[s:republic-of-siena|Republic of Siena]] to Cosimo I de' Medici in 1557, he kept the coastal fortresses of Orbetello, Porto Ercole, Talamone, Porto Santo Stefano and Ansedonia. Porto Longone on Elba was added in 1603.
state-of-the-presidi.r: The Presidi, meaning garrisons, were run as a military district under the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] of the [[s:kingdom-of-naples|Kingdom of Naples]]. Their purpose was strategic: to secure Spanish sea routes between Naples, [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]] and Barcelona and to watch the [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Grand Duchy of Tuscany]]. [[e:spain|Spain]] built powerful fortifications at Porto Ercole and Orbetello. The painter Caravaggio died at Porto Ercole in 1610.
state-of-the-presidi.e: The Presidi passed with Naples to [[e:austria|Austria]] in 1707 and to the [[e:house-of-bourbon|Bourbons]] in 1735. In 1801 the Treaty of [[s:duchy-of-florence|Florence]] ceded them to [[e:france|France]], which joined them to the [[s:kingdom-of-etruria|Kingdom of Etruria]]; after 1815 they became part of [[s:grand-duchy-of-tuscany|Tuscany]].

sulaymanid-emirate.t: A small Alid dynasty related to the Idrisids that ruled Tlemcen and western Algeria in the 9th and 10th centuries.
sulaymanid-emirate.o: Sulayman ibn Abd Allah was a brother of Idris I, founder of the [[s:idrisid-dynasty|Idrisid dynasty]]. Around 814 Idris II granted [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]] to Sulayman's son Muhammad, establishing a branch dynasty, the Sulaymanids, which ruled the city and surrounding region, formerly held by the [[s:banu-ifran-emirate|Banu Ifran emirate]].
sulaymanid-emirate.r: Little is known in detail. The [[e:emirate|emirate]] was divided among family members, who ruled towns such as [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]], Arshgul and Ténès, relying on local Zenata [[e:berbers|Berber]] tribes. Like the [[s:idrisid-dynasty|Idrisids]], the Sulaymanids drew prestige from descent from the Prophet's family, and Tlemcen prospered as a crossroads of trade routes between [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], [[e:ifriqiya|Ifriqiya]] and the [[e:sahara|Sahara]].
sulaymanid-emirate.e: In the early 10th century the Sulaymanid princes were caught in the struggle between the [[s:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate]] and the [[s:caliphate-of-cordoba|Caliphate of Córdoba]]. Fatimid forces ended their rule around 931, and several family members fled to [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]].

swedish-pomerania.t: Baltic territory held by the Swedish crown for nearly two centuries, giving Sweden a foothold and a vote in the Holy Roman Empire.
swedish-pomerania.o: [[e:gustavus-adolphus|Gustavus Adolphus]] landed in [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] in 1630 and occupied the duchy during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]]. When the last Pomeranian duke died in 1637, [[e:sweden|Sweden]] kept control, and the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 granted it [[e:pomerania|Western Pomerania]] with Stettin, Stralsund and the island of [[s:principality-of-rugen|Rügen]], held as an imperial fief.
swedish-pomerania.r: The Swedish king sat in the [[e:imperial-diet|Imperial Diet]] as Duke of [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]], but the territory kept its own estates and German law. Greifswald University continued as a centre of learning. [[e:sweden|Sweden]] lost Stettin and the lands south of the Peene to [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1720, and Stralsund became the seat of government. [[e:serfdom|Serfdom]] was abolished in 1806 under Gustav IV Adolf.
swedish-pomerania.e: Under the Treaty of [[e:kiel|Kiel]] in 1814 [[e:sweden|Sweden]] ceded [[s:duchy-of-pomerania|Pomerania]] to [[e:denmark|Denmark]], which exchanged it with [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in 1815 for Saxe-Lauenburg and money. It became part of the Prussian Province of [[e:pomerania|Pomerania]]; Swedish influence survives in Stralsund's architecture.

saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla.t: British colony joining Saint Kitts, Nevis and Anguilla from 1882, an uneasy union that broke apart when Anguilla rebelled in 1967.
saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla.o: To cut administrative costs after the decline of [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] merged the separate presidencies of [[s:saint-kitts-and-nevis|Saint Kitts and Nevis]], with Anguilla, into a single colony in 1882, governed from Basseterre within the Leeward Islands federal colony. Nevisians and Anguillians resented the loss of their own institutions to the larger island.
saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla.r: [[s:colony-of-saint-christopher|Saint Kitts]] remained a [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] island, its estates consolidated into a central factory after 1912, while [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]] and Anguilla turned to small farming, fishing and emigration. A sugar strike in 1935 helped launch the labour movement, later led by Robert Bradshaw, whose Labour Party dominated politics. The colony joined the [[s:west-indies-federation|West Indies Federation]] in 1958 and became an Associated State with internal self-government in 1967.
saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla.e: Anguillians rejected rule from Basseterre and declared the [[s:republic-of-anguilla|Republic of Anguilla]] in 1967; [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] intervened in 1969, and Anguilla was formally separated in 1980. The remaining islands became independent as [[s:saint-kitts-and-nevis|Saint Kitts and Nevis]] on 19 September 1983, under Prime Minister Kennedy Simmonds.

sheikhdom-of-bahrain.t: Bahrain under the Al Khalifa and British protection, where the first oil on the Arab side of the Gulf was struck in 1932.
sheikhdom-of-bahrain.o: The Al [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]], a clan of the Bani Utbah settled at Zubarah in [[s:sheikhdom-of-qatar|Qatar]], crossed to [[s:state-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] in 1783 and drove out the Al Madhkur governor, who ruled for Persian-backed [[e:bushehr|Bushehr]]. Ahmad ibn Muhammad Al Khalifa, known as al-Fateh, the Conqueror, became the first ruler of the islands.
sheikhdom-of-bahrain.r: [[s:state-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] lived on pearling, date farming and trade, with Manama as its port. Its [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] ruling family governed a population that was largely [[e:shia-islam-idea|Shi'a]]. Treaties with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from 1820, culminating in the exclusive agreements of 1880 and 1892, made it a protected state. Under Isa bin Ali and the British adviser Charles Belgrave, from 1926, reforms created courts, schools and a modern administration. Oil was struck in 1932.
sheikhdom-of-bahrain.e: [[e:iran|Iran]] long claimed [[s:state-of-bahrain|Bahrain]], but a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] survey in 1970 found the people wanted independence. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ended its protection and the State of [[e:bahrain|Bahrain]] became independent in August 1971 under Isa bin Salman Al [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]].

state-of-burma.t: The Japanese-sponsored Burmese state of 1943 to 1945, led by Ba Maw, whose army under Aung San eventually turned against Japan.
state-of-burma.o: [[e:japan|Japan]] invaded [[s:british-burma|British Burma]] in 1942 with the help of the [[s:myanmar|Burma]] Independence Army, formed by Aung San and the Thirty Comrades. On 1 August 1943 Japan granted nominal independence, and Ba Maw, a pre-war premier, became head of state, or Adipadi, of the State of [[e:burma|Burma]], which declared war on [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]].
state-of-burma.r: Ba Maw governed from Rangoon with a cabinet including Aung San as war minister and Thakin Nu as foreign minister, but the Japanese army controlled the economy and military affairs. Forced labour, notably on the Burma-[[e:thailand|Thailand]] Railway, requisitioning and [[e:inflation|inflation]] brought hardship. The Shan and [[s:karenni-states|Karenni]] areas were partly handed to [[s:thailand|Thailand]].
state-of-burma.e: Disillusioned nationalists formed the Anti-Fascist Organisation, and in March 1945 the [[s:myanmar|Burma]] National Army rose against [[e:japan|Japan]]. British forces retook Rangoon in May 1945, ending the state; Ba Maw fled to Japan. Its leaders went on to negotiate independence in 1948.

saqqawist-emirate.t: The nine-month rule of Habibullah Kalakani, a Tajik rebel who seized Kabul from King Amanullah in 1929.
saqqawist-emirate.o: King Amanullah Khan's modernising reforms provoked tribal and religious revolts in late 1928. Habibullah Kalakani, a Tajik bandit leader from the Shomali plain north of [[e:kabul|Kabul]], known as Bacha-i Saqao, 'son of the water carrier', captured Kabul in January 1929, and Amanullah abdicated and fled.
saqqawist-emirate.r: Kalakani proclaimed himself emir as Habibullah II and reversed Amanullah's reforms, closing girls' schools and restoring religious law, with backing from conservative clergy. His regime controlled little beyond [[e:kabul|Kabul]] and the north and was unrecognised by most of the Pashtun tribes, who resented a non-Pashtun ruler.
saqqawist-emirate.e: Mohammad Nadir Khan, a former general, raised Pashtun tribes and took [[e:kabul|Kabul]] in October 1929. Kalakani was captured and executed in November, and [[e:nader-shah|Nadir Shah]] restored the [[s:kingdom-of-afghanistan|Kingdom of Afghanistan]]. Kalakani has been rehabilitated by some Tajik nationalists.

suessiones.t: Belgic people of the Aisne valley whose kings once ruled across Gaul and Britain, and who led the coalition against Caesar in 57 BCE.
suessiones.o: The Suessiones held fertile land along the Aisne, around Soissons. Caesar was told that within living memory their king Diviciacus had been the most powerful ruler in Gaul, holding sway over much of Belgic Gaul and over [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]].
suessiones.r: They shared laws and magistrates with their neighbours the [[s:remi|Remi]], and Caesar credits them with twelve fortified towns and fifty thousand warriors. Their king Galba was chosen to command the Belgic league in 57 BCE.
suessiones.e: After the league dispersed, Caesar besieged their oppidum of Noviodunum, and the Suessiones surrendered and were placed under the [[s:remi|Remi]]. Under [[e:rome|Rome]] their town Augusta Suessionum became Soissons, later capital of the [[s:domain-of-soissons|Domain of Soissons]] and of [[e:frankish-kingdom|Frankish kingdoms]].

second-taifa-of-malaga.t: Málaga under the Zirid prince Tamim, who broke away from his brother's kingdom of Granada until the Almoravids removed both.
second-taifa-of-malaga.o: When the Zirid king Badis of [[e:granada|Granada]] died in 1073, his grandsons divided his realm. Tamim ibn Buluggin received Málaga and ruled it as an independent [[e:taifa|taifa]], while his brother Abd Allah held the [[s:taifa-of-granada|Taifa of Granada]].
second-taifa-of-malaga.r: Tamim governed a prosperous port city producing [[e:silk|silk]], ceramics and dried fruit. The brothers quarrelled and fought over border towns, and both paid tribute to [[e:alfonso-vi-of-castile|Alfonso VI of Castile]]. Tamim joined the Almoravid campaign of 1086 but, like other [[e:taifa|taifa]] kings, was distrusted by their emir [[e:yusuf-ibn-tashfin|Yusuf ibn Tashfin]].
second-taifa-of-malaga.e: In 1090 the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] deposed both Tamim and Abd Allah. Tamim was exiled to the Sus in [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]]. Málaga became an Almoravid city and later re-emerged briefly as the [[s:third-taifa-of-malaga|Third Taifa of Málaga]].

state-of-yan.t: The northernmost of the great Zhou states, centred on Beijing, which nearly destroyed Qi in 284 BCE and sent the assassin Jing Ke against the King of Qin.
state-of-yan.o: Yan was granted after the Zhou conquest to the Duke of Shao, a senior royal kinsman, whose son took up the fief in the far north. Its capital Ji stood in the area of modern [[e:beijing|Beijing]]; the early Yan cemetery at Liulihe has yielded inscribed bronzes confirming the founding.
state-of-yan.r: Isolated on the frontier with the [[s:donghu|Donghu]] and other northern peoples, Yan stayed on the margins for centuries before becoming one of the seven Warring States. A disastrous abdication by King Kuai in 316 BCE provoked civil war and a Qi invasion. King Zhao rebuilt the state, recruited the general Yue Yi and in 284 BCE captured Linzi. Yan built long walls in the north, forerunners of the [[e:great-wall-of-china|Great Wall]].
state-of-yan.e: Crown Prince Dan's attempt to have Jing Ke assassinate the King of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] in 227 BCE provoked a Qin onslaught. Ji fell in 226 BCE and King Xi fled to Liaodong, where he was captured in 222 BCE. The name Yan remains a literary name for [[e:beijing|Beijing]].

sultanate-of-tadjoura.t: An Afar sultanate on the Gulf of Tadjoura that controlled caravan routes to the Ethiopian highlands and became part of French Djibouti.
sultanate-of-tadjoura.o: Tadjoura, one of the oldest towns of the [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]] coast, was the seat of an [[e:afar|Afar]] sultanate from at least the 16th century. Its rulers came from Afar clans of the region and drew their power from the port, which linked the [[e:red-sea|Red Sea]] with the interior.
sultanate-of-tadjoura.r: The sultan ruled with clan elders over pastoral [[e:afar|Afar]] communities. Tadjoura's wealth came from caravans bringing slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and salt from [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]] and [[e:harar|Harar]] to the coast, and from its role as a stopping place for Arab traders. [[e:islam|Islam]] was well established, and the sultans dealt with Ottoman, Egyptian and later European powers.
sultanate-of-tadjoura.e: In 1884 the sultan signed a treaty placing Tadjoura under French protection, and in 1896 it became part of [[s:french-somaliland|French Somaliland]]. The sultanate survives as a traditional office, and Tadjoura remains a regional capital of [[s:djibouti|Djibouti]].

shu-han.t: The Three Kingdoms state of Liu Bei and Zhuge Liang in Sichuan, which claimed to continue the Han dynasty and became the heroic centre of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
shu-han.o: Liu Bei, a distant Han kinsman, allied with Sun Quan to defeat [[e:cao-cao|Cao Cao]] at Red Cliffs in 208, then took Yi province ([[e:sichuan|Sichuan]]) in 214 and Hanzhong in 219. After [[e:cao-pi|Cao Pi]] ended the Han in 220, Liu Bei proclaimed himself emperor at Chengdu in 221, presenting his state as the legitimate Han.
shu-han.r: Liu Bei's attack on [[s:eastern-wu|Eastern Wu]] ended in disaster at Yiling in 222, and he died in 223. The chancellor Zhuge [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]] governed for his son Liu Shan, with strict law, irrigation works and salt and iron monopolies. He pacified the Nanzhong south in 225 and led five northern expeditions against [[s:cao-wei|Cao Wei]], dying at Wuzhang Plains in 234.
shu-han.e: Jiang Wei continued the northern campaigns, exhausting the state. In 263 the Wei general Deng Ai crossed the mountains to Chengdu and Liu Shan surrendered. The later novel Romance of the [[e:three-kingdoms-period|Three Kingdoms]] made Liu Bei, Guan Yu, Zhang Fei and Zhuge [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]] lasting heroes.

state-of-vietnam.t: The French-sponsored Vietnamese state of former emperor Bao Dai, created in 1949 as a non-communist rival to Ho Chi Minh's government.
state-of-vietnam.o: By the Elysee Accords of March 1949, [[e:france|France]] recognised a State of [[s:socialist-republic-of-vietnam|Vietnam]] within the [[s:french-fourth-republic|French Union]], uniting [[s:french-protectorate-of-tonkin|Tonkin]], [[s:french-protectorate-of-annam|Annam]] and [[s:french-cochinchina|Cochinchina]] under Bao Dai as head of state. It replaced the [[s:provisional-central-government-of-vietnam|Provisional Central Government of Vietnam]] and was recognised by the [[s:united-states|United States]] and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1950.
state-of-vietnam.r: The state, based in Saigon, gained ministries, its own army and currency, but [[e:france|France]] kept control of defence and foreign policy until 1954. Its authority was challenged by the [[e:viet-minh|Viet Minh]] in the countryside and by armed religious sects, the Cao Dai and Hoa Hao, and the Binh Xuyen gang in Saigon. Bao Dai spent much of his time in France and at Da Lat.
state-of-vietnam.e: The [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]] Accords of 1954 limited the state to the south of the 17th parallel. Prime Minister Ngo Dinh Diem defeated the sects and in October 1955 won a rigged referendum deposing Bao Dai, proclaiming the [[s:republic-of-vietnam|Republic of Vietnam]].

soran-emirate.t: A Kurdish emirate based at Rawanduz that, under Mir Muhammad Kor, briefly became a powerful state with its own cannon foundry before Ottoman reconquest.
soran-emirate.o: The Soran [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled the mountains between the Great Zab and the Iranian frontier, in the north-east of modern [[e:iraq|Iraq]]. Sharaf Khan Bidlisi's 16th-century history, the Sharafnama, traces their line back to around 1400. For most of their history they were tribal lords under Ottoman suzerainty, competing with the [[s:baban-emirate|Baban emirate]] and the [[s:bahdinan-emirate|Bahdinan emirate]].
soran-emirate.r: Soran reached its height under Mir Muhammad, known as Mir Kor ('the blind prince'), who ruled from about 1814 to 1836. He built a standing army, made [[e:musket|muskets]] and [[e:field-artillery|cannon]] in Rawanduz, imposed order on the tribes and conquered neighbouring districts, including [[s:bahdinan-emirate|Bahdinan]], while his campaigns against the Yazidis were notoriously brutal. The Sorani form of Kurdish takes its name from this region.
soran-emirate.e: In 1836 an Ottoman army under Reşid Mehmed Pasha, supported by [[e:qajar-dynasty|Qajar]] pressure, forced Mir Muhammad to surrender. He was taken to [[e:istanbul|Istanbul]] and disappeared on the return journey, and the [[e:emirate|emirate]] was brought under direct Ottoman rule.

shuruppak.t: A Sumerian city sacred to the grain goddess Ninlil, remembered as the home of the flood hero and source of some of the oldest literary texts ever found.
shuruppak.o: Shuruppak, modern Tell Fara, grew on a branch of the [[e:euphrates|Euphrates]] in the late fourth millennium BCE and flourished in the [[e:early-dynastic-period|Early Dynastic period]]. A layer of river sediment dated around 2900 BCE has sometimes been linked to the flood tradition, in which the last king before the deluge, Ubar-Tutu, and his son Ziusudra (Utnapishtim) ruled at Shuruppak.
shuruppak.r: The city was dedicated to Sud, later identified with Ninlil, the wife of Enlil. Excavations by German and American teams uncovered the Fara archive of about 2600 BCE: land records, lists of workers, lexical lists and early literary works such as the Instructions of Shuruppak, a collection of proverbial advice. The texts show a large and well-organised household economy, but the names of its rulers are barely known.
shuruppak.e: Shuruppak came under the [[s:akkadian-empire|Akkadian Empire]] after 2334 BCE and later served as a provincial town under the [[s:neo-sumerian-empire|Neo-Sumerian Empire]]. It declined soon afterwards and was abandoned by the early second millennium BCE.

syrian-arab-republic.t: The Syrian state since 1961, ruled for over five decades by the Ba'ath party and the Assad family, and transformed by civil war.
syrian-arab-republic.o: After Syrian officers broke away from the [[s:united-arab-republic|United Arab Republic]] in September 1961, the country took the name Syrian Arab Republic. A coup on 8 March 1963 brought the Ba'ath party to power, and a further coup in 1966 brought its radical wing.
syrian-arab-republic.r: Hafez al-Assad took power in 1970 and built a one-party state dominated by the army and security services, drawing heavily on his Alawite community. [[e:syria|Syria]] lost the Golan Heights to [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] in 1967, intervened in [[s:lebanese-republic|Lebanon]] from 1976 and crushed an Islamist uprising at Hama in 1982. Bashar al-Assad succeeded his father in 2000. Repression of protests in 2011 led to a civil war that killed hundreds of thousands and displaced half the population.
syrian-arab-republic.e: On 8 December 2024 a rebel offensive led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham took [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and Bashar al-Assad fled to [[e:russia|Russia]]. Ahmed al-Sharaa became interim president in 2025, leading a transitional government.

saaremaa.t: Estonia's largest island and its seafaring people, the Oeselians, feared raiders of the Baltic who held out against the crusaders until 1227.
saaremaa.o: Saaremaa, known to Germans and Scandinavians as Ösel, was densely settled in the Iron Age, with strong hillforts such as Valjala and Kaarma. Its inhabitants, the Oeselians, appear in Norse sagas and in Henry of [[e:livonia|Livonia's]] chronicle as skilled sailors and [[e:piracy|pirates]].
saaremaa.r: Each parish was led by elders, who joined together for raids and defence. The Oeselians attacked the coasts of [[e:denmark|Denmark]] and [[e:sweden|Sweden]] and, in 1220, destroyed a Swedish garrison at Lihula on the mainland. They also traded across the Baltic and worshipped a god Henry calls Tharapita.
saaremaa.e: In early 1227 a crusader army crossed the frozen sea and took Valjala, forcing the islanders to accept baptism. The island was divided between the [[s:bishopric-of-osel-wiek|Bishopric of Ösel-Wiek]] and the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]]. Its people rebelled repeatedly, notably in 1343, and Saaremaa later passed to [[s:danish-osel|Danish Ösel]].

state-of-qi.t: The great eastern power of ancient China, home of the first hegemon Duke Huan, the reformer Guan Zhong and the Jixia Academy, and the last state to fall to Qin.
state-of-qi.o: After the Zhou conquest the general Jiang Ziya, Lord Taigong, was enfeoffed on the Shandong peninsula, where he founded Qi with its capital at Linzi. Lying among Dongyi peoples, the state grew by absorbing its neighbours and exploiting the coast, and by the 7th century BCE it was the largest power of the east.
state-of-qi.r: Duke Huan of Qi and his minister Guan Zhong made Qi the first hegemon from 679 BCE, organising covenants of the Zhou states, and drew wealth from state monopolies of salt and iron, fisheries and [[e:silk|silk]]. In 386 BCE the Tian clan, descended from exiles of the [[s:state-of-chen|State of Chen]], replaced the Jiang line. Under King Wei and King Xuan, Linzi's Jixia Academy hosted philosophers such as Mencius and Xunzi.
state-of-qi.e: An invasion by the [[s:state-of-yan|State of Yan]] under Yue Yi in 284 BCE overran almost all of Qi until Tian Dan recovered it from Jimo in 279 BCE. Weakened and passive, Qi surrendered without a battle to King [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] of the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] in 221 BCE, completing the unification that created the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]].

smyrna.t: Ancient Greek city on the Gulf of Izmir, a claimed birthplace of Homer, destroyed by Lydia and refounded in the Hellenistic age.
smyrna.o: Old Smyrna, at Bayraklı on the Gulf of Izmir, was settled by Aeolian [[e:greeks|Greeks]] c. 1000 BCE and taken over by Ionian exiles from [[s:colophon|Colophon]], probably in the 8th century BCE. It developed into one of the first Greek cities with planned streets and stone walls, and claimed to be the birthplace of Homer.
smyrna.r: The city prospered from the fertile Hermus plain. Its temple of Athena is among the earliest monumental Ionian sanctuaries. It was not one of the original twelve members of the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]]. Smyrna fought the [[s:kingdom-of-lydia|Kingdom of Lydia]], resisting Gyges, but Alyattes destroyed it c. 600 BCE, after which it survived only as villages.
smyrna.e: [[e:antigonus-i-monophthalmus|Antigonus]] and [[e:lysimachus|Lysimachus]] refounded Smyrna on the slopes of Mount Pagus c. 300 BCE, and it joined the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]]. It sided with [[e:rome|Rome]] against [[e:antiochus-iii-the-great|Antiochus III]] and passed into the province of [[e:asia|Asia]] after 133 BCE, growing into the modern city of Izmir.

seven-slavic-tribes.t: Union of Slavic tribes in Moesia that joined Asparuh's Bulgars in 681, forming one of the two founding peoples of Bulgaria.
seven-slavic-tribes.o: After the collapse of the [[e:danube|Danube]] frontier in the early 7th century, [[e:slavs|Slavs]] settled densely in Moesia between the Danube and the Balkan Mountains. Byzantine chroniclers, chiefly Theophanes, say seven tribes there formed a union, though their names are not recorded.
seven-slavic-tribes.r: Little is known beyond a few lines in Byzantine chronicles. The union was a loose alliance of farming tribes under their own chiefs, probably formed against [[e:avars|Avar]] and Byzantine pressure. When Asparuh's [[e:bulgars|Bulgars]] crossed the [[e:danube|Danube]], the [[e:slavs|Slavs]] were placed to guard the western frontier against the Avars, while the [[s:severians-balkan|Severi]] held the eastern passes.
seven-slavic-tribes.e: In 681 [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] recognised the new [[e:bulgars|Bulgar]] state, and the union was absorbed into the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]]. Over the next two centuries [[e:slavs|Slavs]] and Bulgars merged, and the Slavic language prevailed.

state-of-zhao.t: One of the three successor states of Jin, famed for King Wuling's adoption of nomad cavalry and for its catastrophic defeat by Qin at Changping in 260 BCE.
state-of-zhao.o: The Zhao lineage served as ministers of the [[s:state-of-jin|State of Jin]] for generations. Zhao Xiangzi helped destroy the Zhi clan in 453 BCE, and in 403 BCE the Zhou king recognised his successor, Marquis Lie, as a ruler. Zhao moved its capital to Handan in 386 BCE.
state-of-zhao.r: Bordering the steppe, Zhao learned from its nomadic neighbours: in 307 BCE King Wuling ordered his troops to adopt trousers and mounted archery, then conquered [[s:zhongshan|Zhongshan]]. Zhao produced famous ministers and generals, including Lin Xiangru, Lian Po and Li Mu. But at Changping in 260 BCE the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] destroyed its main army, reportedly killing hundreds of thousands of prisoners.
state-of-zhao.e: Zhao survived a [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] siege of Handan in 257 BCE, but Qin took the city in 228 BCE and captured King Qian. Prince Jia held out at Dai until 222 BCE. Zhao's horse-riding reforms influenced later Chinese warfare.

sultanate-of-tsibiri.t: The refuge state of the Hausa rulers of Gobir in southern Niger, which kept up the war against the Sokoto Caliphate for most of the 19th century.
sultanate-of-tsibiri.o: The [[s:kingdom-of-gobir|Kingdom of Gobir]] was the first target of [[e:usman-dan-fodio|Usman dan Fodio's]] [[e:jihad|jihad]], and its capital Alkalawa fell in 1808. Its ruling family survived in exile, and in the 1830s they established a new capital at Tsibiri, north of the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]], in alliance with the [[e:hausa|Hausa]] exiles of the [[s:sultanate-of-maradi|Sultanate of Maradi]].
sultanate-of-tsibiri.r: Tsibiri preserved the titles and traditions of [[s:kingdom-of-gobir|Gobir]] and acted as a base for raids into the [[e:caliphate|caliphate]]. In 1836 [[e:gobir|Gobir]] and [[s:sultanate-of-maradi|Maradi]] forces were defeated by [[e:muhammad-bello|Muhammad Bello]] at the battle of Gawakuke, and the Gobir ruler was killed, but the war continued for decades. Tsibiri's rulers were Muslims, yet they opposed the political authority of [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]].
sultanate-of-tsibiri.e: French forces occupied the area in 1899, and Tsibiri was absorbed into the territory that became the [[s:colony-of-niger|Colony of Niger]]. The [[e:sultan|Sultan]] of [[s:kingdom-of-gobir|Gobir]] still reigns at Tsibiri as a traditional ruler.

sahib-ataids.t: A beylik around Afyonkarahisar founded by the family of Sahib Ata, the great Seljuk vizier and builder of Konya.
sahib-ataids.o: Sahib Ata Fakhr al-Din Ali was [[e:vizier|vizier]] of the [[s:sultanate-of-rum|Sultanate of Rum]] for decades under Mongol overlordship. In the 1270s his sons were granted Karahisar, Kutahya and nearby lands, which the family held as a semi-independent domain after Seljuk authority collapsed.
sahib-ataids.r: Sahib Ata was one of the greatest patrons of Seljuk architecture, building the Ince Minareli [[e:madrasa|madrasa]] and his own mosque complex in [[e:konya|Konya]] and works in Kayseri and Sivas. His descendants ruled a small [[e:beylik|beylik]] in western [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], built mosques and schools in Afyonkarahisar and kept close ties with the Mevlevi order.
sahib-ataids.e: The [[e:beylik|beylik]] was squeezed by the [[s:germiyanids|Germiyanids]], who absorbed its lands by around 1341.

saudi-arabia.t: The Al Saud kingdom covering most of the Arabian Peninsula, guardian of Mecca and Medina and one of the world's largest oil producers.
saudi-arabia.o: Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] ibn Saud unified the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd|Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd]] as the Kingdom of Saudi [[e:arabia|Arabia]] on 23 September 1932, completing three decades of conquest begun with the [[s:emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa|Emirate of Nejd and Hasa]]. The [[s:idrisid-emirate-of-asir|Idrisid Emirate of Asir]] was absorbed by 1934, and the Treaty of Ta'if with [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] fixed the southern border.
saudi-arabia.r: Saudi [[e:arabia|Arabia]] is an absolute monarchy whose kings rule with the support of the Wahhabi religious establishment. Oil found at Dammam in 1938 and developed by Aramco funded a vast state. King Faisal used the 1973 [[e:us-oil-embargo-against-japan|oil embargo]] as a political weapon. The 1979 seizure of the Grand Mosque led to stricter religious policies, and the kingdom hosted coalition forces in the Gulf War of 1990-1991.
saudi-arabia.e: Succession has passed among the sons of Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]]. Under King Salman, from 2015, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman launched the Vision 2030 programme to diversify the economy and relaxed some social restrictions, while concentrating power further.

salankayana-dynasty.t: A small Andhra dynasty ruling from Vengi in the Godavari-Krishna delta between the Ikshvakus and the Vishnukundinas.
salankayana-dynasty.o: The Salankayanas emerged in the coastal Andhra region around the 4th century, after the fall of the [[s:ikshvaku-dynasty|Ikshvaku dynasty]]. Their capital was Vengi, near modern Eluru. A Hastivarman of Vengi appears among the southern kings defeated and then reinstated by [[e:samudragupta|Samudragupta]] of the [[s:gupta-empire|Gupta Empire]], as recorded in his Allahabad pillar inscription.
salankayana-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known from about a dozen [[e:copper|copper]]-plate charters recording land grants to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]], written first in Prakrit and later in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]], which document the shift in courtly language in the [[e:deccan|Deccan]]. The kings described themselves as devotees of Chitrarathasvamin, apparently a form of the Sun god. The fertile delta supported [[e:rice|rice]] farming and coastal trade.
salankayana-dynasty.e: In the 5th century the Salankayanas were displaced by the expanding [[s:vishnukundina-dynasty|Vishnukundina dynasty]], which absorbed Vengi.

sufi-dynasty.t: A short-lived Qungrat dynasty that ruled Khwarazm from Urgench in the late 14th century until Timur destroyed the city.
sufi-dynasty.o: As the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] fell into civil war after 1359, Husayn [[e:sufism|Sufi]], a leader of the Qungrat tribe, made himself independent ruler of [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] around 1361, with his capital at Urgench ([[e:gurganj|Gurganj]]). He also seized southern Khwarazm, including Kath and [[e:khiva|Khiva]], which [[e:timur|Timur]] claimed for the Chagatai lands.
sufi-dynasty.r: The Sufids ruled a rich trading oasis on the routes between the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] and [[e:transoxiana|Transoxiana]], and Urgench was a large city of mosques and mausoleums. They allied with the [[e:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] khan Tokhtamysh against [[e:timur|Timur]], who campaigned in [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] several times from 1372, besieging Urgench in 1373 and marrying his son Jahangir to a Sufid princess, Khanzada.
sufi-dynasty.e: After repeated revolts, [[e:timur|Timur]] destroyed Urgench in 1388, levelled the city and ordered barley sown on its site. [[e:khwarazm|Khwarazm]] was absorbed into the [[s:timurid-empire|Timurid Empire]], and Urgench was later partly rebuilt.

southern-qi.t: The second of the Southern Dynasties, short-lived and bloody, but remembered for the literary salon of Prince Jingling and the Yongming style of poetry.
southern-qi.o: Xiao Daocheng, a general who had become the power behind the [[s:liu-song|Liu Song]] throne, forced its last emperor to abdicate in 479 and founded the Qi dynasty at Jiankang. Historians call it Southern Qi to distinguish it from the [[s:northern-qi|Northern Qi]].
southern-qi.r: Under [[e:emperor-wu-of-han|Emperor Wu]] (483 to 493) the south enjoyed relative peace. His son Xiao Ziliang, Prince of Jingling, gathered scholars and Buddhists at his residence, including the Eight Friends of Jingling such as Shen Yue and Xiao Yan, who developed the tonal rules of Yongming-style verse. Later rulers, especially Emperor Ming and Xiao Baojuan, killed ministers and relatives in large numbers.
southern-qi.e: In 501 Xiao Yan, a distant relative and governor at [[e:xiangyang|Xiangyang]], rebelled against Xiao Baojuan, took Jiankang and in 502 founded the [[s:liang-dynasty|Liang dynasty]].

second-taifa-of-niebla.t: Niebla's brief independence under Yusuf al-Bitruji during the 1140s revolts against the Almoravids in the far west of al-Andalus.
second-taifa-of-niebla.o: In 1145 Yusuf ibn Ahmad al-Bitruji, a local leader, took control of the walled town of Niebla on the Tinto river, as the revolt begun by Ibn Qasi in the Algarve spread through the south-west.
second-taifa-of-niebla.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Niebla was one of several small regimes that rose and fell in quick succession. Its ruler was drawn into conflicts with Almoravid loyalists in [[e:seville|Seville]] and with neighbouring rebels.
second-taifa-of-niebla.e: Niebla submitted to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] around 1150. A century later it became independent again as the [[s:third-taifa-of-niebla|Third Taifa of Niebla]].

suebi.t: A broad grouping of Germanic peoples between the Elbe and the Rhine whose name Roman writers used for half of Germania and which later gave Swabia its name.
suebi.o: The Suebi enter history in 58 BCE when [[e:julius-caesar|Julius Caesar]] fought their leader Ariovistus in Alsace, after he had crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] about 72 BCE to aid the [[s:sequani|Sequani]]. Caesar describes the Suebi as the largest and most warlike people of Germania. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] later used the name for a whole cluster of peoples around the Elbe, including the Semnones, [[s:marcomanni|Marcomanni]] and [[s:quadi|Quadi]].
suebi.r: The Suebi were less a single state than a loose family of tribes sharing cult and customs. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]] describes the 'Suebian knot' hairstyle worn by free warriors and an annual sacrifice in the sacred grove of the Semnones, regarded as the oldest and noblest of the group. Leadership rested with kings or war-leaders chosen for campaigns, and their economy combined farming with [[e:cattle|cattle]] raising.
suebi.e: After the 3rd century the name was absorbed into new groupings, especially the [[s:alemanni|Alemanni]], whose land became known as Swabia. A separate Suebian group crossed the [[e:rhine|Rhine]] in 406 and founded a kingdom in [[s:gallaecia|Gallaecia]] in north-west [[e:spain|Spain]], which lasted until the [[e:visigoths|Visigoths]] conquered it in 585.

state-of-shen.t: A Jiang-clan state in the Nanyang basin whose marquis helped the Quanrong sack the Zhou capital in 771 BCE, ending the Western Zhou.
state-of-shen.o: Shen was an old Jiang-clan state. Around 821 BCE King Xuan of Zhou moved his maternal uncle, the Earl of Shen, to Xie near modern Nanyang in Henan, to guard the southern approaches against Chu and the Huai peoples; the Book of [[e:song-dynasty|Songs]] celebrates the founding.
state-of-shen.r: Shen controlled the Nanyang basin, a fertile corridor between the Central Plain and the [[e:han-river|Han River]]. Its rulers were closely tied to the Zhou royal house by marriage. When King You demoted his queen, a daughter of the Marquis of Shen, in favour of Bao Si, the Marquis allied with the Quanrong and the State of Zeng and sacked Haojing in 771 BCE.
state-of-shen.e: King Wen of Chu conquered Shen around 688 BCE and made it a Chu county, whose levies became one of Chu's main armies for northern campaigns. The site remained a key military base on Chu's northern frontier.

sheikhdom-of-mohammerah.t: An Arab sheikhdom at the mouth of the Karun whose last ruler, Sheikh Khaz'al, protected Britain's first great oil refinery at Abadan.
sheikhdom-of-mohammerah.o: The Muhaysin, a branch of the [[s:banu-kab-sheikhdom|Banu Ka'b sheikhdom]], developed the port of Mohammerah (modern Khorramshahr) at the confluence of the Karun and the Shatt al-Arab in the early 19th century. Under Hajji Jabir Khan it became the dominant power in the Arab lowlands of Khuzestan, known as Arabistan, nominally under [[s:qajar-iran|Qajar Iran]].
sheikhdom-of-mohammerah.r: The sheikhs profited from river and Gulf trade, especially after the Karun was opened to foreign steamers in 1888. Sheikh Khaz'al ibn Jabir, who took power in 1897 by killing his brother Mizal, became a semi-independent prince. In 1909 he leased land on Abadan island to the Anglo-Persian Oil Company for its refinery, and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] gave him guarantees of protection. He ruled from his palace at Failiyeh near Mohammerah, dealing directly with British officials.
sheikhdom-of-mohammerah.e: After Khaz'al rebelled against the central government in 1924, Reza Khan's army entered Khuzestan, and in 1925 he was arrested and taken to Tehran, where he died in 1936. The sheikhdom was absorbed into [[s:pahlavi-iran|Pahlavi Iran]].

cr.a: East India Company, the Board of Control, the India Office, or other British Government Department

salyes.t: Celto-Ligurian confederation inland of Marseille whose wars with Greek Massalia drew Rome into Gaul and led to the founding of Aix-en-Provence.
salyes.o: The Salyes were a league of Ligurian and Celtic communities in lower [[s:county-of-provence|Provence]], between the Rhône and the Var. Greek writers mention them from the 4th century BCE as troublesome neighbours of [[s:massalia|Massalia]]. Their chief stronghold was the oppidum of Entremont on a plateau north of modern Aix, fortified in the 2nd century BCE.
salyes.r: Entremont is known for its stone sculptures of seated warriors and carved severed heads, and for a portico where real skulls were displayed, reflecting a warrior cult of the head. The Salyes farmed olives and cereals, pressed oil and traded with the Greek coast while raiding it.
salyes.e: [[s:massalia|Massalia]] appealed to the [[s:roman-republic|Roman Republic]], and campaigns in 125 to 123 BCE under Marcus Fulvius Flaccus and Gaius Sextius Calvinus destroyed Entremont. Their king Teutomalius fled to the [[s:allobroges|Allobroges]]. In 122 BCE the [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] founded Aquae Sextiae (Aix-en-Provence) nearby, and the territory became part of Gallia Narbonensis.

sipsong-panna.t: The Tai Lue kingdom of the upper Mekong, centred on Chiang Hung (Jinghong), which balanced Chinese and Burmese overlords for over seven centuries.
sipsong-panna.o: Tai Lue chronicles date the kingdom to 1180, when Phaya Choeng united the Tai principalities of the upper [[e:mekong-river|Mekong]] valley in southern Yunnan and founded his capital at Chiang Hung. The later name Sipsong [[s:panna-state|Panna]] means 'twelve thousand [[e:rice|rice]] fields', referring to its administrative districts.
sipsong-panna.r: The ruler, the chao phaendin or saopha, governed with a council of nobles over [[e:rice|rice]]-growing Tai Lue villages and surrounding hill peoples such as the Akha. [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]] and the Tai Tham script tied it to [[s:lan-na|Lan Na]] and the Burmese world. From the Yuan period it was a native chieftaincy of [[e:china|China]], but it also paid tribute to Burmese kings, including the [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]], often to both at once.
sipsong-panna.e: Qing and Republican governments increasingly intervened, and the People's Liberation Army took control in 1950. In 1953 the Xishuangbanna Dai Autonomous Prefecture replaced the old monarchy; the last ruler, Chao Mom Kham Le (Dao Shixun), became an official of the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]].

swedish-ingria.t: Swedish province at the head of the Gulf of Finland that cut Russia off from the Baltic, until Peter the Great built St Petersburg on its land.
swedish-ingria.o: [[e:sweden|Sweden]] captured the fortresses of Ivangorod, Jama and Koporye during the [[e:livonian-war|Livonian War]], confirmed by the Truce of Plussa in 1583, but returned them to [[e:russia|Russia]] in 1595. During the Time of Troubles Sweden reconquered the area, and the Treaty of Stolbovo in 1617 gave [[e:ingria|Ingria]] to Sweden permanently, cutting Russia off from the sea.
swedish-ingria.r: [[e:ingria|Ingria]] was a thinly populated frontier, governed from Narva together with [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]]. Many [[e:eastern-orthodox-church|Orthodox]] inhabitants left, and Lutheran Finns from Savonia and [[s:karelians|Karelia]] settled, forming the Ingrian Finns. The fortress of Nyenskans and the town of Nyen at the mouth of the Neva controlled trade with [[e:russia|Russia]].
swedish-ingria.e: In the [[e:great-northern-war|Great Northern War]] [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great]] captured Nyenskans in 1703 and founded St Petersburg nearby. Narva fell in 1704, and the [[e:treaty-of-nystad|Treaty of Nystad]] in 1721 confirmed [[e:ingria|Ingria]] as Russian. It became the core of the St Petersburg [[e:governorate|Governorate]].
swedish-ingria.la: Finnish, Swedish, Russian, Votic and Izhorian

shanghai-french-concession.t: The French-governed district of Shanghai, known for its leafy avenues, its gangsters and as the birthplace of the Chinese Communist Party.
shanghai-french-concession.o: After Shanghai was opened to foreign trade in 1843, the French consul Charles de Montigny obtained from the local Chinese authorities in 1849 a concession between the walled Chinese city and the British settlement. When the British and American settlements merged in 1863, [[e:france|France]] chose to keep its area separate.
shanghai-french-concession.r: The concession was run by the French consul-general with an elected municipal council, under French law and with its own police. Its tree-lined streets, such as the Avenue Joffre, became a favoured residential district. The French police tolerated and employed Green Gang bosses such as [[s:state-of-huang|Huang]] Jinrong and Du Yuesheng, and political exiles found refuge there: the Chinese Communist Party held its first congress in the concession in 1921.
shanghai-french-concession.e: [[e:japan|Japan]] occupied the rest of Shanghai in 1941 but left the Vichy-run concession in place. In 1943 [[s:vichy-france|Vichy France]] handed it to the Japanese-backed [[s:wang-jingwei-regime|Wang Jingwei regime]], and after 1945 it remained part of Chinese Shanghai.

sicel-league.t: Short-lived union of the native Sicel towns of eastern Sicily under Ducetius, who tried to resist the Greek cities in the mid-5th century BCE.
sicel-league.o: The Sicels were the native people of eastern [[e:sicily|Sicily]], gradually pushed inland by the Greek colonies. After the fall of the tyrants in [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] and [[s:acragas|Acragas]] in the 460s BCE, the Sicel leader Ducetius united most Sicel communities, apart from Hybla, around 460 BCE.
sicel-league.r: Ducetius founded new towns, including Menaenum and Palike, beside the sanctuary of the Palici, twin gods worshipped at volcanic pools that served as a place of oaths and refuge for slaves. He took Morgantina and Inessa and attacked Acragan and Syracusan territory. The league was a military federation built around his leadership.
sicel-league.e: In 450 BCE [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] and [[s:acragas|Acragas]] defeated Ducetius at Nomae; he surrendered and was exiled to [[s:corinth|Corinth]]. He returned to found Kale Akte on the north coast but died around 440 BCE, and Syracuse absorbed the Sicel towns. The Sicels were gradually Hellenised.

state-of-honduras.t: Member state of the Central American Federation, birthplace of its leading champion Francisco Morazán, which seceded in 1838.
state-of-honduras.o: The former province of Comayagua and the mining district of Tegucigalpa formed the State of [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]] within the [[s:federal-republic-of-central-america|Federal Republic of Central America]]. Its first constitution was adopted in 1825, and Dionisio de Herrera, a liberal lawyer, served as first head of state from 1824, with the capital at Comayagua.
state-of-honduras.r: [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]] was poor and thinly populated, living from [[e:cattle|cattle]] ranching, [[e:silver|silver]] mining around Tegucigalpa and the export of mahogany and hides. Rivalry between Comayagua and Tegucigalpa shaped its politics. During the federal civil war Guatemalan forces deposed Herrera in 1827, and the Honduran officer Francisco Morazán won his first victory at La Trinidad that year, launching his career as federal leader. British loggers were active on the north coast.
state-of-honduras.e: As the federation broke apart, [[s:republic-of-honduras|Honduras]] declared itself separate on 26 October 1838, becoming the Republic of Honduras, though its leaders still spoke of reviving the union. Morazán's defeat in 1840 ended hopes of restoring the federation by force.

saka.t: Iranian-speaking horse nomads of the eastern steppe, famed for gold-rich kurgans, who later carved out kingdoms in Bactria, Sistan and north-western India.
saka.o: The Saka were the eastern branch of the wider Scythian world, recorded by Persian inscriptions and Greek writers from about the 7th century BCE. Achaemenid texts name several groups, among them the Saka Tigraxauda, the 'pointed-hat' Saka, and the Saka Haumavarga, and [[e:cyrus-the-great|Cyrus the Great]] and [[e:darius-i|Darius I]] campaigned against them across the [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]].
saka.r: They were not one state but a loose world of pastoral tribes ruled by chieftains and warrior elites. Mobile herding of horses, sheep and [[e:cattle|cattle]] supported them, alongside trade with oasis towns. Their burials, such as the Issyk kurgan with its 'Golden Man' and the frozen tombs of Pazyryk and Berel, display the animal-style art of gold plaques, felt and horse trappings shared across the steppe.
saka.e: In the 2nd century BCE pressure from the [[s:yuezhi|Yuezhi]] drove many Saka south into [[s:greco-bactrian-kingdom|Bactria]], Sistan and the [[e:indus|Indus]] valley, where they founded the Indo-Scythian kingdoms. Others were absorbed by the [[s:wusun|Wusun]] and later [[e:turkic-peoples|Turkic peoples]]. Khotanese and Tumshuqese, the Saka languages of the [[e:tarim-basin|Tarim Basin]], survived into the 10th century.

southern-rhodesia.t: The self-governing British settler colony that became Rhodesia and, after a long war, Zimbabwe.
southern-rhodesia.o: In a 1922 referendum the settlers of the [[e:british-south-africa-company|British South Africa Company's]] southern territory rejected union with [[s:republic-of-south-africa|South Africa]]. On 1 October 1923 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed it as the self-governing Colony of Southern [[s:rhodesia|Rhodesia]], with Charles Coghlan as its first premier and Salisbury as its capital, ending [[s:company-rule-in-rhodesia|Company rule in Rhodesia]].
southern-rhodesia.r: A small white electorate controlled parliament, while [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] kept rarely used reserve powers over African affairs. The Land Apportionment Act of 1930 divided land by race, giving the best farmland to whites. Godfrey Huggins, prime minister from 1933 to 1953, led the colony through rapid growth based on tobacco, mining and white immigration after 1945, while African nationalism grew through the 1950s.
southern-rhodesia.e: Southern [[s:rhodesia|Rhodesia]] led the [[s:federation-of-rhodesia-and-nyasaland|Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland]] from 1953 to 1963. The Rhodesian Front won power in 1962, and on 11 November 1965 Ian Smith's government declared independence unilaterally, creating Rhodesia.

sheikhdom-of-qatar.t: Qatar under the Al Thani, from its recognition by Britain in 1868 through Ottoman and British protection to independence in 1971.
sheikhdom-of-qatar.o: Qatar's coast had been dominated by [[e:bahrain|Bahrain's]] Al [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]]. After a destructive war between them, the British envoy Lewis Pelly signed an agreement with Muhammad bin Thani of Doha in 1868, recognising him as the peninsula's leader. Ottoman troops arrived in Doha in 1871.
sheikhdom-of-qatar.r: Jassim bin Muhammad Al Thani, ruler from 1878 to 1913, is regarded as founder of the state; he defeated an Ottoman force at al-Wajbah in 1893. [[s:state-of-qatar|Qatar]] lived from pearling and fishing and was poor and sparsely populated. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] withdrew during the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], and the Anglo-Qatari Treaty of 1916 made Qatar a British protected state. The collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s caused hardship.
sheikhdom-of-qatar.e: Oil was found at Dukhan in 1939 and exported from 1949, funding development. When [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] withdrew from the Gulf, [[s:state-of-qatar|Qatar]] declined to join the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] and became the independent State of Qatar on 3 September 1971.

sudovians.t: Warlike West Baltic people of the lake and forest country between the Neman and Narew, who held off Rus', Poland and the Teutonic Order for centuries.
sudovians.o: Ptolemy's 'Sudinoi' in the 2nd century are usually taken to be the Sudovians, also called Yotvingians. They occupied the lands around modern Suwałki, Grodno and southern [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]], close kin of the Prussians and [[s:galindians|Galindians]], and were organised as a loose federation of territories led by hillfort chieftains rather than a single state.
sudovians.r: Their economy rested on farming, [[e:cattle|cattle]], hunting and the amber and [[e:fur-trade|fur trade]], supplemented by raiding. They kept Baltic pagan cults and a language close to Old Prussian. Rus' princes campaigned against them from Vladimir the Great's expedition of 983, and Polish dukes repeatedly invaded in the 12th and 13th centuries; Bolesław V the Chaste killed the chief Komata in 1264.
sudovians.e: After 1274 the Teutonic Order turned on Sudovia, and in 1283 its last war leader, Skomantas, submitted. Many Sudovians were resettled in [[s:sambians|Sambia]], in a district long called the Sudauer Winkel, while others fled to the [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Grand Duchy of Lithuania]]. The emptied land became a frontier wilderness, and the language died out.

severians-balkan.t: Slavic tribe in north-eastern Bulgaria whom the Bulgars under Asparuh placed to guard the eastern passes of the Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.o: Known mainly from Byzantine chronicles, the Severi were a Slavic tribe that settled in Moesia in the 7th century, in the area between the [[e:danube|Danube]] delta and the eastern Balkan Mountains.
severians-balkan.r: They lived as a tribal people under their own chiefs. When the [[e:bulgars|Bulgars]] arrived under Asparuh in 680–681, Theophanes records that the Severi were moved to guard the passes towards [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], while the [[s:seven-slavic-tribes|Seven Slavic Tribes]] held other borders.
severians-balkan.e: They became part of the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]], keeping their own leaders for some time; in the 760s the Byzantine emperor Constantine V captured Slavun, chief of the Severi. They then merged into the Bulgarian population.

sanjak-of-alexandretta.t: A Syrian district with a large Turkish population whose status, disputed between France and Turkey, ended in its annexation by Turkey.
sanjak-of-alexandretta.o: By the Treaty of Ankara of 1921 [[e:france|France]] agreed that the district of Alexandretta, which included [[s:principality-of-antioch|Antioch]] and a large Turkish-speaking population alongside [[e:arabs|Arabs]], Alawites and [[e:armenians|Armenians]], should have a special administrative regime within French-ruled [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. It formed an autonomous sanjak attached first to the [[s:state-of-aleppo|State of Aleppo]] and then to [[e:syria|Syria]].
sanjak-of-alexandretta.r: Turkish was an official language and the sanjak had its own administration. When [[e:france|France]] promised [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] independence in 1936, [[e:turkey|Turkey]] demanded the district. The [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] drafted a statute making it a separate entity, and elections held in 1938 under Turkish military presence gave Turks a majority in the assembly.
sanjak-of-alexandretta.e: In September 1938 the assembly proclaimed [[s:hatay-state|Hatay State]], which joined [[e:turkey|Turkey]] in 1939. [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] has never formally recognised the loss.

sultanate-of-bambao.t: The sultanate around Moroni on Grande Comore whose ruler Said Ali united the island under French protection in 1886.
sultanate-of-bambao.o: Bambao was one of the districts of Grande Comore (Ngazidja) ruled by Shirazi-descended lineages from walled coastal towns, including Ikoni and later Moroni. By the 17th century it was among the leading sultanates, contending with the [[s:sultanate-of-itsandra|Sultanate of Itsandra]] for the paramount title of sultan tibe.
sultanate-of-bambao.r: Its sultans governed with the elders of noble lineages under matrilineal rules of succession, and [[e:islam|Islam]] framed law and education. Trade with the [[e:swahili|Swahili]] coast, Madagascar and [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]] brought prosperity, while island politics were dominated by endless wars between the sultanates, which often drew in [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]] and outside powers.
sultanate-of-bambao.e: Said Ali of Bambao, backed by the French adventurer Leon Humblot, became paramount and in 1886 signed a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the whole island. Grande Comore later became a French colony and in 1975 part of the independent Comoros, with Moroni as the capital.

socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.t: Tito's communist federation of six South Slav republics, which broke with Stalin, led the Non-Aligned Movement and broke apart in war in the 1990s.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.o: Tito's Partisans emerged victorious from the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]] after defeating occupiers, the [[s:independent-state-of-croatia|Independent State of Croatia]] and the Chetniks. The AVNOJ council at Jajce in 1943 had set out a federal state, Democratic Federal [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] was formed in 1945, and on 29 November 1945 the monarchy was abolished and a federal people's republic proclaimed, with six republics.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.r: After Tito's split with Stalin in 1948, [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]] developed its own socialism based on workers' self-management and market elements, and in 1961 co-founded the Non-Aligned Movement in [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]]. Its citizens could travel and work abroad. The 1974 constitution decentralised power to the republics and autonomous provinces, while Tito ruled as president for life.
socialist-federal-republic-of-yugoslavia.e: After Tito's death in 1980, debt, [[e:inflation|inflation]] and nationalism grew, notably under Slobodan Milošević in [[s:serbia|Serbia]]. Slovenia and Croatia declared independence in 1991, followed by Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, amid war. In April 1992 [[s:serbia-and-montenegro|Serbia and Montenegro]] formed the [[s:federal-republic-of-yugoslavia|Federal Republic of Yugoslavia]].

sultanate-of-the-maldives.t: An Islamic sultanate of coral atolls in the Indian Ocean that lasted more than eight centuries, famed for its cowrie shells and visited by Ibn Battuta.
sultanate-of-the-maldives.o: According to Maldivian tradition the king Dhovemi converted from [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] to [[e:islam|Islam]] in 1153 under the influence of a Muslim visitor, taking the title of sultan. The islands, previously Buddhist, were rapidly Islamised, and Male became the seat of a sultanate that would be ruled by a series of dynasties.
sultanate-of-the-maldives.r: The sultans ruled the scattered atolls through appointed chiefs and the judges of Islamic law. [[e:cowrie-shell|Cowrie shells]] harvested in the islands served as currency across the [[e:indian-ocean|Indian Ocean]] and [[e:west-africa|West Africa]], and coir rope and dried fish were exported. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]] served as a judge in Male in the 1340s and described a court where women sometimes held the throne, including Sultana Khadija.
sultanate-of-the-maldives.e: The Portuguese occupied Male from 1558 to 1573, until expelled by Muhammad Thakurufaanu. The sultanate became a British [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1887, was briefly replaced by the [[s:first-maldivian-republic|First Maldivian Republic]] in 1953, and gained independence in 1965. A referendum abolished the monarchy in 1968, creating the [[s:republic-of-maldives|Republic of Maldives]].

sultanate-of-mayotte.t: The Shirazi sultanate of Mayotte, whose last ruler, the exiled Sakalava king Andriantsoly, sold the island to France in 1841.
sultanate-of-mayotte.o: A Shirazi Muslim dynasty established itself on [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]] (Maore) around 1500, linked by marriage and trade to the other Comorian islands. The sultans ruled from Tsingoni, where the Friday mosque, dated by inscription to 1538, is among the oldest in the region.
sultanate-of-mayotte.r: The sultanate was a small maritime state trading [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:cattle|cattle]] and slaves with the [[e:swahili|Swahili]] coast, Madagascar and passing European ships. Its rulers were often drawn into the wars of the [[s:sultanate-of-anjouan|Sultanate of Anjouan]], which claimed overlordship, and the island suffered heavy Malagasy slave raids in the late 18th century. The capital later moved to Dzaoudzi.
sultanate-of-mayotte.e: In 1832 Andriantsoly, the former Sakalava king of [[s:boina|Boina]] driven out by the [[s:merina-kingdom|Merina Kingdom]], seized [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]]. Seeking protection, he sold the island to [[e:france|France]] in 1841. Mayotte remained French and is now an overseas [[e:departement|department]].

savanur-state.t: A small Muslim-ruled state in northern Karnataka, held by a Pathan family of Nawabs granted their lands under Aurangzeb.
savanur-state.o: Savanur was founded around 1680 when Abdul Rauf Khan, an Afghan (Miana) officer, received a grant from the Mughal emperor [[e:aurangzeb|Aurangzeb]] in the Carnatic. His descendants ruled as Nawabs of Savanur.
savanur-state.r: The Nawabs ruled a territory of black-soil [[e:cotton|cotton]] and grain country between Dharwad and the Tungabhadra. They lost much land to the [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] and to Hyder Ali and Tipu [[e:sultan|Sultan]] of Mysore in the 18th century, and came under British protection after 1818 in the Southern Maratha Country.
savanur-state.e: Savanur acceded to [[e:india|India]] and merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948, passing to [[s:mysore-state|Mysore State]] (now Karnataka) in 1956. The town lies in Haveri district.

state-of-syria.t: The unified Syrian state created by France in 1925 from Damascus and Aleppo, the setting of the Great Syrian Revolt.
state-of-syria.o: [[e:france|France]] merged the [[s:state-of-damascus|State of Damascus]] and the [[s:state-of-aleppo|State of Aleppo]] into the State of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] with effect from 1 January 1925, with [[e:damascus|Damascus]] as capital and Subhi Barakat as president; the Alawite and Jabal Druze states remained separate.
state-of-syria.r: Months after its creation, the Great Syrian Revolt spread from the Jabal Druze to [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and the countryside; French forces shelled Damascus in October 1925 and suppressed the rising by 1927. French high commissioners appointed governments led by Ahmad Nami and later Taj al-Din al-Hasani. A Constituent Assembly elected in 1928, dominated by the nationalist National Bloc under Hashim al-Atassi, drafted a constitution.
state-of-syria.e: In May 1930 the French high commissioner promulgated a modified constitution, turning the state into the [[s:syrian-republic|Syrian Republic]].

cr.a: F l a n k e r

saudeleur-dynasty.t: The first rulers to unite the island of Pohnpei, remembered for the basalt city of Nan Madol, built on artificial islets in a coral lagoon.
saudeleur-dynasty.o: Pohnpeian oral tradition says two sorcerer brothers, Olisihpa and Olosohpa, came from overseas and built an altar on the reef off Temwen Island, the start of Nan Madol. Olosohpa became the first Saudeleur, meaning lord of Deleur, and his line brought Pohnpei's chiefdoms under one ruler, probably around 1100 to 1200.
saudeleur-dynasty.r: Nan Madol, nearly 100 islets of stacked basalt columns and coral fill, served as royal residence, ceremonial centre and burial ground for the Saudeleur. The rulers demanded heavy tribute in food and labour, and tradition remembers them as increasingly harsh and controlling. Priests tended sacred eels and turtles, and the island's population lived from breadfruit, yams and fishing. The dynasty's history is known almost entirely from oral tradition and archaeology.
saudeleur-dynasty.e: Tradition says the hero Isokelekel, son of the thunder god, came from Kosrae with warriors and overthrew the last Saudeleur, traditionally around 1628. He founded the Nahnmwarki system of chiefdoms that still survives on Pohnpei. Nan Madol was gradually abandoned and became a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 2016.

state-of-el-salvador.t: Indigo-producing member state of the Central American Federation, the liberal heartland that backed Francisco Morazán to the end.
state-of-el-salvador.o: Salvadoran liberals led by the priest José Matías Delgado had resisted annexation to the [[s:first-mexican-empire|First Mexican Empire]], even offering in 1822 to join the [[s:united-states|United States]]. With the creation of the [[s:federal-republic-of-central-america|Federal Republic of Central America]], [[s:republic-of-el-salvador|El Salvador]] became one of its five states under its own constitution of 1824, with Juan Manuel Rodríguez as first head of state.
state-of-el-salvador.r: The economy depended on [[e:indigo|indigo]] grown on [[e:hacienda|haciendas]] and exported through Guatemalan merchants, a source of rivalry with [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] City. Salvadoran liberals fought Guatemalan conservatives in the federal civil war of 1826 to 1829. In 1833 the Nonualco people rose under Anastasio Aquino against land seizures and forced recruitment. From 1834 San [[e:salvador|Salvador]] hosted the federal government, and Francisco Morazán himself served as head of state in 1839 and 1840.
state-of-el-salvador.e: After Morazán's defeat by Rafael Carrera in 1840, [[s:republic-of-el-salvador|El Salvador]] lost its federal role, and a constitution of February 1841 declared it a sovereign state, the Republic of El [[e:salvador|Salvador]].

surgana-state.t: A small hill state in the Sahyadri ranges north of Nashik, ruled by a local chiefly family over a largely tribal population.
surgana-state.o: Surgana lay in the hills on the border of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and Maharashtra, and was ruled by a family of Deshmukhs. The register dates it to around 1700. Its origins are known mainly from local tradition.
surgana-state.r: The chief ruled a forested territory inhabited mostly by Koknas, Warlis and other Adivasi communities, who practised hill farming. In the British period Surgana was a minor non-salute state, later grouped in the [[e:deccan|Deccan]] States Agency. Few further details are recorded.
surgana-state.e: Surgana merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960. It is now a taluka of Nashik district.

shechem.t: Shechem, a fortified Canaanite city in the central hills whose ruler Labayu challenged Egyptian control in the Amarna age.
shechem.o: Shechem, at Tell Balata near modern Nablus, commanded the pass between Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. It appears in Egyptian execration texts and in an account of a campaign by Senusret III of the [[s:middle-kingdom-of-egypt|Middle Kingdom of Egypt]], and by the 17th century BCE was ringed by massive walls.
shechem.r: Its rulers built a great fortress-temple, among the largest in [[e:canaan|Canaan]], and controlled the highlands around. In the 14th century BCE its king Labayu expanded his territory at the expense of neighbouring [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]], provoking complaints in the [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]]; his sons carried on the struggle.
shechem.e: The Canaanite city declined in the 12th century BCE. Shechem later became a centre of the [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Kingdom of Israel]] and of the Samaritans, and the Bible preserves memories of its temple of El-Berith.

syrian-republic.t: The Syrian state of 1930-1958, which won independence from France and then fell into military coups before uniting with Egypt.
syrian-republic.o: The French high commissioner promulgated a constitution in May 1930 that turned the [[s:state-of-syria|State of Syria]] into the Syrian Republic under the French mandate. Muhammad Ali al-Abid became its first president in 1932.
syrian-republic.r: The National Bloc negotiated a 1936 treaty that [[e:france|France]] never ratified. Shukri al-Quwatli, elected president in 1943, led the country to full independence when the last French troops left on 17 April 1946. Defeat in the 1948 war with [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] discredited the civilian leadership, and in 1949 three coups followed, by Husni al-Za'im, Sami al-Hinnawi and Adib Shishakli, who ruled until 1954. Parliamentary rule then returned, with the Ba'ath party gaining influence.
syrian-republic.e: Fearing communist influence and seeking Arab unity, Syrian leaders asked [[e:egypt|Egypt]] for union, and in February 1958 [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] joined the [[s:united-arab-republic|United Arab Republic]].

suriname.t: The Dutch plantation colony on the Guiana coast, notorious for harsh slavery and home to strong maroon nations, which became an independent republic in 1975.
suriname.o: The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] seized the English colony of [[s:willoughbyland|Willoughbyland]] in 1667, and the Treaty of Breda confirmed their possession. From 1683 Suriname was run by the Society of Suriname, owned by the city of [[e:amsterdam|Amsterdam]], the [[e:dutch-west-india-company|Dutch West India Company]] and the Van Aerssen van Sommelsdijck family, whose member Cornelis became governor.
suriname.r: Suriname became one of the richest [[e:dutch|Dutch]] colonies, with hundreds of plantations producing [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and [[e:cacao|cacao]] worked by enslaved Africans under brutal conditions. Many escaped to the interior and formed maroon nations such as the Ndyuka and Saramaka, which won peace treaties in the 1760s. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] occupied the colony from 1799 to 1816. [[e:slavery|Slavery]] was abolished in 1863, and indentured workers then arrived from [[e:india|India]] and [[e:java|Java]], giving Suriname its diverse population.
suriname.e: Suriname gained autonomy within the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]] in 1954 and independence on 25 November 1975. Desi Bouterse seized power in a coup in 1980, and an interior war followed from 1986 to 1992. It has been a democratic republic since 1991.
