second-polish-republic.t: Independent interwar Poland, reborn in 1918 after 123 years of partition, which defeated the Red Army in 1920 and fell to Germany and the USSR in 1939.
second-polish-republic.o: As the partitioning empires collapsed in November 1918, Jozef Pilsudski took power in [[e:warsaw|Warsaw]] from the Regency Council of the [[s:kingdom-of-poland-1916-1918|Kingdom of Poland]] (1916-1918), and independence was proclaimed on 11 November. [[e:poland|Poland's]] borders were settled by war: with the [[s:west-ukrainian-peoples-republic|West Ukrainian People's Republic]], with [[e:germany|Germany]] in [[s:duchy-of-greater-poland|Greater Poland]] and [[s:duchy-of-silesia|Silesia]], and with [[s:russian-sfsr|Soviet Russia]], whose army was defeated at Warsaw in 1920.
second-polish-republic.r: The constitution of 1921 created a parliamentary republic, but after President Gabriel Narutowicz was murdered in 1922 and governments proved unstable, Pilsudski seized power in the May Coup of 1926. His Sanation regime ruled until 1939. About a third of the population were Ukrainians, [[e:jews|Jews]], Belarusians and Germans. The state built the port of Gdynia and the Central Industrial District.
second-polish-republic.e: [[s:nazi-germany|Nazi Germany]] invaded on 1 September 1939 and the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] on 17 September, dividing the country. The government went into exile in [[e:france|France]] and [[e:london|London]], and [[e:poland|Poland]] was re-established in 1945 with new borders under communist rule.

side.t: Side, a Pamphylian port city with its own language and script, famous for its harbour and later its slave market.
side.o: [[e:greeks|Greeks]] from Cyme in Aeolis settled Side in the 7th century BCE on a peninsula of the Pamphylian coast. According to legend, they soon forgot Greek and spoke the local language, called Sidetic, written in a unique alphabet. The city's name means pomegranate.
side.r: Side was a self-governing port that thrived on trade and shipbuilding. It surrendered to Alexander of the [[s:macedonian-empire|Macedonian Empire]] in 333 BCE and came under the [[s:ptolemaic-empire|Ptolemaic Empire]] and the [[s:seleucid-empire|Seleucid Empire]]. In 190 BCE a Rhodian fleet defeated [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] off its shore.
side.e: In the 1st century BCE Side became a centre for Cilician [[e:piracy|pirates]], who sold captives in its market. The [[e:roman-empire|Romans]] suppressed piracy, and in 25 BCE the city was included in the province of [[s:galatia|Galatia]], flourishing under [[e:rome|Rome]].

state-of-somaliland.t: The independent state formed from British Somaliland, which existed for just five days in 1960 before uniting with the south.
state-of-somaliland.o: [[s:british-somaliland|British Somaliland]] received independence on 26 June 1960 as the State of [[s:republic-of-somaliland|Somaliland]], with a legislative assembly elected earlier that year and Muhammad Haji Ibrahim Egal as prime minister. Some 35 countries, including the [[s:united-kingdom|United Kingdom]], recognised it.
state-of-somaliland.r: There was no time for a separate state to take shape. Its leaders had already agreed to unite with the south, and the union was rushed through with an act signed hastily and never properly ratified by both sides, a fact later cited by northern separatists.
state-of-somaliland.e: On 1 July 1960 the State of [[s:republic-of-somaliland|Somaliland]] united with the [[s:trust-territory-of-somaliland|Trust Territory of Somaliland]] to form the [[s:somali-republic|Somali Republic]]. Its short-lived independence is the legal basis claimed by the Republic of [[e:italian-somaliland|Somaliland]], which declared its independence in 1991.

silla.t: The longest-lived of Korea's Three Kingdoms, which unified most of the peninsula in the 7th century and built a Buddhist golden age at Gyeongju.
silla.o: Silla began as Saro, one statelet of the [[s:jinhan|Jinhan confederacy]] at modern Gyeongju, traditionally founded in 57 BCE by Bak Hyeokgeose. Three clans, Bak, Seok and Kim, shared the throne in early centuries; by the 4th century the Kim had made it hereditary and Saro had absorbed its Jinhan neighbours.
silla.r: Society was ordered by the bone-rank system, which fixed every family's rank and office by birth. King Beopheung adopted [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] in 527 and a law code; Jinheung expanded into the Han river valley and conquered Gaya, and the hwarang youth corps trained elites. Allied with [[e:tang-dynasty|Tang China]], Silla destroyed [[s:baekje|Baekje]] in 660 and [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]] in 668, then expelled [[s:later-tang|Tang]] forces by 676. Unified Silla built Bulguksa and the Seokguram grotto.
silla.e: From the late 8th century aristocratic feuds and regional strongmen weakened the throne, and rebels founded [[s:later-baekje|Later Baekje]] and [[s:taebong|Taebong]]. In 935 King Gyeongsun surrendered peacefully to [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]], which absorbed Silla's aristocracy and culture.

swedish-wismar.t: Baltic port in Mecklenburg held by Sweden from the Peace of Westphalia until 1803, when it was pawned to Mecklenburg-Schwerin for a century.
swedish-wismar.o: [[e:sweden|Sweden]] occupied [[e:wismar|Wismar]] during the [[e:thirty-years-war|Thirty Years' War]], and the [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Peace of Westphalia]] in 1648 gave it the town, the island of Poel and the district of Neukloster as an imperial fief. Wismar became one of Sweden's footholds on the southern Baltic, with [[s:swedish-pomerania|Swedish Pomerania]] and [[s:duchies-of-bremen-and-verden|Bremen-Verden]].
swedish-wismar.r: [[e:sweden|Sweden]] turned [[e:wismar|Wismar]] into a heavily fortified naval base and placed there, from 1653, the Wismar Tribunal, the supreme court of appeal for all of Sweden's German possessions. The town kept its Hanseatic council and German law, while a Swedish governor commanded the garrison. Its trade suffered from the wars fought over it, and Danish and Prussian forces besieged it in 1675 and 1711-1716.
swedish-wismar.e: In 1803 [[e:sweden|Sweden]] pawned [[e:wismar|Wismar]] to the Duke of [[s:duchy-of-mecklenburg|Mecklenburg-Schwerin]] for 1,250,000 riksdaler for 100 years, in the Treaty of Malmö. The loan was never repaid, and in 1903 Sweden renounced its rights, leaving Wismar to [[e:germany|Germany]].

sui-dynasty.t: The short dynasty that reunited China in 589, built the Grand Canal and laid the institutional foundations of the Tang.
sui-dynasty.o: Yang Jian, an aristocrat of mixed Han and [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] background and father-in-law of a [[s:northern-zhou|Northern Zhou]] emperor, seized power as regent and took the throne in 581 as Emperor Wen. He built a new capital, Daxing, beside old [[e:changan|Chang'an]], absorbed [[s:western-liang-555-587|Western Liang]] in 587 and conquered the [[s:chen-dynasty|Chen dynasty]] in 589.
sui-dynasty.r: Emperor Wen issued the Kaihuang Code, kept the [[e:equal-field-system|equal-field]] land system and [[e:fubing-system|fubing]] militia, reformed local administration, took regular [[e:census|censuses]] and began recruiting officials by examination. He was a fervent patron of [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]]. His son [[e:emperor-yang-of-sui|Emperor Yang]] built the eastern capital at [[e:luoyang|Luoyang]] and linked the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] and [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] with the [[e:grand-canal|Grand Canal]], using vast forced labour.
sui-dynasty.e: Three failed invasions of [[s:goguryeo|Goguryeo]] between 612 and 614 drained manpower and sparked revolts across the empire. [[e:emperor-yang-of-sui|Emperor Yang]] withdrew to Jiangdu, where he was murdered in 618; [[e:emperor-gaozu-of-tang|Li Yuan]], who had taken [[e:changan|Chang'an]], founded the [[s:tang-dynasty|Tang Dynasty]], which kept most Sui institutions.

shabankara.t: A Kurdish tribal confederation of eastern Fars that overthrew the last Buyids of Shiraz and ruled from the fortress of Ij for three centuries.
shabankara.o: The Shabankara were Kurdish pastoral tribes in the uplands of eastern [[e:fars|Fars]], around Darabgerd. In 1062 their chief Fadluya (Fadlawayh) seized [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] from the last Buyid ruler. He soon came into conflict with the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]], which defeated him, and he died a prisoner around 1071.
shabankara.r: After Fadluya the Shabankara chiefs held the region of Shabankara with its capital at the fortress of Ij, near modern Estahban, ruling as [[e:vassal|vassals]] of the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]], the [[s:salghurid-dynasty|Salghurid dynasty]] and later the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]]. Their society combined pastoral nomadism with control of irrigated farmland and [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] between [[e:fars|Fars]] and [[e:kerman|Kerman]]. Under the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] they paid tribute while keeping their tribal leadership.
shabankara.e: In the 14th century the Shabankara were weakened by Ilkhanid succession wars. In 1355 the [[s:muzaffarid-dynasty|Muzaffarid dynasty]] took Ij and ended their rule.

sultanate-of-angoche.t: A Swahili Muslim sultanate on the Mozambique coast that traded inland past the Portuguese and resisted colonial conquest until 1910.
sultanate-of-angoche.o: Angoche was founded on coastal islands in the late 15th century by [[e:swahili|Swahili]] settlers linked to [[s:kilwa-sultanate|Kilwa]]. It was already an established trading town when the Portuguese arrived, and it served as an alternative outlet for gold and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from the [[e:zambezi|Zambezi]] valley, bypassing Portuguese-controlled [[e:sofala|Sofala]] and later [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]] Island.
sultanate-of-angoche.r: The sultan ruled with a council of leading [[e:swahili|Swahili]] lineages, and the town was a centre of Islamic learning and [[e:sufism|Sufi]] brotherhoods for the coast. Trade in [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and, in the 19th century, slaves for French and Brazilian buyers made it wealthy. Under Musa Mohamed Sahib Quanto in the 1860s Angoche expanded inland among the Makua.
sultanate-of-angoche.e: Portuguese forces occupied Angoche in 1861 and again in the 1890s, but resistance led by the Makua and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] continued. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Farelay fought on until his capture in 1910, when the sultanate was absorbed into [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]].

scalovians.t: Baltic people of the lower Neman river, between the Prussians and Lithuanians, conquered by the Teutonic Order in the 1270s.
scalovians.o: The Scalovians, or Skalvians, lived on both banks of the lower Neman in what is now the Kaliningrad region of [[e:russia|Russia]] and western [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]]. They were related to the Prussians and [[s:curonians|Curonians]], and their territory lay on the river route linking the Baltic coast with inland [[e:lithuania|Lithuania]].
scalovians.r: They lived in farming and fishing communities defended by hillforts, including Ragnit on the Neman. Their position made them a buffer between the Teutonic Order and [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]], and they traded and intermarried with both Prussians and Lithuanians.
scalovians.e: The Teutonic Order campaigned against them from the 1270s, and by 1277 Scalovia was subdued. The Order built Ragnit castle in 1289 on the site of a Scalovian fort. Many Scalovians fled to [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]], and the region later became part of the area known as [[e:lithuania|Lithuania]] Minor.

saguntum.t: The Iberian town of Arse, Rome's ally, whose siege and destruction by Hannibal in 219 BCE started the Second Punic War.
saguntum.o: Saguntum, called Arse by its inhabitants, grew in the 5th century BCE on a long rocky hill above the Palancia river, near the coast north of [[e:valencia|Valencia]], within the Edetanian world. Greek writers wrongly believed it had been founded by settlers from Zakynthos.
saguntum.r: It was a prosperous Iberian town trading by sea with [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and [[e:phoenicians|Phoenicians]] and minting [[e:silver|silver]] coins with the legend Arse. In the 220s BCE it made an alliance with [[e:rome|Rome]], though it lay south of the [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]], the limit agreed between Rome and Hasdrubal in 226 BCE.
saguntum.e: In 219 BCE [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] besieged Saguntum for eight months and took it, and [[e:rome|Rome's]] declaration of war on [[e:carthage|Carthage]] followed. The Scipios recaptured the town in 212 BCE and restored its people. Saguntum flourished as a Roman municipium, whose [[e:theatre|theatre]] and walls still survive.

state-of-buenos-aires.t: The province of Buenos Aires as a separate state, which broke away from the Argentine Confederation in 1852 and then reunited the nation on its terms.
state-of-buenos-aires.o: After Justo José de Urquiza overthrew Juan Manuel de Rosas at Caseros in 1852, he called a congress that would reduce Buenos Aires's control of customs revenue. On 11 September 1852 the province rebelled against him, rejected the national constitution of 1853 and in 1854 adopted its own constitution as the State of Buenos Aires.
state-of-buenos-aires.r: Buenos Aires kept the revenues of its port, the country's main source of income, while the [[s:argentine-confederation|Argentine Confederation]] governed from Paraná. Leaders such as Valentín Alsina and Bartolomé Mitre built schools, railways and a modern administration. Immigration and wool exports grew. Tension with the confederation led to tariff wars and armed conflict.
state-of-buenos-aires.e: Urquiza defeated Buenos Aires at Cepeda in 1859, and the Pact of San José de Flores brought it back into the confederation after constitutional amendments. Conflict resumed, and Mitre's victory at Pavón in 1861 led to national reunification under Buenos Aires's leadership as the [[s:argentine-republic|Argentine Republic]].

seljuk-sultanate-of-iraq.t: The western branch of the Great Seljuks, ruling western Iran and Iraq from Hamadan while real power slipped to their atabegs and the caliphs.
seljuk-sultanate-of-iraq.o: When [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Muhammad I Tapar died in 1118, his son Mahmud II succeeded to the western lands of the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]], while his uncle Sanjar kept Khurasan as senior sultan. The western sultanate, centred on [[e:hamadan|Hamadan]], covered 'Persian [[e:iraq|Iraq]]' (the Jibal), [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] and Arab Iraq.
seljuk-sultanate-of-iraq.r: The sultans depended on Turkish [[e:emir|emirs]] who served as atabegs (guardians) of young princes and often held real power, most notably the [[s:eldiguzids|Eldiguzids]] of [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]]. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mas'ud defeated the [[e:caliphate|caliph]] al-Mustarshid, who was murdered in 1135, but the Abbasid caliphs gradually regained control of [[e:iraq|Iraq]], and Muhammad II's siege of [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]] in 1157 failed. Persian court culture and patronage continued, with poets and historians at [[e:hamadan|Hamadan]].
seljuk-sultanate-of-iraq.e: [[e:tughril|Tughril]] III tried to free himself from the [[s:eldiguzids|Eldiguzids]], but he was killed near Ray in 1194 by the Khwarazmshah Tekish of the [[s:khwarazmian-empire|Khwarazmian Empire]], ending Seljuk rule in [[e:iran|Iran]].

seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.t: The Aleppo share of Tutush's realm under his son Ridwan, a weak state that paid tribute to Antioch and allied with the Assassins.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.o: After Tutush I fell in battle in 1095, his son Ridwan secured [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] and northern [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]], while his brother Duqaq took [[e:damascus|Damascus]]. Their quarrels divided Muslim [[e:syria|Syria]] at the moment the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] arrived.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.r: Ridwan lost territory to the [[s:principality-of-antioch|Principality of Antioch]] and paid tribute to Tancred. Unpopular with the [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] population, he relied on the [[e:nizari-ismaili-state|Nizari Ismailis]], allowing them a mission house in [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] and using their assassins against rivals. He also rejected a Seljuk-led counter-[[e:crusade|crusade]] in 1111 by closing the city's gates. After his death in 1113 his sons [[e:alp-arslan|Alp Arslan]] al-Akhras and [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Shah were puppets of the [[e:eunuch|eunuch]] Lu'lu' and other officers.
seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo.e: Threatened by the [[s:franks|Franks]], [[e:aleppo|Aleppo's]] notables turned to outside protectors, and in 1117-1118 the city passed to the Artuqid Ilghazi, later part of the [[s:artuqids-of-mardin|Artuqids of Mardin]]'s sphere and then the [[s:zengid-dynasty|Zengid dynasty]].

second-taifa-of-mertola.t: A Sufi-led rebel state in the Algarve whose leader Ibn Qasi rose against the Almoravids and opened the way for the Almohads.
second-taifa-of-mertola.o: Ibn Qasi, a former tax official turned [[e:sufism|Sufi]] teacher, gathered disciples called the Muridun in the western Algarve. In 1144, as Almoravid rule weakened, his followers seized Mértola, and he proclaimed himself [[e:imam|imam]] and mahdi.
second-taifa-of-mertola.r: The movement combined religious reform with rebellion against Almoravid taxes and jurists. Ibn Qasi was allied for a time with Ibn al-Mundhir of Silves and Sidray ibn [[e:wazir|Wazir]] of Beja, but they soon turned against him. He was among the first to appeal to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] in [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], then sought support from [[e:afonso-i-of-kongo|Afonso I]] of Portugal.
second-taifa-of-mertola.e: His alliance with Portugal angered his own supporters, who killed him in Silves in 1151. Mértola passed to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]], and his mystical writings were later studied by Ibn Arabi.

seljuk-sultanate-of-kerman.t: A branch of the Seljuk dynasty that ruled Kerman in south-eastern Iran for nearly 150 years and extended its power across the sea to Oman.
seljuk-sultanate-of-kerman.o: Qavurt (Qara Arslan), elder brother of [[e:alp-arslan|Alp Arslan]], took the province of [[e:kerman|Kerman]] in the 1040s as the [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] expanded across [[e:iran|Iran]]. He conquered the mountain tribes of the region and crossed the Gulf to make [[e:oman|Oman]] tributary. He later rebelled against his nephew Malik-Shah and was executed in 1074, but his sons kept Kerman.
seljuk-sultanate-of-kerman.r: The [[e:kerman|Kerman]] [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]] ruled from Bardasir (Kerman city) with Turkish troops and Persian officials. Arslan Shah I (1101 to 1142) presided over a period of prosperity based on trade routes from the Gulf ports of [[s:kingdom-of-ormus|Hormuz]] and Tiz to Khurasan, and the rulers built mosques, [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] and [[e:caravanserai|caravanserais]]. The dynasty was largely independent of the main Seljuk line.
seljuk-sultanate-of-kerman.e: After [[e:tughril|Tughril]] Shah's death in 1170, his sons fought a long civil war, inviting outside intervention. In 1186 [[e:oghuz-turks|Oghuz Turks]] under Malik [[e:dinar|Dinar]] took [[e:kerman|Kerman]], ending the dynasty.

shailodbhava-dynasty.t: A dynasty of coastal Odisha ruling the land of Kongoda, linked to some of the earliest surviving temples of Bhubaneswar.
shailodbhava-dynasty.o: The Shailodbhavas, whose name means born of the rock, ruled Kongoda, the coastal region of southern Odisha around Ganjam and Puri, from the 6th century. Madhavaraja II began as a feudatory of Shashanka of the [[s:gauda-kingdom|Gauda Kingdom]] and asserted independence after Shashanka's death.
shailodbhava-dynasty.r: The dynasty is known from [[e:copper|copper]]-plate grants in [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]], which describe a legendary origin from a rock and record land given to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]]. The kings were Shaivas, and the Parashurameshvara temple in Bhubaneswar, one of the oldest surviving temples of the [[s:kingdom-of-kalinga|Kalinga]] style, is generally dated to their time. Xuanzang described Kongoda as a strong kingdom with good harbours.
shailodbhava-dynasty.e: In the first half of the 8th century the Shailodbhavas were displaced by the [[s:bhauma-kara-dynasty|Bhauma-Kara dynasty]], which unified much of coastal Odisha.

sumbawa-sultanate.t: Sultanate of the Samawa people in western Sumbawa, closely tied to Makassar and known for its great wooden palace.
sumbawa-sultanate.o: The Samawa lands of western Sumbawa accepted [[e:islam|Islam]] in the 17th century under the influence of the [[s:gowa-sultanate|Gowa Sultanate]] of Makassar, which had campaigned on the island. After the fall of Makassar the region came under the [[s:dutch-east-india-company-territories|Dutch East India Company]], and a Muslim sultanate based at Sumbawa Besar was established by the 1670s, its rulers marrying into Makassarese and Bugis royal families.
sumbawa-sultanate.r: The sultan ruled with a council of ministers and Islamic officials over [[e:rice|rice]]-growing lowlands and upland villages. Sumbawa exported horses, sappanwood, honey and rice. The Istana Dalam Loka, a vast [[e:timber|timber]] palace on stilts built in 1885, remains a celebrated example of Sumbawan architecture.
sumbawa-sultanate.e: The sultanate continued as a self-governing domain of the [[s:dutch-east-indies|Dutch East Indies]] and joined the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] after independence. Its administrative powers were abolished in 1958, though the royal title was revived in a ceremonial form in 2011.

sultanate-of-dahlak.t: An island sultanate in the Red Sea off Eritrea that controlled pearl fisheries and shipping between Egypt, Arabia and Ethiopia.
sultanate-of-dahlak.o: The Dahlak archipelago was drawn into the Islamic world early, serving as a place of exile under the [[e:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyads]]. By the 10th century a local Muslim dynasty ruled from Dahlak Kebir, the largest island, controlling the sea approaches to the Ethiopian coast and the port of [[e:massawa|Massawa]].
sultanate-of-dahlak.r: The sultans grew rich from pearls, from customs on ships trading slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and hides from the African mainland, and from their position on the route to [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] and [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. Hundreds of Arabic tombstones from the 10th to 13th centuries record merchants, scholars and officials. The sultans often paid tribute to rulers in [[e:yemen|Yemen]] and dealt with Christian [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] as both trade partner and rival.
sultanate-of-dahlak.e: The sultanate declined as trade shifted, and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] took [[e:massawa|Massawa]] and the islands in 1557, incorporating them into the [[s:habesh-eyalet|Habesh Eyalet]]. Its cemeteries and cisterns on Dahlak Kebir are among the main medieval Islamic sites in the [[e:horn-of-africa|Horn of Africa]].

southwestern-caucasian-republic.t: A short-lived Muslim provisional government centred on Kars after the Ottoman withdrawal of 1918, dissolved by the British in 1919.
southwestern-caucasian-republic.o: Under the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|Armistice]] of Mudros in October 1918, the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] had to withdraw from Kars, Ardahan and Batum, lands it had gained by the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk. Local Muslim leaders, encouraged by departing Ottoman officers, formed a provisional national government in Kars in December 1918 to keep the region out of Armenian control.
southwestern-caucasian-republic.r: Led by Cihangiroglu Ibrahim Bey and a council of local notables, the government claimed Kars, Ardahan, Batum, Nakhchivan and adjoining districts, organised militias and held elections. It had little real administration and lacked international recognition, while Armenian and Georgian forces pressed their claims.
southwestern-caucasian-republic.e: In April 1919 British troops occupied Kars, arrested its leaders and deported them to Malta, and the district was handed to the [[s:first-republic-of-armenia|First Republic of Armenia]]. Kars returned to [[e:turkey|Turkey]] in 1920 after the Turkish-Armenian War.

state-of-muskogee.t: A self-proclaimed Creek and Seminole state in Spanish Florida led by the adventurer William Augustus Bowles, which challenged Spain for four years.
state-of-muskogee.o: William Augustus Bowles, a Maryland-born Loyalist who had married into the [[s:muscogee-confederacy|Muscogee Confederacy]], returned to Florida in 1799 after escaping Spanish captivity. Backed by British trading interests and some Creek and [[s:seminole-nation|Seminole]] leaders, he proclaimed the State of Muskogee, with its seat at the Miccosukee towns near present-day Tallahassee, and declared himself its director general.
state-of-muskogee.r: Muskogee was less a working state than Bowles's project for an independent Native nation allied to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]]. He issued proclamations, granted commissions to privateers and declared war on [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1800, briefly capturing the Spanish fort of San Marcos de Apalache. He tried to break the trading monopoly of the firm Panton, Leslie and Company.
state-of-muskogee.e: [[e:spain|Spain]] offered a reward for Bowles, and Creek leaders allied with the [[s:united-states|United States]] turned against him. In 1803 he was seized at a council at Hickory Ground and handed to the Spanish. He died in Morro Castle in Havana in 1805, and the state vanished with him.

sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate.t: The British colony at Freetown, founded as a home for freed slaves, which became the base of the anti-slave-trade squadron and the cradle of Krio culture.
sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate.o: After the failure of the [[s:province-of-freedom|Province of Freedom]], the [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]] Company brought about 1,100 Black Loyalists from [[s:colony-of-nova-scotia|Nova Scotia]] under John Clarkson, who founded Freetown in 1792. [[s:jamaican-maroons|Jamaican Maroons]] arrived in 1800. The company could not pay its way, and in 1808 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] made the settlement a crown colony.
sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate.r: Freetown became the base of the [[e:royal-navy|Royal Navy]] squadron suppressing the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] and the seat of courts that freed captured slaves. Tens of thousands of these liberated Africans settled there, and with the earlier settlers formed the Krio people, Protestant and English-educated. Fourah Bay College, founded in 1827, trained clergy and clerks for much of [[e:west-africa|West Africa]]. In 1896 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the interior.
sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate.e: A hut tax provoked the Hut Tax War of 1898, led by Bai Bureh. Elections and constitutional reforms in the 1950s brought Milton Margai to power, and [[e:sierra-leone|Sierra Leone]] became independent on 27 April 1961.
sierra-leone-colony-and-protectorate.re: Protestant Christianity, Sunni Islam, traditional religion

sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.t: The seat of the Qawasim, a seafaring dynasty whose fleets challenged the British in the Gulf and who joined the UAE in 1972.
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.o: The Qawasim, an Arab tribe on the northern coast of the [[e:oman|Oman]] peninsula, established themselves at [[e:ras|Ras]] al-Khaimah, near the old port of Julfar, in the early 18th century. They built a maritime power with branches on both shores of the Gulf, including Lingeh in [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sharjah]].
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.r: The Qawasim lived from pearling, trade and sea warfare. Their attacks on shipping, partly linked to alliance with the [[s:emirate-of-diriyah|Emirate of Diriyah]], led the British to call the area the Pirate Coast. British expeditions in 1809 and 1819 destroyed their fleet and town, and the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 made the sheikhdom one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]]. It was ruled with [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sharjah]] at times and separated permanently in 1921.
sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah.e: [[e:ras|Ras]] al-Khaimah stayed out of the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] at its founding in 1971, hoping for oil and a dispute over the Tunb islands, seized by [[e:iran|Iran]]. It joined in February 1972 under Sheikh Saqr bin Muhammad Al Qasimi.

seha-river-land.t: The Seha River Land, a Hittite vassal kingdom of western Anatolia, caught between the Hittites and the Mycenaean Greeks.
seha-river-land.o: The Seha River Land formed part of the old [[s:arzawa|Arzawa]] coalition in the valley of a western Anatolian river, probably the Bakırçay or Gediz. After the fall of Arzawa c. 1320 BCE, Mursili II confirmed Manapa-Tarhunta as its king under a Hittite treaty.
seha-river-land.r: Its rulers governed the river valley and, at times, the nearby island of Lazpa, probably Lesbos. A letter from Manapa-Tarhunta reports on events in [[s:wilusa|Wilusa]], and King Masturi married a sister of [[e:muwatalli-ii|Muwatalli II]] of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]].
seha-river-land.e: Under [[e:tudhaliya-iv|Tudhaliya IV]] a king backed by [[s:ahhiyawa|Ahhiyawa]] rebelled and was defeated. The kingdom fades from the record with the collapse of the [[s:hittite-empire|Hittite Empire]] c. 1180 BCE.

serbian-vojvodina.t: Self-proclaimed Serbian autonomous province in southern Hungary during the revolution of 1848, whose name lives on in today's Vojvodina.
serbian-vojvodina.o: As [[e:hungary|Hungary]] asserted its independence in spring 1848, [[e:serbs|Serbs]] of southern Hungary feared Magyarisation. A national assembly at Sremski Karlovci in May 1848 proclaimed the Serbian Vojvodina in Srem, Baranya, Bačka and Banat, elected Josif Rajačić patriarch and Colonel Stevan Šupljikac voivode, and set up a Main Board led by Đorđe Stratimirović.
serbian-vojvodina.r: The Vojvodina was a wartime administration rather than a settled state. Its forces, joined by volunteers from the [[s:principality-of-serbia|Principality of Serbia]], fought Hungarian revolutionary armies in bitter ethnic warfare across Bačka and Banat. The Serb leaders allied with the [[s:county-of-habsburg|Habsburg]] court against [[e:budapest|Budapest]], hoping for autonomy as a reward.
serbian-vojvodina.e: After [[e:hungary|Hungary's]] defeat in 1849, [[e:vienna|Vienna]] created the [[s:voivodeship-of-serbia-and-banat-of-temeschwar|Voivodeship of Serbia and Banat of Temeschwar]], an Austrian crown land run by German-speaking officials rather than by the [[e:serbs|Serbs]]. The name Vojvodina, however, became established for the region.

second-french-empire.t: Napoleon III's empire, which rebuilt Paris, built railways and a colonial empire, and collapsed after defeat by Prussia at Sedan in 1870.
second-french-empire.o: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, president of the [[s:french-second-republic|French Second Republic]], seized dictatorial power in a coup in December 1851. A plebiscite approved restoring the empire, and on 2 December 1852 he became Emperor [[e:napoleon-iii|Napoleon III]].
second-french-empire.r: The early empire was authoritarian, with censorship and managed elections. Baron Haussmann rebuilt [[e:paris|Paris]] with boulevards and sewers, and railways, banks and [[e:departement|department]] stores expanded. [[e:france|France]] fought in the [[e:crimea|Crimea]], helped unify [[e:italy|Italy]] and gained Nice and [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Savoy]] in 1860, but the Mexican intervention failed. From 1860 the regime liberalised, becoming a parliamentary 'Liberal Empire' under Émile Ollivier in 1870.
second-french-empire.e: Provoked by [[e:otto-von-bismarck|Bismarck]], [[e:france|France]] declared war on [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] in July 1870. [[e:napoleon-iii|Napoleon III]] was captured at [[s:principality-of-sedan|Sedan]] on 2 September, and two days later the [[s:french-third-republic|French Third Republic]] was proclaimed in [[e:paris|Paris]]. He died in exile in [[e:england|England]] in 1873.

sidicini.t: Small Oscan people of northern Campania whose appeal for help against the Samnites in 343 BCE set off Rome's first war with Samnium.
sidicini.o: The Sidicini lived around Teanum Sidicinum (modern Teano) in the hills between the Roccamonfina volcano and the Volturno, bordering the [[s:aurunci|Aurunci]] and Campanians. They were an Oscan-speaking people, possibly related to the [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]] or the Ausones; their earlier history is unknown.
sidicini.r: Known mainly from Livy, they formed a small community centred on Teanum, which later issued its own coins in Oscan. In 343 BCE the [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]] attacked them; the Sidicini sought help from [[s:capua|Capua]], and Capua's appeal to [[e:rome|Rome]] began the First Samnite War. They joined the [[e:latins|Latins]] and Campanians against Rome in 340 BCE.
sidicini.e: [[e:rome|Rome]] founded the [[e:latin|Latin]] colony of Cales on land taken from the Sidicini and [[s:aurunci|Aurunci]] in 334 BCE, ending their independence. Teanum Sidicinum became a Roman ally and later a municipium and colony.

second-turkic-khaganate.t: The revived Turkic empire of Mongolia, whose Orkhon inscriptions are the earliest surviving texts in a Turkic language.
second-turkic-khaganate.o: After fifty years of [[s:later-tang|Tang]] rule, [[e:ilterish-qaghan|Ilterish Qaghan]] led a revolt in 682 and restored an independent Turkic state, with the support of the strategist [[e:tonyukuk|Tonyukuk]]. His brother Qapaghan extended its power from [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]] to the [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]].
second-turkic-khaganate.r: The [[e:khagan|khagans]] ruled from the Otuken highlands in [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]], leading a confederation of Turkic tribes in wars against the [[s:later-tang|Tang]], the Kyrgyz and the [[s:turgesh-khaganate|Turgesh Khaganate]]. Under [[e:bilge-qaghan|Bilge Qaghan]] and his brother, the general Kul Tegin, the state reached its cultural height. Their memorial stelae on the Orkhon River, written in the Old Turkic runic script, proclaim the duties of the khagan and warn the Turks against Chinese luxury.
second-turkic-khaganate.e: After [[e:bilge-qaghan|Bilge Qaghan]] was poisoned in 734, succession struggles weakened the khaganate. In 744 an alliance of the [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]], [[e:basmyls|Basmyls]] and [[s:karluk-yabgu|Karluks]] killed the last [[e:khagan|khagan]], and the [[s:uyghur-khaganate|Uyghur Khaganate]] took its place.

swedish-livonia.t: Livonia under the Swedish crown, home to Riga, one of the largest cities of the Swedish realm, and to the university founded at Dorpat in 1632.
swedish-livonia.o: Gustav II Adolf captured Riga from Poland-[[e:lithuania|Lithuania]] in 1621, and the Truce of Altmark in 1629 confirmed Swedish possession of most of the [[s:duchy-of-livonia|Duchy of Livonia]], including southern [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]] and the island of Ösel after 1645. Latgale in the south-east stayed Polish.
swedish-livonia.r: A Swedish governor-general ruled from Riga, while the Baltic German knighthood kept its diet and Lutheran church. Gustav II Adolf founded the University of Dorpat in 1632, and the pastor Ernst Glück translated the Bible into Latvian in 1685-1689. Riga's exports of grain, [[e:flax|flax]] and [[e:timber|timber]] made it one of the busiest ports of the Swedish empire. [[e:charles-xi-of-sweden|Charles XI's]] reduction of noble estates provoked the opposition of Johann Reinhold Patkul.
swedish-livonia.e: In the [[e:great-northern-war|Great Northern War]] Russian troops besieged and took Riga in 1710 after a plague-stricken defence. The [[e:treaty-of-nystad|Treaty of Nystad]] in 1721 ceded [[s:livonian-confederation|Livonia]] to [[e:russia|Russia]], where it became the [[s:governorate-of-livonia|Governorate of Livonia]]. Later Latvians and Estonians remembered the Swedish period as 'the good Swedish times'.

surasena.t: The ancient kingdom of Mathura on the Yamuna, early home of the cult of Krishna and a junction of northern trade routes.
surasena.o: Surasena emerged around Mathura on the Yamuna river, a region linked in tradition with the Yadava clans. By the 6th century BCE Buddhist sources counted it among the sixteen mahajanapadas. Its king Avantiputra, whose mother was apparently a princess of [[s:kingdom-of-avanti|Avanti]], became a follower of the Buddha through the monk Mahakaccana.
surasena.r: Mathura stood where routes from the [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]] met roads to the west and to [[e:malwa|Malwa]], which made it a busy commercial city. Buddhist texts describe it as dusty and inhospitable, yet it became a stronghold of the worship of Vasudeva-Krishna. Around 300 BCE the Greek envoy Megasthenes described the Sourasenoi as honouring Herakles, usually taken to mean Krishna, at their cities Methora and Cleisobora.
surasena.e: Surasena was absorbed by the [[s:nanda-empire|Nanda Empire]] in the 4th century BCE and then passed to the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]]. Mathura went on to become a great centre of Kushan sculpture and of [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] pilgrimage, which it remains today.

swat-state.t: A 20th-century Pashtun kingdom in the Swat valley, built by the Wali Miangul Abdul Wadud and abolished in 1969.
swat-state.o: In 1915 the Yusufzai tribes of Swat chose Sayyid Abdul Jabbar Shah as their ruler. He was replaced in 1917 by Miangul Abdul Wadud, grandson of the revered Akhund of Swat, who united the valley by force and diplomacy. The British recognised him as Wali in 1926.
swat-state.r: Abdul Wadud, known as Badshah Sahib, built a centralised state with a standing army, telephone lines, roads and forts, ruling according to Islamic law and Pashtun custom. His son Miangul Jahanzeb, Wali from 1949, expanded schools, hospitals and colleges at Saidu Sharif.
swat-state.e: Swat acceded to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in 1947 but kept internal autonomy until 1969, when it was abolished and merged into the North-West Frontier Province, now Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

second-brazilian-republic.t: The years of Getúlio Vargas's rise after the Revolution of 1930, when Brazil centralised power, gave women the vote and drifted towards dictatorship.
second-brazilian-republic.o: The Revolution of 1930 ended the [[s:first-brazilian-republic|First Brazilian Republic]] and installed Getúlio Vargas as head of a provisional government. He dissolved Congress and the state legislatures and appointed interventors to govern the states, breaking the power of the old oligarchies.
second-brazilian-republic.r: Vargas created a Ministry of Labour and began social legislation. [[e:sao-paulo|São Paulo]] rose in the Constitutionalist Revolution of 1932, which was defeated. The constitution of 1934 gave women the vote and introduced corporatist representation, and Congress elected Vargas president. Politics polarised between the fascist-inspired Integralists and the left-wing National Liberation Alliance, which launched a failed communist uprising in 1935.
second-brazilian-republic.e: Citing an invented communist plot, the Cohen Plan, Vargas staged a coup on 10 November 1937, closing Congress and creating the authoritarian [[s:estado-novo-brazil|Estado Novo (Brazil)]]. The 1934 constitution, [[e:brazil|Brazil's]] third, had lasted barely three years.

savantvadi-state.t: A Maratha state of the southern Konkan coast, ruled by the Bhonsle Sawants and known for its lacquered toys and painted Ganjifa cards.
savantvadi-state.o: The Sawant family, Bhonsle [[e:maratha-empire|Marathas]] who had served the Adil Shahi sultans of Bijapur, established themselves as rulers of the Konkan country around Sawantwadi in 1627. They were often at odds with [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]] and the later Maratha powers, as well as with the Portuguese of [[e:goa|Goa]].
savantvadi-state.r: The Sawants ruled a coastal and hilly territory of [[e:rice|rice]], coconut and cashew. Their state was long troubled by piracy disputes and internal revolts, and British officers administered it for periods in the 19th century. The court fostered crafts such as lacquered wooden toys and Ganjifa playing cards.
savantvadi-state.e: Sawantwadi merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of Maharashtra in 1960, in Sindhudurg district. Its craft traditions still flourish.

sallarid-emirate.t: A Daylamite dynasty that briefly ruled Azerbaijan and the eastern Caucasus in the 10th century, part of the so-called Iranian intermezzo between Arab and Turkic rule.
sallarid-emirate.o: The [[s:sallarid-dynasty|Sallarids]], also called Musafirids, were a Daylamite family from Tarom in the mountains south of the Caspian. After the [[s:sajid-emirate|Sajid Emirate]] collapsed, Marzuban ibn Muhammad seized [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] in 941, taking [[e:ardabil|Ardabil]] and [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]] and extending his authority to [[s:caucasian-albania|Arran]], [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] and [[s:armenia|Armenia]].
sallarid-emirate.r: Marzuban ruled through Daylamite soldiers and local governors and drew tribute from Armenian and Albanian princes and the [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvanshahs]]. The [[s:sallarid-dynasty|Sallarids]] were Ismaili-leaning Shiites ruling a largely [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] population. In 943-944 Rus raiders seized Barda, and Marzuban besieged them until disease and his forces drove them out.
sallarid-emirate.e: Marzuban was captured by the [[s:buyid-dynasty|Buyids]] in 948, and after his death in 957 his sons fought among themselves. Local Kurdish and Arab dynasties broke away, and around 981 the [[s:rawwadid-emirate|Rawwadid Emirate]] took over their remaining lands in [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

selaparang-kingdom.t: The leading Sasak kingdom of eastern Lombok, an early Muslim state of the island until conquered by Balinese Karangasem in 1740.
selaparang-kingdom.o: Selaparang was one of several Sasak principalities on Lombok, centred in the east of the island near the coast facing Sumbawa. Its early history is known mainly from Sasak tradition and the Babad Lombok. The register's founding date of 1300 is approximate, and the kingdom is said to have been subject to [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] in the 14th century.
selaparang-kingdom.r: [[e:islam|Islam]] reached Selaparang in the 16th century, traditionally through preachers sent by Sunan Prapen of [[s:giri-kedaton|Giri Kedaton]] in [[e:java|Java]]. The kingdom had ties with [[s:gowa-sultanate|Makassar]] and with Sumbawa across the strait, and its people farmed [[e:rice|rice]] and traded horses and [[e:cotton|cotton]].
selaparang-kingdom.e: From the 17th century Balinese princes of [[s:kingdom-of-karangasem|Karangasem]] expanded into western Lombok. Selaparang allied with Sumbawa against them but was defeated, and around 1740 it fell. Lombok remained under Balinese rule until the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] conquest of 1894, and Selaparang's memory endures in Sasak identity.

samanid-empire.t: A Persian dynasty ruling from Bukhara that revived New Persian as a literary language and made Transoxiana a centre of Islamic learning.
samanid-empire.o: The Samanids descended from Saman Khuda, a Persian landowner near Balkh who converted to [[e:islam|Islam]]. In 819 the Abbasid [[e:caliphate|caliph]] [[e:al-mamun|al-Ma'mun]] gave his four grandsons governorships of [[e:samarkand|Samarkand]], [[s:principality-of-ferghana|Ferghana]], [[s:principality-of-chach|Chach]] and [[e:herat|Herat]]. Nasr ibn Ahmad unified their holdings, and his brother Isma'il ibn Ahmad defeated the [[s:saffarid-dynasty|Saffarids]] in 900, ruling [[e:transoxiana|Transoxiana]] and Khurasan as Abbasid governors.
samanid-empire.r: From [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]] the [[e:emir|emirs]] ran a sophisticated bureaucracy of divans modelled on the [[e:caliphate|caliphate]], with powerful [[e:vizier|viziers]] such as al-Bal'ami and al-Jayhani. [[e:silver|Silver]] [[e:dirham|dirhams]] from Samanid mints flowed to [[e:scandinavia|Scandinavia]] through the [[e:volga|Volga]] trade in slaves and [[e:fur-trade|furs]]. The court patronised the poet Rudaki and commissioned Persian translations, while scholars such as Ibn Sina and al-Razi worked under their rule. [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni Islam]] spread to the Turkic steppe.
samanid-empire.e: Turkic slave generals gained power in the 10th century, and the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]] took Khurasan. In 999 the [[s:kara-khanid-khanate|Kara-Khanid Khanate]] captured [[e:bukhara|Bukhara]] and ended the dynasty. The Samanids are remembered in [[s:tajikistan|Tajikistan]] as founders of Tajik statehood.

shang-dynasty.t: The first Chinese dynasty confirmed by its own writing, whose oracle-bone inscriptions and bronze vessels from Anyang open the recorded history of China.
shang-dynasty.o: According to tradition [[s:later-tang|Tang]] of Shang overthrew Jie, last ruler of the Xia, around 1600 BCE. The Shang moved their capital several times, at sites such as Zhengzhou and Yanshi, until King Pan Geng settled at Yin, near modern Anyang in Henan, around 1300 BCE. From there the kings ruled the middle [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] plain.
shang-dynasty.r: The king was chief priest as well as war leader, consulting royal ancestors and the high god Di by cracking ox scapulae and turtle shells and carving the questions on them: the oldest substantial Chinese writing. Workshops cast massive bronze ritual vessels, [[e:chariot|chariots]] arrived from the steppe, and royal tombs held [[e:human-sacrifice|human sacrifices]]. The tomb of Fu Hao, a consort of King Wu Ding and a general, survived intact.
shang-dynasty.e: In 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king, Di Xin, at the Battle of Muye, and the [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]] took power. Shang descendants were given the [[s:state-of-song|State of Song]] to continue their ancestral sacrifices. The rediscovery of oracle bones in 1899 and excavations at Anyang from 1928 turned the Shang from legend into history.

shubria.t: Shubria, a Hurrian kingdom of the upper Tigris highlands that sheltered fugitives from Assyria until Esarhaddon conquered it.
shubria.o: Shubria lay in the mountains north of the upper [[e:tigris|Tigris]], between [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Kingdom of Urartu]]. It emerged as a kingdom after the [[e:late-bronze-age|Late Bronze Age]], inhabited by Hurrian speakers whose culture survived longer there than elsewhere.
shubria.r: Its kings, ruling from Uppumu, played [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] and [[s:kingdom-of-urartu|Urartu]] against each other. Shubria was known as a refuge where fugitives, deserters and escaped slaves from the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] could find asylum, a practice its kings defended.
shubria.e: When King Ik-Teshub refused to hand over fugitives, [[e:esarhaddon|Esarhaddon]] of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] captured Uppumu in 673 BCE and annexed Shubria, recording the campaign in a letter to the god [[e:assur|Ashur]].

shakya-republic.t: The small clan republic at the foot of the Himalaya into which Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, was born.
shakya-republic.o: The Shakyas were a clan claiming descent from the Ikshvaku kings, settled in the Terai on the border of modern [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Nepal]] and [[e:india|India]]. By the 7th or 6th century BCE they governed themselves from Kapilavastu, now identified either with Tilaurakot in [[e:nepal|Nepal]] or with Piprahwa in India.
shakya-republic.r: The Shakyas were ruled by an assembly of clan heads that met in a council hall, with an elected chief; the Buddha's father Suddhodana was one such leader, later remembered as a king. They farmed [[e:rice|rice]] and were proud of their lineage. Politically they were dependants of the [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kingdom of Kosala]]. A relic casket found at Piprahwa carries an inscription naming the Shakyas.
shakya-republic.e: Shortly before or after the Buddha's death the Kosalan king Vidudabha attacked Kapilavastu and massacred many Shakyas, ending the republic as an independent state. Their territory became part of [[s:kingdom-of-kosala|Kosala]] and then of [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]], and the Buddha is still called Shakyamuni, sage of the Shakyas.

seraikela-state.t: A Singh Deo-ruled state of the Chota Nagpur plateau, cradle of the masked Seraikela style of Chhau dance.
seraikela-state.o: Seraikela was founded around 1620 by Bikram Singh, a member of the Singh Deo family of Porahat, who carved out his own principality on the Kharkai river. The neighbouring state of [[s:kharsawan-state|Kharsawan]] later branched from the same family.
seraikela-state.r: The Rajas ruled a population of Ho, Santal and Oriya-speaking peasants. From 1820 the state came under British protection and later the Eastern States Agency. The court patronised the Chhau dance, whose Seraikela form uses distinctive painted masks.
seraikela-state.e: Seraikela was briefly merged into Orissa in January 1948 but was transferred to Bihar later that year after local opposition. It is now part of Seraikela [[s:kharsawan-state|Kharsawan]] district of Jharkhand.

sultanate-of-damagaram.t: A Kanuri-ruled sultanate centred on Zinder in modern Niger, which grew rich from the trans-Saharan caravan trade and became the first capital of French Niger.
sultanate-of-damagaram.o: Damagaram was founded around 1731 by Kanuri nobles from the [[s:kanem-bornu-empire|Kanem-Bornu Empire]], who settled among [[e:hausa|Hausa]] and other peoples east of the [[s:hausa-kingdoms|Hausa kingdoms]]. It began as a small [[e:vassal|vassal]] state of [[e:bornu|Bornu]], and in the mid-18th century its rulers moved their seat to Zinder, which became the capital.
sultanate-of-damagaram.r: The sultan ruled through Kanuri titled officials and slave officers, in a court modelled on [[e:bornu|Bornu]]. Zinder lay on the caravan route from [[e:kano|Kano]] to [[s:county-of-tripoli|Tripoli]] across the [[e:sahara|Sahara]], and the sultanate taxed traffic in [[e:ostrich-feather|ostrich feathers]], [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], hides, slaves and salt. Under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Tanimoune in the mid-19th century it threw off Bornu's overlordship, built up an army with firearms and locally made [[e:field-artillery|cannon]], and expanded by conquest.
sultanate-of-damagaram.e: In July 1899 a French column killed [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ahmadu dan Bassa and occupied Zinder. It served as the capital of the French territory, later the [[s:colony-of-niger|Colony of Niger]], until 1926. The sultan's palace survives and the sultanate continues as a traditional institution.

swiss-confederation.t: Modern Switzerland, a federal state of cantons that became a model of neutrality, direct democracy and multilingual government.
swiss-confederation.o: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] Act of Mediation of 1803 replaced the centralised [[s:helvetic-republic|Helvetic Republic]] with a confederation of 19 cantons, including new cantons such as Vaud, Aargau and Ticino formed from former subject lands. After Napoleon's fall the Federal Treaty of 1815 and the [[e:congress-of-vienna|Congress of Vienna]] added [[s:republic-of-geneva|Geneva]], Valais and Neuchâtel and recognised Swiss neutrality.
swiss-confederation.r: Tensions between liberal Protestant and conservative Catholic cantons led to the Sonderbund War of 1847. The federal constitution of 1848 created a federal state with a two-chamber parliament and a seven-member Federal Council, with Bern as federal city. Referendums and popular initiatives were added in 1874 and 1891. Industry, banking and tourism grew, and German, French, Italian and Romansh are national languages.
swiss-confederation.e: [[e:switzerland|Switzerland]] stayed neutral in both world wars. Women gained the federal vote only in 1971, and the canton of Jura was created in 1979. It joined the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] in 2002 but remains outside the [[e:european-union|European Union]].
