second-republic-of-venezuela.t: The republic restored by Bolívar's Admirable Campaign of 1813, which fell within a year to the royalist llanero cavalry of José Tomás Boves.
second-republic-of-venezuela.o: In 1813 Simón Bolívar invaded [[s:venezuela|Venezuela]] from New [[e:granada|Granada]] in the Admirable Campaign, while [[s:spanish-jamaica|Santiago]] Mariño liberated the east. Bolívar issued the Decree of War to the Death in June 1813 and entered Caracas in August, where he was acclaimed as the Liberator.
second-republic-of-venezuela.r: Bolívar ruled as dictator in the west and Mariño in the east, with little formal constitution. The war became extremely brutal. José Tomás Boves raised the llaneros, plainsmen of mixed race, against the [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] patriots, turning the conflict into a social war. In February 1814 Bolívar ordered the execution of hundreds of Spanish prisoners at La Guaira.
second-republic-of-venezuela.e: Boves defeated Bolívar at La Puerta in June 1814, and the population of Caracas fled east in the Emigration to the East. Boves was killed at Urica in December 1814, but the republic had collapsed, and Bolívar went into exile in [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]].

shah-armens.t: A Turkish dynasty that ruled Ahlat on Lake Van for a century, taking the title Shah-Armen, King of the Armenians.
shah-armens.o: In 1100 Sokmen al-Qutbi, a mamluk officer of the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]], took Ahlat on the north-western shore of Lake Van from the [[s:marwanids|Marwanids]]. His descendants built a principality around the lake that took its title, Shah-Armen, from the region's Armenian past.
shah-armens.r: Ahlat became a thriving city on the trade road between [[e:iran|Iran]], the Jazira and [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]], with a Muslim population alongside many [[e:armenians|Armenians]]. The longest reign was that of Sokmen II (1128-1185), who fought the Georgians and married into the Artuqid and Zengid families. The great Seljuk-era cemetery of Ahlat, with its tall carved tombstones, reflects the city's wealth in this period.
shah-armens.e: After Sokmen II died without an heir in 1185, his mamluk Begtimur ruled, followed by other slave commanders amid Ayyubid and Georgian pressure. In 1207 the Ayyubid al-Awhad took Ahlat, ending the dynasty.

sarir.t: A Christian mountain kingdom of the Avars in Dagestan, famed among Arab geographers for its golden throne and its power over the North Caucasus highlands.
sarir.o: Sarir took shape in the 6th century in the [[e:avars|Avar]] lands of mountainous [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]], centred on Khunzakh. Arab writers say its name came from a golden throne said to have been given by a Sasanian king. Little is known of its early history beyond these later accounts.
sarir.r: Its kings ruled clans of mountain farmers and herders and were reported to control many thousands of villages. Ibn Rusta and al-Masudi describe a Christian ruler and church while most subjects followed older beliefs. Sarir was tributary to the [[s:khazar-khaganate|Khazar Khaganate]], allied with the [[s:kingdom-of-alania|Kingdom of Alania]] through royal marriages, and fought the Muslim rulers of Derbent.
sarir.e: After the fall of the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]], [[e:islam|Islam]] spread into the mountains and the Christian monarchy faded in the 11th and 12th centuries. Its lands and traditions passed to the [[s:avar-khanate|Avar Khanate]], centred on the same town of Khunzakh.

spanish-louisiana.t: Spain's vast Mississippi province, ruled from New Orleans for four decades before Napoleon took it back and sold it to the United States.
spanish-louisiana.o: In the secret Treaty of Fontainebleau of 1762 [[e:france|France]] handed [[s:french-louisiana|French Louisiana]] west of the [[e:mississippi-river|Mississippi]], together with New Orleans, to its ally [[e:spain|Spain]] as compensation for losses in the [[e:seven-years-war|Seven Years' War]]. Spanish authority arrived slowly: the first governor, Antonio de Ulloa, was driven out by French [[e:criollo-people|Creole]] rebels in 1768, and Alejandro O'Reilly crushed the revolt in 1769.
spanish-louisiana.r: [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]] was governed as a dependency of the [[s:captaincy-general-of-cuba|Captaincy General of Cuba]], under [[s:new-spain|New Spain]]. [[e:spain|Spain]] kept French law and the French-speaking elite largely in place, welcomed Acadian refugees and Canary Islanders, and opened New Orleans to trade. Plantations grew [[e:indigo|indigo]], [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and later [[e:cotton|cotton]] with enslaved African labour. During the American Revolution Bernardo de Gálvez used the colony as a base to seize British posts in the [[s:province-of-west-florida|Province of West Florida]].
spanish-louisiana.e: By the Treaty of San Ildefonso in 1800 [[e:spain|Spain]] secretly returned [[e:louisiana|Louisiana]] to [[e:france|France]]. Spanish officials still governed until 1803, when the colony was handed to France and, weeks later, to the [[s:united-states|United States]] under the Louisiana Purchase, doubling American territory.

state-of-han.t: The smallest of the three states carved from Jin, home of the administrator Shen Buhai and the philosopher Han Fei, and the first state conquered by Qin.
state-of-han.o: The Han lineage, ministers of the [[s:state-of-jin|State of Jin]], shared in the destruction of the Zhi clan in 453 BCE and the partition of Jin. In 403 BCE the Zhou king recognised Marquis Jing as a ruler. In 375 BCE Han conquered the [[s:state-of-zheng|State of Zheng]] and moved its capital to Xinzheng in Henan.
state-of-han.r: Han held a central but exposed position on the routes from [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] to the eastern plain. Under Marquis Zhao the minister Shen Buhai developed methods for controlling officials, and Han's [[e:crossbow|crossbows]] and swords were renowned. Its prince Han Fei wrote the classic statement of [[e:legalism|Legalism]]. Han's attempt to exhaust Qin by having the engineer [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] Guo build a canal backfired by enriching Qin.
state-of-han.e: Han was the first of the six states to fall: in 230 BCE the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]] captured King An and made his land a commandery. The name Han was later revived for the kingdom granted to a royal descendant in 206 BCE.

sheikhdom-of-sancul.t: A Swahili Muslim sheikhdom on the mainland opposite Mozambique Island, alternately ally and rival of the Portuguese.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.o: Sancul developed on the coast south of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]] Island as a settlement of [[e:swahili|Swahili]] Muslim families, many connected to [[s:sultanate-of-angoche|Angoche]] and other coastal towns. By the 18th century it was governed by its own sheikhs, who held land and authority over neighbouring Makua communities.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.r: The sheikhs combined Islamic leadership with control of trade between the Makua interior and the coast. They sometimes allied with the Portuguese at [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]] Island and sometimes resisted their demands. In the 19th century Sancul profited from the [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]] to the Comoros, Madagascar and the French islands.
sheikhdom-of-sancul.e: Sancul joined the coastal resistance to Portuguese occupation in the late 19th century. Portuguese campaigns against the [[e:swahili|Swahili]] sheikhdoms and the [[s:sultanate-of-angoche|Sultanate of Angoche]] brought it under colonial control by 1910.

socialist-republic-of-vietnam.t: Reunified Vietnam since 1976, a one-party communist state that has become one of Asia's fastest-growing economies since the Doi Moi reforms of 1986.
socialist-republic-of-vietnam.o: After the fall of Saigon in 1975, the [[s:democratic-republic-of-vietnam|Democratic Republic of Vietnam]] and the [[s:republic-of-south-vietnam|Republic of South Vietnam]] were merged by a national assembly elected for the whole country. On 2 July 1976 the Socialist [[s:republic-of-vietnam|Republic of Vietnam]] was proclaimed, with [[e:hanoi|Hanoi]] as capital and Saigon renamed Ho Chi Minh City.
socialist-republic-of-vietnam.r: The Communist Party of [[e:vietnam|Vietnam]] rules as the sole party. Early years brought re-education camps, collectivisation in the south, the exodus of boat people, the invasion of [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia|Cambodia]] in 1978 and a border war with [[e:china|China]] in 1979. In 1986 the Doi Moi reforms introduced a market economy, and Vietnam became a major exporter of [[e:rice|rice]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]], textiles and electronics.
socialist-republic-of-vietnam.e: [[e:vietnam|Vietnam]] continues today, having normalised relations with the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1995 and joined ASEAN in 1995 and the World Trade Organization in 2007. It balances relations with [[e:china|China]] and the [[e:united-states|United States]] while disputing claims in the [[e:south-china-sea|South China Sea]].

sealand-dynasty.t: A kingdom of the southern marshes that broke away from Hammurabi's heirs and ruled the far south of Mesopotamia for nearly three centuries.
sealand-dynasty.o: Around 1732 BCE [[e:ilum-ma-ili|Ilum-ma-ili]] rebelled against [[e:samsu-iluna|Samsu-iluna]], son of [[e:hammurabi|Hammurabi]], and established control over the marshlands at the head of the Gulf, known as the Sealand. He survived Babylonian counter-attacks, and his successors held the old Sumerian heartland as the [[s:babylonian-empire|Babylonian Empire]] contracted.
sealand-dynasty.r: The Sealand kings left few monuments, and their capital is unknown, though recently published archives from the dynasty and excavations at Tell Khaiber near Ur show an organised state collecting grain and dates. Kings such as Ishkibal, Peshgaldaramesh and Ayadaragalama took archaic Sumerian-style names, and scribes copied Sumerian literature and omens, suggesting a self-conscious cultural revival. At times the dynasty held [[s:nippur|Nippur]] and Ur, and it probably controlled Gulf trade with [[s:dilmun|Dilmun]].
sealand-dynasty.e: After the [[e:hittite-sack-of-babylon|Hittite sack of Babylon]] in 1595 BCE, the [[e:kassites|Kassites]] took the north. Around 1460 BCE the Kassite king Ulamburiash conquered the Sealand, and its last king, Ea-gamil, fled to [[e:elam|Elam]]. The south was then joined to [[s:kassite-babylonia|Kassite Babylonia]].

state-of-jin.t: The dominant northern power of the Spring and Autumn period, whose hegemon Duke Wen defeated Chu at Chengpu and whose break-up in 403 BCE opened the Warring States era.
state-of-jin.o: King [[s:cheng-han|Cheng]] of Zhou enfeoffed his younger brother [[s:later-tang|Tang]] Shu Yu in the Fen River valley of southern [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]], among Rong and Di peoples. The early Jin rulers' cemetery at Beizhao near Tianma-Qucun has confirmed the location. In 678 BCE a junior branch of the house, from Quwo, seized power and made Jiang its capital.
state-of-jin.r: Duke Xian expanded Jin by conquering neighbours such as [[s:western-guo|Western Guo]] and the [[s:state-of-yu|State of Yu]], and Duke Wen, the long-exiled Chong'er, became hegemon after defeating the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] at Chengpu in 632 BCE. Jin dominated the north for a century and a half, but its dukes barred their own kinsmen from office and power passed to ministerial lineages commanding the state's armies.
state-of-jin.e: After the ministerial families of Han, Zhao and Wei destroyed the Zhi clan in 453 BCE, they divided Jin among themselves and were recognised as rulers by the Zhou king in 403 BCE, creating the [[s:state-of-han|State of Han]], the [[s:state-of-zhao|State of Zhao]] and the [[s:state-of-wei|State of Wei]]. The last Jin dukes were stripped of their remaining lands in 376 BCE.

socialist-republic-of-chile.t: A Chilean socialist republic proclaimed by military officers in June 1932, which lasted only twelve days before a counter-coup.
socialist-republic-of-chile.o: [[s:republic-of-chile|Chile]] was hit severely by the Great Depression, which collapsed nitrate and [[e:copper|copper]] exports. On 4 June 1932 the air force commander Marmaduke Grove and other officers, with the politicians Carlos Dávila and Eugenio Matte, overthrew President Juan Esteban Montero and proclaimed the Socialist Republic of Chile.
socialist-republic-of-chile.r: A governing junta announced radical measures, including the dissolution of Congress, the distribution of land, the release of goods pawned by the poor, and plans to nationalise key industries. Divisions quickly emerged between Grove's more radical socialism and Dávila's moderate state socialism. Opposition from the army and conservative groups grew.
socialist-republic-of-chile.e: On 16 June 1932 Dávila ousted Grove and Matte, who were exiled to Easter Island. Dávila ruled until September, and after further instability, elections in October 1932 returned Arturo Alessandri to the presidency of the [[s:republic-of-chile|Republic of Chile]]. Grove later helped found the Socialist Party.

sudamra-state.t: A minor chiefship of the Kathiawar peninsula, held by co-sharers of a local ruling family.
sudamra-state.o: Sudamra, also spelled Sudamda, was a small estate in Kathiawar held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is poorly documented.
sudamra-state.r: Like many small Kathiawar holdings, it was shared among members of the ruling family and supervised after 1807 by the British Kathiawar Agency. Little else is recorded in standard works.
sudamra-state.e: Sudamra merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960.

swedish-gold-coast.t: Sweden's brief foothold in West Africa, centred on Carolusborg at Cape Coast, lost to Denmark and the Dutch within thirteen years.
swedish-gold-coast.o: The Swedish [[e:africa|Africa]] Company was founded in 1649 by Louis De Geer, a Dutch-born industrialist in Swedish service. Its agent Hendrik Carloff obtained land from the local Fante rulers, and in 1653 the company built Fort Carolusborg at Cape Coast, on the coast of modern [[e:ghana|Ghana]], along with smaller lodges.
swedish-gold-coast.r: The colony was a trading enterprise, exchanging European goods for gold, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and enslaved people. It relied on agreements with local African rulers and on [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and Swedish crews, and it faced constant rivalry from the [[e:dutch-west-india-company|Dutch West India Company]] and the Danes.
swedish-gold-coast.e: In 1658 Carloff, now serving [[e:denmark|Denmark]], seized Carolusborg. The fort changed hands several times before the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] took it in 1663, ending Swedish presence in [[e:africa|Africa]]. As Cape Coast Castle under the English from 1664, it became one of the main centres of the British [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]].

sultanate-of-singora.t: A Muslim port sultanate at Songkhla on the Thai peninsula that defied Ayutthaya in the 17th century before being destroyed in 1680.
sultanate-of-singora.o: Around 1605 Dato Mogol, a Muslim leader said to be of Persian or Malay origin, established a fortified port at Singora, present-day Songkhla, on the east coast of the peninsula. It grew under his son Sulaiman, who declared independence from [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]] around 1642.
sultanate-of-singora.r: Singora prospered from trade in [[e:pepper|pepper]], [[e:tin|tin]] and [[e:rice|rice]], attracting [[e:dutch|Dutch]] and English merchants. Its rulers built strong fortifications on the hills above the town and repelled several Siamese expeditions in the mid 17th century. The population included Malays, Thais and Chinese, and the sultans were Muslims.
sultanate-of-singora.e: Under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Mustafa, King Narai of the [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya Kingdom]] sent a large force that destroyed Singora in 1680. The ruling family was spared and resettled; Sulaiman's descendants served Siam as officials, and the town was later refounded across the lagoon. The sultan's tomb survives at Hua Khao Daeng.

segontiaci.t: British people recorded only by Julius Caesar, one of five groups that submitted to him in 54 BCE during his second campaign in Britain.
segontiaci.o: The Segontiaci appear once in Caesar's Gallic War, among the peoples who surrendered after the [[s:trinovantes|Trinovantes]] made terms with [[e:rome|Rome]] in 54 BCE. The others were the [[s:iceni|Cenimagni]], [[s:ancalites|Ancalites]], [[s:bibroci|Bibroci]] and [[s:cassi|Cassi]].
segontiaci.r: Nothing is known of their government or way of life. Their territory has often been placed in northern Hampshire, around the later Roman town of Calleva, partly because a Roman-period name there has been compared with theirs, but this remains a guess.
segontiaci.e: They disappear from the record after 54 BCE. If they lived around Silchester, their lands were later part of the realm of the [[s:atrebates-britain|Atrebates (Britain)]] before the Roman conquest of 43.

southern-court.t: The rival imperial court founded by Emperor Go-Daigo in the mountains of Yoshino, which held out against the Ashikaga for more than half a century.
southern-court.o: After his [[s:kenmu-restoration|Kenmu Restoration]] collapsed, Go-Daigo escaped from [[e:kyoto|Kyoto]] late in 1336 and established his court at Yoshino in the mountains south of Nara, insisting that the regalia he carried made him the only rightful emperor.
southern-court.r: The Southern Court relied on loyal warrior families such as the Kusunoki, Kitabatake and Nitta, and on regional bases in Kyushu, where Prince Kaneyoshi held power for years and dealt with Ming envoys. Kitabatake Chikafusa wrote the Jinno shotoki to argue its legitimacy. Its emperors after Go-Daigo were Go-Murakami, Chokei and Go-Kameyama.
southern-court.e: Militarily outmatched, Go-Kameyama agreed in 1392 to hand the regalia to the Northern emperor on a promise that the lines would alternate, which was never kept. In 1911 the government declared the Southern line legitimate.

sardargadh-state.t: A minor chiefship of southern Kathiawar, one of the small estates under British supervision.
sardargadh-state.o: Sardargadh was a small estate in the [[s:junagadh-state|Sorath]] region of Kathiawar, held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is poorly documented.
sardargadh-state.r: The ruler held a few villages and paid tribute to [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh]], coming under British supervision after 1807 in the Kathiawar Agency. Standard references record little else.
sardargadh-state.e: Sardargadh merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960.

segovellauni.t: Small Gallic people of the middle Rhône valley around Valence, absorbed into Rome's first province in Gaul.
segovellauni.o: Known only from Pliny and Ptolemy, the Segovellauni lived on the left bank of the Rhône around modern Valence, between the [[s:allobroges|Allobroges]] to the north and the [[s:cavares|Cavares]] to the south. They may have been dependents of the Allobroges or the Cavares.
segovellauni.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or society beyond their position on the Rhône corridor, the main route between the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] and central Gaul.
segovellauni.e: Their land passed under Roman control after the victories over the [[s:allobroges|Allobroges]] and [[s:arverni|Arverni]] in 121 BCE. The Roman colony of Valentia (Valence) was founded in their territory, probably under Caesar or Augustus.

sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.t: The independent Sicily proclaimed in the revolution of 1848, which deposed the Bourbons and held out for sixteen months.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.o: On 12 January 1848 Palermo rose against Ferdinand II of the [[s:kingdom-of-the-two-sicilies|Kingdom of the Two Sicilies]], one of the first revolutions of that year in [[e:europe|Europe]]. The rebels took most of the island, revived the Sicilian constitution of 1812 and formed a government under the veteran admiral Ruggero Settimo.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.r: The Sicilian parliament declared the [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] dynasty deposed in April 1848 and in July offered the crown to Ferdinando, Duke of [[s:republic-of-genoa|Genoa]], son of Charles Albert of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]], who declined. The state had a government, parliament and army, but was divided between moderates and radicals and lacked foreign support.
sicilian-kingdom-of-1848.e: Ferdinand II's troops bombarded and took Messina in September 1848. The [[s:ile-bourbon|Bourbon]] offensive resumed in 1849, Catania fell in April and Palermo surrendered in May 1849, ending the kingdom.

shonai-domain.t: A Sakai family domain on the Sea of Japan coast that fought unbeaten for the shogunate in 1868 and was then treated leniently.
shonai-domain.o: In 1622 the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] moved [[s:sakai|Sakai]] Tadakatsu, from a trusted Tokugawa [[e:vassal|vassal]] family, to Shonai in Dewa with about 138,000 koku. He made Tsuruoka his castle town; the port of Sakata lay within the domain.
shonai-domain.r: Shonai's [[e:rice|rice]] plain was among the most productive in the north, and the Homma merchant family of Sakata, among the richest in [[e:japan|Japan]], backed the domain's finances. In 1840 the [[e:shogun|shogunate]] ordered Shonai's lord to be transferred, but protests by farmers and townspeople led to the order being cancelled. In the 1860s Shonai policed Edo and in 1867 burned the [[e:satsuma-domain|Satsuma]] residence there.
shonai-domain.e: In the [[e:boshin-war|Boshin War]] Shonai troops won their battles but surrendered in 1868 after allies collapsed. Saigo Takamori arranged lenient terms, and Shonai men later compiled his sayings. The domain became part of Yamagata Prefecture in 1871.

second-taifa-of-badajoz.t: Badajoz under the Banu Wazir family, one of the western regimes that arose when Almoravid rule broke down in the 1140s.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.o: In 1145 members of the Banu [[e:wazir|Wazir]], the family of Sidray ibn Wazir of the [[s:taifa-of-beja-and-evora|Taifa of Beja and Évora]], took control of [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]] as part of the revolt against the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] that had begun in the Algarve.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, the state was a frontier territory on the Guadiana facing the [[s:kingdom-of-portugal|Kingdom of Portugal]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-leon|Kingdom of León]], governed by a military family that switched alliances as needed.
second-taifa-of-badajoz.e: By 1150 the Banu [[e:wazir|Wazir]] had submitted to the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]], who kept [[e:badajoz|Badajoz]] as a frontier stronghold. Alfonso IX of León took the city in 1230.

sultanate-of-bangassou.t: The Nzakara sultanate on the Mbomou River, a slave-raiding state that survived by dealing with both Belgian and French colonisers.
sultanate-of-bangassou.o: The Nzakara state on the Mbomou River was ruled by a Bandia dynasty related to the Zande kingdoms. In the later 19th century its ruler Bangassou, whose name was given to the state and its capital, built it into a regional power.
sultanate-of-bangassou.r: Bangassou took captives and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] from neighbouring peoples and sold them to northern traders from the [[e:nile|Nile]] basin and [[s:sultanate-of-dar-al-kuti|Dar al Kuti]], acquiring guns in return. Visitors described a large court with many wives and dependants. Power rested on control of trade and on armed retainers rather than on fixed borders.
sultanate-of-bangassou.e: Bangassou signed a treaty with the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] in 1890, but the 1894 Franco-Congolese agreement put his capital on the French side. He died in 1907, and the French reduced the sultanate to an administrative chiefdom within [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]].

surakarta-sunanate.t: Senior successor of the Javanese Mataram dynasty, whose Susuhunan kept an influential court at Surakarta until the revolution of 1946.
surakarta-sunanate.o: After the Chinese War sacked the court at Kartasura in 1742, Susuhunan Pakubuwono II moved the [[s:mataram-sultanate|Mataram]] capital to Surakarta in 1745. The Treaty of Giyanti in 1755 divided the realm, leaving Pakubuwono III with the eastern half while the [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta Sultanate]] took the west, and in 1757 further lands went to [[s:mangkunegaran|Mangkunegaran]].
surakarta-sunanate.r: The Susuhunan presided over the most elaborate court of [[e:java|Java]], regarded as the guardian of Javanese tradition, with royal poets such as Ronggowarsito, gamelan ensembles, bedhaya dances and Islamic ritual. Real power rested increasingly with the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] resident, while royal lands were leased to European [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and tobacco planters in the 19th century.
surakarta-sunanate.e: Unlike [[s:yogyakarta-sultanate|Yogyakarta]], the court did not win popular support during the Indonesian revolution. An anti-royalist movement in 1946 led the [[s:indonesia|Republic of Indonesia]] to end its special status, and Surakarta became an ordinary city. The kraton survives with a ceremonial Susuhunan.

sultanate-of-the-geledi.t: A Somali sultanate of the fertile lower Shabelle valley that became the strongest power in southern Somalia in the 19th century.
sultanate-of-the-geledi.o: In the early 18th century the Geledi clan, led by the Gobroon dynasty, rose to power at Afgooye on the Shabelle river after the fall of the [[s:ajuran-sultanate|Ajuran Sultanate]]. Its founder Ibrahim Adeer is remembered for overthrowing local rivals and establishing the dynasty's religious prestige.
sultanate-of-the-geledi.r: The sultans controlled rich farmland where grain and [[e:cotton|cotton]] were grown, partly by slave labour, and exported produce through [[s:sultanate-of-mogadishu|Mogadishu]], Merca and [[s:barawa|Barawa]]. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Yusuf Mahamud Ibrahim made the Geledi the leading power of the south, attacking the Bardera jihadists in 1843. Islamic learning flourished, and the sultans held annual ceremonies at Afgooye.
sultanate-of-the-geledi.e: [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ahmed Yusuf was killed fighting the Bimaal in 1878, and the sultanate declined. In 1908 the Geledi accepted Italian authority, and the sultanate was absorbed into [[s:italian-somaliland|Italian Somaliland]], the Gobroon line surviving as a traditional house.

serbian-empire.t: Stefan Dušan's short-lived Serbian Empire, the largest medieval Balkan state of its day, with its own patriarchate and law code.
serbian-empire.o: Stefan Dušan, king of the [[s:kingdom-of-serbia-medieval|Kingdom of Serbia (medieval)]] from 1331, took advantage of the Byzantine civil war to conquer Macedonia, [[s:albania|Albania]], Epirus and Thessaly. In 1346 he raised the Serbian archbishopric to a patriarchate at Peć and was crowned Emperor of the [[e:serbs|Serbs]] and [[e:greeks|Greeks]] at Skopje.
serbian-empire.r: Dušan ruled through Serbian nobles and Byzantine-style titles, issuing a law code, Dušan's Code, in 1349 and 1354. Greek lands kept Byzantine administration, and [[e:silver|silver]] mines such as Novo Brdo financed the state. Monasteries on [[s:monastic-community-of-mount-athos|Mount Athos]] received his patronage. He aimed at [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] itself but died suddenly in 1355.
serbian-empire.e: Under his son Uroš V the great nobles became effectively independent. The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] destroyed the army of Vukašin and Jovan Uglješa at the Maritsa in 1371, and Uroš died the same year, ending the empire. Its lands passed to [[s:moravian-serbia|Moravian Serbia]], the [[s:kingdom-of-prilep|Kingdom of Prilep]] and other successors.

sultanate-of-ifat.t: The leading Muslim power of medieval Ethiopia, ruled by the Walasma dynasty and the main rival of the Solomonic emperors for over a century.
sultanate-of-ifat.o: In 1285 Umar Walasma, of a family claiming Arab descent, conquered the old [[s:sultanate-of-shewa|Sultanate of Shewa]] and founded a new state in the eastern highlands of [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]]. [[e:ifat-sultanate|Ifat]] controlled the trade route from the interior to the port of [[e:zeila|Zeila]] and soon drew other Muslim principalities, such as [[s:sultanate-of-dawaro|Dawaro]] and [[s:fatagar-sultanate|Fatagar]], into its orbit.
sultanate-of-ifat.r: [[e:ifat-sultanate|Ifat]] was a prosperous Muslim state of towns, farms and caravans, exporting slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]], gold and horses through [[e:zeila|Zeila]] to [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. The Arab writer [[e:al-umari|al-Umari]] described it as the largest of the seven Muslim states of Abyssinia, with a well-ordered court. Its sultans alternated between paying tribute to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] and rebelling: Sabr ad-Din I's revolt was crushed by [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] in 1332.
sultanate-of-ifat.e: Repeated wars ended in disaster when the emperor Yeshaq's forces killed [[e:sultan|Sultan]] [[e:saad-ad-din-ii|Sa'ad ad-Din II]], traditionally near [[e:zeila|Zeila]], in the early 15th century. His sons fled to [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]], returned and founded the [[s:adal-sultanate|Adal Sultanate]] further east, which carried on the Walasma line and the struggle against [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]].

sirmur-state.t: A Rajput hill state of the Shivaliks ruled from Nahan, whose name was given to the Sirmoor Battalion, the first of the British Army's Gurkha regiments.
sirmur-state.o: The ruling Prakash dynasty traditionally dates its rule to 1095, when a [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] prince settled in the hills between the Yamuna and the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]]. Raja Karam Prakash founded the town of Nahan as the capital in 1621.
sirmur-state.r: Sirmur's Rajas held a strategic position on the routes from the plains to the hills and to the Doon valley. Like its neighbours it fell to the Gurkhas of the [[s:kingdom-of-nepal|Kingdom of Nepal]], from 1803 to 1815. Raja Shamsher Prakash (r. 1856–1898) modernised the state, founding the Nahan Foundry and building roads and schools.
sirmur-state.e: The British restored the dynasty in 1815 and raised the Sirmoor Battalion there from former Gurkha soldiers. Sirmur merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948 and is now Sirmaur district.

sorbs.t: West Slavic tribes between the Saale and the Bóbr whose descendants, the Sorbs of Lusatia, are still a recognised minority in Germany.
sorbs.o: Slavic groups settled the lands east of the Saale and Elbe in the 6th and 7th centuries. The Chronicle of Fredegar records that in 631 the Sorb prince Dervan left Frankish allegiance and joined [[s:samos-empire|Samo's Empire]]. Their territory included the regions later called Daleminzia, Milzenland (Upper Lusatia) and Lusatia.
sorbs.r: The Sorbs were organised in small tribal territories, each centred on fortified strongholds (gords) such as those at Tornow and Raddusch, with no lasting central ruler. They farmed, raised livestock and worshipped Slavic gods. Frankish sources record frequent wars and tribute payments, and [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne's]] Limes Sorabicus marked the boundary with them.
sorbs.e: [[e:east-francia|East Francia's]] king Henry the Fowler took the Daleminzian stronghold of Gana in 929 and founded Meissen. By 932 the Sorbian tribes were tributary, and the [[s:marca-geronis|Marca Geronis]] and later the [[s:margraviate-of-meissen|Margraviate of Meissen]] and Lusatia absorbed them. Sorbs survive today in Lusatia, keeping their language.

strandzha-commune.t: Short-lived insurgent administration in the Strandzha mountains during the Preobrazhenie Uprising of 1903 against Ottoman rule.
strandzha-commune.o: In August 1903, alongside the Ilinden Uprising in Macedonia, the Adrianople revolutionary district of the Internal Macedonian-Adrianople Revolutionary Organisation launched the Preobrazhenie Uprising in eastern Thrace, on the Feast of the Transfiguration. Bulgarian rebels drove Ottoman forces out of much of the Strandzha mountains, near the Bulgarian border and the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]].
strandzha-commune.r: In the liberated villages the rebels set up a provisional administration, later called the Strandzha Commune, with Vasiliko as a centre. Leaders influenced by anarchist ideas, notably Mihail Gerdzhikov, organised local self-government, supplies and defence, and promised fair treatment to Greek and Turkish villagers. It lasted only about three weeks.
strandzha-commune.e: Large Ottoman forces suppressed the uprising by early September 1903, burning villages and driving thousands of refugees into [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]]. Northern Strandzha joined [[e:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] after the [[e:balkan-wars|Balkan Wars]], and the commune is remembered as an early experiment in revolutionary self-rule.

saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.t: Multi-island state in the Windwards, independent since 1979, shaped by bananas, volcanic eruptions and long-serving prime ministers.
saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.o: The [[s:colony-of-saint-vincent|Colony of Saint Vincent]] became independent with the northern Grenadines on 27 October 1979 under Prime Minister Milton Cato. Weeks later a brief armed uprising on Union Island was put down with help from [[s:barbados|Barbados]].
saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.r: James Mitchell of the New Democratic Party governed from 1984 to 2000, and Ralph Gonsalves of the Unity Labour Party from 2001 to 2025. Bananas sustained farmers until European preferences ended, and the economy turned toward tourism, yachting in the Grenadines and offshore services. Voters rejected a new constitution that would have made the country a republic in 2009. Argyle International Airport opened in 2017.
saint-vincent-and-the-grenadines.e: La Soufrière erupted in April 2021, forcing thousands to evacuate, and Hurricane Beryl devastated the southern Grenadines in 2024. The New Democratic Party under Godwin Friday won the election of November 2025, and the country remains a parliamentary monarchy.

spanish-puerto-rico.t: Spain's island colony and fortress in the eastern Caribbean for four centuries, guarding the route of the treasure fleets until 1898.
spanish-puerto-rico.o: Juan Ponce de León began the conquest of [[e:puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] in 1508, founding Caparra; the settlement moved to San Juan on its bay around 1521. The Taíno were forced into gold mining, and their uprising of 1511 was crushed.
spanish-puerto-rico.r: With little gold, [[e:puerto-rico|Puerto Rico]] became a military bastion, its fortresses of El Morro and San Cristóbal paid for by [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] from [[s:new-spain|New Spain]]. It repelled Drake in 1595, the [[e:dutch|Dutch]] in 1625 and the British in 1797, though the Earl of Cumberland held San Juan briefly in 1598. [[e:sugar-plantation|Sugar]], [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and tobacco grew in the 19th century, worked partly by enslaved Africans until abolition in 1873.
spanish-puerto-rico.e: After the Grito de Lares revolt of 1868, [[e:spain|Spain]] granted autonomy in 1897, but the [[s:united-states|United States]] invaded in 1898 during the [[e:spanish-american-war|Spanish-American War]], and the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] transferred the island to [[s:puerto-rico-united-states|Puerto Rico (United States)]].

state-of-wei.t: The first great power of the Warring States, whose Marquis Wen pioneered legal and administrative reform, later ruling from Daliang and known as Liang.
state-of-wei.o: The Wei lineage were ministers of the [[s:state-of-jin|State of Jin]] who joined Zhao and Han in destroying the Zhi clan in 453 BCE and dividing Jin. Marquis Wen led the family, and in 403 BCE the Zhou king recognised Wei as a state, with its capital at Anyi in southern [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]].
state-of-wei.r: Marquis Wen made Wei the leading state through reforms by Li Kui, whose Canon of Laws became a model for later codes, the irrigation works of Ximen Bao and the professional army of Wu Qi. In 361 BCE Wei moved its capital to Daliang ([[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]]), so its rulers were called kings of [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]]. Defeats by the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]] at Guiling and Maling ended its dominance.
state-of-wei.e: Squeezed by the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]], Wei lost its western lands, though Lord Xinling briefly rallied the states to save Handan in 257 BCE. In 225 BCE the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] general Wang Ben flooded Daliang by diverting the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]] and captured King Jia.

shirvan-khanate.t: A khanate in the old Shirvan heartland around Shamakhi, which rose after Nader Shah's death and was absorbed by Russia in 1820.
shirvan-khanate.o: After [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] death in 1747, local leaders in [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] formed an independent khanate around Shamakhi, the old capital of the Shirvanshah State. Its early years were divided between rival families and two capitals, Old Shamakhi and New Shamakhi, also called Aghsu.
shirvan-khanate.r: [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] was a land of [[e:silk|silk]], grain and [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]], but earthquakes and wars had reduced Shamakhi from its former greatness. The khanate was for a time dominated by Fatali Khan of the [[s:quba-khanate|Quba Khanate]]. Mustafa Khan, who ruled from 1792, reunited it and built a mountain stronghold at Fit-dagh, balancing between [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:russia|Russia]].
shirvan-khanate.e: Mustafa Khan accepted Russian protection in 1805 but remained restless. In 1820 he fled to [[e:persia|Persia]], and the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished the khanate, making [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] a province. Shamakhi later became the seat of a Russian governorate until a devastating earthquake in 1859 moved it to [[e:baku|Baku]].

state-of-cai.t: A Ji-clan state of the Huai plain, founded by a rebellious royal brother, that was crushed between Chu and Wu and finally annexed by Chu in 447 BCE.
state-of-cai.o: King Wu of Zhou gave Cai to his brother Du, Cai Shu, with its capital at Shangcai in south-central Henan. Cai Shu joined the rebellion of the Three Guards against the regency of the Duke of Zhou and was banished, but his son Cai Zhong was later restored to the fief.
state-of-cai.r: Cai stood directly in the path of the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] and spent much of the Spring and Autumn period as its reluctant client. King Ling of Chu annexed it in 531 BCE, but it was restored in 529 BCE. Resentment of Chu led Cai to help the [[s:state-of-wu|State of Wu]] sack the Chu capital in 506 BCE. [[e:bronze|Bronzes]] from the tomb of Marquis Zhao of Cai at Shouxian show a refined court culture.
state-of-cai.e: Under pressure from Chu, Cai moved its capital to Xincai and then in 493 BCE to Zhoulai in Anhui, under Wu's protection. After Wu fell to Yue, Chu annexed Cai in 447 BCE. The surname Cai traces its origin to the state.

scythian-kingdom-of-crimea.t: The last Scythian kingdom, ruled from Scythian Neapolis near Simferopol after Sarmatians drove the Scythians from the open steppe.
scythian-kingdom-of-crimea.o: As Sarmatian tribes overran the steppe in the 3rd century BCE, the [[e:scythians|Scythians]] who survived withdrew into the Crimean foothills and the lower [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]]. There they built a new state with a fortified royal seat, Scythian [[s:neapolis|Neapolis]], on the edge of modern Simferopol.
scythian-kingdom-of-crimea.r: The Late [[e:scythians|Scythians]] were more settled than their ancestors, farming, building stone houses and trading through the Greek cities of the coast. Their kings sought to control [[s:chersonesus-taurica|Chersonesos]] and the grain trade. King Skilurus struck coins at [[s:olbia-pontica|Olbia]], and a stone mausoleum at [[s:neapolis|Neapolis]] holding dozens of burials and rich goods is often attributed to him.
scythian-kingdom-of-crimea.e: Palakus was defeated around 110 BCE by Diophantes, general of Mithridates VI of [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]], and the kingdom lost its leading role. It survived in a weaker form, often in conflict with the [[s:bosporan-kingdom|Bosporan Kingdom]], until Goths and other invaders destroyed [[s:neapolis|Neapolis]] in the mid 3rd century CE.

samos.t: Ionian island state that under the tyrant Polycrates became the leading naval power of the Aegean and built the famous Tunnel of Eupalinos.
samos.o: Ionian settlers occupied [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]], opposite Mount Mycale, c. 1000 BCE, beside an older cult of Hera at the Heraion. Samos joined the [[s:ionian-league|Ionian League]] and by the 7th century BCE was a seafaring state: the Samian Colaeus reached [[s:tartessos|Tartessos]] in [[e:spain|Spain]], and the city founded colonies such as [[s:perinthus|Perinthus]].
samos.r: Polycrates seized power c. 538 BCE and built a fleet of a hundred ships, a harbour mole, the 1,036 metre aqueduct tunnel of Eupalinos and a vast new temple of Hera. Pythagoras left to escape his rule. [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]] was later a privileged ship-providing member of the [[s:delian-league|Delian League]], birthplace of Aristarchus and Epicurus.
samos.e: Pericles crushed a Samian revolt in 440 to 439 BCE, and Athenian settlers held the island from 365 to 322 BCE. [[s:principality-of-samos|Samos]] then served as a Ptolemaic naval base before passing under [[e:pergamenes|Pergamene]] and finally Roman control, becoming part of the province of [[e:asia|Asia]] in 129 BCE.

sakya-regime.t: The first Tibetan government under Mongol patronage, in which the abbots of Sakya monastery and their administrators ruled Tibet for the Yuan emperors.
sakya-regime.o: In 1244 the scholar Sakya Pandita answered a summons from the Mongol prince Köden and negotiated [[e:tibet|Tibet's]] submission. His nephew Phagpa became spiritual teacher to Kublai, who made him Imperial Preceptor and in the 1260s gave the Sakya lamas authority over [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], organised after a [[e:census|census]] into thirteen myriarchies.
sakya-regime.r: The Sakya lamas spent much time at the Yuan court, while an administrator, the ponchen, governed from Sakya with Mongol backing; Shakya Zangpo was the first. Phagpa devised a new script for Kublai's empire in 1269. Rivalry with other monastic orders was intense, and a revolt by the Drikung was crushed with Mongol troops in 1290.
sakya-regime.e: As Yuan power waned, the myriarch Changchub Gyaltsen of [[s:phagmodrupa-dynasty|Phagmodru]] fought the Sakya administrators and by 1354 controlled central [[s:tibet-1912-1951|Tibet]], founding the Phagmodrupa dynasty. Sakya remained a major monastery and school of [[e:tibetan-buddhism|Tibetan Buddhism]].

shaki-khanate.t: A khanate in the silk country of north-western Azerbaijan, founded in a revolt against Nader Shah and known for the painted Palace of the Shaki Khans.
shaki-khanate.o: In 1743 Hajji Chelebi, a local notable, led a rising against the heavy taxes of [[e:nader-shah|Nader Shah's]] [[s:afsharid-empire|Afsharid Empire]] and defeated the forces sent against him. He made Shaki an independent khanate, one of the first of the Caucasian khanates, and after a mudflow destroyed old Shaki the capital moved to Nukha.
shaki-khanate.r: The khans ruled a land rich in [[e:silk|silk]], orchards and crafts, and Nukha became a major centre of silk weaving. Hajji Chelebi fought the Georgian kings and neighbouring khans. The Palace of the Shaki Khans, built in the late 18th century, is famous for its painted interiors and stained-glass shebeke windows.
shaki-khanate.e: Weakened by family feuds, the khanate accepted Russian protection in 1805. After the death of Ismail Khan in 1819, the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished it and created the Shaki province. The palace survives and, with the historic centre of Shaki, is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.t: A Republican regional government in Asturias that declared itself sovereign when cut off from the rest of Republican Spain in 1937.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.o: After Bilbao fell to Franco in June 1937, and as Santander fell in late August, Asturias and part of León were isolated from the Republican government in [[e:valencia|Valencia]]. On 24 August 1937 the Interprovincial Council at Gijón, led by the Socialist miners' leader Belarmino Tomás, declared itself sovereign.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.r: The council took over all civil and military powers, issued its own decrees and money, and tried to organise defence of the mountains and the mining valleys with exhausted troops and few supplies. The central government saw the declaration as a step too far, but could do little.
sovereign-council-of-asturias-and-leon.e: Nationalist forces broke through in October 1937. Leaders and soldiers fled by sea, and Franco's troops entered Gijón on 21 October 1937, ending the war in the north.

state-of-wu.t: The lower Yangtze kingdom that rose suddenly under Helü and Fuchai, sacked the Chu capital in 506 BCE and fell to its rival Yue in 473 BCE.
state-of-wu.o: Wu, also called Gouwu, claimed descent from Taibo and Zhongyong, uncles of King Wen of Zhou, who were said to have settled among the tattooed peoples of the south. It enters the record in 585 BCE under King Shoumeng, and Jin sent the exile Wu Chen to teach [[e:chariot|chariot]] warfare so that Wu would harass Chu.
state-of-wu.r: Wu's rulers called themselves kings and ruled from Gusu (Suzhou) amid lakes and rivers, fighting with fleets as well as armies and casting famous bronze swords. With the advisers Wu Zixu and, by tradition, Sun Tzu, King Helü captured the Chu capital Ying in 506 BCE. King Fuchai defeated Yue, dug the Han Canal linking the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] and the Huai, and claimed precedence over Jin at Huangchi in 482 BCE.
state-of-wu.e: While Fuchai was in the north, King Goujian of the [[s:state-of-yue|State of Yue]] attacked. After a long siege Yue took Gusu in 473 BCE and Fuchai killed himself. Wu's story became a classic of Chinese storytelling about pride and revenge.

state-of-the-teutonic-order.t: Crusader state of the Teutonic Knights on the Baltic, which conquered the pagan Prussians, ruled from Marienburg and became the Duchy of Prussia in 1525.
state-of-the-teutonic-order.o: In 1226 Duke Konrad of Masovia invited the Teutonic Order to fight the pagan Prussians, and Emperor [[e:frederick-ii|Frederick II's]] [[e:golden-bull-of-1356|Golden Bull]] of [[s:lordship-of-rimini|Rimini]] granted Grand Master Hermann von Salza the conquered lands. Over fifty years the knights subdued [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]], absorbing the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]] in 1237 and seizing Danzig in 1308.
state-of-the-teutonic-order.r: The Grand Master ruled from Marienburg from 1309 through a network of brick castles, with commanders governing districts. The knights brought in German peasants and townsmen, founded towns such as Thorn and Königsberg and profited from the grain and amber trade through the [[s:hanseatic-league|Hanseatic League]]. Under Winrich von Kniprode in the 14th century the state reached its height, launching [[e:crusade|crusades]] against [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]].
state-of-the-teutonic-order.e: Defeat by [[e:poland|Poland]] and [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] at Grunwald in 1410 and the Thirteen Years War cost the Order West [[e:kingdom-of-prussia|Prussia]] at the Second Peace of Thorn in 1466. In 1525 Grand Master Albert of Brandenburg-Ansbach turned Lutheran and secularised the rest as the [[s:duchy-of-prussia|Duchy of Prussia]].

sudasna-state.t: A small Parmar Rajput chiefship of the Mahi Kantha country in northern Gujarat.
sudasna-state.o: Sudasna was held by a branch of Parmar [[e:rajputs|Rajputs]] and emerged as a separate estate by around 1600. Its early history is known mainly from family tradition and colonial gazetteers.
sudasna-state.r: The Thakor ruled a small group of villages, paying tribute through the [[e:gaekwads|Gaekwads]] of [[s:baroda-state|Baroda]] and supervised in the British period by the Mahi Kantha Agency. Little else is recorded in standard works.
sudasna-state.e: Sudasna merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in present Mehsana district.

suigam-state.t: A small Rajput chiefship on the edge of the Rann of Kutch in northern Gujarat.
suigam-state.o: Suigam was a small estate in the Banas Kantha region bordering the Rann of [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]], held by a Chauhan [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] family from around 1700. Its early history is known mainly from local tradition.
suigam-state.r: The ruler governed a dry, sparsely settled territory of grazing land and [[e:millet|millet]] fields on the edge of the salt desert. In the British period it was a minor state under the Banas Kantha Agency. Little else is recorded.
suigam-state.e: Suigam merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Banaskantha district.

smertae.t: People of the interior of Sutherland in northern Scotland, named only in Ptolemy's Geography.
smertae.o: The Smertae are known solely from Ptolemy's Geography of about 150, which places them inland in the far north of [[e:scotland|Scotland]], usually located in central Sutherland around the upper Oykel and Shin valleys. Their name may be linked to the Celtic god Smertrios, or to a word meaning 'smeared', perhaps referring to body paint.
smertae.r: Nothing is recorded of their rulers or customs. The interior of Sutherland was a land of moorland and river valleys, with scattered roundhouses and brochs along the straths, and the population lived mainly by herding [[e:cattle|cattle]] and sheep and growing small crops of barley.
smertae.e: The Smertae are not mentioned again. Their region later formed part of the lands of the northern Picts and, from the 9th century, came under Norse influence as the name Sutherland, the 'southern land' of the Norse earls, shows.

silaharas-of-kolhapur.t: A Silahara branch of southern Maharashtra that ruled from Kolhapur and built temples such as the Kopeshvara at Khidrapur.
silaharas-of-kolhapur.o: The [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] Silaharas arose in the mid-10th century as feudatories of the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]], in the region around Karad and Kolhapur. Like the other Silahara branches, they claimed descent from the legendary Jimutavahana. After 973 they served the [[s:western-chalukya-empire|Western Chalukya Empire]].
silaharas-of-kolhapur.r: The kingdom covered southern Maharashtra and parts of the Konkan and [[e:goa|Goa]]. Gandaraditya and Vijayaditya were active patrons, granting land to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] and Jain monks; Jainism was particularly strong. The Kopeshvara Shiva temple at Khidrapur, completed in the early 13th century, is their most famous monument, and the Mahalakshmi temple at [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] grew in importance. Vijayaditya helped the Kalachuri Bijjala seize the Chalukya throne.
silaharas-of-kolhapur.e: Bhoja II, the last major king, asserted independence as Chalukya power collapsed, but around 1212 the Yadava king Singhana conquered [[s:kolhapur-state|Kolhapur]] and ended the dynasty.

seneca-nation.t: The largest nation of the Iroquois Confederacy, the Keepers of the Western Door, and birthplace of the Longhouse religion of Handsome Lake.
seneca-nation.o: The Seneca lived in western [[e:new-york|New York]] between Seneca Lake and the Genesee River, the westernmost of the five founding [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Haudenosaunee]] nations. Joining the Iroquois [[s:confederate-states-of-america|Confederacy]] around the mid-15th century, according to tradition, they guarded its western flank, and towns such as Ganondagan grew into some of the largest settlements in the region.
seneca-nation.r: The Seneca sent eight chiefs to the [[e:grand-council-qing|Grand Council]] and, as the most numerous nation, supplied many warriors in the Beaver Wars against the [[s:huron-confederacy|Huron Confederacy]], [[s:neutral-confederacy|Neutral Confederacy]] and [[s:erie-nation|Erie Nation]]. In 1687 the French governor Denonville burned Ganondagan. In the late 18th century the war chief Cornplanter and the orator Red Jacket led the nation, and in 1799 Handsome Lake began the teaching that became the Longhouse religion.
seneca-nation.e: After siding with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], the Seneca sold most of their lands in the Treaty of Big Tree in 1797. In 1848 the Allegany and Cattaraugus communities formed the Seneca Nation of Indians, an elected republic, while Tonawanda kept traditional chiefs. Kinzua Dam flooded Allegany land in the 1960s.

state-of-qin.t: The western frontier state that turned itself into a war machine through Shang Yang's reforms and conquered all its rivals to unify China in 221 BCE.
state-of-qin.o: The Ying clan of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] traced their rise to Feizi, who bred horses for King Xiao of Zhou and was granted the small fief of Qin in eastern Gansu in the 9th century BCE. After Duke Xiang escorted King Ping east in 770 BCE, he was made a full lord and promised the old Zhou heartland if he could win it from the Rong.
state-of-qin.r: [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] moved its capital eastward to Yong, Yueyang and, from 350 BCE, Xianyang. Duke Mu dominated the west in the 7th century BCE. From 356 BCE the minister [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] Yang reorganised Qin under Duke Xiao: counties ruled by appointed officials, harsh collective punishments, and ranks earned by heads taken in battle or grain produced. Victories such as Changping in 260 BCE broke the [[s:state-of-zhao|State of Zhao]].
state-of-qin.e: King [[s:state-of-zheng|Zheng]] conquered the [[s:state-of-han|State of Han]], Zhao, Wei, Chu, Yan and Qi between 230 and 221 BCE and took the new title of First Emperor, transforming the state into the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]]. The name [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] is the likely origin of the Western word [[e:china|China]].

saxons.t: A confederation of north German peoples who raided Roman coasts, settled England and fought Charlemagne for thirty years before forced conversion.
saxons.o: A people called Saxones is probably named by Ptolemy in the 2nd century, though the reading is disputed; the Saxons appear as sea raiders on the coasts of Gaul and [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] from the late 3rd century. They absorbed older peoples such as the [[s:chauci|Chauci]], [[s:angrivarii|Angrivarii]] and [[s:cherusci|Cherusci]], spreading from [[s:county-of-holstein|Holstein]] across the plains between the Elbe and the [[e:rhine|Rhine]]. From the 5th century many settled in [[e:britain|Britain]].
saxons.r: Continental Saxony had no king. Bede records that it was ruled by many [[e:satrapy|satraps]], and later sources describe an assembly at Marklo where representatives of nobles, freemen and [[e:freedmen|freedmen]] from [[e:peace-of-westphalia|Westphalia]], Engern and Eastphalia met. Their sacred places included the Irminsul, a great pillar or tree.
saxons.e: [[e:charlemagne|Charlemagne]] attacked Saxony in 772, destroying the Irminsul. The [[e:saxon-wars|Saxon Wars]], with the resistance of Widukind and the massacre at [[e:verden|Verden]] in 782, ended with [[e:deportation|deportations]] in 804. Saxony was baptised and incorporated into the Frankish realm, later forming the [[s:duchy-of-saxony|Duchy of Saxony]], whose dukes became [[e:east-francia|East Francia's]] kings in 919.

sint-maarten.t: Southern half of a small island shared with France since 1648, a country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands since 2010.
sint-maarten.o: Sint Maarten was part of the [[s:netherlands-antilles|Netherlands Antilles]] until that country was dissolved on 10 October 2010. Islanders had voted in 2000 for separate status, and it became an autonomous country within the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]], with Sarah Wescot-Williams as first prime minister. The island's division with French Saint-Martin dates from the Treaty of Concordia of 1648.
sint-maarten.r: Sint Maarten has its own parliament, government and constitution in Philipsburg, while the [[s:kingdom-of-the-netherlands|Netherlands]] oversees defence, foreign affairs and, through a board, public finances. Its economy depends on tourism, especially cruise ships and visitors flying in to Princess Juliana Airport. English is the everyday language, and much of the population is of migrant origin. Governments have been unstable, with frequent changes of prime minister.
sint-maarten.e: Hurricane Irma devastated the island in 2017, and [[e:dutch|Dutch]] reconstruction aid came with conditions on governance. Sint Maarten remains a country within the kingdom, debating its relationship with The Hague.

swedish-guadeloupe.t: Caribbean island promised to Sweden for joining the coalition against Napoleon, nominally Swedish for about a year before returning to France.
swedish-guadeloupe.o: British forces captured [[s:colony-of-guadeloupe|French Guadeloupe]] in 1810. In the Treaty of Stockholm of 1813, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ceded the island to [[e:sweden|Sweden]] as a reward for Crown Prince Charles John, the former French marshal Bernadotte, bringing Sweden into the coalition against [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]].
swedish-guadeloupe.r: Swedish rule was brief and largely nominal. The British garrison remained, and the colonial administration, laws and plantation society based on [[e:slavery|slavery]] continued with little change.
swedish-guadeloupe.e: The Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1814 restored [[s:colony-of-guadeloupe|Guadeloupe]] to [[e:france|France]]. In compensation [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] paid [[e:sweden|Sweden]] 24 million francs, money that went into the so-called Guadeloupe Fund, which paid an annual sum to the Bernadotte family until 1983. The island remains part of France.

sparta.t: Militarised city-state of Laconia with two kings and a helot workforce, the dominant land power of Classical Greece and victor over Athens in 404 BCE.
sparta.o: Dorian [[e:greeks|Greeks]] settled the Eurotas valley in Laconia in the 10th century BCE, and four villages joined to form Sparta, later absorbing nearby Amyclae. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE Sparta conquered [[s:messene|Messenia]], reducing its people to helots, state serfs who farmed the land for Spartan citizens.
sparta.r: Sparta had two hereditary kings, from the Agiad and Eurypontid houses, a council of elders, five annual [[e:ephor|ephors]] and an assembly, a system credited to the lawgiver Lycurgus. Male citizens underwent the agoge training and lived in messes. Sparta led the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]] and the [[s:hellenic-alliance|Hellenic Alliance]] against [[e:persia|Persia]], where Leonidas I fell at [[e:battle-of-thermopylae|Thermopylae]] in 480 BCE.
sparta.e: Sparta defeated [[s:athens|Athens]] in 404 BCE, but [[s:thebes|Thebes]] broke its power at Leuctra in 371 BCE and freed [[s:messene|Messenia]]. The reformer Cleomenes III was defeated in 222 BCE. Sparta was forced into the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]] in 192 BCE and came under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE as a free city.

saint-domingue.t: France's richest colony, the world's leading sugar and coffee producer, whose enslaved population rose in 1791 and created independent Haiti.
saint-domingue.o: French buccaneers and planters spread from [[s:tortuga|Tortuga]] onto the western part of Hispaniola in the mid-17th century. In 1665 the French West [[e:india|India]] Company appointed Bertrand d'Ogeron governor, who organised settlement, and [[e:spain|Spain]] recognised French possession of the west of the island in the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697.
saint-domingue.r: By the 1780s Saint-Domingue produced around 40 per cent of [[e:europe|Europe's]] [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and over half its [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]]. About half a million enslaved Africans, worked under the Code Noir with appalling mortality, vastly outnumbered some 30,000 whites and a similar number of free people of colour. Cap-Français was the cultural capital and Port-au-Prince the seat of government from 1770. Racial hierarchy and planter resentment of metropolitan trade rules ran deep.
saint-domingue.e: The revolution in [[e:france|France]] set off struggles among planters, free people of colour and, from August 1791, a vast slave uprising. France abolished [[e:slavery|slavery]] in 1793 to 1794. [[e:toussaint-louverture|Toussaint Louverture]] rose to govern the colony, but [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] attempt to restore control failed, and [[e:jean-jacques-dessalines|Jean-Jacques Dessalines]] proclaimed [[e:haiti|Haiti's]] independence on 1 January 1804.

sogaya.t: A small Gaya state on the southern coast at modern Goseong, one of the six Gaya polities of the founding legend.
sogaya.o: Sogaya, meaning Little Gaya, grew up around the bay of Goseong on the south coast. It is often identified with Goja-guk, one of the [[s:byeonhan|Byeonhan]] statelets named in Chinese records, and in legend its founder was one of the six brothers born from golden eggs in 42 CE.
sogaya.r: As a coastal polity it depended on fishing and sea trade along the southern shore. Korean chronicles say it joined the war of the eight port states against [[s:ara-gaya|Ara Gaya]] in the early 3rd century, which [[s:silla|Silla]] helped repel. Tombs at Songhak-dong show contacts with [[s:baekje|Baekje]], Silla and [[e:japan|Japan]].
sogaya.e: Sogaya was absorbed by [[s:silla|Silla]] during its conquest of the remaining Gaya states around 562, becoming part of Silla's local administration.

surguja-state.t: A large forest state of the Chota Nagpur plateau ruled by Rakshel Rajput Maharajas from Ambikapur.
surguja-state.o: Surguja was ruled by a Rakshel family whose traditions trace their arrival to the hill country of northern Chhattisgarh centuries earlier. The register dates the state to around 1600. In the 18th century it came under [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] pressure from the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Bhonsles of Nagpur]].
surguja-state.r: The Maharajas governed a vast upland of sal forest, with Oraon, Gond, Kanwar and other Adivasi communities forming much of the population. Under British paramountcy from 1818, Surguja was one of the Chota Nagpur tributary states, transferred to the Central Provinces in 1905 and later to the Eastern States Agency.
surguja-state.e: Surguja merged into the Central Provinces and Berar in 1948, later Madhya Pradesh. Since 2000 its territory has been in Chhattisgarh, where Surguja is a district with its seat at Ambikapur.

samthar-state.t: A Gujar-ruled principality in Bundelkhand near Jhansi, unusual among the region's Rajput-ruled states.
samthar-state.o: Samthar's ruling family were Gujars who served the Bundela rulers of [[s:datia-state|Datia]] and established their own chiefship around Samthar in the 1730s as Bundela authority fragmented. The British recognised it by treaty in 1817.
samthar-state.r: Samthar was a salute state of the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency, governed by a Raja over a compact, mainly agricultural territory. Few details of its internal history are recorded in standard sources.
samthar-state.e: Samthar acceded to [[e:india|India]] after 1947 and was absorbed by 1950. The town lies in [[s:jhansi-state|Jhansi]] district of Uttar Pradesh.

state-of-zou.t: A small Shandong state, called Zhu and later Zou, that endured for eight centuries beside Lu and was the homeland of the philosopher Mencius.
state-of-zou.o: Zhu was ruled by the Cao clan, said to descend from the legendary Zhuanxu, and was recognised by the Zhou as a minor state in south-western Shandong, just south of Qufu. Its rulers initially held only the low rank of viscount.
state-of-zou.r: Zhu fought frequent border wars with its larger neighbour, the [[s:state-of-lu|State of Lu]], while balancing between Qi, [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] and later Chu. Duke Wen of Zhu moved the capital to Yi in 614 BCE after divination, saying the ruler's task was to benefit the people. By the Warring States period the state was known as Zou, and Mencius was born there.
state-of-zou.e: Zou survived into the late Warring States period before being annexed by the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] around 261 BCE. Its name lives on in Zoucheng, Shandong, where the Mencius Temple and the tombs of the Meng family still stand.

state-of-yu.t: A Ji-clan state in southern Shanxi that let Jin's army through to attack its neighbour Guo and was destroyed on the way back, the origin of the saying 'lips gone, teeth cold'.
state-of-yu.o: Yu traced its founding to Zhongyong, brother of Taibo and great-uncle of King Wen of Zhou; after the conquest his descendants were confirmed at Yu, near modern Pinglu in south-western [[e:shanxi|Shanxi]], on the north bank of the [[e:yellow-river|Yellow River]].
state-of-yu.r: Yu was a small duchy close to both the [[s:state-of-jin|State of Jin]] and [[s:western-guo|Western Guo]], and its security rested on cooperation with Guo. Little else is known of its institutions beyond the episode that ended it, recorded in the Zuo zhuan and Gongyang commentary.
state-of-yu.e: In 658 and 655 BCE Duke Xian of Jin gave the Duke of Yu fine jade and horses in exchange for passage to attack Guo. The minister Gong Zhiqi warned that Yu and Guo were like lips and teeth, but was ignored. After taking Guo in 655 BCE Jin seized Yu as well.

spanish-trinidad.t: Spain's long-neglected colony on Trinidad, transformed in its last years by French Catholic planters before British conquest in 1797.
spanish-trinidad.o: [[e:christopher-columbus|Columbus]] sighted Trinidad in 1498, but [[e:spain|Spain]] made no lasting settlement until 1592, when Antonio de Berrío founded San José de Oruña as a base for searching for El Dorado on the Orinoco. Walter Raleigh burnt it in 1595.
spanish-trinidad.r: For nearly two centuries Trinidad was a poor, underpopulated outpost with a few Spanish settlers, missions and indigenous communities. The capital moved to Port of [[e:spain|Spain]] in 1757. In 1783 the Cedula of Population offered land to Catholic settlers, drawing French planters and enslaved Africans from the French [[e:caribbean|Caribbean]] and creating a [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and cocoa economy.
spanish-trinidad.e: In 1797 a British force under Ralph Abercromby captured the island, and Governor José María Chacón surrendered. [[e:spain|Spain]] ceded Trinidad at the Treaty of Amiens in 1802, and it became the [[s:colony-of-trinidad|Colony of Trinidad]].

sotuta.t: The Maya province of the Cocom lineage in central Yucatán, bitter enemies of the Xiu and leaders of resistance to the Spanish conquest.
sotuta.o: The Cocom had been the leading lineage of the [[s:league-of-mayapan|League of Mayapan]]. When the Xiu-led revolt destroyed Mayapan around 1441 and massacred the Cocom, a surviving son established a new realm centred on Sotuta in central Yucatán.
sotuta.r: Sotuta was ruled by a halach uinic (supreme lord) of the Cocom lineage over the batabs of its towns. Its feud with the Xiu of [[s:mani|Maní]] dominated regional politics: in 1536 Nachi Cocom killed a Xiu embassy, including the lord Ah Dzun Xiu, at Otzmal while they travelled to [[s:chichen-itza|Chichen Itza]]. Sotuta refused alliance with the Spanish.
sotuta.e: Sotuta was among the last provinces to submit and took part in the Great Maya Revolt of 1546-47, which was crushed. It was then absorbed into the [[s:province-of-yucatan|Province of Yucatán]]. Nachi Cocom later accepted baptism as Juan Cocom.

second-taifa-of-silves.t: Silves under the rebel Ibn al-Mundhir, one of the Algarve leaders who rose with Ibn Qasi against the Almoravids in 1144.
second-taifa-of-silves.o: In 1144 Abu Muhammad ibn al-Mundhir, a local notable and disciple of the [[e:sufism|Sufi]] leader Ibn Qasi, took Silves during the uprising of the Muridun against the [[e:almoravid-empire|Almoravids]] and governed it as an independent lord.
second-taifa-of-silves.r: Known only from brief chronicle references, Ibn al-Mundhir's rule was one of the short-lived regimes of the second [[e:taifa|taifa]] period. He first backed Ibn Qasi of the [[s:second-taifa-of-mertola|Second Taifa of Mértola]], then joined Sidray ibn [[e:wazir|Wazir]] of Beja against him.
second-taifa-of-silves.e: Around 1150 Silves accepted [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohad]] authority. Ibn Qasi was killed in the city in 1151. Silves was taken briefly by Sancho I of Portugal in 1189, lost again, and finally conquered by Portugal in 1242.

state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.t: Brief state of the South Slavs of Austria-Hungary, proclaimed in Zagreb in October 1918 and merged into Yugoslavia a month later.
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.o: As [[e:austro-hungarian-empire|Austria-Hungary]] disintegrated, the National Council of [[e:slovenes|Slovenes]], [[e:croats|Croats]] and [[e:serbs|Serbs]] in Zagreb, formed earlier in October 1918, took power. On 29 October the Croatian Sabor broke ties with [[e:hungary|Hungary]] and [[e:austria|Austria]], and the new state was proclaimed, covering Slovenia, [[s:kingdom-of-croatia-slavonia|Croatia-Slavonia]], [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]], Bosnia and Herzegovina and Vojvodina, with the Slovene politician Anton Korošec as president.
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.r: The state had no army and no international recognition, and its authority was weak in the countryside, where returning soldiers and peasants rioted. The Austro-Hungarian fleet at Pola was handed to it, but [[e:italy|Italy]] seized [[s:histria|Istria]] and parts of [[e:dalmatia|Dalmatia]] under the [[e:armistice-of-11-november-1918|armistice]]. Svetozar Pribićević led those pushing for rapid union with [[s:serbia|Serbia]].
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.e: Fearing Italian expansion, the National Council sent a delegation to [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]], and on 1 December 1918 the state united with the [[s:kingdom-of-serbia|Kingdom of Serbia]] to form the [[s:kingdom-of-yugoslavia|Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes]], later called the Kingdom of [[e:yugoslavia|Yugoslavia]].
state-of-slovenes-croats-and-serbs.re: Catholic and Orthodox Christianity, Sunni Islam

seljuk-sultanate-of-syria.t: The Syrian realm of Tutush, brother of the Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah, whose death split Syria just before the First Crusade.
seljuk-sultanate-of-syria.o: In 1079 Malik-Shah sent his brother Tutush to aid Atsiz against the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]]; Tutush had Atsiz killed and took [[e:damascus|Damascus]]. In 1086 he defeated and killed the Rum Seljuk Suleiman ibn Qutalmish near [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] and extended his rule over most of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]].
seljuk-sultanate-of-syria.r: Tutush ruled as a Seljuk prince with Turkish commanders as governors, among them Aq Sunqur in [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] and the [[s:artuqids-of-mardin|Artuqids]] in [[e:jerusalem|Jerusalem]]. The state rested on [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] cavalry and [[e:iqta|iqta]] land grants, and its revenues came from the cities of [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and Aleppo and the trade of the coast. After Malik-Shah died in 1092, Tutush claimed the sultanate itself and executed Aq Sunqur in 1094.
seljuk-sultanate-of-syria.e: Tutush was killed in battle near [[e:rayy|Rayy]] in 1095 fighting his nephew Berkyaruq. [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] was divided between his sons: Ridwan in the [[s:seljuk-emirate-of-aleppo|Seljuk Emirate of Aleppo]] and Duqaq in the [[s:seljuk-emirate-of-damascus|Seljuk Emirate of Damascus]], whose rivalry left [[e:syria|Syria]] divided when the [[e:crusader-states|Crusaders]] arrived.

selonians.t: Small Baltic people on the south bank of the Daugava, the first of the Latvian tribes to fall to the German crusaders in 1208.
selonians.o: The Selonians settled in what is now south-eastern [[s:republic-of-latvia|Latvia]] and north-eastern [[s:grand-duchy-of-lithuania|Lithuania]] during the first millennium, between the [[s:semigallians|Semigallians]] and the Latgalians. Their name survives in the region of Sēlija. They lived in communities centred on hillforts, without a single ruler.
selonians.r: Archaeology shows farming villages, fortified hills and graves rich in bronze ornaments. Their position on the Daugava trade route brought them under the influence of Polotsk and, by the 12th century, of the Lithuanians, who used their main fortress, Sēlpils, as a base for raids.
selonians.e: In 1208 [[e:bishop|Bishop]] Albert of Riga and the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]] besieged and took Sēlpils, and the Selonians accepted baptism. Their land was later divided between the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]] and the [[s:archbishopric-of-riga|Archbishopric of Riga]], and a short-lived [[s:bishopric-of-semigallia|Bishopric of Selonia]] was founded. The Selonians merged into the Latvian and Lithuanian peoples.

spanish-florida.t: Spain's oldest North American colony, centred on St Augustine, the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the United States.
spanish-florida.o: Juan Ponce de León named La Florida in 1513, but several attempts at settlement failed. When French Huguenots built [[s:french-florida|Fort Caroline]] in French Florida, Philip II sent Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, who founded St Augustine in 1565 and destroyed the French colony. Florida became a military frontier guarding the route of the Spanish treasure fleets through the Bahama Channel.
spanish-florida.r: Florida was a poor garrison colony, supported by a royal subsidy from [[s:new-spain|New Spain]]. Franciscans built a chain of missions among the Timucua, Guale and [[s:apalachee-chiefdom|Apalachee]], who supplied food and labour. The stone Castillo de San Marcos, begun in 1672, resisted English sieges in 1702 and 1740, and Pensacola was founded in 1698. Fort Mose, established in 1738 for people escaping [[e:slavery|slavery]] in [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]], was the first legally free Black town in [[e:north-america|North America]].
spanish-florida.e: English raids wrecked the missions after 1702. [[e:spain|Spain]] ceded Florida to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] in 1763, when it was split into the [[s:province-of-east-florida|Province of East Florida]] and the [[s:province-of-west-florida|Province of West Florida]], regained it in 1783, and sold it to the [[s:united-states|United States]] by the Adams-Onís Treaty of 1819, effective in 1821.

spanish-oran.t: Spain's fortress city on the Algerian coast, held for nearly three centuries as a frontier presidio facing the Ottoman Regency of Algiers.
spanish-oran.o: After taking Mers el-Kébir in 1505, [[s:kingdom-of-castile|Castile]] captured Oran in 1509 in an expedition financed and led by Cardinal Cisneros, with Pedro Navarro commanding the troops. The conquest continued the [[e:reconquista|Reconquista]] into [[e:africa|Africa]] and aimed to stop raids on the Spanish coast and control the trade of the [[s:zayyanid-kingdom-of-tlemcen|Zayyanid Kingdom of Tlemcen]].
spanish-oran.r: Oran was a garrison town ruled by captains-general, ringed with forts and supplied from [[e:spain|Spain]]. Its governors allied with or raided neighbouring tribes and played politics in [[e:tlemcen|Tlemcen]]. The Count of Alcaudete, governor from 1534, died in a failed attack on Mostaganem in 1558. Oran's Jewish community was expelled in 1669, and the town also served as a penal settlement.
spanish-oran.e: The Bey of the [[s:beylik-of-the-west|Beylik of the West]] took Oran in 1708, but [[e:spain|Spain]] recaptured it in 1732. After a devastating earthquake in 1790, Spain negotiated its handover to the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]], completed in 1792.

sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman.t: Oman's Al Bu Said sultanate after the loss of Zanzibar, a coastal state in tension with the interior imams until the 1970 coup.
sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman.o: When Said ibn [[e:sultan|Sultan]] of the [[s:omani-empire|Omani Empire]] died in 1856, his son Thuwaini took [[e:muscat|Muscat]] and another son Majid took [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]]. The Canning Award of 1861, arbitrated by the [[e:viceroy-of-india|Viceroy of India]], confirmed the split, with Zanzibar paying Muscat an annual subsidy.
sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman.r: Cut off from East African wealth and steamship trade, [[e:muscat|Muscat]] declined and depended on British support. The interior Ibadi tribes resented the coastal sultans; Azzan ibn Qais briefly held Muscat as [[e:imam|imam]] in 1868-1871, and the [[s:imamate-of-oman|Imamate of Oman]] rose in 1913, kept at bay by the Treaty of Seeb in 1920. Said bin Taimur, sultan from 1932, kept the country isolated, won the Jebel Akhdar War of 1954-1959 and sold Gwadar to [[s:islamic-republic-of-pakistan|Pakistan]] in 1958.
sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman.e: Oil exports began in 1967 but development stayed slow while the Dhofar rebellion grew. In July 1970 Said's son Qaboos deposed him and renamed the country the [[s:sultanate-of-oman|Sultanate of Oman]].

sheikhdom-of-ajman.t: The smallest of the Trucial sheikhdoms, ruled by the Al Nuaimi since 1816 and a founding member of the UAE.
sheikhdom-of-ajman.o: In 1816 Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi, leader of the Na'im tribe, took the coastal fort of Ajman, between [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sharjah]] and [[s:sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain|Umm al-Quwain]], and established a sheikhdom ruled by his descendants ever since. It also held the inland enclaves of Masfut and Manama.
sheikhdom-of-ajman.r: Ajman lived from fishing, pearling and dhow building. It signed the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 and became one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] under British protection. Its rulers often had to manoeuvre between the larger [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sheikhdom of Sharjah]] and other neighbours. Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi III ruled from 1928 to 1981.
sheikhdom-of-ajman.e: Ajman joined the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] at its foundation in December 1971 and is the smallest of its seven [[e:emirate|emirates]].
ru: Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi I
Rashid bin Humaid Al Nuaimi III
