sheikhdom-of-dubai.t: The Al Maktoum sheikhdom on Dubai Creek, which turned free trade and merchant migration into the Gulf's leading commercial hub.
sheikhdom-of-dubai.o: In 1833 about 800 members of the Al Bu Falasah section of the Bani Yas left the [[s:sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi|Sheikhdom of Abu Dhabi]] and settled at Dubai Creek under Maktoum bin Butti and Obaid bin Said. Maktoum's descendants, the Al Maktoum, have ruled since.
sheikhdom-of-dubai.r: Dubai joined the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] system and lived from pearling, fishing and trade. Low taxes drew merchants, especially from the Persian port of Lingeh after 1902, and Dubai became the main [[e:entrepot|entrepot]] of the coast. Saeed bin Maktoum ruled from 1912 to 1958, facing a reform movement in 1938. His son Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum dredged the creek and opened an airport in 1960.
sheikhdom-of-dubai.e: Offshore oil was found in 1966 and funded further building. Rashid worked with Zayed of [[s:sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi|Abu Dhabi]] to form the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]], which Dubai joined at its foundation in December 1971.

state-of-zheng.t: The commercial heart of the Central Plain, whose Duke Zhuang humbled the Zhou king and whose minister Zichan published China's first written law code.
state-of-zheng.o: In 806 BCE King Xuan of Zhou enfeoffed his younger brother, Duke Huan of [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]], in the Wei valley. Foreseeing the fall of the [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]], Huan moved his family and wealth east; his son Duke Wu conquered [[s:eastern-guo|Eastern Guo]] and Kuai and built a new capital at Xinzheng in Henan.
state-of-zheng.r: Duke Zhuang made [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] the leading state of the early Spring and Autumn period, and in 707 BCE his [[e:archery|archers]] wounded King Huan of Zhou at Xuge, shattering royal prestige. Zheng had a strong merchant class bound to the state by covenant. In 536 BCE the minister Zichan had the penal laws cast on bronze tripods, making law public for the first time. Confucians condemned the music of Zheng as licentious.
state-of-zheng.e: Caught between Jin and Chu, [[s:zheng-wang-shichong|Zheng]] was a constant battlefield. After the partition of Jin, the [[s:state-of-han|State of Han]] conquered it in 375 BCE and moved its capital to Xinzheng, which remained the Han capital until 230 BCE.

sarila-state.t: A small Bundela principality of Bundelkhand, one of the holdings created from the lands of Chhatrasal's descendants.
sarila-state.o: Sarila was founded in the 1760s by a member of the Bundela family descended from Maharaja Chhatrasal, through the [[s:jaitpur-state|Jaitpur]] line. It was confirmed by a British sanad in the early 19th century.
sarila-state.r: The Raja ruled a compact agricultural territory as a non-salute state of the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] Agency. Few details of its internal history are recorded.
sarila-state.e: After independence Sarila was merged with the [[e:bundelkhand|Bundelkhand]] states into [[s:vindhya-pradesh|Vindhya Pradesh]] and was absorbed by 1950; the town is now in Hamirpur district of Uttar Pradesh.

second-sealand-dynasty.t: A brief Babylonian dynasty of three kings around 1000 BCE, founded by Simbar-Shipak in a time of Aramean raids and famine.
second-sealand-dynasty.o: Simbar-Shipak, who claimed descent from the southern marshlands, took the throne of [[e:babylon|Babylon]] in 1025 BCE after the end of the [[s:second-dynasty-of-isin|Second Dynasty of Isin]]. Babylonian king lists call his line the dynasty of the [[s:sealand-dynasty|Sealand]].
second-sealand-dynasty.r: The dynasty ruled a weakened [[e:babylonia|Babylonia]] troubled by Aramean and Sutean incursions. Simbar-Shipak restored the throne of Enlil in the Ekur at [[s:nippur|Nippur]], damaged by raiders, and is mentioned in later chronicles. He was murdered after eighteen years; his successor Ea-mukin-zeri reigned only months, and Kashshu-nadin-ahi ruled for three years amid shortages that halted temple offerings.
second-sealand-dynasty.e: The dynasty ended around 1005 BCE and was replaced by the [[s:bazi-dynasty|Bazi Dynasty]].

silures.t: Warlike people of south-east Wales who resisted Rome for nearly thirty years, until legions at Caerleon held their land and Caerwent became their town.
silures.o: The Silures lived in the valleys and coastal plain of [[s:lordship-of-glamorgan|Glamorgan]] and [[s:kingdom-of-gwent|Gwent]], defended by hillforts such as Llanmelin. [[e:tacitus|Tacitus]], noting their dark complexions and curly hair, speculated that they had come from [[e:spain|Spain]], a guess no longer accepted. They first appear in 47, when [[e:rome|Rome]] began its advance into Wales.
silures.r: Little is known of their leadership; they seem to have been a confederation of communities rather than a single kingdom, without a coinage of their own. Their warfare relied on raids and ambush in difficult country. Caratacus fought alongside them after 47, and in 52 they defeated a legion under Manlius [[e:valens|Valens]]; the governor Ostorius Scapula died worn out by the campaign.
silures.e: Julius Frontinus finally subdued them around 74 to 78 and founded the [[e:legion|legionary]] fortress of Isca at Caerleon. Their territory became a civitas within [[s:roman-britain|Roman Britain]] with its centre at Venta Silurum, Caerwent, where an inscription records the council of the Silures. The later [[s:kingdom-of-gwent|Kingdom of Gwent]] grew in the same region.

siris.t: Short-lived Ionian Greek city on the Gulf of Taranto, proverbial for wealth, destroyed by its Achaean neighbours in the 6th century BCE.
siris.o: [[e:ionia|Ionian Greeks]] from [[s:colophon|Colophon]] in [[e:asia-minor|Asia Minor]], fleeing Lydian attacks, founded Siris around 680 BCE near the mouth of the Siris (Sinni) river, apparently taking over an existing native settlement. The poet Archilochus praised its land as fair and lovely.
siris.r: Little is known of its government. Siris was famous for its fertile land and luxury, like its neighbour [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]], and became a rival to the Achaean cities of [[s:metapontum|Metapontum]], Sybaris and [[s:croton|Croton]]. Some scholars link the hill of Policoro with its main settlement. [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] records that [[s:athens|Athens]] later claimed a right to the site.
siris.e: Around 530 BCE an alliance of [[s:metapontum|Metapontum]], [[s:sybaris|Sybaris]] and [[s:croton|Croton]] captured Siris and destroyed it, reportedly killing suppliants at the altar of Athena. In 433 BCE [[s:taras|Taras]] and [[s:thurii|Thurii]] founded [[s:perinthus|Heraclea]] on or near its territory.

saint-lucia.t: Windward island independent since 1979, a parliamentary monarchy known for its Pitons, its Kwéyòl culture and two Nobel laureates.
saint-lucia.o: The [[s:colony-of-saint-lucia|Colony of Saint Lucia]] became independent on 22 February 1979, with John Compton of the United Workers Party as prime minister and the British monarch as head of state.
saint-lucia.r: Politics has alternated between the United Workers Party and the Saint Lucia Labour Party, whose Kenny Anthony led governments from 1997. Bananas, sold under preferential access to [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], were the economic backbone until the 1990s, when the end of European preferences forced a turn to tourism, which now dominates. The Pitons were declared a World Heritage Site in 2004. Derek Walcott, born in Castries, won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992, after Arthur Lewis's economics prize in 1979.
saint-lucia.e: Saint Lucia remains a parliamentary democracy and Commonwealth realm. Philip J. Pierre of the Labour Party became prime minister in 2021, and Kwéyòl, French place names and Catholic traditions continue to shape national identity.

santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico.t: The Spanish province of New Mexico, a remote frontier of New Spain along the upper Rio Grande, scene of the Pueblo Revolt of 1680.
santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico.o: In 1598 Juan de Oñate led settlers, soldiers and Franciscans up the Camino Real from [[s:mexico|Mexico]] and claimed the upper Rio Grande, setting up headquarters at the Tewa pueblo of Ohkay Owingeh. His brutal punishment of Ácoma Pueblo in 1599 led to his recall. Around 1610 governor Pedro de Peralta founded Santa Fe as the new capital.
santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico.r: Governors ruled from the Palace of the Governors, while Franciscan missions sought to convert the Pueblo peoples, who were burdened with tribute and forced labour under [[e:encomienda|encomienda]]. The province depended on caravans along the Camino Real to Chihuahua and [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]], and Hispanic villages grew along the river. Raids by Apache, Navajo and later Comanche shaped frontier life until governor Juan Bautista de Anza made peace with the Comanche in 1786.
santa-fe-de-nuevo-mexico.e: The Pueblo Revolt of 1680, led by Popé, drove the Spanish out until Diego de Vargas returned in 1692. After 1821 the province belonged to [[s:mexico|Mexico]]. American troops under Stephen Kearny occupied Santa Fe in 1846, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ceded it to the [[s:united-states|United States]] in 1848.

saint-barthelemy-swedish.t: Sweden's only long-lasting colony, a small Caribbean island whose free port of Gustavia boomed in the age of revolutionary wars.
saint-barthelemy-swedish.o: In 1784 King Gustav III obtained Saint Barthélemy from [[e:france|France]] in exchange for French trading rights at Gothenburg. The Swedes renamed the main harbour, Le Carénage, as Gustavia, after the king, and in 1785 declared it a free port.
saint-barthelemy-swedish.r: A Swedish governor ran the colony, at first with the Swedish West [[e:india|India]] Company. During the wars of the French Revolution and [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], neutral Gustavia thrived as an [[e:entrepot|entrepôt]] for goods, including enslaved people, and its population rose to several thousand. The island had little farmland and depended on trade. [[e:slavery|Slavery]] was abolished in 1847.
saint-barthelemy-swedish.e: After peace returned, trade declined, and hurricanes and fires damaged Gustavia. [[e:sweden|Sweden]] sold the island back to [[e:france|France]] by a treaty of 1877, after the inhabitants voted almost unanimously for the transfer, and it passed to France in 1878. Gustavia keeps its Swedish name and some Swedish buildings.

sri-ksetra-kingdom.t: The largest and most powerful Pyu city, near modern Pyay, whose stupas, gold manuscripts and royal urns reveal a sophisticated Buddhist kingdom.
sri-ksetra-kingdom.o: Sri Ksetra, meaning 'field of glory', rose on the lower Irrawaddy near present-day Pyay from around the 5th century, though occupation of the site began earlier. Burmese chronicles say it was founded by princes from [[s:tagaung-kingdom|Tagaung]], and its great circular wall, nearly 14 km around, made it the biggest of the [[s:pyu-city-states|Pyu city-states]].
sri-ksetra-kingdom.r: Its kings, known from inscribed funerary urns of the Vikrama dynasty, ruled a city that enclosed palaces, fields and [[e:reservoir|reservoirs]] within its walls. Pali texts on gold leaves found at the Khin Ba mound are among the oldest [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada]] Buddhist writings in [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]]. Massive cylindrical stupas such as the Bawbawgyi and Payagyi still stand, and [[e:silver|silver]] coins circulated in trade.
sri-ksetra-kingdom.e: Sri Ksetra declined from the 8th century, perhaps as the Irrawaddy shifted and power moved north, and [[s:nanzhao|Nanzhao]] raids in the 9th century finished its prominence. The [[s:pagan-kingdom|Pagan Kingdom]] inherited much of its Buddhist culture. The site is part of the Pyu Ancient Cities World Heritage Site.

seminole-nation.t: A people formed in 18th-century Florida from Muscogee migrants and escaped Africans, whose resistance in three wars made them the 'unconquered' Seminole.
seminole-nation.o: After English raids emptied northern [[s:spanish-florida|Spanish Florida]] of its earlier peoples, Muscogee towns, especially Hitchiti-speakers from the Lower Creek, moved into the region. From around 1750 the chief Cowkeeper led a group to the Alachua prairie, and others followed. The Spanish called them cimarrones, wild or runaway people, which became Seminole. Africans escaping [[e:slavery|slavery]] in [[s:georgia|Georgia]] and [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] joined them as allies.
seminole-nation.r: Seminole towns were autonomous, led by chiefs and war leaders and organised in matrilineal clans, with the Green Corn ceremony at their centre. They raised [[e:cattle|cattle]] on the Florida grasslands and farmed. Black Seminoles lived in their own villages, owing tribute and fighting as allies. Andrew Jackson's invasion in the First Seminole War of 1817 to 1818 helped push [[e:spain|Spain]] to sell Florida.
seminole-nation.e: In the Second Seminole War of 1835 to 1842, led by Osceola and Micanopy, the Seminole fought the [[s:united-states|United States]] to a costly standstill, but most were removed to Indian Territory, where Wewoka became their capital. A few hundred stayed in the Everglades; their descendants form the Seminole Tribe of Florida.

cr.a: State Library and Archives of Florida

sanhaja-confederation.t: The veiled camel-herding Sanhaja tribes of the western Sahara, masters of the caravan routes and forerunners of the Almoravids.
sanhaja-confederation.o: The Saharan Sanhaja, including the [[e:lamtuna|Lamtuna]], Massufa and Guddala (Juddala), were [[e:berbers|Berber]] [[e:camel|camel]] nomads of what is now [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]] and Western [[e:sahara|Sahara]]. Their men wore the face veil, as the [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] still do. By the 9th century they had formed a confederation controlling the routes between [[e:sijilmasa|Sijilmasa]] and the [[s:ghana-empire|Ghana Empire]], centred on the trading town of Awdaghust.
sanhaja-confederation.r: The confederation was led by chiefs of the [[e:lamtuna|Lamtuna]], and its power rose and fell with its unity. According to the 11th-century geographer al-Bakri, the Lamtuna king Tinbarutan in the mid-10th century ruled a large territory and received tribute from Sudanese kings. The Sanhaja grew rich from caravan taxes, livestock and the salt and [[e:gold-trade|gold trade]], and had converted to [[e:islam|Islam]], though their practice was loosely observed.
sanhaja-confederation.e: Around 990 the [[s:ghana-empire|Ghana Empire]] captured Awdaghust, and the confederation broke apart. Around 1040 the Guddala chief [[e:yahya-ibn-ibrahim|Yahya ibn Ibrahim]] brought the scholar [[e:abdallah-ibn-yasin|Abdallah ibn Yasin]] from [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]], whose reform movement united the Sanhaja anew as the [[s:almoravid-empire|Almoravid Empire]].

salihids.t: The Banu Salih, the leading Arab allies of the Eastern Roman Empire in the 5th century, between the Tanukhids and the Ghassanids.
salihids.o: The Salih were an Arab tribe of the Quda'a group who entered Roman territory in [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] and [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Transjordan]]. During the 5th century they displaced the [[s:tanukhids|Tanukhids]] as the principal foederati, guarding the desert frontier and supplying troops in return for annual payments.
salihids.r: Known mainly from later Arabic sources and scattered Greek references, the [[s:emirate-of-nekor|Salihids]] were Christian and their leaders appear to have founded monasteries; Arabic tradition remembers a king named Dawud who built one. They helped defend the frontier against nomad raids and the Lakhmid allies of [[e:persia|Persia]]. Details of their government and territory are uncertain.
salihids.e: According to Arabic tradition, disputes over the tribute they collected from newly arrived Ghassanid tribes led to fighting in which the [[s:ghassanid-kingdom|Ghassanids]] prevailed. Around 502 [[e:rome|Rome]] concluded a treaty with the Ghassanids, who took the Salihids' place. The Salih survived as a tribe and fought on the Byzantine side against the early Muslim armies.

suessetani.t: A little-known people of the Cinco Villas region of Aragon, whose town Corbio fell to Rome in 184 BCE.
suessetani.o: The Suessetani lived north of the middle [[e:ebro-river|Ebro]], probably in the Cinco Villas area of modern [[e:kingdom-of-aragon|Aragon]], between the [[s:sedetani|Sedetani]] and the [[s:vascones|Vascones]]. Their origins and language are uncertain; some scholars think they were of Celtic rather than Iberian stock. They appear only in Livy's account of the Roman wars.
suessetani.r: Nothing is known of their institutions beyond their main town, Corbio. They joined the [[s:ilergetes|Ilergetes]] in raids and in the anti-Roman revolts of the early 2nd century BCE.
suessetani.e: In 184 BCE the Roman praetor Aulus Terentius Varro captured Corbio and sold its inhabitants into [[e:slavery|slavery]]. The Suessetani disappear from history soon afterwards, and their lands seem to have passed to neighbouring peoples, possibly the [[s:vascones|Vascones]].

sheikhdom-of-sharjah.t: The main seat of the Al Qasimi family on the Trucial Coast, home of the first airport in the Gulf and a founding member of the UAE.
sheikhdom-of-sharjah.o: Sharjah grew in the 18th century as a town of the [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Qawasim]], the seafaring tribe led from the Sheikhdom of [[e:ras|Ras]] al-Khaimah. Sheikh [[e:sultan|Sultan]] bin Saqr Al Qasimi, who ruled for most of 1803 to 1866, made it the family's chief seat after British attacks on Ras al-Khaimah.
sheikhdom-of-sharjah.r: After the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 Sharjah was one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] under British protection. Its economy rested on pearling, fishing and trade, and its ruler long held authority over [[s:sheikhdom-of-ras-al-khaimah|Ras al-Khaimah]] and other dependencies, including [[s:sheikhdom-of-kalba|Kalba]]. In 1932 Imperial Airways opened a rest house and airfield at Sharjah, later an RAF base, on the route to [[e:india|India]].
sheikhdom-of-sharjah.e: [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] deposed Sheikh Saqr bin [[e:sultan|Sultan]] in 1965 for his Arab nationalist sympathies. His successor Khalid bin Muhammad agreed a shared arrangement with [[e:iran|Iran]] over Abu Musa and joined the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] on its founding in December 1971; he was killed in a coup attempt in 1972.

sallarid-dynasty.t: A Daylamite dynasty from the castle of Tarom that ruled Azerbaijan and much of Armenia in the mid-10th century, part of the Iranian intermezzo.
sallarid-dynasty.o: The [[s:sallarid-emirate|Sallarids]], also called Musafirids or Langarids, were lords of Tarom with their stronghold at Shamiran on the Qezel Ozan. Muhammad ibn Musafir married into the [[s:justanid-dynasty|Justanid dynasty]] and became the leading power in Daylam. In 941 his sons Marzuban and Wahsudan seized control of their father's lands, and Marzuban took [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].
sallarid-dynasty.r: Marzuban ibn Muhammad ruled from [[e:ardabil|Ardabil]] and [[e:tabriz|Tabriz]], extending his authority over [[s:caucasian-albania|Arran]], [[s:shirvanshah-state|Shirvan]] and Armenian princes and defending against the Rus raid on Barda'a in 943 to 944. Sources say he favoured [[e:ismailism|Ismaili]] missionaries. Daylamite soldiers formed the core of his army. In 948 he was captured by the Buyid Rukn al-Dawla, and his family's hold on [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] weakened in later succession quarrels.
sallarid-dynasty.e: [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] passed to the [[s:rawwadid-emirate|Rawwadid Emirate]], while the [[s:sallarid-emirate|Sallarids]] kept Tarom. In 1062 the Seljuk sultan [[e:tughril|Tughril]] took the submission of the last ruler, ending the dynasty.

sinope.t: Milesian colony with the best harbour on the southern Black Sea, birthplace of Diogenes the Cynic and later capital of the Kingdom of Pontus.
sinope.o: [[s:miletus|Miletus]] founded Sinope on a peninsula on the north coast of [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]]; ancient sources give dates in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, and the register follows c. 631 BCE. Its sheltered harbour made it the main Greek port of the southern [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]].
sinope.r: Sinope founded colonies of its own, including [[s:trapezus|Trapezus]], Cerasus and Cotyora, and traded tuna, [[e:timber|timber]] and red ochre called Sinopic earth. It was under the [[s:achaemenid-empire|Achaemenid Empire]] and later independent. Pericles's [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] expedition of c. 437 BCE installed Athenian settlers. Diogenes the Cynic was born there c. 412 BCE.
sinope.e: Pharnaces I of the [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Kingdom of Pontus]] captured Sinope in 183 BCE and made it his capital; Mithridates VI was born there. [[e:rome|Rome]] took it in 70 BCE. It is the modern Turkish town of Sinop.

severians.t: An East Slavic tribe on the Desna, Seym and Sula rivers, whose lands became Chernigov and kept the regional name Siveria.
severians.o: The Severians settled the wooded steppe east of the [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]] along the Desna, Seym and Sula in the 8th century. Archaeologists connect them with the Romny culture of [[e:hill-fort|hill forts]]. Like the Polans and [[s:vyatichi|Vyatichi]] they paid tribute to the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]].
severians.r: They lived in fortified settlements on river bluffs and farmed the black earth, trading with the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazar]] lands and the Arab world, from which large numbers of [[e:silver|silver]] coins reached them. [[e:chernigov|Chernigov]], Novgorod-Seversky and Lyubech grew up in their territory. They faced the steppe directly and bore the brunt of nomad raids.
severians.e: In 884 Oleg forced them to pay tribute to Kiev instead of the [[e:khazar-khaganate|Khazars]]. Their land became part of [[s:kievan-rus|Kievan Rus']] and later the [[s:principality-of-chernigov|Principality of Chernigov]] and the [[s:principality-of-novgorod-seversky|Principality of Novgorod-Seversky]]. The name Siveria survived for the region, and the Severians are last mentioned as a people in the 11th century.

sultanate-of-shewa.t: One of the earliest Muslim states of the Ethiopian interior, ruled by the Makhzumi dynasty in eastern Shewa.
sultanate-of-shewa.o: According to a late Arabic chronicle, the Makhzumi dynasty, claiming descent from an Arab clan of [[e:mecca|Mecca]], founded a sultanate in eastern [[s:kingdom-of-shewa|Shewa]] in 896. The date and the dynasty's origins are uncertain, but the state reflects the spread of [[e:islam|Islam]] inland from the [[e:gulf-of-aden|Gulf of Aden]] along [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] linking the coast at [[e:zeila|Zeila]] with the highlands.
sultanate-of-shewa.r: Very little is known about its government. It was a Muslim trading state among largely non-Muslim neighbours, dealing in slaves, [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and highland produce passed down to the coast. In the 13th century it was weakened by succession disputes among rival members of the dynasty, which gave outside powers a chance to intervene.
sultanate-of-shewa.e: In 1285 Umar Walasma, ruler of neighbouring [[e:ifat-sultanate|Ifat]], conquered the sultanate and absorbed it into the [[s:sultanate-of-ifat|Sultanate of Ifat]]. The Walasma dynasty that followed carried on Muslim power in the region for two more centuries.

san-lorenzo.t: The earliest great Olmec centre, on the Coatzacoalcos river, where colossal stone heads and the first large-scale planned settlement in Mesoamerica appeared.
san-lorenzo.o: Farming villages on a raised plateau above the Coatzacoalcos river floodplain in southern Veracruz grew into a major centre from about 1400 BCE. Control of fertile levee land and river trade routes allowed an elite to emerge, and by 1200 BCE San Lorenzo was the largest settlement in [[e:mesoamerica|Mesoamerica]].
san-lorenzo.r: Its rulers are known only through sculpture: ten colossal basalt heads, thought to be portraits of chiefs, and large table-thrones. Basalt was hauled from the Tuxtla Mountains some 60 kilometres away, showing great command of labour. The plateau was artificially levelled and fitted with stone drains. Obsidian, magnetite and fine pottery moved through wide exchange networks.
san-lorenzo.e: Around 900 BCE San Lorenzo declined, possibly through river shifts or political change, and many monuments were deliberately defaced and buried. Leadership of the Olmec world passed to [[s:la-venta|La Venta]]. Its sculptural style shaped later Mesoamerican art and kingship.

sultanate-of-touggourt.t: An oasis sultanate of the Oued Righ in the Algerian Sahara, ruled by the Banu Djellab dynasty for over four centuries until the French conquest.
sultanate-of-touggourt.o: The Banu Djellab, traditionally said to be of Marinid descent, established themselves as rulers of Touggourt and the oases of the Oued Righ valley around 1414. Their town lay on [[e:caravan-trade|caravan routes]] linking the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] coast with the [[e:sahara|Sahara]].
sultanate-of-touggourt.r: The sultans governed a chain of palm oases producing dates, depending on [[e:well|wells]] and irrigation. The population mixed Arabic-speaking and Berber-speaking groups, as well as people of sub-Saharan origin. Touggourt rivalled the nearby [[s:sultanate-of-ouargla|Sultanate of Ouargla]] and was at times tributary to the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]], whose beys of Constantine sent expeditions to collect tribute.
sultanate-of-touggourt.e: Dynastic quarrels weakened the state in the 19th century. [[s:french-algeria|French Algeria]] occupied Touggourt in 1854 and installed a pliant ruler, ending Djellab independence; the town became a military post in the French [[e:sahara|Sahara]].

shapsugs.t: The largest of the self-governing Circassian peoples on the Black Sea coast, who overthrew their nobility and fought Russia until 1864.
shapsugs.o: The Shapsugs lived along the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast and inland hills between the [[s:natukhaj|Natukhaj]] and the [[s:ubykhia|Ubykhs]], around modern Tuapse, and on the northern slopes towards the Kuban. They emerged as a distinct Adyghe community of [[s:circassia|Circassia]] by the 17th century; earlier history is not separately recorded.
shapsugs.r: In the late 18th century Shapsug commoners rose against their nobles and defeated them and their [[s:principality-of-bzhedugh|Bzhedugh]] allies at Bziyuqo in 1796. Afterwards they were governed by assemblies of elders and representatives of free households. They farmed, herded and traded with Ottoman ships. In the 1840s and 1850s they joined the assemblies that coordinated Circassian resistance.
shapsugs.e: The [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] conquered their territory in 1864, and most Shapsugs were expelled to the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]]. A small community remained near Tuapse and Lazarevskoye, the only Circassians left on the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] coast.

state-of-cao.t: A Ji-clan state on the eastern plain founded by a brother of King Wu, best remembered for an insult to a wandering prince that brought down the wrath of Jin.
state-of-cao.o: After the Zhou conquest King Wu enfeoffed his younger brother Zhenduo, known as Cao Shu, at Taoqiu, near modern Dingtao in south-western Shandong. The site lay in a rich trading region of the eastern plain.
state-of-cao.r: Cao was a modest Ji-clan state that usually followed the leading power of the day. Its most famous episode came when Duke Gong of Cao spied on the exiled Prince Chong'er of Jin in his bath to see his reputedly joined ribs. After Chong'er became Duke Wen of Jin he invaded Cao in 632 BCE and captured its ruler.
state-of-cao.e: Caught between the [[s:state-of-song|State of Song]] and the northern powers, Cao was conquered by [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] in 487 BCE and its last ruler killed. The surname Cao, one of [[e:china|China's]] most common, is traditionally traced in part to this state.

scythia.t: The kingdom of the Royal Scythians, Iranian horse nomads who ruled the Pontic steppe and left lavish gold-filled burial mounds.
scythia.o: Scythian groups moved west from [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]] onto the steppe north of the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] in the 8th and 7th centuries BCE, displacing or absorbing the [[s:cimmerians|Cimmerians]]. After raids deep into the [[e:near-east|Near East]], they settled into a confederation led by the Royal [[e:scythians|Scythians]] on the lower [[e:dnieper|Dnieper]], with the vast fortified site at Kamianka serving as a centre from about 400 BCE.
scythia.r: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] describes kings ruling over subject tribes of nomads and farmers, oaths sealed in blood and horse sacrifices at royal funerals. Wealth came from tribute and from grain, slaves and hides sold to Greek colonies such as [[s:olbia|Olbia Pontica]]. [[e:kurgan|Kurgans]] like Solokha, Chertomlyk and Tovsta Mohyla, with its gold pectoral, show Greek craftsmen working to Scythian taste.
scythia.e: In about 513 BCE the [[e:scythians|Scythians]] wore down the invading army of [[e:darius-i|Darius I]] by retreating across the steppe. King Ateas extended his power to the [[e:danube|Danube]] but died fighting [[e:philip-ii-of-macedon|Philip II of Macedon]] in 339 BCE. In the 3rd century BCE Sarmatian pressure collapsed the steppe kingdom, and Scythian rule survived only in the [[e:crimea|Crimea]].

sultanate-of-agadez.t: Sultanate of the Air mountains in the Sahara, whose sultan arbitrated among Tuareg confederations and guarded caravan routes between Hausaland and North Africa.
sultanate-of-agadez.o: The [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] confederations of the Air massif agreed in the early 15th century to accept a sultan who stood outside their rivalries; tradition says the first came from the north or even from [[e:istanbul|Istanbul]]. The seat moved from [[e:tin|Tin]] Shaman to the oasis town of Agadez around 1449, and the town grew as a caravan halt.
sultanate-of-agadez.r: The sultan was chosen from a single family but installed by the [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] leaders, whose consent limited his power. He collected tolls on caravans, judged disputes and led the salt caravans to Bilma. Agadez had a mixed Tuareg and Hausa-speaking population, Muslim scholars, and a tall mud-brick minaret. The [[s:songhai-empire|Songhai Empire]] under [[e:askia-muhammad|Askia Muhammad]] made the sultanate a tributary around 1500.
sultanate-of-agadez.e: French forces occupied Agadez around 1900. In 1916 and 1917 [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Tegama joined the [[e:tuareg|Tuareg]] revolt of Kaocen, which besieged the French garrison; he was captured and killed. The sultanate survives in a ceremonial form, and Agadez's old town is a World Heritage Site.

salassi.t: Alpine people of the Aosta valley who controlled the Great and Little St Bernard passes and their gold, and resisted Rome until 25 BCE.
salassi.o: The Salassi lived in the Aosta valley and around Eporedia (Ivrea), at the foot of the passes over the western [[e:alps|Alps]]. Ancient writers called them Celts, though they probably mixed with earlier Ligurian peoples. They appear in Roman history in the 2nd century BCE.
salassi.r: The Salassi controlled the routes over the Alpine passes, charging tolls on travellers and armies. They worked gold deposits in the Dora Baltea valley by washing, and their disputes with Roman contractors over water rights, recorded by Strabo, led to conflict. They lived in villages and fortified places and had no known central capital.
salassi.e: Appius Claudius Pulcher fought them in 143 BCE, and [[e:rome|Rome]] founded Eporedia in 100 BCE. In 25 BCE Aulus Terentius Varro Murena conquered them for Augustus, selling some 36,000 into [[e:slavery|slavery]], and founded Augusta Praetoria, modern Aosta, on their land.

sultanate-of-rum.t: The Seljuk state that turned Anatolia into a Turkish and Muslim land, with a Persianate court at Konya and the caravan roads of Asia Minor.
sultanate-of-rum.o: Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, a distant cousin of the Great Seljuk sultans, exploited Byzantine civil wars after [[e:battle-of-manzikert|Manzikert]] to seize much of [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] and made Nicaea his capital around 1077-1080. After the [[e:first-crusade|First Crusade]] retook Nicaea in 1097, his son Kilij Arslan I rebuilt the state around [[e:konya|Konya]].
sultanate-of-rum.r: Kilij Arslan II destroyed a Byzantine army at Myriokephalon in 1176, and under Kaykhusraw I and Kayqubad I the sultanate reached Antalya, Alanya and [[s:sinope|Sinop]] and controlled trade between the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] and the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]]. A network of [[e:caravanserai|caravanserais]] such as the [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Han served merchants. The court used Persian, built mosques and [[e:madrasa|madrasas]] in [[e:konya|Konya]], Kayseri and Sivas, and welcomed Rumi, whose family had left [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]] as the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] advanced and settled in Konya.
sultanate-of-rum.e: The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] crushed the Seljuk army at Kose Dag in 1243, and the sultans became Ilkhanid [[e:vassal|vassals]]. Real power passed to [[e:vizier|viziers]] and [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] beys, and [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] fragmented into [[e:beylik|beyliks]] such as the [[s:karamanids|Karamanids]] and the early [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]]. The last sultan, Mesud II, died around 1308.

sulu-sultanate.t: A Muslim sea power of the Sulu archipelago that fought Spain for three centuries and whose claim to Sabah is still disputed today.
sulu-sultanate.o: A ruler of Sulu, Paduka Batara, visited the Ming court in 1417 and died there; his tomb survives at Dezhou in [[e:china|China]]. Sulu tradition credits Sharif ul-Hashim, an Arab scholar from [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor]], with founding the sultanate in the mid-15th century. Its capital was Jolo.
sulu-sultanate.r: Sulu's wealth came from pearls, sea cucumbers and birds' nests sold to [[e:china|China]], and in the 18th and 19th centuries from [[e:slave-raiding|slave raiding]] by Iranun and Balangingi fleets across the [[s:philippines|Philippines]] and [[s:indonesia|Indonesia]]. Its sultans resisted repeated Spanish attacks in the Moro wars and controlled much of northern [[e:borneo|Borneo]], granted by [[s:brunei-sultanate|Brunei]].
sulu-sultanate.e: In 1878 [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Jamalul Alam leased or ceded [[s:north-borneo|North Borneo]] to a British syndicate, the origin of the Philippine claim to Sabah. [[e:spain|Spain]] took Jolo in 1876; the Americans signed the Bates Treaty in 1899, and in 1915 Jamalul Kiram II gave up temporal power under the Carpenter Agreement.

state-of-south-haiti.t: Short-lived breakaway state in southern Haiti, set up by the veteran revolutionary André Rigaud and reabsorbed into Pétion's republic in 1812.
state-of-south-haiti.o: André Rigaud, who had led the free people of colour in the south during the [[e:haitian-revolution|Haitian Revolution]] and lost the War of the Knives to [[e:toussaint-louverture|Toussaint Louverture]] in 1800, returned from exile in [[e:france|France]] in 1810. Discontent with Alexandre Pétion's leadership in the south allowed him to set up a separate government based at Les Cayes in November 1810.
state-of-south-haiti.r: Little is recorded of its institutions. It was essentially a regional military government under Rigaud, drawing support from officers and landowners of the southern peninsula, which had long been his stronghold. Like Pétion's republic it was dominated by the mixed-race elite and relied on [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] and smallholder agriculture.
state-of-south-haiti.e: Rigaud died in September 1811, and command passed to General Jean-Baptiste Borgella. Facing pressure from Henri Christophe's [[s:kingdom-of-haiti|Kingdom of Haiti]], Borgella reconciled with Pétion, and the south rejoined the [[s:republic-of-haiti-1806-1849|Republic of Haiti]] in March 1812.

spanish-texas.t: Spain's thinly settled frontier province of Tejas, founded to block the French, whose missions and ranches at San Antonio laid foundations for modern Texas.
spanish-texas.o: Alarmed by La Salle's French colony on Matagorda Bay, [[e:spain|Spain]] sent Alonso de León to east Texas, where the mission of San Francisco de los [[s:hasinai-confederacy|Tejas]] was founded among the Hasinai [[s:confederate-states-of-america|Confederacy]] in 1690. It was abandoned in 1693, but French traders at Natchitoches prompted Spain to return in 1716, and in 1718 Martín de Alarcón founded San Antonio.
spanish-texas.r: Texas was a military and missionary frontier of [[s:new-spain|New Spain]]. Franciscan missions, among them San Antonio de Valero, later known as the Alamo, gathered Coahuiltecan peoples, while presidios guarded the roads. From 1729 to 1772 the capital was Los Adaes, near the French border; it then moved to San Antonio de Béxar. Canary Islanders settled San Antonio in 1731, and ranching thrived. Apache and Comanche raids constrained settlement until a peace with the Comanche in 1785.
spanish-texas.e: The province suffered in the Mexican War of Independence, including a republican revolt crushed at the [[e:medina|Medina]] River in 1813. In 1821 it passed to independent [[s:mexico|Mexico]], and Anglo-American colonists under Stephen F. Austin began arriving, leading eventually to the [[s:republic-of-texas|Republic of Texas]].

cr.a: Stephen F. Austin / Henry Schenck Tanner

saint-kitts-and-nevis.t: The smallest sovereign state in the Americas, a two-island federation independent since 1983 whose constitution allows Nevis to secede.
saint-kitts-and-nevis.o: After Anguilla's separation, the remaining part of [[s:saint-christopher-nevis-anguilla|Saint Christopher-Nevis-Anguilla]] became independent on 19 September 1983 as the Federation of Saint Christopher and [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]], with Kennedy Simmonds as prime minister and the British monarch as head of state.
saint-kitts-and-nevis.r: The constitution gave [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]] its own island assembly and the right to secede by a two-thirds vote; a referendum in 1998 produced a majority for separation but fell short of the threshold. Denzil Douglas of the Labour Party governed from 1995 to 2015. The state-owned [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] industry, the islands' economic mainstay for over three centuries, was closed in 2005, and tourism and the citizenship by investment programme, begun in 1984, became the main sources of revenue.
saint-kitts-and-nevis.e: The federation remains a parliamentary democracy within the Commonwealth. Terrance Drew became prime minister in 2022. Relations between Saint Kitts and [[s:colony-of-nevis|Nevis]], and dependence on passport sales, continue to shape its politics.

sheikhdom-of-zahir-al-umar.t: The autonomous domain of Zahir al-Umar, a Bedouin sheikh who made Acre a thriving cotton port and defied Ottoman rule in Galilee.
sheikhdom-of-zahir-al-umar.o: Zahir al-Umar of the Zaydani clan was a tax farmer in [[e:galilee|Galilee]]. From the 1730s he took Tiberias, and over the following decades he extended his control over Galilee and the coast, moving his seat to [[e:acre|Acre]] around 1750.
sheikhdom-of-zahir-al-umar.r: Zahir encouraged settlement, guaranteed security on the roads and brought in Jewish, Christian and Muslim settlers. He controlled the export of [[e:cotton|cotton]] and grain to French merchants, which made [[e:acre|Acre]] the leading port of the region, and rebuilt its walls. Though he usually paid his taxes to the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]], he acted as an independent ruler and in 1771 joined Ali Bey of [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in an attack that briefly took [[e:damascus|Damascus]].
sheikhdom-of-zahir-al-umar.e: In 1775, after the Ottoman fleet bombarded [[e:acre|Acre]] and his own men turned against him, Zahir was killed. His successor in Acre, the Ottoman governor Jezzar Pasha, continued his policies under direct Ottoman authority.

sena-dynasty.t: The Hindu dynasty that replaced the Palas in Bengal, patron of the poet Jayadeva, until Bakhtiyar Khalji's raid on Nadia.
sena-dynasty.o: The Senas came from Karnataka and settled in western [[e:bengal|Bengal]], where Samantasena was a chief. His grandson Vijayasena took advantage of the decline of the [[s:pala-empire|Pala Empire]] to seize much of Bengal in the late 11th and early 12th centuries, also defeating the [[s:varman-dynasty-of-bengal|Varman dynasty of Bengal]].
sena-dynasty.r: The Senas promoted orthodox Brahmanical [[e:hinduism|Hinduism]], granting land to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]] and reshaping Bengali [[e:caste|caste]] society; Ballalasena is credited with the Kulinism system of Brahmin rank and wrote works on ritual. Lakshmanasena's court at Nabadwip hosted the poet Jayadeva, author of the Gita Govinda, and other [[e:sanskrit|Sanskrit]] poets. Their capitals included Nabadwip, Vikramapura and Lakhnauti.
sena-dynasty.e: Around 1204 Bakhtiyar Khalji raided Nabadwip, and the aged Lakshmanasena fled east. North-west [[e:bengal|Bengal]] became the base of Muslim rule, while the Senas held eastern Bengal from Vikramapura until about 1230.

south-peruvian-republic.t: The southern Peruvian state created by Andrés de Santa Cruz in 1836 as one of three members of the Peru-Bolivian Confederation.
south-peruvian-republic.o: After Andrés de Santa Cruz's Bolivian army defeated his Peruvian opponents, an assembly of the southern [[e:departement|departments]] of [[e:peru|Peru]], Arequipa, Cusco, Puno and Ayacucho, met at Sicuani in March 1836 and declared the South Peruvian Republic. It was designed to join the [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Republic of Bolivia]] and the [[s:north-peruvian-republic|North Peruvian Republic]] in the [[s:peru-bolivian-confederation|Peru-Bolivian Confederation]].
south-peruvian-republic.r: Santa Cruz held effective power, with local presidents, including Ramón Herrera and later Juan Pío de Tristán, governing under his supervision. The southern [[s:andecavi|Andes]] had close economic links with [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]], and many in Arequipa and Cusco favoured the union. The state adopted Santa Cruz's legal codes and sent delegates to the Congress of Tacna in 1837.
south-peruvian-republic.e: After the Chilean and Peruvian exile victory at Yungay in January 1839, the confederation collapsed, and Agustín Gamarra reunited the south with the rest of the [[s:republic-of-peru|Republic of Peru]]. Santa Cruz's project of joining southern [[e:peru|Peru]] with [[s:republic-of-bolivia|Bolivia]] was never revived.

sultanate-of-maradi.t: The refuge state of the exiled Hausa rulers of Katsina in southern Niger, which spent the 19th century raiding the Fulani emirates to the south.
sultanate-of-maradi.o: When [[e:fula|Fulani]] jihadists took [[s:katsina-kingdom|Katsina]] in 1807, its [[e:hausa|Hausa]] ruling family fled north. After years of wandering they settled at Maradi around 1819, where local Katsinawa rose against their Fulani governors. Under Dan Kassawa the exiles founded a new state that claimed to continue the Katsina Kingdom and refused to recognise the [[s:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto Caliphate]].
sultanate-of-maradi.r: Maradi kept the titles and court of old [[s:katsina-kingdom|Katsina]]. Most of its people practised [[e:islam|Islam]], but the state allied with the [[e:hausa|Hausa]] of [[s:kingdom-of-gobir|Gobir]], later the [[s:sultanate-of-tsibiri|Sultanate of Tsibiri]], and with non-Muslim groups against [[e:sokoto-caliphate|Sokoto]]. Its army raided the [[s:katsina-emirate|Katsina Emirate]] and other [[e:emirate|emirates]] almost every year, and the frontier between the two Katsinas was a zone of constant warfare.
sultanate-of-maradi.e: In 1899 French forces reached the area, and Maradi was absorbed into the territory that became the [[s:colony-of-niger|Colony of Niger]]. The town grew into a major commercial centre for [[e:groundnut|groundnuts]], and its sultan remains a traditional ruler.

sultanate-of-oman.t: Modern Oman under Sultan Qaboos and his successor, transformed since 1970 from isolation into a stable, neutral Gulf state.
sultanate-of-oman.o: On 23 July 1970 Qaboos bin Said deposed his father Said bin Taimur, ending the isolation of the [[s:sultanate-of-muscat-and-oman|Sultanate of Muscat and Oman]], and renamed the country the Sultanate of [[e:oman|Oman]]. He invited exiles home and launched a programme of roads, schools and hospitals funded by oil.
sultanate-of-oman.r: Qaboos ended the Dhofar rebellion by 1975 with British, Iranian and Jordanian help and with development aid to the south. [[e:oman|Oman]] is an absolute monarchy; the Basic Statute of 1996 codified the system, and an elected consultative council has limited powers. The country's Ibadi tradition, foreign policy of neutrality and role as mediator, including between [[e:iran|Iran]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]], set it apart in the region.
sultanate-of-oman.e: Qaboos died in January 2020 after nearly fifty years in power. His cousin Haitham bin Tariq succeeded him and introduced fiscal reforms and a named crown prince.

second-spanish-republic.t: Spain's democratic republic of the 1930s, whose sweeping reforms and deep divisions ended in civil war and Franco's dictatorship.
second-spanish-republic.o: After republican parties won the cities in the municipal elections of 12 April 1931, Alfonso XIII left [[e:spain|Spain]] and the republic was proclaimed on 14 April, ending [[s:restoration-spain|Restoration Spain]]. The Constitution of December 1931 created a secular, democratic state with women's suffrage.
second-spanish-republic.r: Governments led by Manuel Azaña pursued land reform, army reform, separation of Church and state and Catalan autonomy. A centre-right coalition reversed many reforms after 1933, and the Asturian miners' revolution of 1934 was crushed. The Popular Front won the elections of February 1936 amid rising political violence.
second-spanish-republic.e: A military coup on 17-18 July 1936 began the Spanish Civil War. The Republic, aided by the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]] and the International [[e:brigade|Brigades]], lost to Franco's Nationalists. [[e:madrid|Madrid]] fell in March 1939, and the war ended on 1 April, giving way to [[s:francoist-spain|Francoist Spain]].

sultanate-of-dar-al-kuti.t: A Muslim slave-raiding sultanate on the northern edge of the Central African forest, ruled from Ndele by the warlord al-Sanusi.
sultanate-of-dar-al-kuti.o: Dar al Kuti arose in the 19th century as a frontier province of [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]], where Muslim traders and settlers from Dar Runga established themselves among the [[s:kingdom-of-banda|Banda]] and Kara peoples south of the Chari basin. Its rulers were tributaries of the [[s:wadai-empire|Wadai Empire]].
sultanate-of-dar-al-kuti.r: The economy depended on [[e:slave-raiding|slave raiding]] into the populous lands to the south and on trading captives and [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] north to [[e:wadai-empire|Wadai]] and [[e:darfur-sultanate|Darfur]]. Muhammad al-Sanusi, who took power in 1890 with the backing of [[s:rabih-az-zubayrs-state|Rabih az-Zubayr]], built a fortified capital at Ndele from 1896, with mosques, granaries and a firearm-equipped army, and carried out large raids each dry season.
sultanate-of-dar-al-kuti.e: Al-Sanusi accepted a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1897, but [[e:france|France]] turned against him and he was killed in 1911. The sultanate was absorbed into [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]], and its raids left much of the region depopulated.

state-of-huang.t: A Ying-clan state of the Huai valley whose lavish tombs at Guangshan reveal a rich court, destroyed by Chu in 648 BCE for refusing tribute.
state-of-huang.o: Huang was a long-established state of the Ying clan on the Huai River plain, centred near modern Huangchuan in south-eastern Henan. Its rulers, ranked as lords, were recognised under the [[s:western-zhou|Western Zhou]] and controlled fertile land on the route between the Central Plain and the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]].
state-of-huang.r: Huang joined Qi's alliance under Duke Huan and refused to send tribute to the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]], trusting in Qi's distant support. The tombs of Lord Meng of Huang and his wife, excavated at Guangshan in 1983, contained fine bronzes, jades and lacquer, showing a wealthy aristocratic culture close to that of the Central Plain.
state-of-huang.e: Chu destroyed Huang in 648 BCE, and Qi did not intervene. Its lands became part of Chu's northern frontier. The common surname Huang is traditionally traced to the state.

saar-territory.t: Coal-mining region on the French border governed by the League of Nations for 15 years before voting to return to Germany.
saar-territory.o: The [[e:treaty-of-versailles|Treaty of Versailles]] separated the Saar basin from [[e:germany|Germany]] in 1920 and placed it under the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] for 15 years, with [[e:france|France]] granted ownership of its [[e:coal|coal]] mines as reparation for damage to French mines. A plebiscite was to decide its future afterwards.
saar-territory.r: A five-member Governing Commission appointed by the League ran the territory, with [[e:france|France]] holding the chair for many years. The French franc became the currency and the area was within the French customs zone. [[e:coal|Coal]] and [[e:steel|steel]] dominated the economy. After 1933 opponents of Hitler sought refuge there and campaigned for keeping the status quo.
saar-territory.e: In the plebiscite of 13 January 1935, about 90.7 per cent voted for reunion with [[e:germany|Germany]]. The territory returned to Germany on 1 March 1935, a propaganda triumph for the Nazis.

sangli-state.t: The most important of the Patwardhan Brahmin states of the southern Maratha country, ruled from Sangli on the Krishna river.
sangli-state.o: The Patwardhans were Chitpavan [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] generals of the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]], rewarded with lands in the southern [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] country. In 1782 Chintamanrao Patwardhan, known as Appa Saheb, separated from the family seat at Miraj and made Sangli his own state, building its fort and the Ganpati temple.
sangli-state.r: After the fall of the [[e:peshwa|Peshwa]] in 1818 Sangli became a British protected state of the Southern [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] Country, later the [[e:deccan|Deccan]] States Agency, with a 9-gun salute. Its rulers promoted schools and trade, and Sangli grew into a major market for turmeric and other produce. Chintamanrao II introduced representative institutions in the 20th century.
sangli-state.e: Sangli acceded to [[e:india|India]] and was merged into Bombay State in 1948; since 1960 it has been part of Maharashtra as Sangli district.

southern-liang.t: A kingdom of the Tufa Xianbei in eastern Qinghai and the Hexi Corridor, which broke away from Later Liang in 397 and fell to Western Qin in 414.
southern-liang.o: The Tufa were a [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] clan of the same origin as the Tuoba, settled around the Huangshui valley. In 397 their chief Tufa Wugu rebelled against [[s:later-liang-386-403|Later Liang]] and proclaimed himself king; the capital became Ledu in eastern Qinghai.
southern-liang.r: Southern [[s:liang-liang-shidu|Liang]] was a frontier state of [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] cavalry and Chinese and Qiang farmers. Under Tufa Rutan it acknowledged [[s:later-qin|Later Qin]] and in 406 received Guzang, the old Liang capital, but lost it after defeats by [[s:northern-liang|Northern Liang]]. Rutan promoted Chinese officials and learning but waged costly wars.
southern-liang.e: While Rutan campaigned against the Yifu tribes in 414, [[s:western-qin|Western Qin]] seized Ledu. He surrendered and was poisoned the next year. His son Tufa Poqiang fled to [[s:northern-wei|Northern Wei]], where he became a noted general under the name Yuan He.

state-of-haiti.t: Henri Christophe's northern Haitian state, a military republic in name that he turned into a kingdom in 1811.
state-of-haiti.o: After the killing of Jacques I in October 1806, the constituent assembly at Port-au-Prince adopted a constitution that left the presidency weak. Henri Christophe, the senior general in the north, refused to accept it, marched on the capital and was repulsed. In February 1807 he set up his own State of [[s:first-empire-of-haiti|Haiti]], with its capital at Cap-Haïtien and himself as president for life.
state-of-haiti.r: Christophe governed through his army, enforcing plantation labour to restore [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] and [[e:coffee-economy|coffee]] exports, which made the north richer than Pétion's republic in the south. Military discipline extended to farm workers, who were bound to estates and paid a share of crops. The state fought an inconclusive civil war with the [[s:republic-of-haiti-1806-1849|Republic of Haiti]] along the Artibonite and traded with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and the [[s:united-states|United States]].
state-of-haiti.e: In March 1811 a council of state proclaimed Christophe King Henri I, and the State of [[s:first-empire-of-haiti|Haiti]] became the [[s:kingdom-of-haiti|Kingdom of Haiti]], which lasted until his death in 1820.

socialist-republic-of-romania.t: Communist Romania, which under Nicolae Ceaușescu combined independence from Moscow with one of Eastern Europe's harshest dictatorships.
socialist-republic-of-romania.o: With the Soviet army in [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]], the communists took power step by step after 1945, and on 30 December 1947 King Michael I was forced to abdicate, ending the Kingdom of [[e:romania|Romania]]. The Romanian People's Republic was proclaimed the same day, led by Gheorghe Gheorghiu-Dej.
socialist-republic-of-romania.r: The regime nationalised industry, collectivised land and sent opponents to prisons and labour camps such as those on the Danube-[[e:black-sea|Black Sea]] Canal. Soviet troops left in 1958. Nicolae Ceaușescu, leader from 1965, renamed the country the Socialist Republic, refused to join the 1968 invasion of [[s:czechoslovakia|Czechoslovakia]] and won Western favour, but built a personality cult, banned abortion in 1966 and imposed severe austerity in the 1980s to pay off foreign debt.
socialist-republic-of-romania.e: Protests in Timișoara in December 1989 spread to Bucharest. The army turned against Ceaușescu, who was captured and executed with his wife Elena on 25 December 1989 after a summary trial. The National Salvation Front took power, founding post-communist [[s:kingdom-of-romania|Romania]].

cr.a: Various, see File History below for details.

sambyeolcho.t: Rebel Goryeo military units that refused to submit to the Mongols and set up a rival court on Jindo and Jeju from 1270 to 1273.
sambyeolcho.o: The Sambyeolcho, or Three Elite Patrols, were military units formed under the Choe military regime. When King Wonjong ended the military regime and returned the court from Ganghwa island to Kaegyong in 1270, accepting Mongol overlordship, the units under Bae Jung-son rebelled and proclaimed a royal kinsman, Wang On, as king.
sambyeolcho.r: The rebels sailed south to Jindo island, built the Yongjang fortress and controlled much of the southwestern coast and its grain shipments. They sent envoys to [[e:japan|Japan]] seeking support against the [[e:mongols|Mongols]].
sambyeolcho.e: A combined [[s:goryeo|Goryeo]] and Mongol force took Jindo in 1271, killing Wang On and Bae Jung-son. Survivors under Kim Tong-jeong held out on Jeju until 1273. The [[e:mongols|Mongols]] then set up horse pastures on Jeju.

sharifate-of-mecca.t: Nearly a thousand years of rule by the Hashemite Sharifs, descendants of the Prophet, over Mecca, Medina and the pilgrimage.
sharifate-of-mecca.o: Around 967 Ja'far ibn Muhammad, a descendant of al-[[e:hasan-ibn-ali|Hasan ibn Ali]], took control of [[e:mecca|Mecca]] as the [[s:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimid Caliphate]] rose in [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. The Sharifs, as these Hasanid nobles were known, then governed the holy city under whichever power controlled Egypt. In 1201 Qatada ibn Idris founded the line that ruled until 1925.
sharifate-of-mecca.r: The Sharifs kept order in [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and the pilgrimage roads, collected dues from pilgrims and Jeddah's port and balanced Bedouin tribes. Their suzerains, the [[e:fatimid-caliphate|Fatimids]], [[s:ayyubid-empire|Ayyubid Empire]], [[s:mamluk-sultanate|Mamluk Sultanate]] and, from 1517, the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]], sent annual grain and [[e:subsidy|subsidies]]. Family feuds over succession were frequent, and the overlord often chose between rival sharifs. Abu Numayy II secured a long reign in the 16th century.
sharifate-of-mecca.e: The [[s:emirate-of-diriyah|Emirate of Diriyah]] held [[e:mecca|Mecca]] from 1803 to 1813. Ottoman control tightened in the 19th century, and in 1916 Sharif Hussein ibn Ali launched the Arab Revolt and proclaimed the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Kingdom of Hejaz]].

state-of-quito.t: An early patriot state in the Ecuadorian highlands that issued one of the first constitutions in Spanish America before royalist forces crushed it.
state-of-quito.o: Quito's first junta of 10 August 1809 was suppressed, and on 2 August 1810 royalist troops massacred imprisoned patriots in Quito. A second junta formed in September 1810 under [[e:bishop|Bishop]] José Cuero y Caicedo, with Carlos Montúfar, a royal commissioner who sided with the patriots. In December 1811 it broke with the Regency Council in [[e:spain|Spain]].
state-of-quito.r: In February 1812 a congress adopted the Solemn Pact of Society and Union, a constitution creating the State of Quito, which still recognised Ferdinand VII in principle while asserting self-rule. Bitter rivalry between the Montúfar faction and the Sánchez de Orellana family weakened the government, and Cuenca and Guayaquil remained royalist.
state-of-quito.e: Forces sent by the [[e:viceroy-of-india|viceroy]] of [[e:peru|Peru]] under Toribio Montes took Quito in November 1812 and defeated the last patriots at Ibarra in December. The [[s:royal-audiencia-of-quito|Royal Audiencia of Quito]] was restored until independence in 1822.

silaharas-of-north-konkan.t: A coastal dynasty around Thane and Mumbai that ruled the North Konkan for nearly five centuries and built the Ambarnath temple.
silaharas-of-north-konkan.o: The Silaharas of North Konkan were established around 800 when the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakuta dynasty]] appointed Kapardin I to govern the coastal strip around Thane, Mumbai and [[e:raigad|Raigad]]. They claimed descent from the legendary Jimutavahana. Their capital, Puri, is not securely located, and Sthanaka, modern Thane, was another centre.
silaharas-of-north-konkan.r: The Silaharas served as feudatories first of the [[s:rashtrakuta-dynasty|Rashtrakutas]] and then of the [[s:western-chalukya-empire|Western Chalukya Empire]]. The coast's ports, such as Sanjan, Sopara and Chaul, were busy with Arab and Persian merchants, and the kings granted privileges to foreign traders, including [[e:parsis|Parsi]] and Muslim communities. Their many [[e:copper|copper]]-plate grants are among the main sources for coastal Maharashtra. King Mummuni completed the Shiva temple at Ambarnath in 1060.
silaharas-of-north-konkan.e: The dynasty fought the [[s:kadambas-of-goa|Kadambas of Goa]] and the Yadavas. Around 1265 the Yadava king Mahadeva conquered the North Konkan, killing the last Silahara ruler, Someshvara.

saruhanids.t: A Turkish beylik of western Anatolia centred on Manisa, a partner in the 14th-century naval raids on the Aegean.
saruhanids.o: Saruhan Bey, a [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] commander, took Magnesia (Manisa) from the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]] in 1313 and made it the capital of a [[e:beylik|beylik]] in the Hermus valley, north of the [[s:aydinids|Aydinids]].
saruhanids.r: The Saruhanids joined the [[s:aydinids|Aydinids]] in raiding the [[e:aegean|Aegean]] islands and the Greek mainland, and at times sent troops to help Byzantine factions, including John VI Kantakouzenos. The fertile Gediz plain made the [[e:beylik|beylik]] prosperous, and Ishak Bey built the Great Mosque of Manisa in 1366-1367. The beylik also traded with [[s:lordship-of-phocaea|Genoese Phocaea]].
saruhanids.e: [[e:bayezid-i|Bayezid I]] annexed Saruhan in 1390. [[e:timur|Timur]] restored it after the battle of Ankara in 1402, but the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] absorbed it again around 1410, and Manisa became the seat of Ottoman princes.

somavamshi-dynasty.t: A dynasty of western and coastal Odisha that built the Lingaraja and Mukteshvara temples of Bhubaneswar.
somavamshi-dynasty.o: The Somavamshis were a branch of the lunar-line dynasty earlier known as the [[s:panduvamshis-of-dakshina-kosala|Panduvamshis of Dakshina Kosala]]. In the late 9th century Janamejaya I established them in western Odisha, and his successors took over the coastal lands from the declining [[s:bhauma-kara-dynasty|Bhauma-Kara dynasty]], uniting much of Odisha.
somavamshi-dynasty.r: Their capital moved between Yayatinagara and Jajpur. The kings were Shaivas who granted land to [[e:brahmins|Brahmins]], and tradition credits King Yayati Keshari with bringing Brahmins from the north. The temples of Bhubaneswar reached maturity under their rule: the Mukteshvara temple and the great Lingaraja temple, with its soaring tower, date from this period, as does the Brahmeshvara temple built by Queen Kolavati.
somavamshi-dynasty.e: Weakened by invasions from the [[s:chola-empire|Chola Empire]] and the [[s:kalachuris-of-tripuri|Kalachuris of Tripuri]], the Somavamshis were conquered around 1110 by Anantavarman Chodaganga of the [[s:eastern-ganga-dynasty|Eastern Ganga dynasty]].

setsen-khanate.t: The eastern of the three Khalkha khanates of Outer Mongolia, in the Kherlen valley, which submitted to the Qing with the rest of Khalkha in 1691.
setsen-khanate.o: Among the descendants of Geresenje, son of Dayan Khan of the [[s:northern-yuan|Northern Yuan]], the princes of eastern Khalkha along the Kherlen river took the title Setsen Khan in the late 16th century, forming one of the three great divisions of Khalkha alongside the [[s:tusheet-khanate|Tüsheet Khanate]] and [[s:zasagt-khanate|Zasagt Khanate]].
setsen-khanate.r: Its khans ruled herding peoples of the eastern steppe under a council of Chinggisid nobles. Being nearest to [[e:manchuria|Manchuria]], the khanate had early contact with the rising [[e:manchus|Manchu]] state. Sholoi Setsen Khan exchanged embassies and sent tribute to the [[s:later-jin-1616-1636|Later Jin]] (1616-1636) and the early [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]], sometimes clashing with them over raids and border subjects. Gelug [[e:buddhism|Buddhism]] spread here as across Khalkha.
setsen-khanate.e: When the [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] ruler Galdan invaded Khalkha in 1688, the Setsen Khan's people fled towards Inner [[s:mongolia|Mongolia]]. At the assembly of Dolon Nor in 1691 the Khalkha princes accepted Qing rule, and the khanate became a Qing administrative league.

samal.t: Sam'al, a small Aramaean-Luwian kingdom at Zincirli whose kings left some of the most vivid inscriptions of the Iron Age.
samal.o: Sam'al arose in the 10th century BCE in a valley east of the Amanus mountains, near modern Islahiye. According to its own inscriptions, a ruler named Gabbar founded the dynasty, and the land was also called Ya'diya. Its capital at Zincirli was a circular walled city.
samal.r: King Kilamuwa's inscription boasts that he hired the king of [[e:assyrian-empire|Assyria]] against his enemies and improved the lot of his poor subjects. Later kings wrote in a local [[e:aramaic|Aramaic]] dialect; Bar-Rakib built palaces as a loyal [[e:vassal|vassal]] of Tiglath-Pileser III. The Kuttamuwa stele, found in 2008, shows a belief in a soul dwelling in the stone.
samal.e: Sam'al became an Assyrian province by c. 680 BCE; [[e:esarhaddon|Esarhaddon]] set up a victory stele in the city in 671 BCE. German excavations from 1888 and University of Chicago excavations from 2006 uncovered its gates and palaces.

shimazu-clan-domain.t: The domain of the Shimazu of southern Kyushu, who nearly conquered the whole island before submitting to Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1587.
shimazu-clan-domain.o: The Shimazu had been governors of [[e:satsuma-domain|Satsuma]] since the Kamakura period but had splintered into rival branches. Shimazu Takahisa reunited the clan and province by about 1550, ruling from Kagoshima. Portuguese guns reached the Shimazu [[e:vassal|vassals]] on Tanegashima in 1543, and Francis Xavier landed at Kagoshima in 1549.
shimazu-clan-domain.r: Takahisa's son Yoshihisa and his brothers Yoshihiro, Toshihisa and Iehisa formed a formidable military team. They conquered Osumi and Hyuga, crushed the Otomo at Mimikawa in 1578 and the Ryuzoji at Okitanawate in 1584, and by 1586 controlled most of Kyushu. The domain drew strength from a large warrior class and trade through its ports.
shimazu-clan-domain.e: [[e:toyotomi-hideyoshi|Toyotomi Hideyoshi]] invaded Kyushu in 1587 and Yoshihisa surrendered, keeping [[e:satsuma-domain|Satsuma]] and Osumi. After fighting for the losing side at [[e:battle-of-sekigahara|Sekigahara]] in 1600, the Shimazu negotiated to keep their lands as the [[s:satsuma-domain|Satsuma Domain]].

salinas-grandes-confederation.t: A powerful indigenous confederation on the Argentine pampas led by the Mapuche chief Calfucurá, which raided the frontier for decades.
salinas-grandes-confederation.o: Around 1835 the [[s:araucania|Mapuche]] leader Juan Calfucurá crossed from Araucanía to the pampas and seized control of the Salinas Grandes, the great salt flats on the edge of modern La Pampa and Buenos Aires provinces. After eliminating rival Boroano chiefs at Masallé, he built a confederation of Mapuche, Ranquel and other pampas groups.
salinas-grandes-confederation.r: Calfucurá controlled the [[e:salt-trade|salt trade]] and the [[e:cattle|cattle]] routes to [[s:republic-of-chile|Chile]], where stolen livestock was sold. His warriors carried out malones, large raids on frontier towns and ranches. He negotiated treaties and rations with Juan Manuel de Rosas and later with the governments of the [[s:argentine-confederation|Argentine Confederation]] and the [[s:state-of-buenos-aires|State of Buenos Aires]], playing them against each other.
salinas-grandes-confederation.e: The Argentine army defeated Calfucurá at San Carlos in 1872, and he died in 1873. His son Manuel Namuncurá led the confederation until Julio Argentino Roca's Conquest of the Desert from 1878 to 1879 destroyed it. Namuncurá surrendered in 1884.

sheikhdom-of-kalba.t: A short-lived Trucial sheikhdom on the Gulf of Oman coast, recognised by Britain in 1936 in exchange for an emergency airstrip.
sheikhdom-of-kalba.o: Kalba, a town on the east coast of the [[e:oman|Oman]] peninsula, was ruled by a branch of the Al Qasimi family as part of the [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sheikhdom of Sharjah]]. In 1936 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised its sheikh, Said bin Hamad Al Qasimi, as an independent ruler among the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]], in return for permission to build an emergency landing ground for Imperial Airways flights to [[e:india|India]].
sheikhdom-of-kalba.r: The sheikhdom was tiny, living from fishing and date gardens. After Said's death in 1937 his young son succeeded under a regent, and the family's internal disputes, together with rival claims by [[s:sheikhdom-of-fujairah|Fujairah]], left it unstable.
sheikhdom-of-kalba.e: After a violent succession dispute in 1951, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] allowed Kalba to be reincorporated into [[s:sheikhdom-of-sharjah|Sharjah]], and it remains part of that [[e:emirate|emirate]] within the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]].

state-of-chu.t: The vast southern kingdom of the middle Yangtze whose distinctive culture produced the poetry of Qu Yuan and which was Qin's most formidable rival.
state-of-chu.o: The Mi clan of Chu claimed that Xiong Yi was enfeoffed by King [[s:cheng-han|Cheng]] of Zhou at Danyang, in the hills of the [[e:han-river|Han River]] region. Treated by the Zhou states as semi-barbarian, the rulers took the title of king from Xiong Tong (King Wu) in 704 BCE and moved the capital to Ying, near modern Jingzhou in Hubei.
state-of-chu.r: Chu annexed dozens of small states, organising conquests into counties run by appointed officials. King Zhuang became hegemon after defeating Jin at Bi in 597 BCE. Chu culture was distinctive: shamanistic rites, [[e:lacquerware|lacquerware]], [[e:silk|silk]] painting and textiles, and the [[e:song-dynasty|Songs]] of Chu, attributed to the poet Qu Yuan. In 506 BCE the [[s:state-of-wu|State of Wu]] sacked Ying, and in 278 BCE the [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] general Bai Qi took it again.
state-of-chu.e: Chu moved its capital east to Chen and then Shouchun. [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] armies under Wang Jian destroyed it in 223 BCE. A popular saying held that even if only three households remained, Chu would destroy Qin; and Chu rebels led by Chen Sheng, [[e:xiang-yu|Xiang Yu]] and [[e:liu-bang|Liu Bang]] did overthrow the [[s:qin-dynasty|Qin dynasty]].

salghurid-dynasty.t: Turkmen atabegs of Fars whose submission to the Mongols spared Shiraz, and whose patronage is remembered in the works of the poet Saadi.
salghurid-dynasty.o: The Salghurids were [[e:turkmen|Turkmen]] of the Salghur tribe who entered [[e:iran|Iran]] with the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]]. In 1148 Sunqur ibn Mawdud seized [[e:fars|Fars]] from Seljuk officials and ruled from [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]] as atabeg, formally a guardian for Seljuk princes but in practice independent.
salghurid-dynasty.r: The atabegs ruled a prosperous province of farmland, towns and trade routes to the Gulf. Sa'd I ibn Zangi (1198 to 1226) built walls and mosques in [[e:shiraz|Shiraz]]. His son Abu Bakr ibn Sa'd submitted to the Mongol [[e:great-khan|Great Khan]] Ögedei, paying tribute and keeping [[e:fars|Fars]] from destruction. Saadi took his pen name from Abu Bakr's son Sa'd and dedicated the Bustan (1257) and Gulistan (1258) to the dynasty.
salghurid-dynasty.e: After Abu Bakr's death in 1260 a series of short reigns followed. The last ruler, Abish Khatun, was married to the Mongol prince Mengü-Temür, and by 1282 [[e:fars|Fars]] passed under direct control of the [[s:ilkhanate|Ilkhanate]].

segesta.t: Chief city of the Elymians of western Sicily, whose rivalry with Selinous drew both Athens and Carthage into Sicily.
segesta.o: Segesta was the main town of the Elymians, a people of north-western [[e:sicily|Sicily]] who claimed Trojan descent; Thucydides says they were Trojan refugees joined by Phocians. The city grew on Monte Barbaro in the 7th century BCE and became increasingly Hellenised while keeping close ties with the [[e:phoenicians|Phoenicians]] of [[s:motya|Motya]] and [[s:panormus|Panormus]].
segesta.r: Segesta minted coins with Greek legends and wrote its own Elymian language in Greek letters, known from short inscriptions. Its unfinished Doric temple of the late 5th century BCE and its hilltop [[e:theatre|theatre]] are among the best-preserved Greek monuments in [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. Its long border dispute with [[s:selinous|Selinous]] led it to seek Athenian help in 416 BCE, prompting the Sicilian Expedition, and then Carthaginian help, which ended in the destruction of Selinous in 409 BCE.
segesta.e: Agathocles of [[s:syracuse|Syracuse]] massacred many citizens in 307 BCE. In the [[e:first-punic-war|First Punic War]] Segesta went over to [[e:rome|Rome]], citing shared Trojan ancestry, and after 241 BCE it was a privileged free town of Roman [[e:sicily|Sicily]]. It was abandoned in the Middle Ages.

susquehannock.t: An Iroquoian people of the lower Susquehanna valley, powerful middlemen in the 17th-century fur trade until wars with the Iroquois and colonists broke them.
susquehannock.o: The Susquehannock moved down the Susquehanna River into southern Pennsylvania in the 16th century, settling near modern Lancaster in large palisaded towns. When John Smith met them in 1608 on Chesapeake Bay he described them as tall and well armed. They spoke an Iroquoian language but were long-standing enemies of the [[s:iroquois-confederacy|Iroquois Confederacy]].
susquehannock.r: Controlling routes between the interior and the Chesapeake and Delaware bays, the Susquehannock traded beaver pelts for European goods with [[e:virginia|Virginia]], Maryland, [[s:new-netherland|New Netherland]] and [[s:new-sweden|New Sweden]], which supplied them with guns. Their towns were run by councils of chiefs, and they farmed [[e:maize|maize]] and hunted. In 1652 they made a treaty with the [[s:province-of-maryland|Province of Maryland]], ceding land along the bay.
susquehannock.e: Epidemics and wars with the [[s:seneca-nation|Seneca]] wore them down, and in 1675 they abandoned their homeland. Attacked by Maryland and [[e:virginia|Virginia]] militia at their fort on the Potomac, their raids helped spark Bacon's Rebellion. Survivors joined the Iroquois; the last Conestoga were killed by the Paxton Boys in 1763.

sloboda-ukraine.t: A frontier land of free Cossack settlements east of the Dnieper, founded by refugees and organised into regiments under the tsars.
sloboda-ukraine.o: From the 1630s, and especially after the wars that followed 1648, Ukrainian peasants and [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]] fled from Polish-ruled lands into the empty steppe borderland of the [[s:tsardom-of-russia|Tsardom of Russia]]. [[e:moscow|Moscow]] granted them freedom from taxes and land in return for guarding its southern frontier. Their settlements, called slobody, gave the region its name, and Kharkiv was founded around 1654.
sloboda-ukraine.r: The region was organised into five [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] regiments, Kharkiv, Sumy, Okhtyrka, Izium and Ostrogozhsk, each led by a colonel. Unlike the [[s:cossack-hetmanate|Cossack Hetmanate]], there was no [[e:hetman|hetman]], and the regiments answered directly to [[e:moscow|Moscow]]. The settlers farmed the black earth, traded and defended the frontier against Crimean [[e:tatars|Tatar]] raids. The philosopher Hryhorii Skovoroda taught at the Kharkiv Collegium.
sloboda-ukraine.e: In 1765 [[e:catherine-the-great|Catherine II]] abolished the [[e:cossacks|Cossack]] regiments and created the Sloboda [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]] [[e:governorate|Governorate]], turning the Cossacks into ordinary subjects. The region later formed the core of the Kharkiv province of the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]].

serbian-despotate.t: Last medieval Serbian state, which held out against the Ottomans for half a century from its fortresses on the Danube and its rich silver mines.
serbian-despotate.o: After the battle of Kosovo in 1389, Lazar's son Stefan Lazarević ruled [[s:moravian-serbia|Moravian Serbia]] as an Ottoman [[e:vassal|vassal]]. Following the Ottoman defeat at Ankara in 1402, the Byzantine emperor granted him the title of despot, and he made [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]] his capital with Hungarian backing. In 1427 the despotate passed to his nephew Đurađ Branković.
serbian-despotate.r: The despotate drew great wealth from the [[e:silver|silver]] mines of Novo Brdo and Srebrenica, worked partly by [[e:saxons|Saxon]] miners and traded through [[s:republic-of-ragusa|Ragusa]]. Stefan Lazarević was a writer and patron, and the Resava school of scribes refined Serbian Church Slavonic. When [[e:belgrade|Belgrade]] returned to [[e:hungary|Hungary]], Đurađ built the vast fortress of Smederevo on the [[e:danube|Danube]] between 1428 and 1430.
serbian-despotate.e: The [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] overran [[s:serbia|Serbia]] in 1439, but the Peace of Szeged restored Đurađ in 1444. After his death in 1456 and that of his son Lazar in 1458, internal quarrels left Smederevo exposed, and [[e:mehmed-ii|Mehmed II]] took it in 1459, ending Serbian independence until the 19th century.

sitamau-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state of Malwa, branch of the Ratlam house, whose prince Raghubir Sinh became a noted historian.
sitamau-state.o: Sitamau was founded in 1701 by Keshav Das, a member of the Rathore family of [[s:ratlam-state|Ratlam]], who received the territory as his own holding. Its rulers belonged to the same line that founded Ratlam and [[s:sailana-state|Sailana]].
sitamau-state.r: The Rajas ruled a small plateau territory of wheat and opium. In the 18th century the state paid tribute to Sindhia, and after 1818 it came under British paramountcy as a salute state of the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] Agency. Maharaj Kumar Raghubir Sinh founded a research library on Indian history at Sitamau.
sitamau-state.e: Sitamau joined [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and Madhya Pradesh in 1956. The Raghubir Library remains a centre for historical research in Mandsaur district.

second-east-turkestan-republic.t: A Soviet-backed republic in the Ili region of northern Xinjiang, founded during the Ili Rebellion of 1944 and absorbed into the People's Republic in 1949.
second-east-turkestan-republic.o: In 1944 resentment against the [[e:xinjiang|Xinjiang]] governor Sheng Shicai and Nationalist rule, encouraged by the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], erupted in the Ili Rebellion. Rebels took Ghulja (Yining), and on 12 November 1944 proclaimed the East Turkestan Republic, with the [[e:uzbeks|Uzbek]] cleric Elihan Töre as president.
second-east-turkestan-republic.r: With Soviet weapons and advisers, the republic built an army of [[e:uyghurs|Uyghurs]], [[e:kazakhs|Kazakhs]] and other peoples and held the three northern districts of Ili, Tarbagatai and [[e:altai-mountains|Altai]]. In 1946 it joined a coalition provincial government with the [[s:nationalist-government|Nationalist government]], negotiated by Zhang Zhizhong. Elihan Töre was removed to the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], and the secular Ahmetjan Qasimi led the region.
second-east-turkestan-republic.e: In August 1949 Ahmetjan Qasimi and other leaders died in a plane crash on their way to [[e:beijing|Beijing]]. The remaining leadership, with Saifuddin Azizi, accepted the People's Liberation Army, and the region became part of the [[s:peoples-republic-of-china|People's Republic of China]].
