spanish-protectorate-in-morocco.t: Spain's zone of Morocco, covering the Rif and the north coast, scene of the Rif War and the launchpad of Franco's 1936 coup.
spanish-protectorate-in-morocco.o: After the Treaty of [[e:fez|Fez]] created the [[s:french-protectorate-in-morocco|French protectorate in Morocco]] in 1912, a Franco-Spanish treaty of November 1912 assigned [[e:spain|Spain]] a northern zone along the [[e:mediterranean|Mediterranean]] coast, including the Rif and Jbala mountains, and a southern zone around Cape Juby. Tetouan became the capital.
spanish-protectorate-in-morocco.r: The sultan was represented by a [[e:khalifa|khalifa]] at Tetouan, while a Spanish high commissioner held real power. The mountain tribes resisted fiercely: the Rif War and the disaster at Annual in 1921 cost [[e:spain|Spain]] thousands of lives. Spain later recruited Moroccan troops, and in July 1936 Francisco Franco launched his rising from the [[e:protectorate|protectorate]], bringing the Army of [[e:africa|Africa]] to the mainland.
spanish-protectorate-in-morocco.e: Following French recognition of Moroccan independence, [[e:spain|Spain]] ended its [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in April 1956, and the northern zone joined the [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Kingdom of Morocco]]; the Tarfaya strip followed in 1958. [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] and Melilla remained Spanish.

sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi.t: The Al Nahyan sheikhdom of the Bani Yas, which grew from a pearling settlement into the oil-rich heart of the United Arab Emirates.
sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi.o: According to tradition, Bani Yas tribesmen hunting on the island of Abu Dhabi found fresh water in 1761, and a settlement grew there. The Al Nahyan sheikhs, leaders of the Bani Yas, moved their seat from the Liwa oases to the island in the 1790s.
sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi.r: Abu Dhabi controlled a large desert hinterland, including Liwa and part of the Buraimi oasis, and lived from pearling, dates and [[e:camel|camels]]. From 1820 it was one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] under British protection. Zayed bin [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]], ruling from 1855 to 1909, made it the strongest sheikhdom on the coast. The collapse of the pearl trade in the 1930s brought great poverty.
sheikhdom-of-abu-dhabi.e: Oil was found offshore in 1958 and exported from 1962. In 1966 Zayed bin [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Al Nahyan replaced his brother Shakhbut and used the revenues for development. He led the creation of the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] in 1971 and became its first president.

sixteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: A short-lived Theban dynasty of the Second Intermediate Period that held Upper Egypt against the Hyksos.
sixteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: When the Thirteenth Dynasty collapsed and the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] took Memphis around 1650 BCE, a line of kings established itself at [[s:thebes|Thebes]], controlling [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]] from [[s:abydos|Abydos]] to Elephantine. Its existence as a separate dynasty was clarified by the reconstruction of the Turin King List by Kim Ryholt.
sixteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The kings ruled a small, embattled realm, and their stelae speak of war and famine. Neferhotep III and Nebiryraw I are among the better-attested rulers; stelae of Neferhotep III boast of rescuing [[s:thebes|Thebes]] in a time of hunger. They relied on the god [[e:amun|Amun]] and local garrisons, and were pressed by both the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Fifteenth Dynasty of Egypt]] to the north and [[s:kerma|Kerma]] to the south.
sixteenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Around 1580 BCE the line seems to have been overrun by [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] campaigns or replaced from within [[s:thebes|Thebes]], and it was followed by the [[s:seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Seventeenth Dynasty of Egypt]], which led the war of liberation.

sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain.t: The small Al Mualla sheikhdom on the Trucial Coast, one of the founding members of the United Arab Emirates.
sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain.o: The Al Ali tribe, led by the Al Mualla family, founded a fortified settlement at Umm al-Quwain on a sandy peninsula of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial Coast]] in 1775 under Rashid bin Majid Al Mualla. It also held the inland oasis of Falaj al-Mualla.
sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain.r: The sheikhdom lived from fishing, pearling and boatbuilding, with the lagoon and its mangroves at its centre. It signed the General Maritime Treaty of 1820 and became one of the [[s:trucial-states|Trucial States]] under British protection. It was among the poorest of the sheikhdoms, without significant oil, and Ahmad bin Rashid Al Mualla ruled it from 1929 to 1981.
sheikhdom-of-umm-al-quwain.e: Umm al-Quwain joined the [[s:united-arab-emirates|United Arab Emirates]] at its foundation in December 1971 and remains one of its seven [[e:emirate|emirates]].

spanish-bougie.t: Bejaia under Spanish occupation, a contested fortress that resisted the Barbarossa brothers for decades before falling to Ottoman Algiers.
spanish-bougie.o: In January 1510 Pedro Navarro captured Bejaia, then ruled by a Hafsid prince, as part of [[e:spain|Spain's]] campaign along the North African coast after the fall of [[e:granada|Granada]]. The conquest made Bejaia a Spanish presidio comparable to [[s:spanish-oran|Spanish Oran]].
spanish-bougie.r: The Spanish held only the town and its forts, with a garrison cut off from the hinterland, where the [[s:kingdom-of-kuku|Kingdom of Kuku]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-ait-abbas|Kingdom of Ait Abbas]] held sway. The corsair Oruç Barbarossa attacked Bejaia in 1512 and 1514 and lost his arm in the first attempt. The port's trade declined sharply.
spanish-bougie.e: In 1555 Salah Rais, beylerbey of the [[s:regency-of-algiers|Regency of Algiers]], besieged and took Bejaia. Its governor Alonso de Peralta surrendered and was executed in [[e:spain|Spain]] for doing so. The city became part of Ottoman [[e:algeria|Algeria]].

seongsan-gaya.t: A Gaya polity at Seongju on the middle Nakdong, one of the six Gaya states of legend, closely tied to Silla.
seongsan-gaya.o: Seongsan Gaya, also called Byeokjin Gaya, is identified with Byeokjin-guk, a [[s:byeonhan|Byeonhan]] statelet, and is listed in the Samguk yusa as one of the six Gaya states founded in 42 CE. Its centre lay in the Seongju basin north of [[s:daegaya|Daegaya]].
seongsan-gaya.r: Few records survive. The large tombs at Seongsan-dong contain stoneware and metalwork largely of [[s:silla|Silla]] style, suggesting that its elite fell under Silla influence early while remaining nominally part of the Gaya world.
seongsan-gaya.e: It was absorbed by [[s:silla|Silla]], at the latest during the final conquest of the Gaya states around 562, and became a Silla district.

shunga-empire.t: The Brahmin dynasty that seized power from the last Mauryas and ruled the Ganges plain and central India for over a century.
shunga-empire.o: Around 185 BCE Pushyamitra Shunga, commander of the Maurya army, assassinated the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha, during a military parade and took the throne at [[e:pataliputra|Pataliputra]]. The new kingdom was smaller than the [[s:maurya-empire|Maurya Empire]], covering [[s:kingdom-of-magadha|Magadha]], the middle [[e:ganges-plain|Ganges plain]] and the Vidisha region of central [[e:india|India]].
shunga-empire.r: Pushyamitra performed Vedic horse sacrifices, signalling a revival of Brahmanical kingship; Buddhist texts accuse him of persecution, though Buddhist art flourished in the Shunga period at Bharhut and Sanchi. The Shungas fought the [[s:indo-greek-kingdom|Indo-Greek Kingdom]] and Kharavela of [[s:kingdom-of-kalinga|Kalinga]]. [[e:kalidasa|Kalidasa's]] play Malavikagnimitram is set at the court of Agnimitra in Vidisha, where the Heliodorus pillar records a Greek envoy honouring Vasudeva.
shunga-empire.e: The empire broke into regional centres as power shifted to Vidisha. Around 73 BCE the last king, Devabhuti, was killed at the instigation of his minister Vasudeva, who founded the [[s:kanva-dynasty|Kanva dynasty]]. Shunga descendants may have survived as local rulers in central [[e:india|India]].

suket-state.t: A Sen dynasty hill state south of Mandi whose people's 1948 protest movement, the Suket Satyagraha, helped bring about the formation of Himachal Pradesh.
suket-state.o: Tradition holds that Bir Sen, of a Sen family from [[e:bengal|Bengal]], founded the state around 765, with an early capital at Pangna. [[s:mandi-state|Mandi State]] was later established by a junior branch of the same family, and the two states were frequent rivals.
suket-state.r: The Rajas moved their capital several times, to Lohara and Kartarpur and finally to Banaid, renamed Sundernagar. Suket was a small agricultural state on the route between the [[e:sutlej-river|Sutlej]] and [[e:beas|Beas]] valleys. It came under the [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] in the early 19th century and under British protection after 1846.
suket-state.e: In February 1948 the Suket Satyagraha, led by local Praja Mandal activists, forced Raja Lakshman Sen to cede control. Suket was merged into Himachal Pradesh in April 1948, and Sundernagar is now a town in [[s:mandi-state|Mandi]] district.

sirohi-state.t: The Deora Chauhan Rajput state of south-western Rajasthan, which held Mount Abu and its Dilwara Jain temples and was famed for its swords.
sirohi-state.o: The Deora branch of the Chauhans, descended from the [[s:chahamanas-of-jalor|Chahamanas of Jalor]], ruled the hills around Abu in the 14th century. In the early 15th century they established their seat at Sirohi, which became the capital of the state.
sirohi-state.r: Sirohi was a rugged state on the routes between [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] and [[s:jodhpur-state|Marwar]], often at war with Marwar. Its territory included Mount Abu, with the marble Dilwara Jain temples, and Sirohi blades were renowned across [[e:india|India]]. The state signed a treaty with the British in 1823, and in 1845 leased part of Mount Abu for a sanatorium, which became headquarters of the Rajputana Agency.
sirohi-state.e: Sirohi joined Rajasthan in 1949, though Abu was briefly given to Bombay State before returning to Rajasthan in 1956. It is now a district of Rajasthan.

siba-state.t: A tiny Rajput hill state in the Kangra region, an offshoot of Guler, absorbed into the Sikh Empire in the early 19th century.
siba-state.o: Siba was founded by a branch of the ruling family of [[s:guler-state|Guler State]], itself descended from the Katoch dynasty of [[s:kangra-state|Kangra]]; tradition places the split in the 15th century.
siba-state.r: Siba was a small state of a few villages and forts in the [[e:beas|Beas]] valley, with little recorded history of its own.
siba-state.e: The [[s:sikh-empire|Sikh Empire]] took control of Siba around 1830, and after 1846 the British confirmed the family in a [[e:jagir|jagir]]. The area is now in [[s:kangra-state|Kangra]] district, Himachal Pradesh.

spanish-netherlands.t: The southern Low Countries under the Spanish Habsburgs, battleground of Europe and home of Rubens, which survived the Dutch Revolt but lost land to France.
spanish-netherlands.o: In 1555–1556 [[e:charles-v-holy-roman-emperor|Charles V]] passed the [[s:habsburg-netherlands|Habsburg Netherlands]] to his son [[e:philip-ii-of-spain|Philip II of Spain]]. Philip's persecution of Protestants, new bishoprics and taxes provoked the [[e:dutch-revolt|Dutch Revolt]] from 1566. After the [[e:fernando-alvarez-de-toledo-3rd-duke-of-alba|Duke of Alba's]] harsh rule, the southern provinces made peace with Philip through the Union of Arras in 1579.
spanish-netherlands.r: The Duke of [[s:duchy-of-parma-and-piacenza|Parma]] reconquered [[s:county-of-flanders|Flanders]] and [[s:duchy-of-brabant|Brabant]], taking [[e:antwerp|Antwerp]] in 1585, while the north became the [[s:dutch-republic|Dutch Republic]]. The Archdukes Albert and Isabella governed from 1598 to 1621 and agreed the Twelve Years' Truce. The provinces became a Counter-[[e:protestant-reformation|Reformation]] stronghold; Rubens worked in Antwerp. The Treaty of Münster of 1648 closed the Scheldt, hurting Antwerp's trade.
spanish-netherlands.e: [[e:louis-xiv|Louis XIV]] took [[s:county-of-artois|Artois]], Lille, [[s:prince-bishopric-of-cambrai|Cambrai]] and other lands between 1659 and 1678. After the [[e:war-of-the-spanish-succession|War of the Spanish Succession]], the Treaties of [[s:lordship-of-utrecht|Utrecht]] and Rastatt in 1713–1714 gave the territory to [[e:austria|Austria]] as the [[s:austrian-netherlands|Austrian Netherlands]].

sicyon.t: City of the northern Peloponnese ruled by Greece's longest tyranny, a famed centre of painting and sculpture and the home of Aratus, leader of the Achaean League.
sicyon.o: Sicyon lay in a fertile plain west of [[s:corinth|Corinth]], near the Gulf of Corinth. It was settled by Dorians from [[s:argos|Argos]] in the early Iron Age and became an independent city. In the 7th century BCE it fell under the Orthagorid tyrants, whose rule [[e:aristotle|Aristotle]] called the longest-lasting in [[e:greece|Greece]].
sicyon.r: The tyrant Cleisthenes, early 6th century BCE, renamed the Dorian tribes, fought [[s:argos|Argos]] and helped win the First Sacred War; his daughter Agariste married into the Athenian Alcmaeonids. Sicyon was later an oligarchy and a member of the [[s:peloponnesian-league|Peloponnesian League]]. It became famous for bronze sculpture, especially Lysippus, and for its school of painting, where Apelles studied.
sicyon.e: Demetrius Poliorcetes moved the city to a defensible plateau in 303 BCE. Aratus freed Sicyon from tyranny in 251 BCE and joined it to the [[s:achaean-league|Achaean League]], which he then led. Sicyon passed under [[e:rome|Rome]] in 146 BCE, gaining from the destruction of [[s:corinth|Corinth]].

saito-clan-domain.t: The short-lived domain of the Saito in Mino, founded by the notorious usurper Saito Dosan, the viper of Mino, and taken by Oda Nobunaga in 1567.
saito-clan-domain.o: Saito Dosan, whose rise from obscurity later legends ascribed to a former oil merchant though modern scholars credit part of it to his father, served the Toki governors of Mino. Around 1542 he expelled Toki Yorinari and made himself master of the province from Inabayama castle.
saito-clan-domain.r: Dosan governed by force and intrigue and married his daughter to [[e:oda-nobunaga|Oda Nobunaga]] to secure peace with Owari. His position rested on Mino's rich farmland and its location on routes between eastern [[e:japan|Japan]] and [[e:kyoto|Kyoto]].
saito-clan-domain.e: Dosan's son Yoshitatsu rose against him and killed him at the Nagara river in 1556. Yoshitatsu's son Tatsuoki lost Inabayama to Nobunaga in 1567; Nobunaga renamed it Gifu and made it his base.
