sultanate-of-quitangonha.t: A small Swahili sultanate north of Mozambique Island that grew rich on the 19th-century slave trade before Portuguese conquest.
sultanate-of-quitangonha.o: Quitangonha lay on the coast and islands north of [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Mozambique]] Island, around Matibane. [[e:swahili|Swahili]] Muslim families established a ruling house there by the 18th century, closely tied by marriage to [[s:sheikhdom-of-sancul|Sancul]], [[s:sultanate-of-angoche|Angoche]] and the Comoros.
sultanate-of-quitangonha.r: Its rulers held authority over [[e:swahili|Swahili]] coastal towns and drew on alliances with Makua chiefs inland. In the 19th century Quitangonha became a centre of the clandestine [[e:atlantic-slave-trade|slave trade]], shipping captives to Madagascar, the Comoros and French plantation islands, despite Portuguese and British efforts to suppress it.
sultanate-of-quitangonha.e: The sultanate resisted Portuguese control in alliance with Makua chiefs, but it was subdued during Portuguese military campaigns of the mid-1890s and absorbed into [[s:portuguese-mozambique|Portuguese Mozambique]].

sailendra-kingdom.t: The Buddhist dynasty of Central Java that built Borobudur, the largest Buddhist monument in the world, in the late 8th and early 9th centuries.
sailendra-kingdom.o: The [[e:sailendra-dynasty|Sailendras]], 'lords of the mountain', appear in inscriptions from the 770s. The Kalasan inscription of 778 records a temple to the goddess Tara built under their patronage. Whether they were a separate kingdom or a branch ruling within the [[s:medang-kingdom|Medang Kingdom]] is still debated, as is their possible origin in [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]] or mainland [[e:southeast-asia|Southeast Asia]].
sailendra-kingdom.r: The dynasty were patrons of [[e:mahayana-buddhism|Mahayana Buddhism]]. Under Samaratungga the great stupa-mountain of [[e:borobudur|Borobudur]] was completed around 825, alongside Mendut and Pawon. They kept close ties with [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]], and their power was felt as far as the [[e:malay-peninsula|Malay Peninsula]] and possibly [[s:kingdom-of-cambodia-1953-1970|Cambodia]].
sailendra-kingdom.e: Samaratungga's daughter Pramodhawardhani married Rakai Pikatan of the Sanjaya line, and the [[e:sailendra-dynasty|Sailendras]] lost their hold on Central [[e:java|Java]] in the mid-9th century. Her half-brother Balaputradewa went to [[e:sumatra|Sumatra]] and became king of [[e:srivijaya|Srivijaya]], where the Sailendra name continued for centuries.

somali-democratic-republic.t: Somalia under the military rule of Siad Barre, a socialist state whose defeat in the Ogaden and repression of clans led to its collapse in 1991.
somali-democratic-republic.o: On 21 October 1969, days after the assassination of President Abdirashid Ali Shermarke, the army led by Mohamed Siad Barre seized power in the [[s:somali-republic|Somali Republic]]. A Supreme Revolutionary Council suspended the constitution, banned parties and renamed the country the [[e:somalis|Somali]] Democratic Republic, declaring scientific socialism in 1970.
somali-democratic-republic.r: Barre allied with the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], nationalised the economy and in 1972 made [[e:somalis|Somali]] a written official language in [[e:latin|Latin]] script, followed by mass literacy campaigns. In 1977 [[s:somalia|Somalia]] invaded [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia's]] [[e:ogaden|Ogaden]], but the Soviets switched sides and Somali forces were defeated in 1978. Barre then relied increasingly on his own clan alliances, and his forces bombed Hargeisa in 1988, killing thousands of [[s:isaaq-sultanate|Isaaq]].
somali-democratic-republic.e: Rebel movements, including the [[e:somalis|Somali]] National Movement in the north and the United Somali Congress in the south, closed in, and in January 1991 Barre fled [[s:sultanate-of-mogadishu|Mogadishu]]. The state collapsed into civil war; the north declared itself the [[s:republic-of-somaliland|Republic of Somaliland]].

state-of-ju.t: A Dongyi state in south-east Shandong that held its own between Qi and Lu for six centuries and sheltered the future Duke Huan of Qi in exile.
state-of-ju.o: Ju was a non-Zhou state of the Dongyi peoples on the coastal hills of south-eastern Shandong, with its capital at Ju (modern Juxian). The Zhou kings recognised it after their conquest, and it was ruled by a lineage whose surname is variously given as Ying or Ji.
state-of-ju.r: Ju appears often in the Zuo zhuan as a middling power that fought and allied with its neighbours the [[s:state-of-lu|State of Lu]] and the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]]. It gave refuge to Prince Xiaobai of Qi, who returned in 685 BCE to become Duke Huan, the first hegemon. Its culture blended Dongyi traditions with Zhou bronze ritual.
state-of-ju.e: The [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]], pushing north into Shandong, conquered Ju in 431 BCE, and the area later passed to Qi. The walled city of Ju survived as a stronghold: in 284 BCE it was one of the last two Qi cities to hold out against the invading [[s:state-of-yan|State of Yan]].

spanish-first-republic.t: Spain's first republic, which went through four presidents in eleven months amid Carlist war, cantonal revolts and war in Cuba.
spanish-first-republic.o: When Amadeo I abdicated on 11 February 1873, the Cortes proclaimed a republic, ending the monarchy of the [[s:sexenio-democratico|Sexenio Democrático]]. Estanislao Figueras became the first head of the executive.
spanish-first-republic.r: The Republic was divided between unitary and federal republicans. A federal constitution dividing [[e:spain|Spain]] into states was drafted in 1873, largely by Emilio Castelar, but never adopted. The government faced the Third Carlist War, the Cuban Ten Years' War and the Cantonal Rebellion, and its presidents, Figueras, Pi, Nicolás Salmerón and Emilio Castelar, followed in quick succession.
spanish-first-republic.e: On 3 January 1874 General Manuel Pavía dissolved the Cortes. A unitary republic under Serrano followed until General Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII in December 1874, beginning [[s:restoration-spain|Restoration Spain]].

sunda-kingdom.t: The Hindu kingdom of West Java, ruled from Pakuan Pajajaran near Bogor, which resisted Majapahit and Islam until Banten took its capital in 1579.
sunda-kingdom.o: Sundanese tradition dates the kingdom to 669, when Tarusbawa took the western half of the former [[s:tarumanagara|Tarumanagara]] lands, the eastern half becoming the [[s:galuh-kingdom|Galuh Kingdom]]. The two crowns were often joined, and in 1482 Sri Baduga Maharaja united them permanently, ruling from Pakuan Pajajaran, the site of modern Bogor.
sunda-kingdom.r: [[e:sunda-strait|Sunda]] was an agrarian realm that exported [[e:pepper|pepper]] through ports such as Sunda Kalapa, later Jakarta. The Batutulis inscription of 1533 honours Sri Baduga for building moats and sacred forests. In 1357 King Linggabuana and his daughter Dyah Pitaloka were killed by [[e:majapahit-empire|Majapahit]] troops in the Battle of Bubat, an episode long remembered in Sundanese literature.
sunda-kingdom.e: In 1522 [[e:sunda-strait|Sunda]] signed a treaty with the Portuguese against the rising Muslim states, but in 1527 forces of [[s:demak-sultanate|Demak]] seized Sunda Kalapa. The [[s:banten-sultanate|Banten Sultanate]] captured Pakuan in 1579 and the kingdom fell. Sundanese language and identity remain strong in West [[e:java|Java]] today.

sexenio-democratico.t: Six turbulent years of revolution in Spain, from the fall of Isabella II through an elected king and a republic to the return of the Bourbons.
sexenio-democratico.o: In September 1868 a military rising led by Generals Juan Prim and Francisco Serrano and Admiral Juan Bautista Topete, known as the Glorious Revolution, drove Isabella II into exile. A provisional government called elections by [[e:universal-suffrage|universal male suffrage]], and the Constitution of 1869 declared [[e:spain|Spain]] a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]].
sexenio-democratico.r: With the throne vacant, Serrano acted as regent while Prim searched [[e:europe|Europe]] for a king, a search that helped trigger the [[e:franco-prussian-war|Franco-Prussian War]]. The Cortes chose Amadeo of [[s:duchy-of-savoy|Savoy]], but Prim was assassinated in December 1870, days before he arrived. Amadeo faced Carlist rebellion, war in [[e:cuba|Cuba]] and fractious parties, and abdicated in February 1873.
sexenio-democratico.e: The [[s:spanish-first-republic|Spanish First Republic]] followed, collapsing into the Pavía coup of January 1874. In December 1874 General Martínez Campos proclaimed Alfonso XII at [[s:saguntum|Sagunto]], opening [[s:restoration-spain|Restoration Spain]].

satara-state.t: The kingdom restored by the British for the descendants of Shivaji after the fall of the Peshwa, and the first state annexed under the doctrine of lapse.
satara-state.o: The Bhonsle [[e:chhatrapati|Chhatrapatis]], heirs of [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]], had been figureheads at Satara while the [[e:peshwa|Peshwas]] held real power. After defeating Peshwa Baji Rao II in 1818, the British set up Pratap Singh as Raja of a small kingdom at Satara to win [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] support.
satara-state.r: Pratap Singh governed with energy, building roads and public works, but the British deposed him in 1839 on charges of intrigue and installed his brother Shahaji. The state remained small and under the close watch of the Bombay government.
satara-state.e: When Shahaji died in 1848 without a natural son, [[e:lord-dalhousie|Lord Dalhousie]] refused to recognise his adopted heir and annexed Satara, the first state taken under the doctrine of lapse. It became a district of the [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Presidency]].

cr.a: Society for the Diffusion of Useful Knowledge (Great Britain)

sauromatae.t: Iranian-speaking nomads between the Don and the southern Urals, ancestors of the Sarmatians, remembered by Herodotus for their armed and riding women.
sauromatae.o: [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]] places the [[s:sarmatians|Sauromatae]] east of the Don, beyond the [[s:scythia|Royal Scythians]], in the 5th century BCE, and tells the legend that they descended from Scythian men and [[e:amazon|Amazons]]. Archaeologists link them to the Early Sarmatian or Sauromatian culture of the lower [[e:volga|Volga]] and southern Urals, which took shape around the 6th century BCE.
sauromatae.r: They lived as pastoral nomads moving between seasonal pastures, burying their dead in kurgans with weapons, bronze mirrors and stone altars. A striking feature of their graves is the number of women buried with arrows, swords and horse gear, which matches [[e:herodotus|Herodotus]]' remark that their women rode, hunted and fought, and could not marry before killing an enemy.
sauromatae.e: From the 4th century BCE the [[s:sarmatians|Sauromatae]] merged into the larger Sarmatian confederations, including the [[s:aorsi|Aorsi]] and Siraces, which pushed west across the Don and displaced the [[e:scythians|Scythians]]. Their name largely gives way to 'Sarmatians' in later Greek and Roman sources.

sweden-norway.t: Personal union of Sweden and Norway under the Bernadotte kings, created in 1814 and peacefully dissolved by Norway in 1905.
sweden-norway.o: By the Treaty of [[e:kiel|Kiel]] in 1814 [[e:denmark|Denmark]] ceded [[e:norway|Norway]] to [[e:sweden|Sweden]], but the Norwegians adopted a constitution at Eidsvoll and elected their own king. After a short war in the summer of 1814, the Convention of Moss allowed Norway to keep its constitution, and the Storting elected Charles XIII of Sweden as king of Norway. The Act of Union of 1815 set the terms.
sweden-norway.r: Each kingdom kept its own parliament, government, laws, army and currency, sharing only the monarch and foreign policy, which was run from Stockholm. The Bernadotte kings, starting with Charles XIV John, tried to strengthen the union, while Norwegian nationalism and parliamentary democracy grew. In 1884 [[e:norway|Norway]] won parliamentary government.
sweden-norway.e: A dispute over a separate Norwegian consular service came to a head when the Storting declared on 7 June 1905 that the king had ceased to rule [[e:norway|Norway]]. Norwegians voted overwhelmingly for dissolution, the Karlstad Convention settled terms peacefully, and Prince Carl of [[e:denmark|Denmark]] became Haakon VII of the [[s:kingdom-of-norway|Kingdom of Norway]].

stavropol-soviet-republic.t: A short-lived Soviet republic centred on Stavropol during the first months of the Russian Civil War in 1918.
stavropol-soviet-republic.o: In early 1918 the Bolsheviks took power in Stavropol [[e:governorate|Governorate]] and proclaimed the Stavropol Soviet Republic as an autonomous part of the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]]. It was one of several regional Soviet republics declared in the south of [[e:russia|Russia]] as the old administration collapsed.
stavropol-soviet-republic.r: Governed by a council of people's commissars, the republic covered the grain lands of Stavropol, where the peasants were largely Russian and Ukrainian settlers. It requisitioned grain and organised Red Guard units to fight the Volunteer Army and anti-Bolshevik [[e:cossacks|Cossacks]]. Little is known of its internal administration.
stavropol-soviet-republic.e: In July 1918 it was merged into the [[s:north-caucasian-soviet-republic|North Caucasian Soviet Republic]]. The Whites took Stavropol later that year, and Soviet power returned only in 1920. The territory was later absorbed into the Soviet North [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]] Krai.

spanish-jamaica.t: Spain's lightly settled colony of Santiago on Jamaica, held for 146 years mainly for cattle and provisions until the English conquest of 1655.
spanish-jamaica.o: [[e:christopher-columbus|Columbus]] reached [[s:jamaica|Jamaica]] in 1494 and was stranded there in 1503-04. In 1509 Juan de Esquivel, sent by Diego Colón, founded Sevilla la Nueva on the north coast. Around 1534 the capital moved to Villa de la Vega, later Spanish Town, on the southern plain.
spanish-jamaica.r: The island was the hereditary domain of the [[e:christopher-columbus|Columbus]] family. With no gold, it became a supply base raising [[e:cattle|cattle]], pigs and horses and producing hides, lard and [[e:cassava|cassava]] for passing fleets and the conquest of the mainland. The Taíno population was nearly wiped out within decades, and enslaved Africans were brought in. The Spanish population remained small.
spanish-jamaica.e: In 1655 an English expedition under Penn and Venables took the island. Spanish [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrillas]] under Cristóbal Arnaldo Ysasi resisted until 1660, and freed Africans formed the [[s:jamaican-maroons|Jamaican Maroons]]. The island became the [[s:colony-of-jamaica|Colony of Jamaica]].

sharifate-of-tazeroualt.t: A sharifian lordship in the Anti-Atlas, ruled from Iligh, that controlled the Sous and its Saharan trade during the Saadi collapse.
sharifate-of-tazeroualt.o: Abu Hassan Ali al-Semlali, a descendant of the saint Sidi Ahmed ou Moussa, built a power base in the Tazeroualt region of the Anti-[[e:atlas-mountains|Atlas]]. As the [[s:saadi-sultanate|Saadi Sultanate]] disintegrated after 1603, he took control of the Sous around 1613 and ruled from Iligh.
sharifate-of-tazeroualt.r: The sharifate combined the prestige of a holy lineage with control of trade routes linking the Sous to [[e:timbuktu|Timbuktu]] and the [[e:sahara|Sahara]], and of Atlantic ports such as Massa. Its ruler dealt with [[e:dutch|Dutch]], English and French merchants, exporting [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]], gold and slaves.
sharifate-of-tazeroualt.e: Moulay al-Rashid of the [[s:alaouite-sultanate|Alaouite Sultanate]] took Iligh in 1670 and destroyed its power. The descendants of the founder remained influential local lords in Tazeroualt into the 19th century.

sark.t: A tiny Channel Island fief, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which kept a feudal constitution under its Seigneur until the 21st century.
sark.o: Sark was virtually empty after the 15th century due to [[e:piracy|pirates]]. In 1565 Elizabeth I granted it as a fief to Helier de Carteret of [[s:bailiwick-of-jersey|Jersey]], on condition that he settle it with at least forty men to defend it. He divided it into forty tenements, whose holders formed its parliament, the Chief Pleas.
sark.r: Sark was governed by its Seigneur and the Chief Pleas under Norman feudal law. Cars are banned, and the island lived from farming, fishing and later tourism. Dame Sibyl Hathaway, Dame of Sark from 1927 to 1974, led the island through German occupation from 1940 to 1945.
sark.e: In 2008 Sark held its first fully democratic elections, ending its feudal constitution. It remains a self-governing part of the [[s:bailiwick-of-guernsey|Bailiwick of Guernsey]] and a Crown Dependency.

syracuse.t: The greatest Greek city of the West, which defeated Carthage and Athens, ruled much of Sicily under its tyrants and kings, and fell to Rome in 212 BCE.
syracuse.o: Corinthian colonists led by Archias founded Syracuse in 734 or 733 BCE on the island of Ortygia, with its freshwater spring of Arethusa and two harbours. The city expanded onto the mainland and founded daughter colonies including [[s:kamarina|Kamarina]], controlling south-eastern [[e:sicily|Sicily]].
syracuse.r: Its politics swung between aristocracy, democracy and powerful tyrants. Gelon made it the leading Greek power and with Theron of [[s:acragas|Acragas]] crushed [[e:carthage|Carthage]] at [[s:himera|Himera]] in 480 BCE. A democracy defeated the Athenian expedition in 415–413 BCE. Dionysius I built the Epipolae walls and an empire over [[e:sicily|Sicily]] and southern [[e:italy|Italy]]; Agathocles later took the title of king. Under Hieron II, [[e:rome|Rome's]] ally from 263 BCE, Syracuse enjoyed peace and Archimedes worked there.
syracuse.e: After Hieron II's death Syracuse sided with [[e:carthage|Carthage]]. Marcus Claudius Marcellus besieged it from 214 BCE and took it in 212 BCE, when Archimedes was killed. It became the seat of the Roman governor of [[e:sicily|Sicily]] and remained a major city; its ancient centre is a [[e:unesco-world-heritage-site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]].

sultanate-of-mogadishu.t: A Muslim port city on the Benadir coast that grew rich on gold, textiles and Indian Ocean trade and minted its own coins.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.o: Mogadishu grew in the 10th century as Arab and Persian merchants settled among [[e:somalis|Somali]] communities on the Benadir coast. By the 13th century it had become the leading town of the region, with stone mosques such as the Mosque of Fakr ad-Din, built in 1269, and a ruling dynasty that took the title of sultan.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.r: The city controlled the [[e:gold-trade|gold trade]] from [[e:sofala|Sofala]] for a time and exported its own [[e:cotton|cotton]] cloth to [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and [[e:arabia|Arabia]]. It issued [[e:copper|copper]] coins from the 13th century. [[e:ibn-battuta|Ibn Battuta]], who visited in 1331, described [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abu Bakr ibn Shaykh Umar, who spoke [[e:somalis|Somali]] (Maqdishi) and Arabic and was advised by [[e:qadi|qadis]] and a council of notables, and an elaborate court ceremonial.
sultanate-of-mogadishu.e: From the 16th century Mogadishu fell under the influence of the [[s:ajuran-sultanate|Ajuran Sultanate]], and Portuguese raids disrupted its trade. With the decline of the Ajuran around 1700, power passed to the [[s:hiraab-imamate|Hiraab Imamate]]. The old town of Hamar Weyne preserves its medieval core.

seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.t: The Damascus share of Tutush's divided realm, ruled by his son Duqaq while the First Crusade marched past.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.o: When Tutush I was killed in 1095, his son Duqaq took [[e:damascus|Damascus]] with the support of the city's garrison and the commander Tughtekin, who became his atabeg, or guardian. His brother Ridwan held [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], and the two became bitter rivals.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.r: Duqaq's [[e:emirate|emirate]] covered [[e:damascus|Damascus]], the Hawran and parts of the Beqaa. Its policy was dominated by the feud with [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]], so neither brother offered serious resistance to the [[e:crusader-states|Crusaders]]. Duqaq joined Kerbogha's relief army at [[s:principality-of-antioch|Antioch]] in 1098, which was defeated, and fought Baldwin of [[s:county-of-boulogne|Boulogne]] on the coast in 1100. Administration was in the hands of Tughtekin and the city's notables.
seljuk-emirate-of-damascus.e: Duqaq died in 1104. Tughtekin briefly ruled in the name of his infant son and then on his own account, founding the [[s:burid-emirate-of-damascus|Burid Emirate of Damascus]].

southern-ireland.t: The home-rule jurisdiction created by the Government of Ireland Act 1920 for twenty-six counties, which existed largely on paper until replaced by the Irish Free State.
southern-ireland.o: The Government of Ireland Act 1920 divided Ireland into two home-rule areas, [[s:northern-ireland|Northern Ireland]] and Southern Ireland, each with its own Parliament under Westminster. Southern Ireland came into existence in May 1921, when elections were held for its House of Commons.
southern-ireland.r: Sinn Fein won 124 of the 128 seats unopposed but treated the election as one for the second Dail of the [[s:irish-republic|Irish Republic]], so the Parliament of Southern Ireland met only twice, in June 1921 and January 1922. Only the four members for Dublin University attended the first meeting.
southern-ireland.e: Its second meeting approved the Anglo-Irish Treaty and set up the Provisional Government under Michael Collins. Southern Ireland was replaced by the [[s:irish-free-state|Irish Free State]] on 6 December 1922.

state-of-guatemala.t: The largest member of the Central American Federation, scene of liberal reform under Mariano Gálvez and of Rafael Carrera's conservative rise.
state-of-guatemala.o: [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]], centre of the old Captaincy General, became one of the five states of the [[s:federal-republic-of-central-america|Federal Republic of Central America]] under the constitution of 1824, with its own head of state and assembly in [[e:guatemala|Guatemala]] City, which was also the federal capital until 1834.
state-of-guatemala.r: The state was the main battleground between liberals and conservatives. Mariano Gálvez, head of state from 1831, introduced civil marriage, the Livingston penal codes, land grants to foreign colonists and a head tax. When cholera struck in 1837, rural Maya and ladino communities rose under Rafael Carrera, who took [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] City in 1838. The western highlands broke away as the [[s:state-of-los-altos|State of Los Altos]] until Carrera crushed it in 1840.
state-of-guatemala.e: After the federation dissolved, [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] acted as a sovereign state under conservative governments dominated by Carrera, in alliance with the church. On 21 March 1847 Carrera formally declared it the independent Republic of [[e:guatemala|Guatemala]].

strymonians.t: Slavic tribe of the lower Strymon valley that joined the sieges of Thessalonica and long resisted Byzantine control.
strymonians.o: Known mainly from the Miracles of Saint Demetrius and Byzantine chronicles, the Strymonians settled along the lower Strymon (Struma) in the early 7th century and took part in the Slavic attacks on Thessalonica around 615.
strymonians.r: They were a tribal people under local chiefs, farming the river valley and controlling routes between Thessalonica and [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]]. In the 670s they again joined attacks on Thessalonica, and in 688 Justinian II campaigned against them and moved many [[e:slavs|Slavs]] to [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]].
strymonians.e: [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]] gradually brought the lower Strymon under control, creating the theme of Strymon by the 9th century, while the upper valley passed to the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]]. The tribe merged into the population of both.

sakbajlan.t: The last stronghold of the independent Lacandon Ch'ol Maya in the forests of eastern Chiapas, conquered by Spain in 1695.
sakbajlan.o: The Ch'ol-speaking Lacandon held an island town, Lacam Tun, in Lake Miramar until a Spanish expedition destroyed it in 1586. The survivors moved deeper into the forest and established a new town, Sakbajlan, on the Lacantún river.
sakbajlan.r: The Lacandon Ch'ol remained independent for more than a century, raiding Spanish-controlled towns and resisting missionaries. Sakbajlan was a modest town of houses and a temple, supported by forest farming, and led by its own chiefs and priests. Little is known of their institutions beyond Spanish reports.
sakbajlan.e: In 1695 Spanish expeditions from [[s:republic-of-guatemala|Guatemala]] and [[e:chiapas|Chiapas]] reached Sakbajlan and renamed it Nuestra Señora de los Dolores del Lacandón. The Ch'ol were resettled in the highlands, where most died of disease. The modern Lacandon people are a different, Yucatec-speaking group.

state-of-aden.t: The former Aden Colony as a member state of the Federation of South Arabia, the scene of the Aden Emergency.
state-of-aden.o: In January 1963 the [[s:colony-of-aden|Colony of Aden]] entered the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] as the State of Aden, keeping its own government under a chief minister, while [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] retained [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] and control of the military base. The merger was opposed by Aden's nationalists, who resented being joined to the hinterland rulers.
state-of-aden.r: Aden's legislature was elected on a narrow franchise. The chief minister Hassan Ali Bayoomi supported the merger; his successor Abdul Qawi Mackawee sided with the nationalists and was dismissed in 1965, after which [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ruled directly. Strikes, bombings and assassinations by the National Liberation Front and FLOSY made Aden the centre of the emergency.
state-of-aden.e: In June 1967 armed nationalists briefly held the Crater district. British forces withdrew in November 1967 and Aden became the capital of [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].

southern-song.t: The Song dynasty's southern phase, ruled from Hangzhou, when China led the world in commerce, technology and learning before falling to the Mongols.
southern-song.o: When the [[e:jurchens|Jurchen]] of the [[s:jin-dynasty-1115-1234|Jin dynasty]] (1115-1234) captured [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]] in 1127, Zhao Gou, a son of [[e:emperor-huizong|Emperor Huizong]], was enthroned as Emperor Gaozong. Pursued south, he eventually fixed his court at Lin'an ([[e:hangzhou|Hangzhou]]). The Treaty of Shaoxing in 1141 recognised the Huai river as the frontier, after the execution of the general Yue Fei.
southern-song.r: Cut off from the north, the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]] flourished in the south. [[e:rice|Rice]] agriculture, [[e:porcelain|porcelain]], [[e:silk|silk]] and [[e:printing-press|printing]] expanded; [[e:paper-money|paper money]] circulated widely; and [[e:quanzhou|Quanzhou]] became one of the world's great ports. A permanent navy guarded the [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] and coast. [[e:zhu-xi|Zhu Xi's]] [[e:neo-confucianism|Neo-Confucianism]] became orthodoxy, and [[e:hangzhou|Hangzhou]] was perhaps the world's largest city.
southern-song.e: [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] joined the [[e:mongols|Mongols]] to destroy Jin in 1234, then faced the [[s:mongol-empire|Mongol Empire]] alone. After the long [[e:siege-of-xiangyang|siege of Xiangyang]] ended in 1273, Lin'an surrendered in 1276. At the naval [[e:battle-of-yamen|Battle of Yamen]] in 1279 the minister Lu Xiufu leapt into the sea with the boy emperor, and the [[s:yuan-dynasty|Yuan Dynasty]] ruled all [[e:china|China]].

cr.a: China - Song Dynasty - cs.svg: User:Mozzan derivative work: Kanguole

shun-dynasty.t: The dynasty of the rebel Li Zicheng, whose capture of Beijing in 1644 ended the Ming but opened the way for the Manchu conquest.
shun-dynasty.o: [[e:li-zicheng|Li Zicheng]], a dismissed courier from northern Shaanxi, became a rebel leader in the 1630s amid famine and military mutiny. Promising to cut taxes and redistribute land, he built a huge army, took Xi'an and early in 1644 proclaimed the dynasty of Great Shun there.
shun-dynasty.r: Shun set up ministries and appointed officials across the north, but it governed mainly by military occupation. When Li took [[e:beijing|Beijing]] in April 1644 and the last Ming emperor hanged himself, his troops tortured Ming officials to extract [[e:silver|silver]], and discipline broke down, alienating the elite.
shun-dynasty.e: The Ming general [[e:wu-sangui|Wu Sangui]] at the [[e:shanhai-pass|Shanhai Pass]] allied with the [[e:manchus|Manchus]], and their combined forces defeated Li in May 1644. He retreated from [[e:beijing|Beijing]] to Xi'an and then into Hubei, where he was killed in 1645. The [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] inherited the north.

south-yemen.t: The only Marxist state in the Arab world, ruled from Aden by the Yemeni Socialist Party until unification with the North in 1990.
south-yemen.o: On 30 November 1967, after [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] withdrew from the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]], the National Liberation Front proclaimed the People's Republic of South [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] with Qahtan al-Shaabi as president. The sultanates and sheikhdoms of the former [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]] were abolished.
south-yemen.r: A leftward shift in 1969 removed al-Shaabi, and in 1970 the country became the People's Democratic [[s:republic-of-yemen|Republic of Yemen]]. The ruling party, from 1978 the Yemeni Socialist Party, nationalised land and industry, expanded education and women's rights and allied with the [[s:soviet-union|Soviet Union]], which used Aden as a base. It supported the Dhofar rebellion in [[e:oman|Oman]]. Aden's port declined after the Suez Canal closed in 1967.
south-yemen.e: Party rivalries erupted in a brief civil war in Aden in January 1986 that killed thousands. Weakened by the end of Soviet aid, South [[s:republic-of-yemen|Yemen]] united with the [[s:yemen-arab-republic|Yemen Arab Republic]] on 22 May 1990 to form the Republic of [[e:yemen|Yemen]].

south-west-africa.t: Namibia under South African rule, a League of Nations mandate turned into a contested apartheid territory until independence in 1990.
south-west-africa.o: South African forces conquered [[s:german-south-west-africa|German South West Africa]] in 1915. In 1920 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] gave [[s:republic-of-south-africa|South Africa]] a class C mandate to administer the territory, which it governed from Windhoek as if it were a fifth province.
south-west-africa.r: Land was handed to white farmers, while Africans were confined to reserves and northern Ovambo men supplied contract labour to mines and farms. The [[s:bondelswarts|Bondelswarts]] rising of 1922 was crushed with aircraft. Apartheid laws were extended after 1948, and the Odendaal Plan of 1964 set up ethnic homelands. The [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] revoked the mandate in 1966, and the International Court of Justice declared the occupation illegal in 1971.
south-west-africa.e: SWAPO waged an armed struggle from 1966, linked to the war in [[s:portuguese-angola|Angola]]. After the 1988 [[e:new-york|New York]] Accords, UN-supervised elections were held, and Namibia became independent on 21 March 1990 under President Sam Nujoma.
south-west-africa.la: Afrikaans, English, German, Oshiwambo, Otjiherero, Khoekhoe

cr.a: Parliament of South Africa (Vector graphics image by Denelson83)

samma-dynasty.t: A Sindhi dynasty of jams that ruled lower Sindh from Thatta for nearly two centuries and left the vast necropolis of Makli.
samma-dynasty.o: The Sammas, a local Sindhi Rajput-descended tribe, replaced the [[s:soomra-dynasty|Soomra dynasty]] in lower Sindh around 1351. Their rulers, styled jam, acknowledged the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]] at times, and Firuz Shah Tughluq campaigned against them, but they gradually established an independent state centred on Thatta in the [[e:indus|Indus]] delta.
samma-dynasty.r: Jam Nizam al-Din, known as Jam Nindo, ruled for more than four decades around 1461 to 1508 and is remembered as a just and pious ruler who defended Sindh against the Arghuns. Thatta grew rich as a port and centre of [[e:cotton|cotton]] weaving and Islamic learning. The tombs of the jams at Makli Hill, now a World Heritage Site, show a blend of local, Gujarati and Persian styles.
samma-dynasty.e: After Jam Nindo's death the dynasty weakened. Shah Beg of the [[s:arghun-dynasty|Arghun dynasty]], pushed south by [[e:babur|Babur]], invaded Sindh and defeated the Sammas in 1520, and by 1524 Samma rule had ended.

second-hungarian-republic.t: Hungary's brief post-war multi-party republic, which suffered the worst hyperinflation in history and was dismantled step by step by the communists.
second-hungarian-republic.o: After the Soviet army drove German forces from [[e:hungary|Hungary]] in 1945, free elections in November 1945 gave the Independent Smallholders' Party an absolute majority. The parliament abolished the monarchy of the [[s:kingdom-of-hungary-1920-1946|Kingdom of Hungary]] (1920-1946) and proclaimed a republic on 1 February 1946, with the Smallholder Zoltán Tildy as president and Ferenc Nagy as prime minister.
second-hungarian-republic.r: Under Soviet occupation the communists of Mátyás Rákosi controlled the interior ministry and police and broke up rival parties by 'salami tactics'. The pengő collapsed in the worst hyperinflation ever recorded until the forint was introduced in August 1946. Land reform divided the great estates. Smallholder leader Béla Kovács was arrested by Soviet forces in 1947 and Nagy forced into exile.
second-hungarian-republic.e: Manipulated elections in 1947, the merger of the Social Democrats into a communist party in 1948 and the arrest of Cardinal Mindszenty ended pluralism. A Soviet-style constitution created the [[s:hungarian-peoples-republic|Hungarian People's Republic]] on 20 August 1949.

swellendam-republic.t: A short-lived republic declared by Cape frontier burghers who expelled the Dutch East India Company's officials in 1795.
swellendam-republic.o: By 1795 [[e:burghers|burghers]] in the Swellendam district east of Cape Town resented the [[e:dutch-east-india-company|Dutch East India Company's]] trade restrictions, taxes and its failure to defend them on the frontier. In June 1795, following the example of Graaff-Reinet, they expelled the landdrost and proclaimed themselves a free republic, choosing Hermanus Steyn as president of their assembly.
swellendam-republic.r: Inspired partly by the ideas of the French Revolution, the [[e:burghers|burghers]] set up an assembly of national representatives to run local affairs. They demanded free trade, lower taxes and a free hand in dealings with the Khoikhoi and the Xhosa.
swellendam-republic.e: British forces occupied the Cape in September 1795 after the Battle of Muizenberg, and the Swellendam [[e:burghers|burghers]] accepted British authority later that year, ending the republic within months.

shaib-sheikhdom.t: One of the smallest states of the British Aden Protectorate, a tribal sheikhdom in the highlands near Dhala.
shaib-sheikhdom.o: The Shaib tribe held a small mountain territory near the [[s:emirate-of-dhala|Emirate of Dhala]], with its seat at Al Awabil. It emerged as a separate sheikhdom around 1800, when the [[s:qasimid-state|Qasimid State]] no longer controlled the region. Its early history is almost unknown.
shaib-sheikhdom.r: The sheikhs governed a few thousand tribespeople who farmed terraced valleys. The sheikhdom was brought into the [[s:aden-protectorate|Aden Protectorate]] by treaty with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] and joined the [[s:federation-of-south-arabia|Federation of South Arabia]] in the 1960s.
shaib-sheikhdom.e: After the National Liberation Front took power in 1967, the sheikhdom was abolished and incorporated into [[s:south-yemen|South Yemen]].

saint-pierre-and-miquelon.t: A small archipelago off Newfoundland that is the last remnant of French North America, and a fishing outpost since the 18th century.
saint-pierre-and-miquelon.o: French fishermen used the islands from the 16th century. Under the Treaty of [[e:paris|Paris]] of 1763, which ended [[s:new-france|New France]] on the mainland, [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] allowed [[e:france|France]] to keep Saint-Pierre and Miquelon as an unfortified shelter for its fishermen on the Grand Banks. Settlers, many of them Acadians, arrived soon afterwards.
saint-pierre-and-miquelon.r: The colony depended almost entirely on cod fishing and salting. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] seized and emptied the islands during wars in 1778, 1793 and later, and French rule was only lasting from 1816. In the 1920s Saint-Pierre prospered by smuggling alcohol into the Prohibition-era [[s:united-states|United States]]. In 1941 [[s:free-france|Free French]] forces took the islands from Vichy control, an early Gaullist success.
saint-pierre-and-miquelon.e: The islands became an overseas territory in 1946, an overseas [[e:departement|department]] in 1976 and a territorial collectivity in 1985. The collapse of the cod fishery and a 1992 maritime boundary ruling in [[e:canada|Canada's]] favour hit the economy hard; the islands still rely on French state support.

selge.t: Selge, a powerful Pisidian mountain city in the Taurus, which claimed Spartan origins and fielded armies of thousands.
selge.o: Selge was founded in the high [[e:taurus-mountains|Taurus]] north of Pamphylia, above the Eurymedon gorge. Its citizens claimed descent from Spartans and from the seer Calchas, but the city grew from a Pisidian community that became increasingly Greek from the 5th century BCE.
selge.r: Selge was a self-governing city controlling fertile upland valleys that produced olives, wine and storax resin used in perfume. Strabo says it could once field 20,000 men, and in 218 BCE it resisted a siege by the Seleucid general Achaeus.
selge.e: Selge kept its independence until [[e:rome|Rome]] organised the region. In 25 BCE it became part of the province of [[s:galatia|Galatia]] and lived on as a Roman provincial town.

seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.t: The Theban kings who began the war that drove the Hyksos from Egypt and paved the way for the New Kingdom.
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.o: Around 1580 BCE a new line of kings took power at [[s:thebes|Thebes]], following the [[s:sixteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Sixteenth Dynasty of Egypt]]. At first they acknowledged the overlordship of the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] Fifteenth Dynasty of [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in the north and the power of [[s:kerma|Kerma]] in the south, and ruled [[e:upper-egypt|Upper Egypt]] from Elephantine to [[s:abydos|Abydos]].
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.r: The Theban court was modest, its kings buried in small pyramids at Dra Abu el-Naga, but it built up a strong army. Seqenenre Tao began open war with the [[s:fifteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Hyksos]] king Apepi, and his mummy shows fatal head wounds from axes. His successor Kamose campaigned north to the walls of Avaris, and his stelae at [[e:karnak|Karnak]] record an intercepted letter from Apepi to the ruler of Kush.
seventeenth-dynasty-of-egypt.e: Kamose's brother [[e:ahmose-i|Ahmose I]] completed the war, taking Avaris around 1550 BCE and reuniting [[e:egypt|Egypt]]. His reign is counted as the start of the [[e:eighteenth-dynasty-of-egypt|Eighteenth Dynasty]] and the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]].

southern-yan.t: The last Murong Xianbei state, founded in Shandong by Murong De after the Northern Wei overran Later Yan, and destroyed by Liu Yu in 410.
southern-yan.o: When [[s:northern-wei|Northern Wei]] took the [[s:later-yan|Later Yan]] capital [[s:zhongshan|Zhongshan]] in 397, Murong De, a younger brother of Murong Chui, led followers south to Huatai, proclaiming himself King of Yan in 398. In 399 he moved east to Guanggu (near Qingzhou, Shandong) and in 400 declared himself emperor.
southern-yan.r: Southern Yan ruled the Shandong region with a [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] military elite and Chinese officials. Murong De's nephew and successor Murong Chao alienated the court and raided the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]], seizing captives to train as court musicians.
southern-yan.e: The raids provoked the [[s:eastern-jin|Eastern Jin]] general Liu Yu, who invaded in 409, besieged Guanggu and took it in 410. Murong Chao was executed at Jiankang and thousands of [[s:xianbei|Xianbei]] nobles were killed, ending the Murong states.

soomra-dynasty.t: A local dynasty of Sindh that ruled the lower Indus for three centuries between the Ghaznavid conquest and the Sammas.
soomra-dynasty.o: The Soomras were a Sindhi clan of debated origin, perhaps local converts linked to the [[e:ismailism|Ismaili]] community. They rose to power in the 11th century as Ghaznavid control of Sindh weakened after the fall of the [[s:habbari-dynasty|Habbari dynasty]], establishing their seat at Thari and later at other towns of lower Sindh.
soomra-dynasty.r: Little is known in detail, as the sources are late Persian histories and Sindhi folk tradition. The Soomras appear to have had [[e:ismailism|Ismaili]] sympathies and to have tolerated [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] customs. Sindhi folk poetry celebrates figures of the period, such as Dodo Soomro, who resisted the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]], and Umar Soomro, the king of the tale of Umar and Marvi. Agriculture on the [[e:indus|Indus]] and trade through its ports sustained the realm.
soomra-dynasty.e: The Soomras faced repeated pressure from the [[s:delhi-sultanate|Delhi Sultanate]]. In the mid-14th century the [[s:samma-dynasty|Samma dynasty]], based at Thatta, displaced them, and the Soomras became local chiefs.

simyra.t: Simyra, a port on the Syrian coast that served as Egypt's northern base and later the capital of Amurru, until Assyria made it a province.
simyra.o: Sumur, probably Tell Kazel near the Lebanese border, controlled the Akkar plain and the gap leading inland to the Orontes. In the 15th century BCE [[e:thutmose-iii|Thutmose III]] of the [[s:egyptian-empire-new-kingdom|Egyptian Empire New Kingdom]] made it a garrison and administrative centre for his Syrian conquests.
simyra.r: The [[e:amarna-letters|Amarna letters]] show an Egyptian commissioner residing there. Abdi-Ashirta and his son Aziru seized it, and it became the capital of the [[s:kingdom-of-amurru|Kingdom of Amurru]]. In the Iron Age it was a Phoenician town whose people, the Zemarites, are listed in Genesis.
simyra.e: Simyra was occupied by Tiglath-Pileser III of the [[s:assyrian-empire|Assyrian Empire]] in 738 BCE and became the centre of an Assyrian province. Later overshadowed by [[s:arwad|Arwad]], it shrank to a minor town.

sambalpur-state.t: A Chauhan Rajput kingdom on the middle Mahanadi in western Odisha, whose annexation by the British in 1849 led to the long rebellion of Surendra Sai.
sambalpur-state.o: Tradition holds that Balaram Deva, a member of the Chauhan ruling family of [[s:patna-state|Patna State]], founded a separate kingdom at Sambalpur at the end of the 15th century. It soon became the leading power among the chiefs of the region.
sambalpur-state.r: Sambalpur controlled the diamond-bearing reaches of the Mahanadi and was known for its weaving and its goddess Samaleswari. In the late 18th century it fell to the [[e:bhonsles|Bhonsles]] of the [[s:nagpur-kingdom|Nagpur Kingdom]]. The British took it in 1803 and restored a Chauhan ruler under their supervision.
sambalpur-state.e: When Raja Narayan Singh died without a male heir in 1849, the British annexed Sambalpur. A claimant, Surendra Sai, led an armed rebellion from 1857 until his surrender in 1862. Sambalpur is now a district of Odisha.

state-of-chen.t: A Zhou state on the Huai plain whose rulers claimed descent from the sage-king Shun, a frequent victim of Chu whose exiled branch later seized the throne of Qi.
state-of-chen.o: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed Gui Man, Duke Hu of Chen, a descendant of the legendary Emperor Shun, at Wanqiu (modern Huaiyang, Henan), and gave him his eldest daughter in marriage. Chen thus combined ancient lineage with close ties to the royal house.
state-of-chen.r: Chen sat on the open plain between the northern states and the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]], and switched allegiance repeatedly. Its court was notorious for intrigue: Duke Ling was killed in 599 BCE by Xia Zhengshu, prompting a Chu intervention. In 672 BCE Prince Wan of Chen fled to the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]], where his descendants, the Tian clan, rose to power. Confucius was famously stranded between Chen and Cai.
state-of-chen.e: Chu occupied Chen twice before King Hui of Chu annexed it for good in 479 BCE. Its capital became an important Chu city, and in 278 BCE served as the Chu capital after Ying fell to [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]]. The Tian lineage descended from Chen ruled Qi until 221 BCE.

sagaing-kingdom.t: A breakaway Burmese kingdom on the west bank of the Irrawaddy that rivalled Pinya for half a century in the 14th century.
sagaing-kingdom.o: In 1315 Saw Yun, a son of Thihathu of the [[s:pinya-kingdom|Pinya Kingdom]], quarrelled with his father and set up his own court at Sagaing, across the Irrawaddy from present-day Mandalay. After Thihathu's death he gained control of the lands north and west of the river, and Pinya recognised Sagaing's independence.
sagaing-kingdom.r: Sagaing controlled the Mu valley [[e:rice|rice]] lands and routes toward the Chindwin and the northern Shan states. Its kings kept up Pagan-style Buddhist patronage and court ceremonial, and the hills of Sagaing began their long history as a monastic centre. Court politics were turbulent, with regents and queens shaping successions.
sagaing-kingdom.e: In 1364 Shan forces of [[s:mong-mao|Mong Mao]] sacked Sagaing and [[s:pinya-kingdom|Pinya]]. Thado Minbya, a Sagaing prince, seized power, executed rivals and in 1365 founded the [[s:ava-kingdom|Ava Kingdom]], uniting the two rival courts. Sagaing later served briefly as a royal capital under the [[s:konbaung-dynasty|Konbaung dynasty]].

senones-400.t: Gaulish people of the Adriatic coast of the Marche, credited with the sack of Rome in 390 BCE and destroyed by Rome in 283 BCE.
senones-400.o: The [[s:senones|Senones]] were, according to Livy, the last of the Celtic peoples to cross into [[e:italy|Italy]], around 400 BCE. They settled on the Adriatic coast between the Utente and Esino rivers, land later called the Ager Gallicus, displacing [[s:umbrians|Umbrians]] and Etruscan settlers.
senones-400.r: They lived in villages and buried their warriors with weapons and imported Etruscan and Greek goods, as at Montefortino and Filottrano. Roman tradition said [[s:senones|Senones]] led by Brennus defeated [[e:rome|Rome]] at the Allia and sacked the city in 390 BCE. They raided central [[e:italy|Italy]] and served as [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]], including for Dionysius I.
senones-400.e: The [[s:senones|Senones]] fought alongside the [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]] at Sentinum in 295 BCE. After they defeated a Roman army at [[s:arretium|Arretium]] in 284 BCE, [[e:rome|Rome]] invaded their land in 283 BCE, killing or expelling the Senones, and founded the colony of Sena Gallica (Senigallia) there.

sohra-state.t: The Khasi state of Cherrapunji, where the British set up their first hill station in the Khasi Hills and Welsh missionaries first wrote the Khasi language.
sohra-state.o: Hima Sohra was one of the Khasi chiefdoms on the southern edge of the Meghalaya plateau, above the plains of Sylhet. Its origins are known from oral tradition, and the register's start date is approximate.
sohra-state.r: Sohra was ruled by a Syiem from a royal clan, with succession through the female line. Its position near the plains made it an early British ally. The British founded a station at Cherrapunji in the 1830s, and from 1841 Welsh Calvinistic Methodist missionaries led by Thomas Jones worked there, writing Khasi in the [[e:latin|Latin]] alphabet.
sohra-state.e: The British headquarters moved to Shillong in 1864. Sohra acceded to [[e:india|India]] in 1948 and is now part of Meghalaya; Cherrapunji is famous as one of the wettest places on Earth.

sosso-kingdom.t: Soninke kingdom whose blacksmith-king Sumanguru Kante seized the Ghana Empire's heartland before being defeated by Sundiata Keita.
sosso-kingdom.o: [[e:sosso-empire|Sosso]] grew out of [[e:kaniaga|Kaniaga]], a [[e:soninke|Soninke]] province of the [[s:ghana-empire|Ghana Empire]] north of the upper [[e:niger-river|Niger]]. As [[e:ghana|Ghana]] weakened in the 12th century, the Kante clan, associated with blacksmithing and its power objects, made Sosso independent and began conquering neighbouring lands.
sosso-kingdom.r: Under Sumanguru Kante, who ruled in the early 13th century, [[e:sosso-empire|Sosso]] took [[e:koumbi-saleh|Koumbi Saleh]], the old capital of [[e:ghana|Ghana]], and subdued the Mande chiefdoms, including the [[s:kingdom-of-kangaba|Kingdom of Kangaba]]. Oral tradition portrays him as a powerful sorcerer and a harsh ruler, and links him with resistance to [[e:islam|Islam]], though such details come from the [[e:sundiata-keita|Sundiata]] epic.
sosso-kingdom.e: The Mande clans rallied behind [[e:sundiata-keita|Sundiata Keita]], who defeated Sumanguru at the battle of [[e:battle-of-kirina|Kirina]] around 1235. [[e:sosso-empire|Sosso]] was absorbed into the new [[s:mali-empire|Mali Empire]], and the epic of its fall is still performed by [[e:griots|griots]] across [[e:west-africa|West Africa]].

second-athenian-league.t: Alliance of Aegean states formed by Athens in 378 BCE to resist Sparta, with promises not to repeat the abuses of the 5th-century empire.
second-athenian-league.o: Spartan high-handedness after the King's Peace of 386 BCE, and a raid on Attica by the Spartan Sphodrias, pushed [[s:athens|Athens]] to found a new alliance in 378-377 BCE. The surviving decree of Aristoteles invites [[e:greeks|Greeks]] and barbarians to join 'so that the Spartans may allow the Greeks to be free', listing members such as [[s:chios|Chios]], [[s:thebes|Thebes]] and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]].
second-athenian-league.r: Members kept their autonomy and constitutions, and [[s:athens|Athens]] renounced garrisons, governors, tribute and Athenian settlement on allied land. [[e:allies|Allies]] sat in a council (synedrion) at [[e:athens|Athens]] that voted alongside the Athenian assembly and paid 'contributions' rather than tribute. At its height some seventy states joined. Chabrias' naval victory off [[s:naxos|Naxos]] in 376 BCE restored Athenian sea power.
second-athenian-league.e: [[s:athens|Athens]] gradually broke its promises, planting settlers on [[s:samos|Samos]]. In the Social War of 357-355 BCE [[s:chios|Chios]], [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]], Cos and [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], encouraged by Mausolus of [[s:hecatomnid-caria|Caria]], left the league. Reduced to a rump, it ended after Philip II's victory at Chaeronea in 338 BCE and the creation of the [[s:league-of-corinth|League of Corinth]].

saltukids.t: One of the first Turkish principalities in eastern Anatolia, ruling Erzurum and fighting Georgia for over a century.
saltukids.o: Tradition holds that the Seljuk sultan [[e:alp-arslan|Alp Arslan]] granted the region of Erzurum to the commander Saltuk after the victory at [[e:battle-of-manzikert|Manzikert]] in 1071. His descendants established a hereditary [[e:emirate|emirate]] there, among the earliest Turkish states in [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]].
saltukids.r: The Saltukids held Erzurum, Tercan, Bayburt and Ispir, on the frontier with the [[s:kingdom-of-georgia|Kingdom of Georgia]], which defeated them several times; Izz al-Din Saltuk II was captured by the Georgians in the 1150s and ransomed. Erzurum prospered from the trade route between [[e:iran|Iran]] and the [[e:black-sea|Black Sea]]. Surviving monuments include the tomb tower of [[e:emir|Emir]] Saltuk and the Tepsi Minaret in Erzurum.
saltukids.e: In 1202 the Rum Seljuk sultan Suleymanshah II, campaigning against [[s:georgia|Georgia]], annexed Erzurum and gave it to his brother Tughrilshah, ending the dynasty.

smolyani.t: Slavic tribe of the Rhodope Mountains and Mesta valley, known from Byzantine sources until it passed under Bulgarian rule in the 9th century.
smolyani.o: The Smolyani were among the Slavic groups who settled the [[e:balkans|Balkans]] in the late 6th and 7th centuries, taking the Rhodopes and the middle Mesta (Nestos) in modern [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]] and [[e:greece|Greece]]. They are named among the tribes that besieged Thessalonica in the 670s.
smolyani.r: Known only from brief Byzantine mentions, they were a tribal people under local chiefs, nominally subject to [[s:byzantium|Byzantium]], farming and herding in the mountain valleys. The modern town of Smolyan preserves their name.
smolyani.e: In 837 the Smolyani rose against Byzantine rule, and Khan Presian of the [[s:first-bulgarian-empire|First Bulgarian Empire]] used the revolt to take their lands, which were absorbed into [[s:bulgaria|Bulgaria]].

spanish-sahara.t: Spain's desert colony on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, whose hasty abandonment in 1975 left the unresolved conflict over Western Sahara.
spanish-sahara.o: In 1884 [[e:spain|Spain]] proclaimed a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the coast of Río de Oro, founding Villa Cisneros, now Dakhla. Agreements with [[e:france|France]] between 1900 and 1912 fixed the borders, adding the Saguia el-Hamra to the north, but Spanish control remained confined to a few coastal posts for decades.
spanish-sahara.r: [[e:spain|Spain]] occupied the interior only in 1934, and El Aaiún later became the capital. The Sahrawi population of nomadic Hassaniya-speaking tribes lived largely by herding. In 1958 the territory became a Spanish province. The rich phosphate deposits of Bou Craa, discovered in 1947, began to be exploited in the early 1970s.
spanish-sahara.e: The Polisario Front launched an independence struggle in 1973, while [[s:kingdom-of-morocco|Morocco]] and [[e:mauritania|Mauritania]] claimed the territory. After [[e:morocco|Morocco's]] Green March in November 1975, the [[e:madrid|Madrid]] Accords handed administration to them, and [[e:spain|Spain]] withdrew in early 1976. Western [[e:sahara|Sahara's]] status remains disputed.

sultanate-of-nejd.t: Ibn Saud's state after the conquest of Ha'il, which fixed its northern borders and launched the conquest of the Hejaz.
sultanate-of-nejd.o: In 1921, after taking Ha'il and ending the [[s:emirate-of-jabal-shammar|Emirate of Jabal Shammar]], Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]] ibn Saud adopted the title [[e:sultan|Sultan]] of Nejd and its Dependencies, replacing the [[s:emirate-of-nejd-and-hasa|Emirate of Nejd and Hasa]]. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], his ally under the Treaty of Darin, recognised the new title.
sultanate-of-nejd.r: The sultanate covered central and eastern [[e:arabia|Arabia]] and, from 1920, highland Asir. Its frontiers with the new British [[e:league-of-nations-mandate|mandates]] were set at the Uqair conference of 1922, which drew the borders with the [[s:sheikhdom-of-kuwait|Sheikhdom of Kuwait]] and the [[s:kingdom-of-iraq|Kingdom of Iraq]] and created two neutral zones. The Ikhwan raided [[s:emirate-of-transjordan|Transjordan]], [[e:iraq|Iraq]] and Kuwait, causing clashes with British forces. In 1924 they attacked the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Kingdom of Hejaz]].
sultanate-of-nejd.e: After [[e:mecca|Mecca]] and then Jeddah fell, Ibn Saud was proclaimed King of the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz|Hejaz]] in January 1926, joining his two realms as the [[s:kingdom-of-hejaz-and-nejd|Kingdom of Hejaz and Nejd]].

septinsular-republic.t: Republic of the Seven Islands under Russian and Ottoman protection, the first self-governing Greek state of modern times.
septinsular-republic.o: In 1798-1799 a joint Russian-Ottoman expedition under Admiral Fyodor Ushakov drove the French from the [[s:united-states-of-the-ionian-islands|Ionian Islands]]. The Treaty of [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]] in 1800 created the Septinsular Republic of [[s:corcyra|Corfu]], Paxos, [[s:leucas|Lefkada]], Ithaca, Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Kythira, under Ottoman suzerainty and Russian protection.
septinsular-republic.r: The republic was governed by a senate in [[s:corcyra|Corfu]] dominated by the island nobility, under a series of constitutions; that of 1803 widened participation. Count Spyridon Theotokis presided over the senate, and the young Ioannis Kapodistrias, later the first governor of [[e:greece|Greece]], served as secretary of state. Greek became an official language alongside Italian.
septinsular-republic.e: At Tilsit in 1807 [[e:russia|Russia]] ceded the islands to [[e:napoleon|Napoleon]], and they returned to French rule as the [[s:french-ionian-islands|French Ionian Islands]]. The republic's experience of self-rule fed the ideas of the Greek national movement.

stellaland.t: A Boer mini-republic around Vryburg, created by mercenaries paid in land, whose fate was decided by imperial rivalry.
stellaland.o: In 1882 the [[s:batlhaping-chiefdom|Tlhaping]] chief Mankurwane and the Korana chief David Massouw fought over land west of the [[s:south-african-republic|Transvaal]], both recruiting white [[e:mercenary|mercenaries]]. Those who served Massouw received farms and proclaimed the Republic of Stellaland, named after a comet, with Gerrit Jacobus van Niekerk as administrator and Vryburg as capital.
stellaland.r: The republic had a Volksraad, issued postage stamps and joined with neighbouring [[s:goshen|Goshen]] in 1883 as the [[e:united-states|United States]] of Stellaland. Its settlers farmed [[e:cattle|cattle]] and sought union with the [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]], which would have cut [[e:britain|Britain's]] road north to the interior.
stellaland.e: Cecil [[s:rhodes|Rhodes]] and the Cape government pressed for British intervention. Sir Charles Warren's expedition arrived in 1885, and Stellaland was absorbed into [[s:british-bechuanaland|British Bechuanaland]]; Vryburg became its capital and later passed with it to the [[s:cape-colony|Cape Colony]].

sonepur-state.t: A Chauhan Rajput state on the Mahanadi in western Orissa, famed for its many temples and known as a second Varanasi.
sonepur-state.o: Sonepur was founded in 1556 when Madan Gopal, a younger son of the Chauhan ruling house of [[e:patna|Patna]] ([[s:patna-state|Patnagarh]]), received the territory around the confluence of the Mahanadi and Tel rivers. The area had earlier been an important centre of the Somavamshi kings.
sonepur-state.r: The Rajas ruled a fertile riverine land of [[e:rice|rice]] farmers, weavers and [[e:brahmins|Brahmin]] settlements. The town's numerous temples earned it the name Paschima Varanasi, and it became known for its Sambalpuri handloom textiles. After 1803 it was a tributary state under British paramountcy, briefly attached to the Central Provinces before returning to Orissa in 1905.
sonepur-state.e: Sonepur merged with the province of Orissa on 1 January 1948. Its territory now forms Subarnapur district of Odisha, and the town retains its temple heritage.

sultanate-of-rafai.t: A Zande sultanate on the Mbomou River whose rulers traded ivory and captives before falling under French rule.
sultanate-of-rafai.o: The Rafai state was one of several Zande-ruled sultanates that formed along the Mbomou River in the 19th century. It took its name from its ruler Rafai, whose followers controlled the area around the town that still bears the name.
sultanate-of-rafai.r: Little is recorded in detail. Like its neighbours, the sultanate depended on armed retainers, tribute and the sale of [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]] and captives to traders coming from the [[e:nile|Nile]] basin, which supplied firearms.
sultanate-of-rafai.e: In the 1890s it dealt with officers of the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]] and then, after the 1894 boundary agreement, with [[e:france|France]]. Its independent power ended when it was absorbed into [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]] in the early 20th century.

simsir.t: A short-lived Muslim principality of the Chechens on the North Caucasus plain, known almost only from the chronicles of Timur's campaign of 1395.
simsir.o: After the Mongol conquest, Chechen communities on the plains north of the mountains came under the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]]. In the 14th century a principality called Simsir formed there, apparently around the middle Sunzha and Argun rivers. Its origins are not recorded.
simsir.r: Persian chroniclers of [[e:timur|Timur]], notably Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, mention its ruler Ghayur Khan and describe Simsir as a Muslim land, one of the first among the Chechens. It paid tribute to the [[s:golden-horde|Golden Horde]] and sided with Tokhtamysh in his war against Timur.
simsir.e: In 1395 [[e:timur|Timur's]] army devastated Simsir during its campaign against Tokhtamysh, and the principality disappears from the record. Its people withdrew to the mountains, and the plain was resettled only later.

state-of-maranhao.t: A separate Portuguese colony covering the Amazon and the north coast of Brazil, governed directly from Lisbon rather than from Salvador.
state-of-maranhao.o: After expelling the French of [[s:equinoctial-france|Equinoctial France]] in 1615 and founding Belém in 1616, Portugal created the State of Maranhão in 1621, separate from the [[s:state-of-brazil|State of Brazil]]. Its capital was São Luís, and it included Grão-Pará, Ceará and the [[e:amazon|Amazon]] basin, which were easier to reach by sea from [[e:lisbon|Lisbon]] than from [[e:salvador|Salvador]].
state-of-maranhao.r: The colony depended on indigenous labour to collect forest products such as [[e:cacao|cacao]], [[e:cloves|cloves]] and sarsaparilla. Pedro Teixeira's expedition up the [[e:amazon|Amazon]] in 1637 to 1639 extended Portuguese claims. The [[e:dutch|Dutch]] held São Luís from 1641 to 1644. The [[e:jesuits|Jesuit]] António Vieira campaigned against the enslavement of indigenous people. Settlers resented Jesuit control and a trading company's monopoly, which led to the Beckman Revolt in 1684.
state-of-maranhao.e: In 1751 the Marquis of Pombal reorganised the colony as the [[s:state-of-grao-para-and-maranhao|State of Grão-Pará and Maranhão]], with its capital moved to Belém and his brother Francisco Xavier de Mendonça Furtado as governor.

second-federal-republic-of-mexico.t: The restored federal Mexico of 1846 to 1863, which lost half its territory to the United States and then fought the Reform War over church and state.
second-federal-republic-of-mexico.o: With war against the [[s:united-states|United States]] beginning, a revolt in August 1846 overthrew the centralist government of Mariano Paredes and restored the federal Constitution of 1824. Antonio López de Santa Anna returned from exile to lead the defence, ending the [[s:centralist-republic-of-mexico|Centralist Republic of Mexico]].
second-federal-republic-of-mexico.r: American armies took [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]] in September 1847, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 ceded California, New [[s:mexico|Mexico]] and the claim to Texas. Santa Anna's final dictatorship from 1853 sold more land in the Gadsden Purchase. The liberal Revolution of Ayutla removed him in 1855 and launched La Reforma: the Ley Juárez and Ley Lerdo curbed church and corporate privileges, and the Constitution of 1857 followed. Conservatives revolted, and Benito Juárez won the Reform War of 1858 to 1861.
second-federal-republic-of-mexico.e: When Juárez suspended payments on foreign debts in 1861, [[e:france|France]] intervened. Mexican forces beat the French at Puebla on 5 May 1862, but they took [[e:mexico-city|Mexico City]] in June 1863, and the [[s:second-mexican-empire|Second Mexican Empire]] was proclaimed, while Juárez kept a republican government on the move.

cr.a: Ludovicus Ferdinandus can have elements by Sodacan and Heralder

sultanate-of-anjouan.t: The leading Comorian sultanate, known to English sailors as Johanna, a provisioning stop on the route to India until French rule.
sultanate-of-anjouan.o: Shirazi-descended families established a sultanate on Anjouan (Ndzuwani) around 1500, with an early capital at Domoni. The ruling house later moved to Mutsamudu on the north-west coast, which grew into a fortified stone town with a citadel overlooking its harbour.
sultanate-of-anjouan.r: The sultan governed with a council of the leading Arab and Shirazi lineages, while much of the rural population lived in dependence or [[e:slavery|slavery]]. Anjouan prospered by supplying [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] and other European ships with water, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and fruit, and English became widely understood at court. The sultans claimed overlordship of [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Mayotte]] and Moheli and fought repeatedly to enforce it.
sultanate-of-anjouan.e: Civil wars and Malagasy raids weakened the island in the 19th century. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abdallah III accepted a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1886, and [[e:france|France]] annexed the island outright in 1912. Anjouan became part of the independent Comoros in 1975, though it attempted secession in 1997.

state-of-xi.t: A small Ji-clan state on the Huai whose fall around 680 BCE is tied to the story of Lady Xi, the silent queen taken by King Wen of Chu.
state-of-xi.o: Xi was a minor Zhou state ruled by the Ji clan, located near modern Xixian in southern Henan, on the northern edge of the Huai River plain. It lay close to the [[s:state-of-cai|State of Cai]] and within reach of the expanding [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]].
state-of-xi.r: Little is recorded about its government. Xi appears in the Zuo zhuan chiefly in a story of feuding: the Marquis of Xi, angered that the Marquis of Cai had insulted his wife, Xi Gui, invited Chu to attack Cai, setting off a chain of events that drew Chu into the region.
state-of-xi.e: King Wen of Chu destroyed Xi around 680 BCE and took Xi Gui as his wife; she bore the future King [[s:cheng-han|Cheng]] but, by tradition, refused to speak to her new husband. Xi became a Chu county, an early example of Chu's administrative districts.

senior-juz.t: The southern division of the Kazakh people in Zhetysu, which suffered Dzungar and Kokandi rule before passing to Russia.
senior-juz.o: The [[e:kazakhs|Kazakhs]] had long been grouped into three juz, or hordes, and after the death of Tauke Khan around 1718 the [[s:kazakh-khanate|Kazakh Khanate]] lost its unity, with each juz under its own khans. The Senior Juz occupied the south-east, from the [[e:syr-darya|Syr Darya]] to the Ili valley in Zhetysu.
senior-juz.r: Its tribes, such as the Dulat, Uysun and Jalayir, were nomadic herders closely tied to the oasis cities of Tashkent and Turkistan. They were hit hardest by the [[e:dzungars|Dzungar]] invasions of the 1720s and partly ruled by the Dzungars until the 1750s. The judge Tole Bi, one of three famous Kazakh biys, was a leading figure.
senior-juz.e: In the early 19th century much of the Senior Juz fell under the [[s:khanate-of-kokand|Khanate of Kokand]] and the [[s:tashkent-hakimate|Tashkent Hakimate]]. From the 1820s its northern clans accepted Russian protection, and by 1848 [[e:russia|Russia]] had abolished the khanship, incorporating it into the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]].

south-seas-mandate.t: The Micronesian islands Japan took from Germany in 1914 and governed under a League of Nations mandate, later fortified and fought over in the Pacific War.
south-seas-mandate.o: Early in the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]] the Japanese navy seized [[e:germany|Germany's]] island colonies north of the equator: the Marianas except [[s:guam|Guam]], the Carolines, Palau and the Marshalls. In 1919 the [[e:league-of-nations|League of Nations]] gave them to [[e:japan|Japan]] as a mandate, and in 1922 a civilian South Seas Government was set up at Koror in Palau.
south-seas-mandate.r: [[e:japan|Japan]] developed [[e:sugar-plantation|sugar]] plantations on Saipan and Tinian through the South Seas Development Company, phosphate mining and fisheries. Japanese settlers, many from Okinawa, came to outnumber the islanders by the late 1930s, and schools taught Japanese. Japan left the League in 1933 but kept the islands and turned Truk into a major naval base.
south-seas-mandate.e: American forces captured the islands in 1944 and 1945 in battles at Saipan, Peleliu and elsewhere; the atomic bomb missions flew from Tinian. In 1947 the [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] placed them under American trusteeship, from which today's island states emerged.

sukhothai-kingdom.t: An early Thai kingdom of the upper Chao Phraya, celebrated in Thai national history as the birthplace of the Thai script and a model of Buddhist kingship.
sukhothai-kingdom.o: Around 1238 two Tai chiefs, Pho Khun Bang Klang Hao and Pho Khun Pha Mueang, drove the [[e:khmer-empire|Khmer]] governor out of Sukhothai, then a Khmer outpost. Bang Klang Hao became king as Si Inthrathit, founding the Phra Ruang dynasty.
sukhothai-kingdom.r: Under Ram Khamhaeng in the late 13th century Sukhothai's influence reached across much of present-day [[s:thailand|Thailand]], though largely through alliances and tribute. The Ram Khamhaeng inscription, whose authenticity has been debated, credits him with creating the Thai alphabet. Sinhalese [[e:theravada-buddhism|Theravada Buddhism]] was adopted, and Li Thai wrote the Traiphum cosmology. Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai produced celadon ceramics.
sukhothai-kingdom.e: After Ram Khamhaeng, Sukhothai's power shrank. [[s:ayutthaya-kingdom|Ayutthaya]] forced it into [[e:vassal|vassalage]] in 1378, and around 1438 it was absorbed as a province. Its ruins at Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai are a World Heritage Site, and its memory shaped modern Thai nationalism.

sultanate-of-hobyo.t: A Somali sultanate on the Indian Ocean coast founded by Yusuf Ali Kenadid, which became an Italian protectorate before conquest in 1925.
sultanate-of-hobyo.o: Yusuf Ali Kenadid, a member of the ruling house of the [[s:majeerteen-sultanate|Majeerteen Sultanate]], quarrelled with his cousin Boqor Osman Mahamuud and left the north. With followers and Hadrami allies he took control of the coastal town of Hobyo in central [[s:somalia|Somalia]] and established a sultanate there around 1878.
sultanate-of-hobyo.r: The sultan ruled with clan elders over pastoral [[e:somalis|Somali]] clans, controlling trade through the port of Hobyo, which exported livestock, hides and gum. In 1888 Yusuf Ali accepted an Italian [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] to secure his position. His son Osman Yusuf Kenadid created the Osmanya script for the Somali language.
sultanate-of-hobyo.e: [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Ali Yusuf Kenadid refused Italian demands in 1925, and Governor Cesare De Vecchi's forces occupied the sultanate, annexing it to [[s:italian-somaliland|Italian Somaliland]]. Its territory is part of the Galmudug region today.

septem.t: The Byzantine fortress of Ceuta on the Strait of Gibraltar, the last outpost of Roman rule in north-west Africa.
septem.o: After Justinian's conquest of the [[s:vandal-kingdom|Vandal Kingdom]] in 534, Byzantine forces occupied Septem ([[e:ceuta|Ceuta]]), named after its seven hills, at the African side of the [[e:strait-of-gibraltar|Strait of Gibraltar]]. Justinian had its walls rebuilt and a church to the Virgin built there, as Procopius records.
septem.r: Septem was a small garrison town, commanded by a tribune and supported by a fleet watching the Strait and Visigothic [[e:spain|Spain]]. It belonged to the province of [[s:kingdom-of-mauretania|Mauretania]] Secunda and later the [[s:exarchate-of-africa|Exarchate of Africa]]. Little is known of its internal life, though it remained Christian and Latin-speaking amid [[e:berbers|Berber]] territory.
septem.e: After the Arab conquest of the rest of [[e:north-africa|North Africa]], Septem stood isolated. Tradition says its governor, Count Julian, aided the Arab invasion of [[e:spain|Spain]], and the town passed to the [[s:umayyad-caliphate|Umayyad Caliphate]] around 711. [[e:ceuta|Ceuta]] later became Portuguese and then Spanish.

soviet-union.t: The world's first communist state and a Cold War superpower, a union of Soviet republics that stretched from the Baltic to the Pacific.
soviet-union.o: After winning the Civil War, the Bolsheviks formalised relations between the Soviet republics. In December 1922 the [[s:russian-sfsr|Russian SFSR]], the [[s:ukrainian-ssr|Ukrainian SSR]], the [[s:byelorussian-ssr|Byelorussian SSR]] and the Transcaucasian republic signed the treaty creating the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics, with [[e:moscow|Moscow]] as capital and Vladimir Lenin as head of government.
soviet-union.r: The Communist Party ruled through a centralised planned economy. Under Joseph Stalin, five-year plans industrialised the country while collectivisation brought famine and the Great Terror killed hundreds of thousands. The Soviet Union lost about 27 million people defeating [[s:nazi-germany|Nazi Germany]], then dominated [[e:eastern-europe|Eastern Europe]], built nuclear weapons and launched Sputnik in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin in 1961.
soviet-union.e: After decades of stagnation, Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms of glasnost and perestroika loosened control, and the republics demanded independence. After a failed hardline coup in August 1991, the leaders of [[e:russia|Russia]], [[e:ukraine|Ukraine]] and Belarus signed the Belovezha Accords, and the Soviet Union was dissolved on 26 December 1991.

south-african-republic.t: The Boer republic of the Transvaal, transformed by the Witwatersrand gold rush and destroyed by Britain in the Second Boer War.
south-african-republic.o: In the Sand River Convention of 1852 [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] recognised the independence of the [[e:boers|Boers]] north of the Vaal. The separate communities, including the [[s:potchefstroom-republic|Potchefstroom Republic]], Lydenburg and [[s:zoutpansberg-republic|Zoutpansberg]], gradually united, adopting a constitution in 1858 under President Marthinus Wessel Pretorius and making Pretoria the capital in 1860.
south-african-republic.r: Only white men could be citizens, and the constitution declared no equality between black and white. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] annexed the bankrupt republic in 1877, but the [[e:boers|Boers]] rebelled and won at Majuba in 1881. Under Paul Kruger, president from 1883, gold discovered on the Witwatersrand in 1886 made it the richest state in [[e:africa|Africa]], attracting foreign uitlanders whom Kruger kept from the vote.
south-african-republic.e: The Jameson Raid of 1895-1896 deepened conflict with [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]], which went to war in 1899. Pretoria fell in 1900, and after [[e:guerrilla-warfare|guerrilla]] war the Treaty of Vereeniging in 1902 made the republic the [[s:transvaal-colony|Transvaal Colony]].

saurashtra-state.t: The union that merged more than 200 Kathiawar princely states into one Indian state in 1948, with its capital at Rajkot.
saurashtra-state.o: Kathiawar was a patchwork of over two hundred [[e:princely-state|princely states]], from [[s:bhavnagar-state|Bhavnagar State]] and Nawanagar to tiny estates. In early 1948, under pressure from V. P. Menon and [[e:sardar|Sardar]] Patel, the rulers agreed to merge their states into the United State of Kathiawar, inaugurated in February 1948; [[s:junagadh-state|Junagadh State]] joined in 1949.
saurashtra-state.r: The Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, Digvijaysinhji, served as Rajpramukh, while an elected government led by U. N. Dhebar ran the administration from [[s:rajkot-state|Rajkot]]. Renamed Saurashtra, it became a Part B state of the Indian Union in 1950. Its governments carried out land reform that abolished the girasdari and barkhali landholdings of the old nobility.
saurashtra-state.e: Under the States Reorganisation Act Saurashtra was merged into the enlarged Bombay State on 1 November 1956. When Bombay was divided in 1960, the region became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].
