sultanate-of-zemio.t: A Zande sultanate on the upper Mbomou whose ruler Zemio allied with Egyptian Sudan and later with Belgian and French officers.
sultanate-of-zemio.o: Zemio, a Zande prince of the Vungara dynasty, established his authority on the upper Mbomou in the 1870s. He built his power in alliance with the administration of [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Egyptian Sudan]] in Bahr al-Ghazal, receiving guns in exchange for [[e:ivory-trade|ivory]].
sultanate-of-zemio.r: Zemio ruled through armed followers and tribute from subject communities, and his court hosted European travellers such as the explorer Wilhelm Junker. After the Mahdist rising cut ties with the [[e:nile|Nile]], he turned to the [[s:congo-free-state|Congo Free State]], whose officers he supplied with men and provisions.
sultanate-of-zemio.e: The 1894 Franco-Congolese agreement placed the sultanate in the French sphere. [[e:france|France]] gradually reduced its rulers' authority, and the sultanate was absorbed into [[s:ubangi-shari|Ubangi-Shari]] by about 1913.

sultanate-of-itsandra.t: One of the rival sultanates of Grande Comore, whose rulers long competed with Bambao for the island's paramount title.
sultanate-of-itsandra.o: Grande Comore (Ngazidja) was divided among several Shirazi-descended lineages from around the 15th century, each ruling a district from a walled stone town. Itsandra, on the west coast north of Moroni, became one of the most powerful of these by about 1500.
sultanate-of-itsandra.r: The sultan ruled with the elders of the leading lineages under a matrilineal succession system, and [[e:islam|Islam]] shaped law and town life. The island's sultans contested the title of sultan tibe, a paramount position over the others, and Itsandra and the [[s:sultanate-of-bambao|Sultanate of Bambao]] were the main rivals. Wealth came from trade with the [[e:swahili|Swahili]] coast and Madagascar.
sultanate-of-itsandra.e: Prolonged wars between the sultanates weakened Itsandra in the 19th century. In 1886 Said Ali of [[s:sultanate-of-bambao|Bambao]] accepted a French [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] over the whole island, ending Itsandra's independence. Grande Comore later became part of the Comoros.

sasanian-egypt.t: Egypt's decade under Persian rule, when Khosrow II's armies took Alexandria during the last great Roman-Persian war.
sasanian-egypt.o: During the war of 602 to 628 between the [[s:byzantine-empire|Byzantine Empire]] and [[e:persia|Persia]], the Sasanian general [[e:shahrbaraz|Shahrbaraz]] invaded [[e:egypt|Egypt]] and took [[e:alexandria|Alexandria]] around 619, after a siege. The conquest of Egypt, with its grain and taxes, was a heavy blow to [[s:roman-egypt|Roman Egypt]] and to [[e:constantinople|Constantinople's]] food supply.
sasanian-egypt.r: The [[e:persians|Persians]] kept much of the existing administration but installed their own officials. Papyri in Middle Persian survive from this period, recording requisitions and military supplies. Coptic sources tell of massacres of monks at the start of the conquest, but the occupiers then tended to favour the Miaphysite church over the Chalcedonian clergy loyal to [[e:constantinople|Constantinople]].
sasanian-egypt.e: After [[e:heraclius|Heraclius]] defeated [[e:persia|Persia]] and [[e:khosrow-ii|Khosrow II]] was overthrown in 628, [[e:shahrbaraz|Shahrbaraz]] agreed to withdraw, and [[e:egypt|Egypt]] returned to Byzantine rule by 629. The disruption weakened Byzantine control, and the Arab conquest followed little more than a decade later.

state-of-bahrain.t: Independent Bahrain since 1971, a Gulf financial centre ruled by the Al Khalifa and a kingdom since 2002.
state-of-bahrain.o: After a [[e:united-nations|United Nations]] mission found that Bahrainis wanted independence rather than union with [[e:iran|Iran]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ended its protection of the [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Sheikhdom of Bahrain]], and the State of [[e:bahrain|Bahrain]] became independent on 15 August 1971 under Isa bin Salman Al [[e:khalifa|Khalifa]].
state-of-bahrain.r: An elected parliament created by the constitution of 1973 was dissolved in 1975. With modest oil reserves, [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] built an offshore banking sector, aluminium smelting and a causeway to [[s:saudi-arabia|Saudi Arabia]], opened in 1986, and hosts the US Fifth Fleet. Tension between the [[e:sunni-islam|Sunni]] ruling family and the [[e:shia-islam-idea|Shi'a]] majority produced unrest in the 1990s. Hamad bin Isa, ruler from 1999, introduced a National Action Charter and proclaimed a kingdom in 2002.
state-of-bahrain.e: In 2011 mass protests at the Pearl Roundabout were suppressed with the help of Saudi and Emirati forces. [[s:sheikhdom-of-bahrain|Bahrain]] remains a [[e:constitutional-monarchy|constitutional monarchy]] with strong royal power; it normalised relations with [[s:kingdom-of-israel|Israel]] in 2020.

state-of-wey.t: A Ji-clan state planted in the old Shang heartland that outlived every other Zhou state, surviving as a single city until 209 BCE.
state-of-wey.o: After the rebellion of the Three Guards, the Duke of Zhou gave the former [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] capital region around Zhaoge in northern Henan to Kang Shu Feng, a younger brother of King Wu, to watch over the conquered Shang population. Wey is spelt so in English to distinguish it from the [[s:state-of-wei|State of Wei]].
state-of-wey.r: Wey was a large and cultured state early in the Spring and Autumn period, and its folk songs make up a large part of the Book of [[e:song-dynasty|Songs]]. In 660 BCE the Di overran it after Duke Yi, notorious for giving his cranes official carriages, was killed. Rebuilt with help from the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]], it moved to Chuqiu and then Diqiu (modern Puyang). Confucius spent years there, and the reformer [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] Yang was a Wey nobleman.
state-of-wey.e: Wey shrank to the area around Puyang, a [[e:vassal|vassal]] first of the [[s:state-of-wei|State of Wei]] and then of the [[s:state-of-qin|State of Qin]], which spared it even after unification. In 209 BCE the Second Emperor of [[e:qin-dynasty|Qin]] deposed Lord Jue and made him a commoner, ending the last Zhou state.

state-of-song.t: The state where the descendants of the Shang kings kept their ancestral rites under Zhou rule, home of Zhuangzi and the scene of China's first disarmament conference.
state-of-song.o: After the failed rebellion of the [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] prince Wu Geng, the Duke of Zhou installed Weizi Qi, an elder brother of the last Shang king, at Shangqiu in eastern Henan, so that the Shang royal sacrifices would continue. [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] was ranked as a duchy, the highest grade of Zhou state.
state-of-song.r: [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] preserved [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] customs, and other states mocked its people as slow-witted in stories like the farmer waiting by a tree stump. Duke Xiang of Song sought the hegemony but lost to the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] at the Battle of Hong in 638 BCE after refusing to attack the enemy mid-crossing. In 546 BCE the Song minister Xiang Xu hosted a peace conference of fourteen states. The philosopher Zhuangzi was a native of Song.
state-of-song.e: King Yan of [[e:song-dynasty|Song]], who took the royal title, conquered the [[s:state-of-teng|State of Teng]] and fought his neighbours until the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]], with Wei and Chu, destroyed Song in 286 BCE and divided its lands. Song was later used as a dynastic name, most notably by the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]].

swaziland-protectorate.t: The British protectorate over the Swazi kingdom, during which King Sobhuza II fought to recover land lost to concessions.
swaziland-protectorate.o: The [[s:south-african-republic|South African Republic]] had administered [[s:swazi-kingdom|Swaziland]] from 1894. After the [[e:second-boer-war|Second Boer War]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] took over in 1903 and placed it under the High Commissioner for [[s:republic-of-south-africa|South Africa]], with Mbabane as the administrative centre.
swaziland-protectorate.r: In 1907 a partition of land left only about a third for Swazi use, the rest going to concession holders and settlers. The queen regent Labotsibeni led opposition until Sobhuza II came of age in 1921; he petitioned the Privy Council and later bought back land through a national fund. Mining of asbestos and iron and forestry grew after the [[e:second-world-war|Second World War]].
swaziland-protectorate.e: [[s:swazi-kingdom|Swaziland]] became independent on 6 September 1968 with Sobhuza II as king, part of the continuity of the Swazi Kingdom. He abolished the constitution in 1973, and the country was renamed Eswatini in 2018.

subalpine-republic.t: A French-controlled republic in Piedmont between Napoleon's victory at Marengo and the region's annexation to France in 1802.
subalpine-republic.o: [[e:napoleon|Napoleon's]] victory at Marengo in June 1800 restored French control over Piedmont, which had been lost in 1799. The French set up a new government for the former mainland territories of the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]], which became known as the Subalpine Republic.
subalpine-republic.r: The republic was administered by a commission under French supervision, with General Jourdan as administrator general from 1801. It introduced French administrative divisions and laws, abolished remaining feudal rights and prepared Piedmont for annexation. Piedmontese opinion was divided between those favouring [[e:france|France]] and those hoping for an Italian republic.
subalpine-republic.e: In September 1802 Piedmont was formally annexed to [[e:france|France]] and divided into French [[e:departement|departments]]. It returned to the [[s:kingdom-of-sardinia|Kingdom of Sardinia]] in 1814.

southern-ming.t: The succession of Ming loyalist courts in southern China that resisted the Manchu conquest for eighteen years after the fall of Beijing.
southern-ming.o: When [[e:li-zicheng|Li Zicheng's]] [[s:shun-dynasty|Shun dynasty]] took [[e:beijing|Beijing]] in 1644 and the Chongzhen Emperor killed himself, officials in Nanjing enthroned the Prince of Fu as the Hongguang Emperor. The [[s:qing-empire|Qing Empire]] soon drove Li Zicheng out of Beijing and turned south.
southern-ming.r: Rival princes and factions undermined every Southern Ming court. Nanjing fell in 1645 after the massacre at Yangzhou, the Longwu Emperor was captured at Fuzhou in 1646, and the Yongli Emperor ruled from Zhaoqing and later the south-west. The Qing order to shave the forehead in 1645 drove many to resist, and former rebels such as Li Dingguo and the coastal power of [[e:koxinga|Koxinga]] fought for the Ming cause.
southern-ming.e: Driven from Yunnan in 1659, the Yongli Emperor took refuge with the [[s:restored-toungoo-kingdom|Restored Toungoo Kingdom]] of [[s:myanmar|Burma]], which handed him to [[e:wu-sangui|Wu Sangui]] in 1662; he was executed at Kunming. Loyalism lived on in the [[s:kingdom-of-tungning|Kingdom of Tungning]] on [[s:republic-of-china|Taiwan]] until 1683.

selangor-sultanate.t: Bugis-founded Malay sultanate whose tin fields gave rise to Kuala Lumpur, now Malaysia's most populous and prosperous state.
selangor-sultanate.o: Bugis warriors who dominated the [[s:johor-sultanate|Johor Sultanate]] in the 18th century settled on the Selangor coast. Raja Lumu, son of the Bugis chief Daeng Chelak, was recognised as [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Salehuddin Shah around 1766, with the sanction of the ruler of [[s:perak-sultanate|Perak]], and ruled from Kuala Selangor.
selangor-sultanate.r: Selangor was divided among river chiefs who taxed [[e:tin|tin]] exported from the interior. Chinese miners poured in during the 19th century, and the rivalry of chiefs and [[e:secret-society|secret societies]] erupted in the Klang War of 1867 to 1874, in which Yap Ah Loy built up Kuala Lumpur. [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Abdul Samad accepted a British resident in 1874.
selangor-sultanate.e: Selangor joined the [[s:federated-malay-states|Federated Malay States]] in 1895, with Kuala Lumpur as federal capital. It became a state of the [[s:federation-of-malaya|Federation of Malaya]] and then [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]], ceding Kuala Lumpur in 1974 and Putrajaya in 2001 as federal territories. The sultanate continues under [[e:sultan|Sultan]] Sharafuddin Idris Shah.

sailana-state.t: A Rathore Rajput state of western Malwa, an offshoot of Ratlam, later known for its rulers' cactus garden and celebrated cookery.
sailana-state.o: Sailana was founded in 1736 by Jai Singh, a younger member of the Rathore ruling house of [[s:ratlam-state|Ratlam]], who received his own share of territory in the hills west of Ratlam. The family descended from the Rathores of Jodhpur.
sailana-state.r: The state paid tribute to the [[e:scindias|Scindias]] of [[s:gwalior-state|Gwalior State]] and later came under British protection within the [[e:malwa|Malwa]] Agency of central [[e:india|India]], with an 11-gun salute. A Raja governed a small, partly tribal hill territory. In the 20th century the rulers became known for a large cactus garden and for the family's recipes, later published as a well-known cookbook.
sailana-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]], Sailana merged into [[s:madhya-bharat|Madhya Bharat]] in 1948 and became part of Madhya Pradesh in 1956; it now lies in [[s:ratlam-state|Ratlam]] district.

state-of-teng.t: A tiny Ji-clan state in Shandong whose ruler asked Mencius how a small state could survive among giants, a dialogue preserved in the Confucian classics.
state-of-teng.o: King Wu of Zhou enfeoffed his younger brother Cuo Shu Xiu at Teng, near modern Tengzhou in south-western Shandong, as part of the network of royal kinsmen planted across the eastern plain after the conquest of the [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]].
state-of-teng.r: Teng was among the smallest Zhou states, ranked as a marquisate but forced to follow larger neighbours such as the [[s:state-of-lu|State of Lu]], the [[s:state-of-qi|State of Qi]] and the [[s:state-of-song|State of Song]]. In the late 4th century BCE Duke Wen of Teng consulted Mencius on mourning rites and the well-field system of land allotment; their conversations form a chapter of the Mencius.
state-of-teng.e: Teng was conquered by the [[s:state-of-song|State of Song]] under its last king, Yan, around 296 BCE, and its lands later passed to Qi and Chu. Its memory survives chiefly through Mencius, and in the name of the city of Tengzhou.

sultanate-of-egypt.t: Egypt as a British protectorate during and after the First World War, under sultans of Muhammad Ali's line, ended by the 1919 revolution.
sultanate-of-egypt.o: When the [[s:ottoman-empire|Ottoman Empire]] entered the [[e:first-world-war|First World War]], [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] ended Ottoman [[e:sovereignty|sovereignty]] over [[e:egypt|Egypt]] in December 1914, deposed Khedive [[e:abbas-ii-of-persia|Abbas II]] of the [[s:khedivate-of-egypt|Khedivate of Egypt]] and declared a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]]. His uncle Hussein Kamel took the title of sultan to mark the break from [[e:istanbul|Istanbul]].
sultanate-of-egypt.r: [[e:egypt|Egypt]] was a major British base for campaigns in [[e:palestine|Palestine]] and the Dardanelles, under martial law. Peasants were conscripted into the Egyptian Labour Corps and crops requisitioned, fuelling resentment. Hussein Kamel died in 1917 and was succeeded by his brother Fuad.
sultanate-of-egypt.e: In 1919 the British exile of Saad Zaghloul and the Wafd delegation sparked a nationwide revolution. [[s:united-kingdom|Britain]] unilaterally declared Egyptian independence in February 1922 with reserved powers, and Fuad became king of the [[s:kingdom-of-egypt|Kingdom of Egypt]].

shamkhalate-of-tarki.t: The Kumyk state on Dagestan's Caspian coast, heir of the old shamkhals, which Peter the Great visited in 1722 and Russia absorbed in 1867.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.o: Around 1642, as the [[s:kazikumukh-shamkhalate|Kazikumukh Shamkhalate]] split, the shamkhals moved their seat from the [[e:lak|Lak]] mountains to Tarki, on the Caspian plain near modern Makhachkala. The new state was centred on the Kumyk people and controlled the coastal road between Derbent and the Terek.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.r: The shamkhals ruled Kumyk nobles and villages and claimed authority over much of northern [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]], receiving [[e:subsidy|subsidies]] from the [[s:safavid-empire|Safavid Empire]] and courting [[e:russia|Russia]] and the [[e:ottoman-empire|Ottomans]] in turn. The plain provided grain, livestock and trade routes. During his Persian campaign [[e:peter-the-great|Peter the Great]] was received at Tarki in 1722 by Shamkhal Adil-Girey, who later rebelled and died in Russian exile.
shamkhalate-of-tarki.e: The shamkhals accepted Russian protection in 1806 and held Russian military rank; Mehdi II was a loyal ally against Shamil. In 1867 the [[s:russian-empire|Russian Empire]] abolished the shamkhalate and incorporated it into the [[e:dagestan|Dagestan]] Oblast.

shahgarh-state.t: A Bundela principality of Bundelkhand whose Raja joined the revolt of 1857, after which the British confiscated it.
shahgarh-state.o: Shahgarh was a small Bundela state in the hills north of Sagar, held by a branch of the Bundela clan. The register dates it to around 1700, though its early history is sparsely recorded.
shahgarh-state.r: The Rajas ruled a forested upland of forts and villages. In 1857 Raja Bakht [[e:bali|Bali]], also called Bakhtbali Shah, rose against the [[e:east-india-company|East India Company]] and fought alongside the Raja of [[s:banpur-state|Banpur]] and other Bundela chiefs.
shahgarh-state.e: After the defeat of the rising in 1858, the British confiscated Shahgarh and annexed it to the Saugor and Nerbudda Territories. Its lands now lie in Sagar district of Madhya Pradesh.

state-of-lu.t: The Shandong state founded for the Duke of Zhou's line, guardian of Zhou ritual, birthplace of Confucius and subject of the Spring and Autumn Annals.
state-of-lu.o: After the Zhou conquest the Duke of Zhou was granted Lu but stayed at court as regent, sending his son Boqin to govern it. Its capital Qufu, in south-western Shandong, was built on land associated with the earlier [[s:shang-dynasty|Shang]] ally Yan, and Lu was charged with keeping order among the eastern peoples.
state-of-lu.r: As the house of the Duke of Zhou, Lu was allowed to perform royal rites and kept the most complete Zhou ritual and musical traditions. Its court chronicle, the Spring and Autumn Annals, covering 722 to 481 BCE, gave its name to the era. Power slipped from the dukes to three ministerial families, the Jisun, Mengsun and Shusun. Confucius, born in Lu in 551 BCE, served briefly in its government.
state-of-lu.e: Lu declined into a minor state during the Warring States period and was annexed by the [[s:state-of-chu|State of Chu]] under King Kaolie in 256 BCE. Qufu remained the centre of the cult of Confucius, and the Temple and Cemetery of Confucius there are now a World Heritage Site.

second-hellenic-republic.t: The Greek republic of 1924-1935, born from the Asia Minor disaster and marked by coups, refugee resettlement and the last Venizelos government.
second-hellenic-republic.o: [[e:greece|Greece's]] defeat in [[e:asia-minor|Asia Minor]] in 1922 discredited the monarchy. A [[e:military-revolution|military revolution]] forced [[e:constantine-i|Constantine I]] to abdicate, and in March 1924 the assembly proclaimed a republic, confirmed by a referendum in April. The [[s:kingdom-of-greece|Kingdom of Greece]] was thus replaced, with Admiral Pavlos Kountouriotis as first president.
second-hellenic-republic.r: The republic had to absorb more than a million refugees from [[e:anatolia|Anatolia]] after the population exchange with [[e:turkey|Turkey]], resettling many in Macedonia. Politics were unstable: General Theodoros Pangalos ruled as dictator in 1925-1926. The Venizelos government of 1928-1932 brought stability, a peace treaty with Turkey and public works, but the Great Depression ended it.
second-hellenic-republic.e: Royalists won the 1933 elections, and a failed Venizelist coup in March 1935 strengthened them. In October 1935 General Georgios Kondylis seized power, and a rigged plebiscite restored the monarchy, bringing back George II.

sayla-state.t: A small Jhala Rajput state of the Jhalawad district of Kathiawar, founded in the mid-18th century.
sayla-state.o: Sayla was established around 1751 by a member of the Jhala [[e:rajputs|Rajput]] clan, kinsmen of the rulers of [[s:dhrangadhra-state|Dhrangadhra State]] and [[s:limbdi-state|Limbdi]], who took the town and set up his own chiefship.
sayla-state.r: The Thakor governed a small dry-farming territory within the Kathiawar Agency. The town is known as a [[e:hinduism|Hindu]] pilgrimage place connected with the saint Lalji Maharaj. Little else is recorded of its political history.
sayla-state.e: After accession to [[e:india|India]] Sayla was merged into the [[s:saurashtra-state|United State of Saurashtra]] in 1948; it is now a town in Surendranagar district of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]].

shaigiya-confederation.t: An Arab tribal confederation of the Nile bend around Merowe, famed for its horsemen, which broke from the Funj and fought the Egyptian invasion of 1820.
shaigiya-confederation.o: The Shaigiya were Arabic-speaking tribes living along the [[e:nile|Nile]] near the fourth cataract, around Merowe and Korti. Subjects of the [[s:abdallab-sheikhdom|Abdallab Sheikhdom]] and the [[s:funj-sultanate|Funj Sultanate]], they rebelled around 1690 and established an independent confederation ruled by their own kings.
shaigiya-confederation.r: Shaigiya society was led by warrior aristocrats who fought on horseback, sometimes in chain mail, and raided neighbouring peoples along the [[e:nile|Nile]] and in the Bayuda desert. Agriculture on the river banks, irrigated by waterwheels, supported the population, and Shaigiya horsemen were feared throughout northern [[e:sudan|Sudan]].
shaigiya-confederation.e: In 1820 the army of [[s:egypt-under-muhammad-ali|Egypt under Muhammad Ali]], led by Ismail Pasha, defeated the Shaigiya under Malik Shawish at Korti; their cavalry could not withstand firearms. They then served the [[s:turco-egyptian-sudan|Turco-Egyptian Sudan]] as irregular cavalry and tax collectors, remaining prominent in Sudanese politics.

saffarid-dynasty.t: A dynasty founded by a coppersmith from Sistan that briefly conquered much of Iran and helped revive Persian as a literary language.
saffarid-dynasty.o: Ya'qub ibn al-Layth, a coppersmith (saffar) turned leader of the ayyar volunteer bands of Sistan, took control of Zaranj in 861 while fighting [[e:kharijites|Kharijites]]. He rapidly conquered [[e:herat|Herat]], [[e:kerman|Kerman]] and [[e:fars|Fars]], ended the [[s:tahirid-dynasty|Tahirid dynasty]] by taking [[e:nishapur|Nishapur]] in 873 and marched on [[e:baghdad|Baghdad]].
saffarid-dynasty.r: Ya'qub's state rested on a professional army and on personal leadership rather than caliphal appointment. He is said to have objected to praise in Arabic, which he did not understand, encouraging poets such as Muhammad ibn Wasif to compose in Persian, an early step in the New Persian literary revival. Defeated at Dayr al-Aqul in 876, he died in 879. His brother Amr ibn al-Layth was recognised as governor of Khurasan by the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]].
saffarid-dynasty.e: Amr was defeated and captured by the Samanid ruler Ismail at Balkh in 900. A reduced Saffarid line held Sistan until Khalaf ibn Ahmad surrendered to Mahmud of the [[s:ghaznavid-empire|Ghaznavid Empire]] in 1003; later Saffarid descendants ruled as the [[s:nasrid-maliks-of-sistan|Nasrid Maliks of Sistan]].

selgovae.t: People of the Scottish Borders recorded by Ptolemy, whose lands around the Eildon Hills were held by the Roman fort of Trimontium.
selgovae.o: The Selgovae are known from Ptolemy's 2nd-century Geography, which places them in southern [[e:scotland|Scotland]], usually located in the upper Tweed valley and the hills of the central Borders. Their name may mean 'the hunters'. They grew from Iron Age communities whose landscape contained many hillforts, including the large enclosure on Eildon Hill North.
selgovae.r: No rulers, coins or written records survive. The heavy Roman military presence around their land, especially the fort of Trimontium at Newstead under the Eildon Hills, has led historians to suggest they were hostile to [[e:rome|Rome]], in contrast to their neighbours the [[s:votadini|Votadini]]. Their society was rural, based on [[e:cattle|cattle]] and small farms.
selgovae.e: Roman control of southern [[e:scotland|Scotland]] ebbed and flowed between the 80s and the 2nd century, after which the region lay beyond Hadrian's Wall. The Selgovae disappear from the record, their lands later forming part of the British kingdoms of the north.

sajid-emirate.t: An Abbasid governorship turned hereditary emirate in Azerbaijan whose emir Yusuf dominated Armenia and executed its king Smbat I.
sajid-emirate.o: The Sajids were descended from a military family from Ushrusana in [[e:central-asia|Central Asia]], in the service of the [[e:caliphate|caliphs]]. In 889 Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Saj was appointed governor of [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]] and ruled it almost independently from [[e:maragha|Maragha]] and later [[e:ardabil|Ardabil]], founding a hereditary [[e:emirate|emirate]] under the [[s:abbasid-caliphate|Abbasid Caliphate]].
sajid-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] controlled north-western [[e:iran|Iran]] and claimed authority over [[s:armenia|Armenia]] and [[s:albania|Albania]] as Abbasid governors, collecting tribute and backing rival Armenian princes. Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj invaded [[e:armenia|Armenia]], captured Smbat I of [[s:bagratid-armenia|Bagratid Armenia]] and had him executed in 914, while crowning Gagik Artsruni of the [[s:kingdom-of-vaspurakan|Kingdom of Vaspurakan]] as a rival king.
sajid-emirate.e: Yusuf was killed in 928 fighting the [[e:qarmatians|Qarmatians]] in [[e:iraq|Iraq]], and the [[e:emirate|emirate]] collapsed in 929 amid struggles among his commanders. The [[s:sallarid-emirate|Sallarid Emirate]] and other local dynasties took over [[s:azerbaijan|Azerbaijan]].

shaddadid-emirate.t: A Kurdish dynasty that ruled Ganja and Arran in the 10th and 11th centuries, a meeting point of Muslim, Armenian and Georgian worlds.
shaddadid-emirate.o: The Shaddadids were a Kurdish family who exploited the decline of the [[s:sallarid-emirate|Sallarid Emirate]]. In 951 Muhammad ibn Shaddad seized Dvin, and his descendants established their seat at [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]] in [[s:caucasian-albania|Arran]], taking over the region between the Kura and the Araxes.
shaddadid-emirate.r: The [[e:emir|emirs]] ruled a mixed population of Muslims and Christians and fought and allied in turn with the Armenian kings of Ani, the Georgians and the [[e:byzantine-empire|Byzantines]]. Abu'l-Aswar Shavur, who ruled from 1049, was a forceful soldier and patron. [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]] prospered as a market city on routes linking the Caspian, [[e:iran|Iran]] and the [[e:caucasus|Caucasus]].
shaddadid-emirate.e: The [[s:seljuk-empire|Seljuk Empire]] took control of [[s:caucasian-albania|Arran]], and in 1075 the Seljuk sultan [[e:malik-shah-i|Malik Shah]] deposed the [[s:ganja-khanate|Ganja]] line. A branch survived as the [[s:shaddadids-of-ani|Shaddadids of Ani]], governing the former Armenian capital for the [[e:seljuk-empire|Seljuks]].

sakala.t: Estonian county around Viljandi, homeland of the elder Lembitu, who led the most determined resistance to the Livonian crusade.
sakala.o: Sakala, in south-western central [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]], was one of the major ancient Estonian lands, with hillforts at Viljandi and Lehola. It bordered the Livonians and Latgalians to the south, with whom it traded and fought, and appears in detail in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry from the early 13th century.
sakala.r: Like other Estonian counties, Sakala was led by elders who commanded the levies of its parishes and negotiated with neighbours. Lembitu of Lehola organised alliances across [[s:republic-of-estonia|Estonia]] and sought help from Novgorod and Pskov against the Germans, an unusually wide coalition for the time.
sakala.e: Lembitu was killed at the Battle of St Matthew's Day near Viljandi in 1217, after which Sakala again submitted to the crusaders. An uprising in 1223 briefly expelled them, but Sakala was reconquered by 1224 and passed to the [[s:livonian-brothers-of-the-sword|Livonian Brothers of the Sword]], later the [[s:livonian-order|Livonian Order]], which built Fellin castle there.

sandur-state.t: A small Maratha state ringed by hills in the Bellary country, ruled by the Ghorpade family and rich in iron and manganese.
sandur-state.o: Sandur was taken around 1713 by Siddoji Rao Ghorpade, of a [[e:maratha-empire|Maratha]] family that had served [[e:shivaji|Shivaji]] and his successors. The Ghorpades held the valley through the struggles between the Marathas, Hyder Ali and Tipu [[e:sultan|Sultan]].
sandur-state.r: The Rajas ruled a small valley enclosed by hills in the [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Presidency]], with temples such as the Kumaraswamy shrine. The surrounding hills held rich deposits of iron and manganese ore. The last ruler, Yeshwantrao Ghorpade, was noted for progressive administration.
sandur-state.e: Sandur merged into [[s:madras-presidency|Madras Province]] in 1949 and passed to [[s:mysore-state|Mysore State]], now Karnataka, in 1953. Mining around Sandur in Ballari district remains important.

sultanate-of-dawaro.t: A Muslim sultanate of south-eastern Ethiopia that rebelled repeatedly against the Christian emperors before being swept away by the Oromo.
sultanate-of-dawaro.o: [[e:dawaro|Dawaro]] lay south of [[e:ifat-sultanate|Ifat]], between the Awash and the upper Wabi Shebelle river, and appears in sources from the 13th century as one of the Muslim states of the Ethiopian interior. Around 1332 its ruler, Haydara, joined a revolt against the emperor [[e:amda-seyon-i|Amda Seyon]] and was defeated, making the state tributary to the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]].
sultanate-of-dawaro.r: [[e:dawaro|Dawaro]] was ruled by local Muslim princes under imperial overlordship and grew rich from its [[e:cattle|cattle]], horses and position on trade routes to [[e:zeila|Zeila]]. The emperors installed governors when it rebelled. It lay on the frontier with Adal, so its loyalties shifted with the balance of power.
sultanate-of-dawaro.e: In the 1530s [[e:dawaro|Dawaro]] joined the forces of [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] in his conquest of [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]]. After his death, [[e:oromo-migrations|Oromo migrations]] overran the territory in the second half of the 16th century, and Dawaro ceased to exist as a state.

sordones.t: People of the Roussillon plain beneath the eastern Pyrenees, whose town Ruscino gave the region its name.
sordones.o: Known only from Greek and Roman writers such as Avienus, Pomponius Mela and Pliny, the Sordones held the coastal plain around Ruscino (Château-Roussillon, near Perpignan). Their culture had strong Iberian ties, and their land lay on the coastal route between [[e:iberia|Iberia]] and Gaul.
sordones.r: Livy reports that in 218 BCE Gallic chiefs gathered at Ruscino to decide whether to let [[e:hannibal|Hannibal]] pass on his march to [[e:italy|Italy]], and he won them over with gifts. Excavations at Ruscino show a hilltop settlement with storage silos and imported Greek and Italian goods.
sordones.e: After 121 BCE the area was absorbed into the Roman province of Gallia Narbonensis. Ruscino became a small Roman town with a forum before declining, and its name survives in Roussillon.

sultanate-of-bale.t: A Muslim state of the Bale highlands in southern Ethiopia, a tributary of the Christian emperors and later a battleground with Adal and the Oromo.
sultanate-of-bale.o: [[e:bale|Bale]] appears in 14th-century sources, notably [[e:al-umari|al-Umari]], as one of the seven Muslim kingdoms of Abyssinia. It lay south of the Wabi Shebelle in the highlands that still bear its name. [[e:islam|Islam]] had spread there through traders and holy men, among them the saint Sheikh Hussein, whose shrine nearby became a major pilgrimage site.
sultanate-of-bale.r: [[e:bale|Bale]] was a fertile land of grain, [[e:cattle|cattle]] and horses, governed by local Muslim rulers. It was conquered by the [[s:ethiopian-empire|Ethiopian Empire]] in the 14th century and held as a tributary province, sometimes under appointed governors. In the 15th century it was fought over by the emperors and the [[s:adal-sultanate|Adal Sultanate]].
sultanate-of-bale.e: [[e:bale|Bale]] sided with [[e:ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi|Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi]] during his invasion of [[s:federal-democratic-republic-of-ethiopia|Ethiopia]] in the 1530s. In the later 16th century the [[e:oromo|Oromo]], whose homeland lay close by, expanded across the region, ending the old state. Bale was reincorporated into [[e:ethiopia|Ethiopia]] under [[e:menelik-ii|Menelik II]] in the 1890s.

state-of-franklin.t: A breakaway state set up by frontier settlers in what is now East Tennessee, which sought admission as the fourteenth state but collapsed within four years.
state-of-franklin.o: In 1784 North [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] offered its western counties beyond the Appalachians to Congress. Settlers who felt neglected met at Jonesborough and declared a separate state, named after Benjamin Franklin, with the Revolutionary War officer John Sevier as governor. Greeneville became the seat of government in 1785.
state-of-franklin.r: Franklin adopted a constitution based on North Carolina's, set up courts and counties, and, short of coin, allowed taxes to be paid in goods such as [[e:fur-trade|furs]], whisky and linen. It signed treaties with Cherokee leaders to open land for settlement, provoking frontier warfare. A petition for statehood fell short of the two-thirds of states needed in Congress.
state-of-franklin.e: North [[s:province-of-carolina|Carolina]] reasserted control, and rival officials clashed until a skirmish at Sevier's opponent John Tipton's farm in 1788. The government faded away that year. The region was ceded to the federal government in 1790 and became part of Tennessee, with Sevier its first governor in 1796.

state-of-damascus.t: One of the states into which France divided Syria in 1920, built around Damascus and later merged into a unified Syrian state.
state-of-damascus.o: After defeating the [[s:arab-kingdom-of-syria|Arab Kingdom of Syria]] at Maysalun in July 1920, the French high commissioner Henri Gouraud divided [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]] into several states to weaken Arab nationalism. The State of [[e:damascus|Damascus]], created in September 1920, covered Damascus, Homs, Hama and the south.
state-of-damascus.r: The state had a local government under a governor, the first being Haqqi al-Azm, with French advisers holding real authority. It was the centre of nationalist politics and resentment at the division of [[s:syrian-arab-republic|Syria]]. In 1922 it joined the [[s:syrian-federation|Syrian Federation]] with the [[s:state-of-aleppo|State of Aleppo]] and the [[s:alawite-state|Alawite State]].
state-of-damascus.e: At the end of 1924 [[e:france|France]] dissolved the federation and merged the states of [[e:damascus|Damascus]] and [[e:aleppo|Aleppo]] into the [[s:state-of-syria|State of Syria]], which took effect in January 1925.

sultanate-of-moheli.t: The smallest Comoran sultanate, founded by a Merina prince and ruled by Queen Djoumbe Fatima before falling under France.
sultanate-of-moheli.o: Around 1830 Ramanetaka, a Merina prince and governor who had fled Madagascar, seized control of Moheli (Mwali) and set himself up as sultan with the Muslim name Abderremane, displacing the island's earlier rulers.
sultanate-of-moheli.r: After Ramanetaka's death in 1842 his young daughter Djoumbe [[e:fatima|Fatima]] became queen. Her long reign saw rival French and British influence and a controversial plantation lease to a French trader, while the small island lived from fishing, farming and trade with [[s:sultanate-of-zanzibar|Zanzibar]]. [[e:islam|Islam]] and [[e:swahili|Swahili]] culture shaped court life at Fomboni.
sultanate-of-moheli.e: [[e:france|France]] imposed a [[e:protectorate|protectorate]] in 1886, and the last queen, Salima Machamba, abdicated before the island was annexed and attached to the [[s:colony-of-mayotte-and-dependencies|Colony of Mayotte and Dependencies]]. Moheli is now part of the Union of the Comoros.

singapore.t: Island city-state that became independent in 1965 and turned itself into one of the world's richest trading and financial hubs.
singapore.o: After two years in [[s:malaysia|Malaysia]], disputes between Lee Kuan Yew's People's Action Party and the federal government over racial politics led to Singapore's separation. On 9 August 1965 it became an independent republic, small, without natural resources and dependent on its port.
singapore.r: The People's Action Party has governed without interruption, combining elections with tight control of the press and opposition. The state attracted foreign manufacturers, built public housing for most citizens through the Housing and Development Board, and fostered a multiracial identity with English, Malay, Mandarin and Tamil as official languages. Its port and airport became among the busiest in the world.
singapore.e: Under Goh Chok Tong from 1990 and Lee Hsien Loong from 2004 Singapore became a centre of finance and technology. Lawrence Wong became prime minister in 2024, the fourth since independence.
singapore.re: Buddhism, Christianity, Sunni Islam, Taoism, Hinduism

second-taifa-of-valencia.t: Valencia's short independence under its qadi after the Almoravid collapse, a prelude to the rise of Ibn Mardanish, the Wolf King.
second-taifa-of-valencia.o: In 1145 the notables of [[e:valencia|Valencia]] expelled the Almoravid governor and recognised their qadi, Marwan ibn Abd [[e:al-aziz|al-Aziz]], as ruler, part of the wave of urban revolts that ended Almoravid rule in eastern [[e:al-andalus|al-Andalus]].
second-taifa-of-valencia.r: The regime rested on the qadi's prestige and the support of the city's elite, but it lacked troops. Real military power in the east lay with commanders such as Ibn Iyad and, after him, Muhammad ibn Mardanish, who soon pushed the qadi aside.
second-taifa-of-valencia.e: By 1147 Ibn Mardanish had taken control of [[e:valencia|Valencia]] and joined it to his realm, the [[s:second-taifa-of-murcia|Second Taifa of Murcia]], which held out against the [[e:almohad-caliphate|Almohads]] until 1172.

sertorian-state.t: The breakaway Roman regime of Quintus Sertorius, who with Iberian allies held most of Hispania against the Senate for nearly a decade.
sertorian-state.o: Quintus Sertorius, a supporter of Marius, was driven from Hispania by Sulla's forces but returned in 80 BCE at the invitation of the [[s:lusitanians|Lusitanians]]. Combining Roman exiles with Lusitanian and Celtiberian warriors, he defeated Sulla's generals and by 77 BCE controlled much of [[s:hispania-citerior|Hispania Citerior]] and Ulterior.
sertorian-state.r: Sertorius ran a rival Roman state with its own senate of exiles and magistrates, while winning Iberian loyalty through fair treatment and personal charisma, aided by a white fawn said to bring him divine messages. At Osca he founded a school where sons of Iberian nobles learned [[e:latin|Latin]] and Greek, partly as hostages. He allied with Mithridates VI of [[s:kingdom-of-pontus|Pontus]] and beat [[e:pompey|Pompey]] at Lauron in 76 BCE.
sertorian-state.e: Worn down by Metellus Pius and [[e:pompey|Pompey]], his alliance frayed. In 73 or 72 BCE he was murdered at a banquet by his lieutenant Marcus Perperna, whom Pompey soon defeated and executed. Hispania returned to Senate rule.

sabines.t: Italic people of the hills north-east of Rome, central to Roman foundation legends, who were absorbed by Rome in the early 3rd century BCE.
sabines.o: The Sabines lived in the central Apennines and the hill country between the [[e:tiber-river|Tiber]] and the Aniene from the early 1st millennium BCE. Ancient writers saw them as the parent stock of several Sabellian peoples, such as the [[s:samnite-league|Samnites]] and [[s:picentes|Picentes]], who were said to have left Sabine land in 'sacred springs' of migration.
sabines.r: Sabine society was rural, made up of villages and small towns such as Cures, Reate, Nursia and Amiternum, with a reputation in Roman eyes for austere virtue. They spoke an Osco-Umbrian language known only from glosses. In Roman legend the abduction of the Sabine women led to joint rule between Romulus and the Sabine king Titus Tatius, and [[e:rome|Rome's]] second king Numa Pompilius came from Cures. The Claudii were said to descend from Attus Clausus, who moved to Rome around 504 BCE.
sabines.e: Manius Curius Dentatus conquered the Sabines in 290 BCE. They received citizenship without the vote, and full citizenship in 268 BCE, an early and complete absorption into the Roman state. Their land was later part of Augustus's Regio IV, and the name survives in the Sabina district north of [[e:rome|Rome]].

southern-tang.t: The largest and most cultured of the southern Ten Kingdoms, ruled from Nanjing by a house that claimed Tang descent and ended with the poet-king Li Yu.
southern-tang.o: Xu Zhigao, adopted son of the regent Xu Wen, took the throne of [[s:wu-ten-kingdoms|Wu (Ten Kingdoms)]] in 937. In 939 he took the name Li Bian, claimed descent from the [[s:later-tang|Tang]] imperial family and renamed his state Tang, ruling from Jinling (Nanjing).
southern-tang.r: Southern [[s:later-tang|Tang]] held the wealthy lower [[e:yangtze-river|Yangtze]] and Jiangxi. Under [[e:li-jing|Li Jing]] it conquered [[s:min-ten-kingdoms|Min (Ten Kingdoms)]] in 945 and [[s:ma-chu|Ma Chu]] in 951 but could not hold them. Its court patronised painting, [[e:calligraphy|calligraphy]] and lyric poetry, and its paper and ink were famous. In 958 [[s:later-zhou|Later Zhou]] took its lands between the Huai and Yangtze, and it became a tributary of the north.
southern-tang.e: Li Yu, a celebrated writer of song lyrics, tried to appease the [[s:song-dynasty|Song Dynasty]], but [[e:song-dynasty|Song]] armies took Jinling in 975. He was taken to [[e:kaifeng|Kaifeng]], where his poems lamenting his lost kingdom were composed, and died in 978, reputedly poisoned.

santalpur-state.t: A minor chiefship on the edge of the Little Rann of Kutch in northern Gujarat.
santalpur-state.o: Santalpur was a small estate in the dry country bordering the Rann of [[s:cutch-state|Kutch]], held by a local chiefly family from around 1700. Its founding is known mainly from local tradition.
santalpur-state.r: The ruler held a few villages of grazing and [[e:millet|millet]] land. In the British period Santalpur was a minor state under the Banas Kantha Agency. Little else is recorded.
santalpur-state.e: Santalpur merged into [[s:bombay-presidency|Bombay Province]] in 1948 and became part of [[e:gujarat|Gujarat]] in 1960, in Patan district.

south-hsenwi.t: The southern half of the old Shan state of Hsenwi, created by the British in 1888 and governed from Mong Yai until 1959.
south-hsenwi.o: After the British annexation of Upper [[s:myanmar|Burma]], the large and war-torn Shan state of [[s:hsenwi-state|Hsenwi]] was partitioned in 1888 to settle the civil war between rival claimants. Its southern part became South Hsenwi, with its capital at Mong Yai, under one of the contending families.
south-hsenwi.r: South [[s:hsenwi-state|Hsenwi]] was ruled by a hereditary saopha under British supervision, in a region of Shan farmers and hill peoples on the routes between the Salween and the plateau. Like other Shan states it collected its own revenues and administered customary law, paying tribute to the British government. It joined the [[s:federated-shan-states|Federated Shan States]] in 1922.
south-hsenwi.e: After Burmese independence in 1948 South [[s:hsenwi-state|Hsenwi]] became part of Shan State within the [[s:myanmar|Union of Burma]]. Its saopha, like the other Shan rulers, surrendered his powers to the state government in 1959. Mong Yai remains a town in northern Shan State.
